title: Delusional disorder
text: Delusional disorder ICD-10 F22 Persistent delusional disorders DSM-5-TR F22 Delusional Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Delusional disorder (ICD-11: 6A24; DSM-5-TR: F22) — a psychotic disorder in which one or several delusions predominate for at least one month, without meeting the full criteria for schizophrenia. The patient’s general behavior and functional level remain relatively intact except for the delusional state.

title: 2. History
text: Kraepelin (1899) — “paranoia” — systematized delusion without hallucinations. Esquirol J.E. (1810s) — the term “monomania”; Kahlbaum K. (1863) and Krafft-Ebing R. — the clinical description of paranoia. DSM-III-R (1987) — “Delusional Disorder” established as an official diagnosis; continuation of Kraepelin’s paranoia concept. ICD-11 (2019): Bizarre delusions are also permitted (in ICD-10 only non-bizarre); induced de

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: ~0.2% (Perälä 2007). Onset: middle age (35–55 years), significantly later than schizophrenia. Sex: approximately equal; differences in some subtypes (erotomania in women). Comorbidity: depression, anxiety, social isolation; high suicide risk.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic load is less than in schizophrenia; however, family history shows increased prevalence of paranoid personality and psychotic disorder. Sensory deprivation (hearing impairment) — increases risk of paranoid delusions in the elderly. Social isolation, migration, language barriers — risk factors. Neurobiological — dopaminergic dysregulation, but more localized than in schizophrenia; increased striatal dopamine sy

title: Subtypes (by delusional content)
text: Persecutory: Most frequent — being followed by others, harm being planned. Jealousy (Othello syndrome): delusion about partner’s betrayal; high criminal risk. Erotomanic (Clérambault syndrome): belief that another person (usually of higher status) loves the patient. Grandiosity: special ability, talent, discovery, religious mission. Somatic: Belief in parasites in the body (Ekbom syndrome), emitting odor, deformity.

title: Functional maintenance
text: Outside the delusion, the patient’s general behavior, affect, cognitive functions are relatively preserved; work and relationships can continue as long as they do not involve delusional content.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR · ICD-11)
text: A. One or more delusions persisting: ICD-11 — at least 3 months (usually much longer), DSM-5-TR — at least 1 month. B. Criterion A for schizophrenia is not met (delusion is the sole or dominant symptom; hallucinations, if present, are minimal and related to the delusional content). C. Functional preservation without a direct effect of the delusion; behavior not bizarre. D. If an affective episode is present, it occur

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11: Permission for bizarre delusions (also removed prohibition in DSM-5-TR); induced delusion (folie à deux) integrated into 6A24. DSM-5-TR: Subtype qualifiers (erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, persecutory, somatic, mixed, unspecified); ‘bizarre type’ additional qualifier.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (general and especially delusional content). Relative/friend interview — premorbid function, onset of delusions. SCID-5 / MINI; PANSS / BPRS Positive Symptom Subscale. Medical and neurological examination. Toxicology screening; sensory (hearing, vision) test — mandatory in the elderly. Brain MRI (at first episode). Comorbid depression and suicide risk assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Disorder Distinguishing features Schizophrenia (6A20) Hallucinations, disorganized speech, negative symptoms dominant; significant impairment in functioning. Schizoaffective disorder (6A21) An affective episode is present during a significant portion of the total illness duration. Body dysmorphic disorder (6B21) Appearance-based; degree of insight is variable, but may be at the level of delusion. OCD — with poor insi

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PANSS / BPRS positive symptom subscale; structured documentation of concrete delusion content. Hearing and vision test (mandatory in the elderly). Laboratory: complete blood count, thyroid, B12, liver, glucose, toxicology screening, syphilis, HIV, ANA (lupus), ceruloplasmin (Wilson). Brain MRI — first episode, atypical clinical picture, elderly patient. Assessment of suicide and violence risk (C-SSRS, especially in j

title: 8. Treatment
text: Atypical antipsychotic at low dose (risperidone 1–3 mg, olanzapine 5–10 mg, aripiprazole 5–15 mg) — first-line. The evidence base is smaller than for schizophrenia; patient adherence is problematic (due to delusional content). Pimozide was historically considered superior in erotomania and somatic delusions (Munro A. studies), but in modern practice it is used less often than the atypicals (QTc, EPS). Psychotherapy —

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Non-confrontational CBT — Explore alternative explanations and evidence with the patient without openly denying the delusional content. Birchwood M., Trower P. studies — effective in schizophrenia and delusional disorder. Supportive therapy and therapeutic alliance — Establish a long-term trusting relationship with the patient; strengthening of adherence. PANSS positive symptom subscale — Standardized assessment of d

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG178 — no separate algorithm for delusional disorder; general psychosis principles. APA 2021 — antipsychotic first-line; insight and adherence difficulty emphasized. Munro A. reviews (Cambridge Univ Press 1999) — subtype-specific clinical guidance.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Prognosis is better than in schizophrenia — functional preservation, late onset. Adherence is the main limitation. Jealousy and somatic delusions relatively more difficult to treat. In older adults, improvement with sensory correction is possible. Monitoring — antipsychotic side effects, delusion severity, violence and suicide risk.

title: Myth 1: “The patient must be convinced of the falseness of their delusion”
text: Clinical logic: open confrontation disrupts therapeutic alliance and may reinforce delusions; the patient arrives at an explanation of his own: the doctor is against me too. Evidence: Birchwood and Trower CBT approaches — a non-confrontational approach allowing the patient to explore alternative explanations themselves is effective.

title: Myth 2: “Delusional disorder can only be treated with psychotherapy, antipsychotics are unnecessary”
text: Evidence: An antipsychotic is the first-line pharmacotherapy; psychotherapy alone is insufficient. APA 2021, NICE CG178.

title: Myth 3: “Erotomania is only a female disorder, absent in males”
text: Evidence: Erotomania occurs in both sexes; higher risk of violence reported in male patients (Menzies R.P. et al. Br J Psychiatry 1995).

title: Myth 4: “Delusional jealousy is a sign of ‘great love’, not a medical condition”
text: Evidence: Othello syndrome is a clinical psychotic condition, high risk of violence and homicide against the partner; requires active medical intervention.

title: Myth 5: “Paranoid delusions in the elderly are ‘normal aging’”
text: Evidence: In older adults, paranoid delusions are often a marker for sensory deprivation (auditory impairment) or early dementia; they can be treatable. Hearing aids or vision correction sometimes yield significant improvement.

title: Myth 6: “Exorcism or religious intervention cures delusions”
text: Evidence: Psychotic symptoms are neurobiological; antipsychotic treatment is delayed.

title: Myth 7: “The delusional patient must be isolated — social contact is harmful”
text: Evidence: Social isolation, conversely, strengthens psychosis; social support and psychotherapy are recommended.

title: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders
text: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders ICD-10 — No ICD-10 equivalent DSM-5-TR F29 Unspecified Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: In ICD-11, 6A25, the group of primary psychotic disorders (6A20–6A24) has a dimensional sub-structure. It is not a separate clinical nosological unit — the diagnosis is added as a qualifier to the primary disorder (e.g., 6A20 Schizophrenia). Six symptom domains; each is assessed separately for severity level (none / mild / moderate / severe). The rationale for the concept is to describe the heterogeneous clinical pre
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 2. History
text: Bleuler’s “4A” symptoms (1911) and Schneider’s “first-rank symptoms” (1959) — categorical approach. Crow T.J. (1980) — Concept of Type I (positive symptom dominant) and Type II (negative dominant) — the basis of the dimensional approach. Liddle P.F. (1987) — three-factor model — reality distortion, disorganization, psychomotor poverty. DSM-5 (2013) — Section III research category proposes dimensional assessment. ICD-
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3. Six symptom domains
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3.1 Positive symptoms
text: Delusion, hallucination — “excessive/added” symptoms in perception and thought processes. Severity: from absence to severe level (according to degree of impact on patient’s daily activities).
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3.2 Negative symptoms
text: Affective flattening, avolition (loss of motivation), alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia, social withdrawal. A major factor in functional impairment; responds poorly to pharmacotherapy.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3.3 Depressive symptoms
text: Low mood, hopelessness, suicidal ideation, psychomotor retardation, anhedonia (emotional component dominant, as opposed to negative symptoms).
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3.4 Manic symptoms
text: Elevated or irritable mood, rapid thinking, grandiose ideas, decreased sleep need, rapid speech, psychomotor agitation.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3.5 Psychomotor symptoms
text: Catatonic components (mutism, negativism, waxy flexibility, posturing), agitation, retardation, stereotypy.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 3.6 Cognitive symptoms
text: Working memory, attention, executive function, processing speed, social cognition. Present in 75–85% of patients; strong impact on long-term functional level.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 4. Clinical use
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 4.1 Assessment tools
text: PANSS (positive, negative, general psychopathology subscales). SANS / SAPS — negative and positive symptoms separately. HAM-D, MADRS — depressive component. YMRS — manic component. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale — psychomotor component. MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MCCB) — cognitive component.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 4.2 Treatment implications
text: Positive symptoms predominate — standard antipsychotic (D2 antagonist). Negative symptoms predominate — atypical antipsychotic superior (cariprazine); amisulpride low dose; clozapine — in treatment-resistant cases; psychosocial rehabilitation. Depressive component — adjunctive SSRI (sertraline) or antidepressant; suicide risk monitoring. Manic component — mood stabilizer (lithium, valproate) adjunct; reassessment for
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 5. Differences between sources
text: ICD-11 (6A25): periodic reassessment recommended as the severity in each domain changes during illness course. DSM-5-TR: Section III research category ‘Clinician-Rated Dimensions of Psychosis Symptom Severity’ — parallel to ICD-11 6A25; not an official diagnostic qualifier, but can be used in practice. NICE CG178: dimensional assessment recommended as a clinical approach — basis for individualized treatment.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: 6. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: Myth 1: “6A25 is a separate disorder, can be diagnosed as such”
text: Reality: 6A25 is not a separate clinical entity — it is a qualifier of the primary disorder (6A20–6A24).
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: Myth 2: “Dimensional approach replaces categorical diagnosis”
text: Reality: the two are complementary — categorical diagnosis provides a nosological unit, dimensional qualifier describes specific clinical presentation.
sub: Symptomatic manifestations of primary psychotic disorders

title: Myth 3: “Negative symptoms are side effects of antipsychotics, not ‘real’”
text: Reality: Primary negative symptoms are a core feature of schizophrenia — observed even before antipsychotics. Secondary negative symptoms (sedation, EPS, depression, positive symptom effect) are distinct and manageable.

title: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder
text: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder ICD-10 F06.1 Organic catatonic disorder DSM-5-TR F06.1 Catatonia Associated With Another Mental Disorder (Catatonia Specifier)
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder (ICD-11: 6A40; 6A41 Catatonia Induced by Substances or Medications; 6E69 Secondary Catatonia Syndrome; DSM-5-TR: F06.1 Catatonia) — syndrome of complex disturbance in psychomotor, behavioral and autonomic functions. Not an independent disorder — clinical syndrome against the background of another psychiatric or medical condition. DSM-5-TR — catatonia is no longer a su
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 2. History
text: Kahlbaum K. (1874) — “Die Katatonie oder das Spannungsirresein” — catatonia as a separate syndrome. Kraepelin (1899) — catatonia integrated as ‘dementia praecox’ subtype. Bleuler (1911) — retained within schizophrenia category. 1970s–1980s — Taylor, Fink — catatonia’s widespread presence in affective disorders has been reconfirmed; catatonia has been recognized as a general syndrome. DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 (2019) —
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: 7–15% of patients admitted to psychiatric hospital have catatonic symptoms (Fink M., Taylor M.A. Catatonia 2003). Catatonia is most prevalent in affective disorders (especially bipolar manic and depressive episodes). In schizophrenia, 10–20% of patients exhibit catatonic features during the course. Organic catatonia — autoimmune encephalitis (especially anti-NMDA-R, anti-LGI1), electrolyte disturbances, uremic and he
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: GABAergic system hypofunction — the rapid clinical effect of lorazepam (within hours) supports this; GABA-A receptor dysfunction is the central mechanism. Dopamine dysregulation — neuroleptic-induced catatonia and falls within the spectrum of NMS; antipsychotic discontinuation causes cholinergic and adrenergic rebound. Glutamate NMDA dysregulation — autoimmune anti-NMDA-R encephalitis presents with a classic catatoni
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 5. Clinical features
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: DSM-5-TR criteria — at least 3 of 12 symptoms:
text: Stupor — psychomotor activity absence, unresponsiveness to surroundings. Catalepsy — maintaining a passively given posture against gravity. Waxy flexibility — posture induced by the examiner is maintained as though molded in wax. Mutism — absence of speech or significant reduction. Negativism — opposition to instructions or external stimuli. Posturing — spontaneous, active posture maintenance (against gravity). Manne
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Severity forms
text: Retarded (stuporous) catatonia — motor reduction, mutism dominant; majority of cases. Excited (manic) catatonia — high agitation, autonomic disturbance, hyperthermia. Malignant catatonia — hyperthermia with excited form, autonomic instability, high CK, mortality risk — coincides with NMS; medical emergency.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR — ≥3 of 12 features; ICD-11 — same clinical features across different categories.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 6.2 Diagnostic tests
text: Lorazepam challenge test: 1–2 mg IV/IM lorazepam → significant reduction of catatonic signs within 10–30 minutes confirms the diagnosis (Bush G. et al. Acta Psychiatr Scand 1996). Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) — 23-item standardized scale; first 14 items screening (≥ 2 signs — positive).
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 6.3 Etiological investigation (mandatory)
text: Complete blood count, liver/renal, electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Mg, P), glucose, ammonia, CK, troponin, thyroid, B12. Toxicology screening. Syphilis, HIV. Brain MRI. EEG — rule out non-convulsive status epilepticus. Lumbar puncture — suspected encephalitis / autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA-R, anti-LGI1 antibodies). ANA, lupus panel.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) History of antipsychotic use; hyperthermia, rigidity, very high CK; clinical overlap — some consider the same spectrum. Serotonin syndrome Serotonergic medication; hyperreflexia, myoclonus, hyperthermia. Non-convulsive status epilepticus EEG — epileptic activity. Akinetic mutism (frontal lobe disorder) Brain MRI — frontal or bilateral thalamic pat
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: BFCRS — baseline ratings and monitoring. The above laboratory and instrumental examinations — an etiological search. Autonomic function (blood pressure, pulse, temperature, urine output) — especially in malignant form. Comorbid mood disorder and psychotic symptom assessment (later, when the patient can speak).
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 8. Treatment
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 8.1 General principles (BAP 2023 · Fink–Taylor protocol)
text: STOP antipsychotics — particularly typical and high D2 antagonists (haloperidol, risperidone high dose) — can enhance catatonia, progress to the malignant form. Lorazepam first-line — 1–2 mg IM/IV, titration based on initial response; typical effective dose 6–24 mg/day; some patients require 30+ mg. ~70–80% of patients respond (Sienaert P. et al. Front Psychiatry 2014 review). ECT — refractory cases (lorazepam non-re
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) — 23-item scale; first 14 items screening (≥ 2 positive); 23 items severity. Bush G. et al. Acta Psychiatr Scand 1996. Lorazepam challenge test — reduction of catatonic signs within 10–30 min after 1–2 mg IM/IV lorazepam administration confirms diagnosis and guides the treatment plan. Bush G. et al. 1996. Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) — The gold standard for catatonia; ev
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: BAP 2023 (British Association for Psychopharmacology) Catatonia Consensus Guidelines — lorazepam is first-line; ECT is for refractory or malignant cases; avoid or use antipsychotics with extreme caution. Fink M., Taylor M.A. Catatonia: A Clinician’s Guide (2003) — classic protocol; lorazepam test and high-dose lorazepam therapy. NICE TA59 — ECT: a clear recommendation for catatonia.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Lorazepam and/or ECT response — most patients achieve full recovery within days to weeks. Relapse risk is high if the underlying disorder is untreated. Complications — aspiration pneumonia from prolonged stupor, DVT, dehydration, skin ulcers. Malignant catatonia — untreated mortality historically ~50%+ (up to 75–100% in some series); with modern treatment (benzodiazepines/ECT) drops to ~10–20%. Monitoring — in etiolo
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 1: “Catatonia is a subtype of schizophrenia”
text: Evidence: DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 (2019) — catatonia as a transdiagnostic syndrome; schizophrenia subtype status abolished. More frequent in the context of affective disorders (Fink & Taylor 2003).
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 2: “Catatonic patient should be treated with antipsychotics”
text: Evidence: An antipsychotic may worsen catatonia and precipitate the malignant form. First-line — lorazepam, then ECT. Antipsychotic if needed for the etiological disorder, cautiously with lorazepam; atypical preferred (clozapine or quetiapine).
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 3: “A catatonic patient has lost consciousness or is in a coma”
text: Evidence: Most catatonic patients are fully aware of surroundings — mutism and psychomotor impairment are not loss of consciousness. Patient often remembers what happened after the episode. Staff should be cautious about conversations near the patient.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 4: “Catatonia is a rare or historical condition, absent in modern psychiatry”
text: Evidence: 7–15% of patients admitted to psychiatric hospitals have catatonic symptoms (Fink & Taylor 2003); the syndrome is recognized far less often than it occurs.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 5: “Lorazepam only sedates, does not provide ‘true’ treatment”
text: Evidence: Lorazepam targets the core mechanism of catatonic syndrome (GABAergic hypofunction); ~70–80% of patients experience dramatic and rapid clinical recovery.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 6: “ECT is dangerous and outdated in catatonia”
text: Evidence: ECT is the gold standard for catatonia, NICE TA59 gives a clear recommendation; life-saving in malignant catatonia.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Myth 7: “The patient must be forced to talk — breaking the psychological barrier”
text: Evidence: Mutism is biologically rooted, not psychological “resistance”; demanding speech increases the patient’s distress and is not therapeutic.
sub: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder

title: Bipolar type I disorder
text: Bipolar type I disorder ICD-10 F31 Bipolar affective disorder DSM-5-TR F31.1x Bipolar I Disorder, Current or Most Recent Episode Manic

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Bipolar type I disorder (ICD-11: 6A60; DSM-5-TR: F31.0–F31.9) — a recurrent disorder characterized by at least one manic episode, often alternating with depressive and/or hypomanic episodes. The presence of a manic episode is sufficient for diagnosis — a depressive episode is not required.

title: 2. History
text: Falret J.P. (1854) — Circular insanity; Baillarger J. (1854) — “folie à double forme”. Kraepelin E. (1899) — Manic-depressive insanity — distinct from schizophrenia (dementia praecox). Leonhard K. (1957) — first distinction between unipolar and bipolar disorders. DSM-III (1980) — term “Bipolar Disorder”. DSM-IV / DSM-5 (2013) / ICD-11 (2019) — Distinction between Type I (full manic episode) and Type II (hypomanic + m

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence Type I: ~0.6–1% (Merikangas K.R. et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2011, WMH). Sex: approximately equal. Onset: mean age approximately 18 years; earlier with a family history. Suicide risk: lifetime 6–7%; highest in youth and in the first years. Comorbidity: anxiety disorders 60%, substance use 40%, ADHD, personality disorders. Mortality is twice as high as in the general population — cardiovascular, sui

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 60–85% (Smoller J.W., Finn C.T. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet 2003 family-twin review). GWAS — 60+ risk loci (Mullins N. et al. Nat Genet 2021). Schizophrenia with extensive genetic overlap (Cross-Disorder Group 2013). Neurobiological — monoaminergic (dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine) dysregulation; circadian rhythm disruption; second messenger (PI/cAMP) system impairment; mitochondrial dysfunction

title: 5.1 Manic episode
text: Abnormally elevated or irritable mood + increased energy ≥ 7 days (or any duration requiring hospitalization). ≥ 3 symptoms from the following (≥ 4 in irritable mood): inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increase in goal-directed activity, risky behaviors. Functional impairment or requirement for hospitalization or psychotic features.

title: 5.2 Major depressive episode (in bipolar context)
text: ≥ 5 symptoms (one of which is low mood or anhedonia) × 2 weeks (DSM-5-TR). Bipolar depressive episode with atypical features (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis) is more common — similar to Type II.

title: 5.3 Mixed features
text: DSM-5-TR — subtype abolished — as a specifier: ≥3 depressive symptoms during a manic episode or ≥3 manic symptoms during a depressive episode.

title: 5.4 Rapid cycling
text: ≥4 episodes within 12 months; poor prognostic marker.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR · ICD-11 consensus points)
text: A. At least one manic episode (the above criteria). B. Manic and depressive episodes are not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, or another psychotic disorder. Depressive and hypomanic episodes are not required for Type I diagnosis, but are typically present.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR: Mixed features specifier (DSM-IV mixed episode abolished); increased energy added as a criterion for manic episode (DSM-IV listed only mood). ICD-11 (6A60): Current episode type and remission status subcodes; rapid cycling as a qualifier. NICE CG185: diagnosis supported by structured interview and family information; antidepressant-triggered hypomanic/manic episode leads to bipolar diagnosis (as noted in th

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + relative/friend information — manic and hypomanic episodes are more easily recognized by family members. Structured interview (SCID-5, MINI). YMRS (Young Mania Rating Scale), HAM-D / MADRS. MDQ (Mood Disorder Questionnaire) or HCL-32 — bipolar screening (self-report). Medical examination + laboratory (thyroid, liver, kidney, glucose, toxicology screening); specific tests before lithium initiation

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Bipolar Type II (6A61) No manic episode ever; hypomanic + major depressive. Cyclothymic disorder (6A62) ≥2 years (1 year in adolescents) subthreshold mood fluctuations. Major Depressive Disorder (6A70/6A71) No manic or hypomanic episode. Schizoaffective disorder (6A21) Psychosis persists during periods outside the affective episode. BPD (6D11.5) Emotional lability over hours to days;

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: YMRS, HAM-D / MADRS, MDQ, HCL-32, C-SSRS. Pre-lithium: complete blood count, creatinine, TSH, calcium, ECG, pregnancy test. Pre-valproate: complete blood count, liver function, pregnancy test (valproate is not prescribed to women of childbearing potential). Before carbamazepine: complete blood count, liver, sodium. Brain MRI — first psychotic episode.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG185 · CANMAT/ISBD 2018 · APA · WFSBP consensus)
text: Acute manic episode: Antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, asenapine) ± mood stabilizer (lithium, valproate). Lorazepam as an adjunct in acute agitation. Acute bipolar depressive episode: quetiapine or lurasidone (FDA approval), olanzapine/fluoxetine combination (Symbyax); lithium or lamotrigine as adjunctive therapy. title: 9. Prognosis
text: Episodic course; relapse 80–90% (untreated); significant reduction with maintenance pharmacotherapy. Suicide risk high (6–7% lifetime); particularly in the first years. Increased cardiovascular mortality (metabolic syndrome). Functional recovery moderate — the majority of patients experience significant social and occupational impairment. Monitoring — mood scales, suicide risk, metabolic indicators, lithium level, ad

title: Myth 1: “Bipolar disorder is simple mood swings — everyone has them”
text: Clinical logic: Bipolar manic episode requires both duration (≥7 days) and functional impairment; it is a distinct clinical condition from daily mood fluctuations. Manic episode may require psychotic features and hospitalization. Evidence: Merikangas Arch Gen Psychiatry 2011.

title: Myth 2: “Bad parenting causes bipolar disorder”
text: Evidence: heritability 60–85%; parental experience not etiology. Smoller & Finn 2003.

title: Myth 3: “A bipolar patient is creative or a ‘marker of genius’”
text: Evidence: Some studies show moderate increase in bipolar prevalence in creative professions (Andreasen N.C. reviews), but most patients experience functional impairment; ‘duality’ explanation leads to romanticization and treatment refusal.

title: Myth 4: “Antidepressants always help a bipolar patient”
text: Evidence: NICE CG185, CANMAT — antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder is contraindicated; risk of manic switch and rapid cycling.

title: Myth 5: “Lithium is ‘outdated’ or dangerous — atypical antipsychotic should be first-line”
text: Evidence: Cipriani BMJ 2013 — lithium reduces suicide significantly more than other mood stabilizers; NICE CG185 and CANMAT 2018 — first-line in maintenance.

title: Myth 6: “The patient can ‘volitionally’ control their mood”
text: Evidence: a bipolar episode reflects neurobiological dysfunction; not voluntarily controllable; requires pharmacotherapy or ECT.

title: Myth 7: “Watchful waiting is sufficient — it will resolve on its own”
text: Evidence: Untreated episodes — long-term functional impairment, cardiovascular mortality, suicide (6–7% lifetime).

title: Myth 8: “Herbal preparations (St John’s Wort, valerian) or omega-3 replace mood stabilizers”
text: Evidence: St John’s Wort reduces the levels of some mood stabilizers (carbamazepine, quetiapine) through cytochrome P450 induction and may trigger a manic switch; omega-3 has a mild adjunctive effect and is not the primary treatment.

title: Myth 9: “Cannabis is a mood stabilizer”
text: Evidence: Cannabis worsens bipolar course, increases psychosis risk, reduces adherence.

title: Myth 10: “Mood stabilizer must be completely discontinued during pregnancy”
text: Evidence: full discontinuation doubles the risk of recurrence, increases the proportion of weeks ill fivefold, and shortens time to recurrence more than fourfold (Viguera A.C. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2007). Valproate is contraindicated, but lamotrigine and quetiapine are relatively safe; individual balance should be assessed (NICE CG192).

title: Bipolar type II disorder
text: Bipolar type II disorder ICD-10 F31 Bipolar affective disorder DSM-5-TR F31.81 Bipolar II Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Bipolar type II disorder (ICD-11: 6A61; DSM-5-TR: F31.81) — a form of bipolar disorder characterized by at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, but never a full manic episode. It is not a ‘milder’ form than Type I — patients spend more of their lifetime in depression; functional impairment and suicide risk are comparable to Type I.

title: 2. History
text: Dunner D.L., Gershon E.S., Goodwin F.K. (1976) — proposal to differentiate bipolar disorder subtypes. DSM-IV (1994) — Bipolar Type II as a separate diagnostic category formalized. DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 (2019) — Type II retained, emphasizing that it is not a ‘mild form’.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: ~0.4–1.1% (Merikangas K.R. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2011 WMH). Sex: more common in females (~1.5:1 — different from Type I). Onset: mean 20–25 years; multiple depressive episodes usually precede a hypomanic episode. Suicide risk comparable to Type I (lifetime ~5–7%); more often due to depressive episodes. Comorbidity: anxiety 60%+, substance use 30–40%, borderline personality disorder.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic basis overlaps with Type I — heritability 60–80%; GWAS loci overlap. Genetic independence of the clinical phenotype from bipolar Type I is debated — some studies assess both types as the same spectrum. Circadian rhythm disturbance and family history.

title: 5.1 Hypomanic episode
text: Abnormally elevated or irritable mood + increased energy ≥ 4 days (≥ 7 in Type I). Same sub-symptoms as manic episode (decreased need for sleep, distractibility, increase in goal-directed activity, etc.); ≥ 3 symptoms (≥ 4 if irritable mood). Functional impairment should not be significant (i.e., hypomanic definition); no psychotic features; no hospitalization required. If these criteria are met — diagnosis changes t

title: 5.2 Major depressive episode
text: ≥ 5 symptoms for 2 weeks (including low mood and/or anhedonia). Bipolar Type II depressive episodes often with atypical features — hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity. Patients are symptomatic during 53.9% of follow-up weeks; depressive symptoms occupy 50.3% of weeks (hypomanic 1.3%, cycling/mixed 2.3%) — Judd L.L. et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003, n=86, mean 13.4 years of follow-up; most

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. At least one hypomanic episode. B. At least one major depressive episode. C. Never had a manic episode. D. Hypomanic and depressive episodes are not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, or another psychotic disorder. E. Symptoms cause significant distress or functional impairment (primarily from depressive episode).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11: functional impairment in hypomanic episode should not be significant; antidepressant-induced hypomanic episode leads to bipolar Type II diagnosis (especially in persistent or recurrent cases). Underdiagnosis problem: Angst J. et al. (BRIDGE study, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2011;68(8):791–798) — ~16% of patients presenting with a depressive episode meet DSM-IV criteria for bipolar disorder (types I and II

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Structured inquiry for hypomanic episodes in every depressive patient (SCID-5 mood module, MDQ, HCL-32). Information from family members — observation of hypomanic episodes is important. Clinical interview + YMRS, HAM-D / MADRS. Laboratory: thyroid, liver, kidney, toxicology, pregnancy test. Comorbidity and suicide risk assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Bipolar Type I (6A60) ≥1 manic episode (functional impairment or hospitalization requirement). Major Depressive Disorder (6A70/6A71) No hypomanic episode. Cyclothymic (6A62) No full major depressive or hypomanic episodes. BPD (6D11.5) Emotional lability hours; identity disturbance; chronic suicidal ideation. ADHD Persistent; not episodic. Hyperthyroidism TSH measurement.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SCID-5 mood module — the gold standard. MDQ (Mood Disorder Questionnaire) and HCL-32 (Hypomania Checklist) — screening. YMRS, HAM-D / MADRS, C-SSRS. Pre-lithium: creatinine, TSH, calcium, ECG.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG185 · CANMAT/ISBD 2018)
text: Bipolar Type II depressive episode (most common presentation): First-line — quetiapine (FDA approved); lithium, lamotrigine — second-line. Lurasidone’s FDA indication covers bipolar I depression only, not type II; CANMAT/ISBD 2018 likewise names quetiapine alone as first-line for the type II depressive episode. Lamotrigine — first-line in maintenance and depressive prophylaxis (evidence mainly in Type I, also used in

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Lamotrigine — Bipolar Type II effective in maintenance and prevention of depressive episodes; titration slow (risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome) — 25 mg/day × 2 weeks, then 50 mg/day × 2 weeks, then gradually to 200 mg/day (doses halved with valproate). Calabrese J.R. et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2003. Quetiapine — FDA approval for bipolar depressive episode; 300–600 mg/day; metabolic side effect monitoring. Interpersonal

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: CANMAT/ISBD 2018: Type II depressive episode first-line — quetiapine; lamotrigine in maintenance. NICE CG185: Types I and II share the same main approach, but lamotrigine’s specific role emphasized in Type II. Calabrese J.R. RCTs — lamotrigine efficacy in maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder type II.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Episodic course; relapse significantly reduced with maintenance pharmacotherapy. Type II is not ‘milder’ than Type I — high functional impairment and depressive burden. Suicide risk is high. Quetiapine and lamotrigine as the main maintenance agents. Monitoring — depressive symptoms, hypomanic triggers, metabolic indicators.

title: Myth 1: “Type II bipolar is a ‘mild form’ requiring little treatment”
text: Evidence: Judd L.L. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003 — Type II patients spend 50.3% of follow-up weeks with depressive symptoms (53.9% symptomatic overall); functional impairment and suicide risk comparable to Type I.

title: Myth 2: “Hypomanic episode is a ‘good period’, no treatment needed”
text: Evidence: hypomanic episode can involve risky behavior, impaired relationships, later productivity decline, and trigger a depressive episode; isolated episodes indicate need for maintenance pharmacotherapy.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant alone can be used in patients with Type II disorder”
text: Evidence: CANMAT 2018 — antidepressant only with mood stabilizer; risk of manic switch and rapid cycling.

title: Myth 4: “Bipolar Type II is only a form of borderline personality disorder”
text: Evidence: There is significant overlap and comorbidity, but these are distinct disorders; bipolar Type II is episodic, whereas BPD follows a continuous pattern.

title: Myth 5: “Lamotrigine cures a manic episode”
text: Evidence: Lamotrigine is effective in the depressive component and maintenance; ineffective for manic episodes — antipsychotic or valproate is required.

title: Myth 6: “St John’s Wort is safe in bipolar because it is a natural antidepressant”
text: Evidence: St John’s Wort can induce mania and decrease the levels of mood stabilizers (CYP induction); contraindicated in bipolar disorder.

title: Myth 7: “ECT is not needed in Type II”
text: Evidence: ECT is indicated for refractory depressive episodes or high suicidality risk; also effective in patients with Type II disorder.

title: Cyclothymic disorder
text: Cyclothymic disorder ICD-10 F34.0 Cyclothymia DSM-5-TR F34.0 Cyclothymic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Cyclothymic disorder (ICD-11: 6A62; DSM-5-TR: F34.0 Cyclothymic Disorder) — over a period of at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents) a subthreshold chronic affective disorder characterized by persistent fluctuation between hypomanic and depressive symptoms. Does not meet criteria for full major depressive, manic, or hypomanic episodes.

title: 2. History
text: Kahlbaum K. (1882) — “cyclothymia” term. Kraepelin (1899) — a mild form of manic-depressive disorder. Akiskal H.S. (1977) — reconceptualization of cyclothymic temperament as a subthreshold stage of the bipolar spectrum. DSM-III (1980), DSM-5 (2013), ICD-11 (2019) — within the category of affective disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 0.4–1% (DSM-5-TR; broad range, precise epidemiological data limited). Sex: approximately equal. Onset: adolescence and early adulthood. Type I or II conversion to bipolar: ~15–50% (Akiskal H.S. reviews). Comorbidity: anxiety, substance use, ADHD, borderline personality disorder.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Shared genetic load with the bipolar spectrum (Akiskal). Increased familial density of bipolar and major depressive disorder. Neurobiological — monoaminergic and circadian dysregulation similar to bipolar disorder, but less pronounced.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Multiple subthreshold hypomanic episodes — brief, low-intensity elevations in energy and mood. Multiple subthreshold depressive episodes — low-intensity depressive symptoms. “Stable period” less than 2 months. Mood changes over days or weeks; patient may describe their mood changes as ‘this is just my nature.’ Interpersonal and occupational impairment is present, but not disruptive.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR · ICD-11)
text: A. At least 2 years (adults) / 1 year (children/adolescents) of numerous hypomanic and depressive subthreshold periods. B. During this period, symptoms are present for ≥ half of the time, and symptom-free periods do not exceed 2 months. C. Criteria for full major depressive, manic, or hypomanic episodes have never been met. D. Not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, or another psychotic disor

title: 6.2 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (mood diary recommended for 4–6 weeks — documentation of patient’s own patterns). SCID-5, MDQ, HCL-32. Comorbidity and family history assessment. Medical and laboratory tests (thyroid function mandatory).

title: 6.3 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Bipolar Type II (6A61) Full hypomanic and major depressive episodes. Dysthymic disorder (6A72) Only depressive subthreshold; no hypomanic episodes. BPD (6D11.5) Mood swings; identity disturbance; impulsivity and interpersonal relationships. ADHD (6A05) Not episodic; attention deficit dominant. Cyclothymic temperament (normal variant) No functional impairment.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Mood diary. MDQ, HCL-32, YMRS, HAM-D. Thyroid function.

title: 8. Treatment
text: First-line psychotherapy — CBT, IPSRT, psychoeducation, behavioral activation, circadian rhythm management. Pharmacotherapy — evidence base is limited: Lithium or valproate — considered adequate in the context of bipolar spectrum. Lamotrigine — when the depressive component is dominant. Atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine) — in moderate-to-severe cases. Antidepressant alone — risk of manic switch and rapid cycling; co

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) — Frank (Frank E.) — Circadian rhythm and interpersonal stress management. CBT for bipolar spectrum — Psychoeducation, behavioral activation, relapse markers. Mood diary — Patient’s documentation of own mood changes — diagnostic and therapeutic tool. Lithium and lamotrigine — Pharmacotherapy for the bipolar spectrum is adequate.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG185, CANMAT 2018 — separate algorithm for cyclothymic disorder is limited; bipolar spectrum principles apply; psychotherapy first-line.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic; spontaneous remission is rare. Risk of conversion to Bipolar Type I/II — annual clinical assessment. Comorbid substance use and BPD risk factors. Functional level improves with adequate treatment.

title: Myth 1: “Cyclothymic temperament is a normal personality trait, does not require treatment”
text: Clinical logic: cyclothymic temperament when it is a normal variant has no functional impairment; clinical diagnosis requires functional impairment. However, many patients have explained it as a ‘creative nature’ for years and do not seek intervention, while quality of life deteriorates.

title: Myth 2: “Cyclothymic disorder will not convert to bipolar”
text: Evidence: Akiskal — 15–50% conversion to bipolar Type I or II; higher risk with a family history.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant alone manages all mood changes”
text: Evidence: Manic switching and rapid cycling risk; should be combined with a mood stabilizer.

title: Myth 4: “A cyclothymic patient will lose their creativity due to treatment”
text: Evidence: appropriate treatment (psychotherapy + mood stabilizer) helps preserve creativity (more stable functioning); romanticized ‘duality’ explanation leads to avoidance of intervention.

title: Myth 5: “Herbal preparations or diet cure cyclothymic disorder”
text: Evidence: St John’s Wort risk of manic switch; omega-3 mild adjunct, not primary treatment.

title: Single episode depressive disorder
text: Single episode depressive disorder ICD-10 F32 Depressive episode DSM-5-TR F32.x Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Single episode depressive disorder (ICD-11: 6A70; DSM-5-TR: Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode — F32.x) — an affective disorder causing functional impairment, accompanied by significant cognitive, somatic, and psychomotor symptoms along with depressed mood and/or anhedonia for at least two weeks. The patient’s history includes only one major depressive episode (in case of recurrence, code 6A71).

title: 2. History
text: Hippocrates (5th–4th centuries BC) — the term “melancholia”. Kraepelin (1899) — Depressive episode within manic-depressive insanity. DSM-III (1980) — official diagnosis “Major Depressive Disorder”; separation from bipolar disorder. DSM-5 (2013) — the “bereavement exclusion” has been removed — a major depressive episode can be diagnosed in a patient even after the loss of a loved one. ICD-11 (2019) — Single episode (6

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 15–20% (NESARC-III; Hasin D.S. et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2018). Annual prevalence: ~6–8%. Sex: 1.5–twice as common in females. Onset: mean 20–30 years; but possible at any age. Suicide: depressive disorder is associated with ~50% of suicide deaths. Comorbidity: anxiety disorders 60%, substance use 25%, pain, cardiovascular, diabetes. Mortality: overall mortality increased 1.5 times (cardiovascular,

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 35–40% (Sullivan P.F. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2000 meta-analysis); lower than in bipolar disorder. GWAS — 100+ risk loci (Howard D.M. et al. Nat Neurosci 2019, n>800,000). Neurobiological — monoaminergic (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine) hypothesis; HPA axis dysregulation, elevated cortisol; hippocampal volume reduction; inflammatory hypothesis (CRP, IL-6). Risk factors: childhood trauma, family histo

title: 5.1 Core symptoms (DSM-5-TR — ≥ 5 symptoms × 2 weeks, at least 1 of which is 1 or 2)
text: Persistent low mood. Anhedonia — loss of interest and pleasure. Weight or appetite changes. Sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia). Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable by others). Fatigue or loss of energy. Worthlessness or excessive guilt. Difficulty concentrating and impaired decision-making. Suicidal thoughts or plan.

title: 5.2 Qualifiers (DSM-5-TR)
text: Severity: mild, moderate, severe. With psychotic features (delusion or hallucination). Atypical features (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis). Melancholic features. Catatonic features. Peripartum onset. Seasonal pattern. Mixed features (manic components). With anxious distress.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR · ICD-11 consensus points)
text: A. The presence of 5 or more symptoms for ≥ 2 weeks; at least one of which must be depressed mood or anhedonia. B. Significant distress or functional impairment. C. Exclusion of substance or medical condition. D. Never had a manic or hypomanic episode.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR: “Bereavement exclusion” removed (in DSM-IV, diagnosis was not made during 2 months of bereavement); grief and depressive episode can co-occur. ICD-11 (6A70): single episode separately coded; severity and psychotic feature qualifiers. NICE NG222 (2022): Severity classification: less severe, more severe (instead of mild/moderate/severe in DSM); treatment algorithms based on severity.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Structured interview (SCID-5, MINI). Scales — PHQ-9 (screening and monitoring), HAM-D, MADRS, BDI-II. Suicide risk (C-SSRS). Bipolar screening (MDQ, HCL-32) — to rule out bipolar episodes. Medical and laboratory (thyroid, B12, folate, ferritin, liver, kidney, pregnancy) — to exclude somatic causes. Toxicology screening (suspect substance use).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Bipolar Type I/II (6A60/6A61) History of manic or hypomanic episode. Dysthymic disorder (6A72) ≥2 years subthreshold depressive symptoms. Adjustment disorder (6B43) Response to stress factor; fewer criteria. Grief (sadness) After loss of a loved one; ‘wave-like’ course; self-esteem is preserved. Hypothyroidism Elevated TSH; somatic symptoms. B12 / folate deficiency Laboratory. Substa

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PHQ-9 — standard in primary care; ≥10 score indicates moderate or more severe depression. HAM-D-17 (Hamilton), MADRS — clinical and research. BDI-II — self-assessment. C-SSRS — suicide risk. Laboratory: complete blood count, thyroid, B12, folate, ferritin, liver and kidney function, glucose. ECG — before starting TCA or QT-prolonging medications.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE NG222 · APA 2010 · CANMAT 2016 Consensus)
text: Stepwise approach based on severity: Mild (PHQ-9 5–9) — guided self-help, CBT-based internet interventions, physical activity, observation. Moderate (PHQ-9 10–14) — CBT or IPT, or pharmacotherapy (SSRI); patient choice. Moderately severe (PHQ-9 15–19) — pharmacotherapy (SSRI) or a high-intensity psychological intervention; combination preferred. Severe (PHQ-9 ≥ 20 or psychotic features) — combination of pharmacothera

title: 8.2 Pharmacotherapy
text: Class Drug Dose range Note SSRIs Sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram Sertraline 50–200 mg; escitalopram 10–20 mg First-line; sexual side effect; SIADH (in elderly); citalopram > 40 mg: QT prolongation. SNRI Venlafaxine, duloxetine Venlafaxine 75–375 mg; duloxetine 60–120 mg Comorbid pain, anxiety. Atypical Mirtazapine, bupropion, agomelatine, vortioxetine Mirtazapine 15–45 mg; bupropion 150–4

title: 8.3 Source-specific clarifications
text: NICE NG222 (2022): stepwise algorithm based on severity; “less severe” — CBT or guided self-help first-line; “more severe” — combination. APA Practice Guideline (2010): SSRI first-line; CBT / IPT first-line alternative. CANMAT 2016: A 4-step algorithm based on severity and clinical presentation. Cipriani A. et al. Lancet 2018 network meta-analysis: Comparison of 21 antidepressants — agomelatine and amitriptyline high

title: 8.4 Treatment methods
text: CBT for depression — Beck (Beck A.) — Cognitive restructuring, behavioral activation; 12–20 sessions. Evidence: Cuijpers P. et al. Cochrane meta-analyses — medium effect, comparable to pharmacotherapy; combination superior to monotherapy in severe cases. Interpersonal Therapy (IPT — Interpersonal Therapy) — Klerman (Klerman G.), Weissman (Weissman M.) — 4 problem areas — grief, role transition, role dispute, interper

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Spontaneous remission occurs in 50% within one year (though most remissions occur without antidepressant treatment); relapse risk is high. The risk of a subsequent episode increases after each episode. Suicide risk is particularly high in the first weeks. Monitoring — PHQ-9 / MADRS, suicide risk, side effects, compliance; more frequent in first 12 weeks. Duration of treatment — 6–12 months after remission in first ep

title: Myth 1: “Depression is just ‘sadness’; it can be overcome voluntarily”
text: Evidence: Depression is a complex neurobiological disorder involving HPA axis dysregulation, monoamine imbalance, and structural changes (e.g., hippocampus); it is not volitionally controllable. The APA, WHO, and NICE define it as a medical condition.

title: Myth 2: “Antidepressants are addictive”
text: Evidence: SSRI and SNRI do not cause addiction — no abuse or tolerance. But a discontinuation syndrome does exist (especially with the short half-life of paroxetine, venlafaxine) — this is not addiction, but physiological adaptation; it resolves with gradual discontinuation.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant changes the patient’s personality”
text: Evidence: Antidepressants reduce the symptoms; they do not change the personality. If a patient says that he or she no longer feels like themselves, that is a side effect — emotional blunting — and the answer is to change the drug or lower the dose.

title: Myth 4: “Antidepressants are no better than placebo”
text: Evidence: Cipriani Lancet 2018 — 21 antidepressants significantly superior to placebo; but effect is modest, especially in mild depression. In moderate-to-severe depression, the effect is clinically significant.

title: Myth 5: “Diet (omega-3, B vitamins, magnesium) replaces antidepressants”
text: Evidence: Some supplements (omega-3, vitamin D in deficiency) may have mild adjunct effect, but do not replace main treatment in moderate-to-severe depression. SMILES study (Jacka F.N. BMC Med 2017) — Mediterranean-type diet as mild adjunct.

title: Myth 6: “St John’s Wort is a natural antidepressant and can replace antidepressants”
text: Evidence: St John’s wort shows efficacy in mild depression (Cochrane Linde K. 2008), but the evidence base is limited in moderate-to-severe depression; due to CYP induction, it reduces the levels of numerous drugs (contraceptives, anticoagulants, antidepressants, antiretrovirals) — a serious interaction.

title: Myth 7: “Only exercise or psychotherapy is sufficient; medication is unnecessary”
text: Evidence: In mild depression, psychotherapy and exercise may sometimes be sufficient, but in moderate-to-severe depression and particularly when suicidal risk is present, pharmacotherapy is necessary; NICE NG222 and APA 2010.

title: Myth 8: “ECT is an outdated or traumatic treatment”
text: Evidence: modern ECT (under anesthesia, with muscle relaxants) is safe and highly effective; it is the gold standard for severe refractory and psychotic depression. UK ECT Review Group Lancet 2003.

title: Myth 9: “Antidepressants cause suicide”
text: Evidence: FDA black box in children and adolescents (especially first weeks) warns of increased risk of suicidal thoughts — requires monitoring of these patients, but long-term antidepressants reduce suicide risk (Stone M. et al. BMJ 2009).

title: Myth 10: “Depression cannot be diagnosed during the grieving period”
text: Evidence: DSM-5 eliminated the bereavement exclusion; grief and major depressive episode can co-occur; pathological forms of grief (prolonged grief disorder — 6B42) are separate.

title: Myth 11: “Depression in healthy patients is a marker of psychological ‘weakness’”
text: Evidence: Depression can occur in any individual; the concept of “psychological strength” is stigmatizing and incorrect; it should be evaluated as a medical condition.

title: Recurrent depressive disorder
text: Recurrent depressive disorder ICD-10 F33 Recurrent depressive disorder DSM-5-TR F33.x Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent Episode

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Recurrent depressive disorder (ICD-11: 6A71; DSM-5-TR: Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent — F33.x) — presence of at least two major depressive episodes, with partial or full remission lasting at least 2 months between episodes. No history of manic or hypomanic episodes (if present, diagnosis is bipolar disorder). Differs from single episode depressive disorder (6A70) only by number of episodes; clinical manifestati

title: 2. History
text: Kraepelin (1899) — within the framework of manic-depressive disorder, recurrent depressive episodes. Leonhard K. (1957) — concept of unipolar depression. DSM-III (1980), DSM-5 (2013) — Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent official designation. ICD-11 (2019) — Single episode (6A70) and recurrent (6A71) are coded separately.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Major depressive disorder lifetime prevalence 15–20%; of which ~50–80% have a recurrent course. The risk of a subsequent episode increases after each episode (Solomon D.A. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2000) — ~50% after the 1st episode, ~70% after the 2nd, ~90% after the 3rd. Suicide risk higher than in single episodes, particularly in untreated episodes.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Same as single episode (6A70) — heritability ~35–40% (Sullivan 2000); GWAS loci. Relapse predisposition — predominantly cognitive predisposition, neurobiological “kindling” (Post R.M.) concept — threshold decreases for the next episode after each one. Risk factors — childhood trauma, family history, chronic stress, comorbid anxiety, somatic illness.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Same as a single episode (see 6A70 §5). In recurrent patients, additional features: Episode presentation may change from previous episodes (atypical features, seasonal pattern). Inter-episode intervals shorten, the role of triggering stress decreases (kindling concept — Post R.M. Am J Psychiatry 1992). Comorbid anxiety disorders with increased frequency. Chronic cognitive deficits may be observed (especially after mu

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR · ICD-11)
text: A. At least 2 major depressive episodes (according to 6A70 §6.1 criteria). B. ≥ 2 months partial or full remission between episodes. C. Never had a manic or hypomanic episode. D. Not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, or another psychotic disorder.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11: current episode severity (mild, moderate, severe) and psychotic feature qualifiers; remission status (partial, full). DSM-5-TR: qualifiers are the same as 6A70. NICE NG222: ≥3 episodes — MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy) is specifically recommended for relapse prevention in patients.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: History — number of previous episodes, duration, triggers, quality of remission. Bipolar screening (MDQ, HCL-32) — to rule out hypomanic episodes. PHQ-9 / HAM-D / MADRS — severity of current episode. C-SSRS — suicide risk (high in recurrent patients). Laboratory (thyroid, B12, folate, ferritin); somatic comorbidity assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Same as 6A70 (see single episode). Special attention — exclude bipolar episodes.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Same as 6A70. Special attention — assessment of cognitive deficits (after multiple episodes).

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE NG222 · APA 2010 · CANMAT 2016)
text: Acute episode treatment — Same as 6A70 (SSRI, CBT, combination). Maintenance pharmacotherapy — long-term. After 2 episodes — continue for 1–2 years after remission. ≥3 episodes — long-term (years) or lifelong maintenance. Effective antidepressant is maintained at the same dose after remission (dose reduction increases relapse risk). MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy) — comparable effect to antidepressant cont

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) — 8-week group program; 2.5-hour sessions + home practice. Effective in relapse prevention for patients with history of ≥3 episodes. RCT: Kuyken W. et al. Lancet 2015. mbct.com. Antidepressant Maintenance Therapy — Long-term use with the same drug and dose; at least 2 years (≥ 3 episodes); gradual discontinuation (4–8 weeks). CBT and IPT maintenance formats — Monthly or ever

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG222 (2022): ≥3 episode history — MBCT or antidepressant maintenance; both are comparably effective. APA 2010: maintenance pharmacotherapy after ≥ 2 episodes; long-term after ≥ 3 episodes. Geddes J.R. et al. Lancet 2003 meta-analysis: Antidepressant continuation significantly superior to placebo in relapse reduction (NNT 5).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Relapse risk increases after each episode (Solomon 2000). Relapse risk significantly reduced with adequate maintenance treatment (NNT 5). Comorbid anxiety, somatic illnesses, compliance disturbance — poor prognosis. Monitoring — PHQ-9 monitoring; relapse markers; antidepressant levels and side effects; suicide risk.

title: Myth 1: “Antidepressants cannot be used lifelong, they cause ‘addiction’”
text: Evidence: SSRI/SNRI do not cause dependency; long-term (for years) maintenance is recommended for those with ≥3 episode history (NICE NG222, APA 2010). Reducing the maintenance dose increases the risk of relapse.

title: Myth 2: “Antidepressants should be stopped immediately after remission”
text: Evidence: After remission continue at least 6–12 months (single episode) or years (recurrent); early discontinuation significantly increases relapse risk (Geddes Lancet 2003).

title: Myth 3: “Medication should be changed with every episode”
text: Evidence: The medication effective in the previous episode should be reused in the next episode (patient-specific efficacy).

title: Myth 4: “Recurrent depressive disorder is a ‘personality weakness’, treatment should not be long”
text: Evidence: Neurobiological ‘kindling’ concept — each episode increases risk of new episode; long-term treatment ‘protects’ the brain.

title: Myth 5: “Only MBCT is sufficient for relapse prevention; pharmacotherapy is unnecessary”
text: Evidence: Kuyken Lancet 2015 — MBCT vs. maintenance antidepressant comparison; but individual choice — based on patient values, accessibility, prior treatment response.

title: 11. Sources

title: Dysthymic disorder
text: Dysthymic disorder ICD-10 F34.1 Dysthymia DSM-5-TR F34.1 Persistent Depressive Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Dysthymic disorder (ICD-11: 6A72; DSM-5-TR: F34.1 Persistent Depressive Disorder) — chronic depressive symptoms lasting at least 2 years (in adults; 1 year in children/adolescents) that do not meet the severity of a major depressive episode. The patient may describe their state as ‘I’ve always been this way’. DSM-5-TR — the term “Persistent Depressive Disorder” combines dysthymia and chronic major depressive disorder

title: 2. History
text: Flemming C.F. (1844) — first psychiatric use of the term “dysthymia”; Kahlbaum (1882) — gave it its modern meaning as a chronic, subthreshold depressive state. Akiskal H.S. (1980s) — dysthymic temperament as a substage of the depressive spectrum. DSM-III (1980) — official diagnosis “Dysthymic Disorder”. DSM-5 (2013) — “Persistent Depressive Disorder” — merger of dysthymia and chronic MDD. ICD-11 (2019) — dysthymic di

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1.1–6.4% (dysthymia); 12-month prevalence in the US ~0.5%, plus 1.5% for chronic major depression (DSM-5-TR). Sex: twice as common in females. Onset: early (childhood/adolescence — early-onset; ≥ 21 years — late-onset). “Double depression” — major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymic disorder — occurs in 76.9% of patients within 5 years (Klein D.N. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2000;157(6):931–9

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Shared genetic and neurobiological predisposition with major depressive disorder. Childhood trauma and chronic psychosocial stress are key environmental risk factors. The frequency of depressive disorder or dysthymia is increased in close relatives.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Persistent low mood — present most of the time (≥ half the time, no symptom-free period > 2 months over 2 years). At least 2 of the following: low or increased appetite, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, concentration difficulty, hopelessness. The patient has adapted to numerous functional compromises — the explanation “I have always been like this” is typical; they often present to the clinic dur

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent depressive mood ≥ 2 years (children ≥ 1 year), most of the day, most of the time. B. ≥ 2 symptoms during depressive episodes (above) C. No symptom-free period longer than 2 months within 2 years (1 year). D. During this period, criteria for a major depressive episode may be continuously present (DSM-5 — new “double depression” synthesis). E. Never had a manic or hypomanic episode. F. Not better explaine

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR: “Persistent Depressive Disorder” — combines dysthymia and chronic MDD; qualifiers — early/late onset, with/without anxious distress, melancholic, atypical, peripartum, seasonal, etc. ICD-11: dysthymic disorder (6A72) separate; chronic depressive episode within 6A70/71 qualifier.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + long-term history (patient may not recall exact onset). SCID-5; PHQ-9, HAM-D, MADRS. Bipolar screening. Personality assessment — differential with BPD. Medical and laboratory (thyroid, anemia, B12).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Major depressive disorder (6A70/6A71) Discrete episodes; mood is normal between symptoms. Cyclothymic disorder (6A62) Hypomanic periods present. BPD (6D11.5) Emotional lability over hours; identity disturbance. Adjustment disorder (6B43) Response to stress factor; ≤ 6 months. Hypothyroidism TSH.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PHQ-9, HAM-D, MADRS. Cornell Dysthymia Rating Scale — dysthymia-specific. Medical and laboratory.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Pharmacotherapy: SSRI (sertraline, fluoxetine) — first-line; the effect may take 6–8 weeks (slower than in major depression). Psychotherapy: CBASP (Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy — McCullough J.) — specifically developed for chronic depression; CBT, IPT. Combination — superior to monotherapy in chronic depression (Keller M.B. et al. NEJM 2000 – nefazodone + CBASP RCT). In “double depression” —

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy (CBASP — Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy) — McCullough (McCullough J.) — Approach specifically developed for chronic depression — situation analysis, interpersonal behavior teaching, use of therapeutic relationship as main tool. Keller M.B. et al. NEJM 2000 RCT. SSRI long-term — Sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram; slow response; prolonged m

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG222 — recommends long-term cognitive behavioral treatment for chronic depressive symptoms (CBASP is not named in the guideline); CBASP is named by APA 2010. APA 2010 — combination superior. Keller M.B. et al. NEJM 2000 — nefazodone + CBASP combination significantly superior to monotherapy.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course; spontaneous remission is rare. “Double depression” — develops in 76.9% of dysthymic patients without a prior major episode within 5 years (Klein D.N. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2000). Functional level improves with long-term treatment. Monitoring — periodic scales, compliance, comorbidity.

title: Myth 1: “Dysthymia is just a ‘gloomy character’, not a medical disorder”
text: Evidence: persistent functional impairment, suicidality risk, development of “double depression”; should be evaluated as a medical disorder.

title: Myth 2: “Dysthymic patient does not respond to antidepressants”
text: Evidence: The response is slow — 6 to 8 weeks, but SSRIs are effective; combination with CBASP superior.

title: Myth 3: “Chronic depression only requires psychotherapy; medications are ineffective”
text: Evidence: Keller NEJM 2000 — nefazodone + CBASP combination superior to monotherapy; pharmacotherapy is a core component.

title: Myth 4: “The patient’s explanation ‘I’ve always been like this’ is not a basis for diagnosis — it should be accepted as adaptation”
text: Evidence: This patient perspective creates a problem of under-detection — long-term functional compromise may be a marker of medical condition.

title: Myth 5: “Herbal preparations are a safe alternative for dysthymia”
text: Evidence: St John’s Wort demonstrates some efficacy in mild depression, but CYP induction interactions; standard antidepressants superior.

title: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) (Premenstrual dysphoric disorder)
text: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) (Premenstrual dysphoric disorder) Premenstrual dysphoric disorder ICD-10 N94.3 Premenstrual tension syndrome DSM-5-TR F32.81 Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (ICD-11: GA34.41; DSM-5-TR: F32.81 / ICD-10: N94.3) — a recurrent disorder with significant emotional and behavioral symptoms in the last week before menstruation (luteal phase), fully remitting within a few days after menses onset. Distinguished from Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) by clinical severity and significant functional impairment.

title: 2. History
text: Frank R.T. (1931) — “Premenstrual tension” term. DSM-IV (1994) — “Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder” is included in Appendix B as a research category. DSM-5 (2013) — officially accepted as a diagnosis in the category of depressive disorders. ICD-11 (2019) — as separate category within mood disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in reproductive-age women: 3–8% (Yonkers K.A. et al. Lancet 2008 review). PMS — milder form — in 30–80% of women. Comorbidity: major depressive disorder, anxiety, bipolar disorder — increases risk. Suicidal thoughts significantly increase in the luteal phase.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic: heritability ~30–50% (Treloar S.A. et al. Psychol Med 2002 twin studies). Hormonal sensitivity: In PMDD patients, ovarian hormones (estrogen, progesterone) are at normal levels; however sensitivity is increased — allopregnanolone (progesterone metabolite) exerts abnormal effect on GABA-A receptors (Schmidt P.J. et al. NEJM 1998 ovarian suppression and hormone supplementation study). Serotonergic dysregulatio

title: 5.1 Affective and behavioral symptoms (in the luteal phase)
text: Affective lability (rapidly changing mood, tearfulness, rejection sensitivity). Irritability and angry outbursts (interpersonal conflict). Low mood, hopelessness, self-criticism. Anxiety, tension.

title: 5.2 Behavioral and somatic symptoms
text: Decreased interest in usual activities. Difficulty concentrating. Lethargy and fatigue. Appetite changes (especially carbohydrate craving) or overeating. Sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia). Sense of loss of control. Somatic — swelling of body, back pain, headache, breast tenderness.

title: 5.3 Duration and rhythm
text: Symptoms begin in luteal phase (1 week pre-menses), completely resolve within a few days post-menses onset; complete remission in follicular phase (post-menses).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR · ICD-11)
text: A. In most menstrual cycles, 5+ symptoms in the last week of luteal phase; diminish within a few days after onset of menses; complete remission in postmenstrual phase. B. At least 1 of the following: Affective lability; Irritability or anger; Low mood or self-criticism; Anxiety and tension. C. Additional symptoms from the following (B + C total 5+): Decreased interest; Difficulty concentrating; Lethargy, fatigue; App

title: 6.2 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview — rhythm of cycle-related symptoms. Prospective mood diary for 2 cycles — DRSP (Daily Record of Severity of Problems, Endicott J.) or PRISM (Prospective Record of the Impact and Severity of Menstrual Symptomatology) — diagnosis cannot be confirmed by retrospective anamnesis. Comorbidity screening (depression, anxiety, bipolar). Medical (thyroid, anemia, polycystic ovary).

title: 6.3 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features PMS (premenstrual syndrome) Soft symptoms, no functional impairment. MDD luteal exacerbation Core disturbance (MDD) is present throughout cycle, intensified in luteal phase. Bipolar disorder Hypomanic/manic episodes present. Thyroid disorder TSH. Endometriosis, dysmenorrhea Pelvic pain dominant; mood symptoms mild.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: DRSP or PRISM mood diary. PHQ-9, GAD-7 — comorbidity. Pelvic examination (gynecologist) and TSH — somatic causes excluded.

title: 8.1 General principles (ACOG · ISPMD · APA 2010)
text: SSRI first-line: Fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine (FDA approved for PMDD), escitalopram. Two modes possible: Persistent (daily): Throughout the entire cycle. Luteal-phase intermittent: From ovulation to start of menses (14 days) — equally effective (Steiner M. et al. NEJM 1995 RCT). Hormonal suppression — combined oral contraceptives (especially those containing drospirenone — Yaz, Beyaz; FDA-approved); GnRH agonis

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP) — Endicott (Endicott J.) — 21 symptoms, daily rating of 1–6 points; prospective 2 cycles required for PMDD diagnosis. SSRI — Luteal Phase Regimen — From ovulation (day 14) until menses onset; as effective as continuous use. Steiner M. et al. NEJM 1995. Drospirenone-containing Oral Contraceptive — Yaz, Beyaz — FDA approval for PMDD; hormonal stabilization. GnRH Agonist (Leup

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: ACOG (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists) Practice Bulletin: SSRI first-line; oral contraceptive second. ISPMD (International Society for Premenstrual Disorders) consensus: continuous or luteal SSRIs equal efficacy; GnRH refractory.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: SSRI or hormonal treatment leads to significant improvement in most patients. Persists during reproductive period; remission after menopause. Monitoring — cycle symptoms, compliance, side effects, comorbidity.

title: Myth 1: “PMDD is ‘female willpower weakness’, not a medical disorder”
text: Evidence: Schmidt P.J. NEJM 1998 — ovarian hormone suppression eliminates symptoms, hormone restart returns symptoms; neurobiologically based disorder. DSM-5 and ICD-11 official diagnosis.

title: Myth 2: “PMDD is also PMS, no difference”
text: Evidence: PMS mild form in 30–80% of women; PMDD characterized by clinical severity and functional impairment — 3–8% of women.

title: Myth 3: “SSRIs show no significant effect in PMDD, should be treated like depression”
text: Evidence: SSRI shows rapid effect (within 1–2 days) in PMDD — different pharmacokinetic mechanism from major depression; direct effect on serotonergic system.

title: Myth 4: “Only hormonal treatment (contraceptives, hormone replacement) is effective”
text: Evidence: SSRI and hormonal treatment both effective; SSRI first-line (for most patients); hormonal — with gynecological comorbidity or patient choice.

title: Myth 5: “Herbal preparations (chasteberry, evening primrose oil, St John’s Wort) cure PMDD”
text: Evidence: Chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus) has mild effect for PMS in some studies; evidence base for PMDD limited. Evening primrose oil — systematic review showed no effect. St John’s Wort — risk of interaction with SSRIs.

title: Myth 6: “Craniosacral therapy, homeopathy, acupuncture cure PMDD”
text: Evidence: Efficacy of these complementary interventions for PMDD has not been proven.

title: Myth 7: “PMDD diagnosis can be made from retrospective history”
text: Evidence: retrospective records are unreliable; Prospective 2-cycle diary is mandatory for diagnosis — this is the most frequent cause of under-detection.
