title: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) (Generalised anxiety disorder)
text: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) (Generalised anxiety disorder) Generalised anxiety disorder ICD-10 F41.1 Generalized anxiety disorder DSM-5-TR F41.1 Generalized Anxiety Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Generalized anxiety disorder (ICD-11: 6B00; DSM-5-TR: F41.1) — a disorder characterized by excessive anxiety that persists for at least several months (≥ 6 months in DSM-5-TR), encompasses multiple life domains (work, family, health, daily topics), is uncontrollable, and lacks sufficient triggers. It is accompanied by significant somatic symptoms (tension, fatigue, sleep disturbance).

title: 2. History
text: 1895–1960s — term ‘anxiety neurosis’ (German: Angstneurose); introduced by Sigmund Freud. DSM-III (1980) — “anxiety neurosis” → separation of panic disorder and GAD; GAD was a residual category. DSM-IV (1994), DSM-5 (2013) — GAD as separate disorder; ≥ 6-month duration; characteristic somatic symptoms. ICD-11 (2019) — has formulated the duration requirement for diagnosis as “several months” (less strict than DSM-5).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 3–9% (Kessler R.C. et al. WMH surveys). Annual prevalence: ~2–3%. Sex: twice as common in females. Onset — bimodal — adolescence and middle age; often chronic course. Comorbidity: MDD ~60%, social anxiety, panic, substance use, somatic (irritable bowel, cardiac complaints).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 30–40% (Hettema J.M. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2001 meta-analysis). Neurobiological — amygdala hyperresponsivity, impaired prefrontal-amygdala regulation; GABAergic and serotonergic dysregulation. Personality traits (neuroticism, behavioral inhibition) are high-risk factors. Environment — childhood trauma, chronic stress, parental overprotection.

title: 5.1 Psychological symptoms
text: Uncontrollable worry covering multiple areas. “Worry about worry” — meta-worry (Wells A. concept). Difficulty concentrating, mind going blank. Irritability.

title: 5.2 Somatic symptoms
text: Muscle tension. Fatigue. Sleep disturbance (difficulty falling asleep, difficulty staying asleep). Autonomic symptoms (tachycardia, sweating, dry mouth, headache). IBS is a common comorbidity, presenting with gastrointestinal complaints.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Excessive anxiety or tension, focused on multiple areas; present most of the time during daily activities; ≥ 6 months (DSM-5-TR) / several months (ICD-11). B. Difficulty managing anxiety. C. ≥ 3 symptoms from the following (1 in children): Restlessness, feeling keyed up or on edge; Easy fatigability; Difficulty concentrating; Irritability; Muscle tension; Sleep disturbance. D. Significant distress or functional im

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR: ≥6 month period; ≥3 somatic symptoms. ICD-11: duration “several months” — less stringent; somatic symptoms are required, but a specific number is not indicated. NICE CG113 (Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management, 2011, 2020 update): Stepped care — psychoeducation + observation → guided self-help → CBT or pharmacotherapy → combination → specialized service in severe case.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (areas of concern, triggers, somatic symptoms, avoidance). SCID-5, MINI. GAD-7 (screening, initial assessment and monitoring) — ≥ 10 moderate-to-severe anxiety. HAM-A (Hamilton Anxiety) — clinician-rated. Comorbidity screening (PHQ-9 depression, panic, social anxiety). Exclude somatic causes — TSH, anemia, cardiac, caffeine or stimulant use.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing features Panic disorder (6B01) Discrete panic attacks. Social anxiety (6B04) Fear of social evaluation dominant. OCD (6B20) Ego-dystonic obsessions, compulsions. PTSD (6B40) Trauma history, intrusive symptoms. Major depressive (6A70/6A71) Affective symptoms predominate. Hyperthyroidism Decreased TSH, somatic symptoms. Caffeine or stimulant intoxication Use history. Arrhythmia, pheochromocytom

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: GAD-7, HAM-A, PSWQ (Penn State Worry Questionnaire). Medical and laboratory (TSH, complete blood count, caffeine and alcohol use assessment). ECG (if cardiac complaint present).

title: 8.1 Stepped approach (NICE CG113 · Katzman 2014)
text: Step 1 — psychoeducation and active monitoring. Step 2 — guided self-help (internet-based CBT), psychoeducation groups. Step 3 — high-intensity CBT or pharmacotherapy. Step 4 — specialist service: combination treatment, refractory cases.

title: 8.2 First-line
text: Psychotherapy — cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). The method with the strongest evidence base; 12–20 sessions. Components: Cognitive restructuring — testing beliefs about anxiety: judgments such as “worrying keeps me prepared” are set against the facts. Work with intolerance of uncertainty (Dugas M.J. model) — the patient deliberately experiences situations with unknown outcomes and builds tolerance. Exposure — ste

title: 8.3 Second-line
text: Pregabalin — approved for this indication in Europe; acts quickly but carries dependence potential. Buspirone — partial effect; as an alternative to benzodiazepines. Mirtazapine — adjunct where sleep disturbance accompanies. Quetiapine — second-line in Katzman 2014; use limited by metabolic adverse effects.

title: 8.4 Short-term use and limits
text: Benzodiazepines — only in the acute period, no longer than 2–4 weeks. Dependence potential is high; continuous use is not recommended.

title: 8.5 Additional methods
text: Mindfulness-based stress reduction and cognitive therapy (MBSR / MBCT) — an 8-week group program; a mild effect in this disorder. Hofmann S.G. et al., J Consult Clin Psychol 2010 meta-analysis. Acceptance-based behavior therapy (close to ACT) — instead of fighting the symptom it teaches living by one’s values alongside it; increases psychological flexibility. Randomized trials by Roemer L. et al. Applied relaxation (

title: 8.6 Duration of treatment
text: Continued for at least 12 months after remission. In a chronic course or with multiple relapses, treatment is planned as long-term. Withdrawal is stepwise: abrupt discontinuation raises the risk of return.

title: 8.7 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG113 (2011, reaffirmed 2020) — stepped approach; SSRIs and SNRIs as first-line pharmacotherapy; benzodiazepines only acutely and briefly. APA — has no separate guideline for this disorder; the only document in the family concerns panic disorder (2009, archived status). Reference is therefore made to NICE CG113 and Katzman 2014. Canadian guideline (Katzman M.A. et al. 2014) — first-line agomelatine, duloxetine,

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course; spontaneous remission is low. Significant symptom reduction and functional improvement with adequate treatment. Comorbid MDD is a marker of poor prognosis. Monitoring — GAD-7 monitoring, side effects, compliance, comorbidity.

title: Myth 1: “Anxiety is a normal life feeling, not a medical condition”
text: Evidence: A clinical distinction exists between normal anxiety and GAD — severity, duration (≥ 6 months), uncontrollability, somatic components, functional impairment. Clinical diagnosis is made based on specific criteria.

title: Myth 2: “Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment for GAD”
text: Evidence: NICE CG113, APA, CANMAT — benzodiazepines only for short-term (2–4 weeks) use; high dependence potential; SSRIs and SNRIs first-line.

title: Myth 3: “Only relaxation or yoga can cure GAD”
text: Evidence: They show moderate adjunctive effects, but in moderate-to-severe cases CBT and/or pharmacotherapy are required.

title: Myth 4: “Antidepressants are ineffective for anxiety — they are for depression”
text: Evidence: SSRI and SNRI effective in anxiety disorders; via effect of serotonergic system on amygdala activity. Katzman 2014, Slee Lancet 2019.

title: Myth 5: “The patient can learn not to be anxious voluntarily”
text: Evidence: GAD is a neurobiological dysregulation; CBT or pharmacotherapy acts at the neurobiological level.

title: Myth 6: “Caffeine restriction is sufficient for GAD”
text: Evidence: Caffeine can exacerbate symptoms; restriction is an adjunct step, not primary treatment.

title: Myth 7: “Herbal preparations (kava, valerian, passiflora) can replace standard treatment”
text: Evidence: Kava causes severe hepatotoxicity (several fatalities — FDA warning); valerian and passiflora effect weak; St John’s Wort (Hypericum perforatum) carries a risk of interaction with antidepressants (SSRIs).

title: Myth 8: “Cannabis (CBD) cures anxiety”
text: Evidence: Preliminary studies exist for CBD, but insufficient for clinical recommendation; THC may exacerbate anxiety or trigger panic attacks.

title: Myth 9: “You will have to use antidepressants for life”
text: Evidence: After 12 months of remission, gradual discontinuation is possible; restart if relapse.

title: Myth 10: “Electroconvulsive therapy is effective in refractory GAD”
text: Evidence: ECT is not indicated for GAD; in refractory cases — medication change, combination, atypical antipsychotic adjunct.

title: Panic disorder
text: Panic disorder ICD-10 F41.0 Panic disorder [episodic paroxysmal anxiety] DSM-5-TR F41.0 Panic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Panic disorder (ICD-11: 6B01; DSM-5-TR: F41.0) — a disorder characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks (acute episodes of fear or anxiety peaking within a few minutes) and persistent worry about recurrence of these attacks, with behavioral changes.

title: 2. History
text: Da Costa J.M. (1871) ‘irritable heart’ — in American Civil War soldiers. Freud (1894) “anxiety neurosis”. Klein D.F. (1964) — distinguishing antidepressant response of panic attacks; basis for splitting ‘anxiety neurosis’. DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis of Panic Disorder. DSM-5 (2013), ICD-11 — Agoraphobia is a separate category from panic disorder.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 2–5%; annual ~2.7% (Kessler R.C. WMH). Sex: twice as common in females. Onset: young to middle adulthood (20–30 years); second peak in middle age. Comorbidity: agoraphobia 30–50%, MDD 50–60%, other anxiety disorders, substance use, mitral valve prolapse.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability ~40% (Hettema 2001 meta-analysis). Neurobiological — amygdala-locus coeruleus-prefrontal circuit hyperreactivity; serotonergic, noradrenergic, GABAergic dysregulation. CO₂ sensitivity hypothesis (Klein D.F. ‘suffocation false alarm’) — patients show sensitivity to hyperventilation and CO₂ accumulation. Personality — anxiety sensitivity (Reiss S.); childhood history of separation anxiety.

title: Panic attack — 4+ symptoms peak within 10 minutes
text: Palpitations, fluttering, tachycardia. Cold sweat, trembling. Shortness of breath, feeling of air insufficiency. Feeling of suffocation. Chest pain or discomfort. Nausea, abdominal discomfort. Dizziness, feeling of impending loss of consciousness. Cold or hot sensations; paresthesia. Derealization, depersonalization. Fear of loss of control or “going crazy.” Fear of death. Attack lasts 5–20 minutes; hospital admissio

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Repeated unexpected panic attacks. B. At least one of the attacks has been followed by ≥ 1 month of one or more of the following: Persistent worry about next attack; Fear of consequences of attacks (heart attack, going crazy); Significant behavioral change associated with attacks (avoidance, safety behaviors). C. Exclusion of substance or medical condition. D. Not better explained by another mental disorder (socia

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — agoraphobia as a separate diagnosis (F40.00); may co-occur. ICD-11 — agoraphobia has its own code 6B02; but no one-month period of concern is required — “persistent concern” is enough. NICE CG113 — diagnosis after exclusion of somatic cause.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + attack history. SCID-5, MINI. PDSS (Panic Disorder Severity Scale), GAD-7 comorbidity. Medical: ECG, TSH, complete blood count, glucose, caffeine/stimulants; pheochromocytoma suspicion — 24-hour urinary metanephrines. Comorbidity (agoraphobia, MDD, substance use).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Agoraphobia (6B02) Avoidance domains are primary; comorbid possible. Social anxiety (6B04) Social evaluation trigger. Specific phobia (6B03) Specific object/situation. PTSD (6B40) Trauma history, intrusive symptoms. Hyperthyroidism TSH. Pheochromocytoma Urine metanephrine. Arrhythmia (SVT) Holter ECG. Substance-induced (caffeine, cocaine) Toxicology.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PDSS, ACQ (Agoraphobic Cognitions Questionnaire), BSQ (Body Sensations Questionnaire). ECG, TSH, complete blood count, glucose. Holter ECG (suspected arrhythmia). Toxicology.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG113 · Katzman 2014)
text: CBT for panic — psychoeducation, interoceptive exposure (building tolerance to bodily sensations), in vivo exposure (to avoided situations), cognitive restructuring. 12–16 sessions. Evidence: Cuijpers P. et al. reviews — large effect. Pharmacotherapy: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine — FDA-approved for panic disorder; escitalopram off-label) or SNRIs (venlafaxine) — first-line. Start at low dose (jittery, ‘a

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: CBT for panic — Clark (Clark D.M.), Barlow (Barlow D.H.) — Interoceptive exposure (deliberately creating body sensation — hyperventilation, spinning, caffeine) + in vivo exposure + cognitive restructuring. Evidence: Barlow D.H. et al. JAMA 2000 RCT. Panic Control Treatment (PCT) — Barlow (Barlow D.H.) — 11-session manually administered protocol; widely used in the US. Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS) — Shear (She

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG113 — CBT and SSRIs first-line; benzodiazepines only short-term. APA Anxiety Guidelines — CBT and pharmacotherapy equally effective. Mitte K. J Affect Disord 2005 meta-analysis — CBT superior to placebo and wait-list.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Remission with treatment in most patients. Comorbid agoraphobia or MDD poor prognosis. Early intervention prevents crystallization of avoidance behavior.

title: Myth 1: “Panic attack is a heart attack”
text: Evidence: symptoms may be similar; but panic attack is short-term, a normal ECG at clinical presentation. Klein’s ‘suffocation false alarm’ hypothesis explains the mechanism.

title: Myth 2: “The patient can voluntarily control panic”
text: Evidence: Panic is a neurobiological dysregulation; CBT and pharmacotherapy are required.

title: Myth 3: “Benzodiazepine is the main treatment for panic”
text: Evidence: For short-term stabilization; addiction potential; SSRIs and CBT first-line.

title: Myth 4: “A panic patient must be protected from panic-inducing situations”
text: Evidence: Avoidance strengthens the symptoms; exposure is the main therapeutic mechanism.

title: Myth 5: “Herbal preparations (kava, valerian) are safe for panic”
text: Evidence: Kava hepatotoxicity (FDA warning); standard treatment superior.

title: Agoraphobia
text: Agoraphobia ICD-10 F40.0 Agoraphobia DSM-5-TR F40.00 Agoraphobia

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Agoraphobia (ICD-11: 6B02; DSM-5-TR: F40.00) — excessive fear and avoidance of situations from which escape is difficult or help may not be available (public transportation, open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds, leaving home alone). The patient fears developing panic attacks or other incapacitating symptoms.

title: 2. History
text: Westphal C. (1872) “agoraphobia” — Greek “agora” (square) + fear. DSM-III (1980) — Together with panic disorder. DSM-5 (2013), ICD-11 — agoraphobia formalized as a SEPARATE category from panic disorder (comorbidity possible, but based on separate diagnosis).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1–2.5%. Sex: twice as common in females. Onset: young to middle adulthood. Comorbidity: panic disorder 50%, MDD, other anxiety, substance use.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability ~48% (Mosing M.A. et al. Depress Anxiety 2009;26(11):1004–1011). Classical conditioning — fear transfer to a specific situation when a panic attack occurs in that situation. Cognitive factors — catastrophizing (“help won’t come”).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Typical avoided situations: Public transportation (bus, train, airplane). Open areas (square, bridge, open ground). Closed spaces (store, cinema theater). Queuing or crowd. Leaving home alone. The patient displays avoidance behaviors, “safety” behaviors (carrying a companion, mobile phone, medication), partial or complete home confinement. In severe cases, housebound.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Significant fear or anxiety in ≥ 2 of the following five categories: Public transportation; Open areas; Enclosed places; Queue or crowd; Leaving home alone. B. These situations are feared because escape is difficult or help will not be available — in the event of a panic attack or incapacitating symptom. C. Situations almost always provoke fear. D. Active avoidance, companion demand, or enduring with acute distres

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — agoraphobia separate from panic disorder; both diagnoses are given if comorbid. NICE CG113 — agoraphobia with panic disorder: similar intervention.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview — avoided situations, panic attack history, functional burden. SCID-5, MINI. Mobility Inventory for Agoraphobia (MIA) — avoidance severity. Comorbidity (panic, MDD, substance). Medical examination.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Panic disorder (6B01) Attack is primary; avoidance areas are limited or absent. Specific phobia (6B03) Concrete single object/situation. Social anxiety (6B04) Fear of social evaluation. PTSD (6B40) History of trauma. Separation anxiety (6B05) Fear of separation from a close person is dominant.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: MIA, ACQ, BSQ. GAD-7, PHQ-9, PDSS comorbidity.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT — exposure-based; graded in vivo exposure to avoided situations; cognitive restructuring. First-line; large effect. SSRI or SNRI — first-line pharmacotherapy (as in panic disorder). Benzodiazepine — only short-term. Virtual reality exposure — alternative means; evidence base developing. Treatment duration — ≥ 12 months after remission.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: In vivo exposure — Staged approach — patient enters avoided situations in structured manner; therapist can accompany (therapist-assisted exposure). First-line method. Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET — Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy) — Virtual environment created in clinical context; alternative to in vivo exposure. Botella C. et al. Clin Psychol Psychother 2007. CBT for panic (Clark, Barlow) — adapted for ag

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG113 — CBT and SSRIs. Katzman 2014 — same. Sánchez-Meca J. et al. Clin Psychol Rev 2010 meta-analysis — CBT-based exposure showed large effect.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Exposure CBT — most patients achieve functional recovery. Chronicity without early intervention (housebound). Comorbid MDD predicts a poor prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Patients with agoraphobia should not be placed in situations”
text: Evidence: Avoidance strengthens the symptoms; exposure is the main therapeutic mechanism.

title: Myth 2: “Agoraphobia is a ‘subtype’ of panic disorder”
text: Evidence: DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 — separate diagnostic categories; comorbidity possible, but can occur without the other.

title: Myth 3: “The patient is ‘lazy’, does not want to leave”
text: Evidence: Agoraphobia is a neurobiological and behavior-based clinical disorder; not a volitional or character problem.

title: Myth 4: “Only medication cures agoraphobia, therapy is unnecessary”
text: Evidence: without exposure-based CBT, sustained remission is difficult; pharmacotherapy alone does not change avoidance behavior.

title: Myth 5: “Ordering online or studying remotely while staying at home is an appropriate lifestyle for a patient with agoraphobia”
text: Evidence: Accommodation provides short-term relief but strengthens illness and reduces functional level.

title: 11. Sources

Clin Psychol Rev 2010;30(1):37–50. Chambless D.L., Caputo G.C., Jasin S.E. et al. The Mobility Inventory for Agoraphobia. Behav Res Ther 1985;23(1):35–44. Botella C., García-Palacios A., Villa H. et al. Virtual reality exposure

title: Specific phobia
text: Specific phobia ICD-10 F40.2 Specific (isolated) phobias DSM-5-TR F40.2xx Specific Phobia

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Specific phobia (ICD-11: 6B03; DSM-5-TR: F40.2xx) — marked, irrational fear and avoidance of a specific object or situation (animals, blood-injection, heights, flying, enclosed spaces). The patient usually recognizes the fear as excessive.

title: 2. History
text: Hippocrates (5th century BC) — descriptions of phobia. Westphal C. (1872) — systematic classification. Marks I.M. (1969) — systematic desensitization and exposure studies. DSM-5 (2013), ICD-11 — subtypes: animal, natural environment, blood-injection-injury, situational, other.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence 7–12% — one of the most common anxiety disorders. Sex: 2–3 times higher in females (blood-injection subtype exception — difference small). Onset: childhood (animal, blood-injection), young adulthood (situational).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability is estimated at approximately 30% (Hettema, 2001). Etiological models include classical conditioning (Watson, ‘Little Albert’, 1920), vicarious learning, and informational transmission. Seligman’s concept of biological preparedness posits a genetic predisposition toward fear of phylogenetically relevant stimuli (e.g., snakes, spiders). In the blood-injection-injury subtype, the characteristic vasovagal r

title: Subtypes
text: Animal — spider, snake, dog, insects. Natural environment — heights, water, storms. Blood-injection-injury — vasovagal reaction (loss of consciousness characteristic). Situational — flight, elevator, tunnel, driving, enclosed place. Other — choking, vomiting, costumed characters, certain sounds.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation. B. Object/situation almost always provokes fear. C. Enduring with active avoidance or acute distress. D. Fear is disproportionate to the actual risk. E. ≥6 months duration (DSM-5-TR). F. Significant distress or functional impairment. G. Not better explained by another mental disorder.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR specifies subtype; ICD-11 has no subtype code. NICE — no separate specific phobia guideline; general anxiety principles.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. FSS (Fear Survey Schedule), specific phobia subscales. Functional burden assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Panic disorder (6B01) Attack is unexpected. Agoraphobia (6B02) Comprehensive situational category. Social anxiety (6B04) Fear of social evaluation. OCD (6B20) Obsession is primary; contamination fear with compulsions. PTSD (6B40) History of trauma. Hypochondriasis (6B23) Fear of illness.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: FSS, specific phobia scale. BAT (Behavioral Avoidance Test) — the degree to which the patient approaches the phobic object.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Exposure therapy is first-line and most effective. Single session 2–3-hour structured exposure (Öst L.G. “one-session treatment”) is effective for most animal and situational phobias. Stepped in vivo exposure — adapted to patient’s pace. Virtual Reality Exposure — particularly suitable for flight, height. In the blood-injection subtype — applied tension (Öst) — the patient is taught to tense the muscles, which preven

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: One-Session Exposure (One-Session Treatment) — Öst (Öst L.G.) — 2–3 hour structured in vivo exposure; 80–90% efficacy for most animal and situational phobias. Öst L.G. Behav Res Ther 1989. Systematic Desensitization (Systematic Desensitization) — Wolpe (Wolpe J.) — Historical method — relaxation + gradual phobic stimulus; superseded by in vivo exposure. Applied Tension (Öst — blood-injection) — Tightening muscles for

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Öst L.G. — one-session exposure demonstrated 80–90% efficacy (Behav Res Ther 1989). Wolitzky-Taylor K.B. et al. Clin Psychol Rev 2008 meta-analysis (33 RCTs) — exposure showed a large effect versus wait-list and a medium effect versus placebo; in vivo contact outperformed other modes of exposure. This meta-analysis made no comparison with pharmacotherapy. APA Anxiety Guidelines — exposure first-line.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Exposure CBT — majority of patients achieve remission. Without treatment, chronicity.

title: Myth 1: “Specific phobia is only a childhood phobia and does not require treatment in adults”
text: Evidence: Specific phobia creates functional impairment in adulthood too (avoidance of flying — occupational limitation; avoidance of medical procedures — health risk).

title: Myth 2: “Forcing the patient into a phobic object causes trauma”
text: Evidence: appropriately applied stepped exposure is safe and highly effective; with patient consent and pace.

title: Myth 3: “Hypnotherapy or NLP rapidly cures phobias”
text: Evidence: systematic evidence base is limited; exposure-based approach is the gold standard.

title: Myth 4: “A patient can live a normal life by completely avoiding the phobic object”
text: Evidence: Avoidance strengthens phobia; situational phobias (flight, elevator) create medical and social restrictions.

title: Myth 5: “Benzodiazepine is an effective treatment for specific situations like flying”
text: Evidence: Possible short-term adjunct role, but not long-term solution; may reduce CBT/exposure efficacy (state-dependent learning).

title: 11. Sources

title: Social anxiety disorder
text: Social anxiety disorder ICD-10 F40.1 Social phobias DSM-5-TR F40.10 Social Anxiety Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Social anxiety disorder (ICD-11: 6B04; DSM-5-TR: F40.10) — intense and persistent fear of negative evaluation or humiliation by others in social situations. The patient avoids situations such as speaking, interaction, and being observed.

title: 2. History
text: Janet P. (1903) — ‘phobie des situations sociales’. Marks I.M., Gelder M.G. (1966) — separation of social phobia from agoraphobia. DSM-III (1980) — “Social Phobia” as an official diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — “Social Anxiety Disorder” — broader and more precise term; performance-only subtype added. ICD-11 — parallel.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 7–13% (Kessler WMH; cultural variability). Sex: more common in females, but males seek clinical help more often. Onset: adolescence (mean 13 years) — one of the earliest onset anxiety disorders. Comorbidity: MDD 60%, other anxiety, alcohol use (as self-medication).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability ~30–40%. Behavioral inhibition (Kagan J.) — childhood temperament as a strong risk factor. Neurobiological — amygdala hyperreactivity to social stimuli; serotonergic dysregulation. Cognitive — self-focused attention, negative self-image, catastrophizing (Clark D.M., Wells A. model). Environment — childhood peer victimization, parental overprotection.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Feared situations — public speaking, asking questions, sharing a meal, writing or eating in front of others, public toilets, talking on the phone. Somatic — flushing, tremor, sweating, tachycardia, dry mouth, voice tremor. Cognitive — negative thoughts about oneself, “post-event processing” (prolonged self-criticism after a situation). Avoidance and ‘safety’ behaviors (avoiding eye contact, speaking less, alcohol use

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Marked fear in one or more social situations — being observed or evaluated by others. B. The patient fears humiliation, rejection by others, or offending others. C. Situations almost always provoke fear. D. Avoidance or endurance with intense discomfort. E. Fear is disproportionate to the social situation. F. ≥6 months duration (DSM-5-TR). G. Functional impairment. H. Not better explained by another mental disorde

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — “performance only” specifier (limited to performance situations). ICD-11 — the duration is “at least several months” (6 months in DSM-5-TR); in children anxiety must occur with peers as well as with adults (DSM-5-TR note). NICE CG159 (Social anxiety disorder: recognition, assessment and treatment, 2013) — individual CBT first-line.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. SCID-5, MINI. Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS), SPIN (Social Phobia Inventory) — scale and monitoring. Comorbidity (MDD, other anxiety, alcohol use).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Agoraphobia (6B02) Difficult escape, help absent; social evaluation absent. Specific phobia (6B03) Specific object/situation. Panic (6B01) Attack is unexpected. Avoidant personality disorder Persistent pattern, broader; comorbidity is common. Autism spectrum (6A02) Social-communication deficit early onset; social interest variable. Selective mutism (6B06) Failure to speak in specific

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: LSAS — gold standard scale (24 items). SPIN — short screening (17 items). BFNE (Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation).

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG159 · Katzman 2014)
text: Individual CBT (Clark D.M. model) first-line — redirecting self-focused attention, video feedback, behavioral experiments, cognitive restructuring, in vivo exposure. 12–16 sessions. NICE CG159 — individual CBT superior to group CBT. SSRI and SNRI first-line pharmacotherapy — escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine (FDA: sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine; escitalopram — EU only). Second-line — moclobemide

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Clark CBT Model — Specifically developed for social anxiety; external redirection of self-focused attention, video feedback (seeing one’s performance through others’ eyes), behavioral experiments (testing fearful beliefs), in vivo exposure. Evidence: Clark D.M. et al. J Consult Clin Psychol 2003 RCT — experimental individual CBT superior to other interventions. Heimberg Group CBT — 12-session group format; Heimberg R

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG159 (2013) — individual CBT (Clark) first-line; SSRIs alternative; group CBT or self-help may be suitable for some patients. Katzman 2014 — first-line escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine. Mayo-Wilson E. et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2014 network meta-analysis — individual CBT has the greatest effect; SSRIs second.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course, high relapse rate without treatment. CBT and SSRIs result in significant improvement in most patients. Early onset and avoidant personality comorbidity as a poor prognosis marker.

title: Myth 1: “Social anxiety — ordinary ‘shyness about life’, does not require treatment”
text: Evidence: Social anxiety disorder is associated with functional impairment, academic and occupational limitations, risk of depression and alcohol use; it is evaluated as a medical condition.

title: Myth 2: “The patient can live a normal life by completely avoiding social situations”
text: Evidence: Avoidance strengthens the symptoms and leads to isolation; exposure is the main therapeutic mechanism.

title: Myth 3: “Alcohol ‘treats’ social anxiety”
text: Evidence: Alcohol provides short-term relief but long-term exacerbates distress and leads to alcohol use disorder; prevalence of this combination is 20–40%.

title: Myth 4: “Benzodiazepines are effective long-term for social anxiety”
text: Evidence: Short-term effect; addiction potential; CBT or SSRIs superior.

title: Myth 5: “Propranolol is effective for all forms of social anxiety”
text: Evidence: propranolol is effective only in the performance subtype (before a performance); it is ineffective in social interaction (parties, relationships).

title: Myth 6: “The patient has avoidant personality disorder, so treatment is unresponsive”
text: Evidence: Comorbid avoidant personality patient may also respond to standard interventions; long-term CBT or schema therapy.

title: Myth 7: “Only hypnotherapy or NLP cures quickly”
text: Evidence: No evidence base; CBT and SSRIs are gold standard.

title: Myth 8: “Cannabis (CBD) is a safe alternative for social anxiety”
text: Evidence: initial studies exist, but insufficient for clinical recommendation; THC may worsen distress.

title: Separation anxiety disorder
text: Separation anxiety disorder ICD-10 F93.0 Separation anxiety disorder of childhood DSM-5-TR F93.0 Separation Anxiety Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Separation anxiety disorder (ICD-11: 6B05; DSM-5-TR: F93.0) — developmentally inappropriate excessive fear and anxiety related to separation from an attachment figure (typically parent) or home. First diagnosable in adults in DSM-5 (limited to childhood in DSM-IV).

title: 2. History
text: Bowlby J. (1969–1980) — attachment theory. DSM-III (1980) — As a childhood disorder. DSM-5 (2013) — age restriction removed; diagnosis possible in adults as well.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in children: ~4%; in adolescents ~1.6%; in adults ~1.9% (Kessler R.C. NCS-R). Sex: more common in females. Onset: typical childhood (6–9 years); may recur or persist in adult form. Comorbidity: specific phobia, panic, GAD, MDD, school avoidance.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability ~40%. Attachment styles (insecure attachment), parental overprotection. History of loss or illness in relatives. Stressful events (moving, school change, parental separation).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Excessive worry about harm or loss to the attachment figure. Avoidance of leaving home or separating from attachment figure. Fear of being alone. Persistent reluctance or refusal to sleep away from home or to go to sleep without the attachment figure nearby (own bedroom, unfamiliar house). Nightmares about separation. Somatic complaints in anticipation of separation (abdominal pain, headache, nausea). In children — s

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. ≥ 3 of the following symptoms: Excessive anxiety about separation from the attachment figure or anticipation thereof; Persistent worry about loss or harm to the attachment figure; Fear of an event that would cause separation from the attachment figure; Avoidance of home, school, or work due to fear of separation; Fear of being alone without the attachment figure; Reluctance to go to sleep without the attachment fi

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — duration ≥6 months in adults; ≥4 weeks in children. ICD-11 — a different duration: “at least several months”; there is no split into 4 weeks for children and 6 months for adults as in DSM-5-TR, and no separate age qualifier.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (also with parent in children). Standardized interview (K-SADS for children, SCID-5 for adults). Scale — SAAS (Separation Anxiety Assessment Scale). Comorbidity screening.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature GAD (6B00) Multiple domains of worry. Social anxiety (6B04) Social evaluation dominant. Agoraphobia (6B02) Avoidance of situations with difficult escape. Panic (6B01) Attack is unexpected. Selective mutism (6B06) Failure to speak in specific contexts. Conduct disorder (school avoidance) Antisocial behavior component. Avoidant personality Persistent pattern across all relationships.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SAAS, K-SADS, MASC (Multidimensional Anxiety Scale for Children). Comorbidity (depression, other anxiety).

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT (Coping Cat, FRIENDS programs for children; standard CBT for adults) — exposure-based, parental involvement critical in children. First-line. SSRIs — in moderate-to-severe cases or when CBT fails; sertraline, fluoxetine (in children). School return programs (school refusal) — graded exposure. Family involvement — parental psychoeducation is recommended; frequent phone calls and visits (accommodation) strengthen s

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: “Coping Cat” program — Kendall (Kendall P.C.) — Manualized CBT for children aged 7–13 years (the C.A.T. Project for ages 14–17) – 16 sessions, psychoeducation + relaxation + exposure + reward system (FEAR plan). FRIENDS Program — Barrett (Barrett P.M.) — In Australia, developed group CBT for child and adolescent anxiety disorders. Stepped School Return — Structured exposure — child gradually returns to school environ

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AACAP Practice Parameter (Connolly S.D., Bernstein G.A. 2007) — CBT and SSRIs effective in children. NICE — general guidelines for childhood anxiety (CBT first-line). Walkup J.T. et al. NEJM 2008 (CAMS — Child/Adolescent Anxiety Multimodal Study) — CBT + sertraline combination superior to monotherapy.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Remission in most children with early CBT. Without treatment, continuation in adulthood leads to risk of other anxiety disorders and depression.

title: Myth 1: “Separation anxiety occurs only in childhood”
text: Evidence: DSM-5 — separation anxiety disorder also diagnosed in adults — prevalence ~1.9%.

title: Myth 2: “The parent must give in to every demand to ‘calm’ the child”
text: Evidence: Accommodation strengthens the symptoms; the SPACE program or parent training is recommended.

title: Myth 3: “Separation anxiety is a result of poor parenting”
text: Evidence: heritability ~40%; attachment and environment modulator. “Bad upbringing” explanation stigmatizing and incorrect.

title: Myth 4: “Leaving a child alone to ‘get used to it’ — this harsh approach cures them”
text: Evidence: “Flooding” or uncontrolled exposure can be traumatic; graded, structured exposure recommended.

title: Myth 5: “Recovery is only possible with medication”
text: Evidence: CBT first-line; SSRIs for moderate-to-severe cases or in combination.

title: Myth 6: “School refusal is a personality weakness and requires discipline”
text: Evidence: School avoidance is a clinical anxiety symptom; punishment-based approach exacerbates the disorder.

title: Selective mutism
text: Selective mutism ICD-10 F94.0 Elective mutism DSM-5-TR F94.0 Selective Mutism

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Selective mutism (ICD-11: 6B06; DSM-5-TR: F94.0) — consistent failure to speak in specific social situations (e.g., school) despite mastery of language, with normal speech in other contexts (e.g., home). A typical childhood anxiety disorder, sometimes misperceived as “extreme shyness.”

title: 2. History
text: Kussmaul A. (1877) — “aphasia voluntaria”. Tramer M. (1934) — “elective mutism” — patient’s voluntary choice expression. DSM-IV (1994) — Replaced with the term ‘selective’ (not voluntary, due to social anxiety). DSM-5 (2013) — moved to the anxiety disorders category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 0.7–1% in school-aged children (Bergman R.L. et al. JAACAP 2002). Sex: relatively higher in girls (1.5–2:1). Onset: 2–5 years; typically detected at school entry. Comorbidity: social anxiety disorder ~70%, GAD, other anxiety, speech or language disorder.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability — anxiety in family history is common (~70% of families have an anxiety disorder). Behavioral inhibition (Kagan) — temperamental predisposition is a key factor. Comorbid developmental speech and language disorders (especially in bilingual environment) — risk factor. Environment — in bilingual families, sometimes mistakenly perceived as a language switch.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Failure to speak in specific social situations (school, public places). Normal speech at home with close ones. Sometimes the use of whispering or gestures. Academic and social impairment (answering questions, peer relationships). Comorbid shyness, social withdrawal, somatic complaints.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent not speaking in specific social situations (where speaking is expected), speech normal in other situations. B. Significant impairment in academic, occupational, or social communication. C. Duration ≥ 1 month (excluding the first month of school). D. Does not result from not learning a language or not being comfortable in that language. E. Not better explained by a communication disorder (e.g., a fluency

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — in the anxiety disorders category; ‘selective’ — not voluntary choice, but situation-specific anxiety response.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Parent, teacher interview. Home video recordings of speech — diagnostic confirmation. SMQ (Selective Mutism Questionnaire). Speech-language assessment (SLT) — communication disorder exclusion. Hearing test. Comorbid anxiety, autism, language disorder screening.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Developmental language disorder (6A01.2) Language is poor in all contexts. Autism spectrum (6A02) Social-communication deficit in all contexts. Bilingual environment transient During adaptation to a new language — typically months. Hearing impairment Audiometry. Social anxiety (6B04) Comorbidity is common — the patient speaks but fears social evaluation. Mutism in trauma context Histo

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SMQ — gold standard; SAS (School Anxiety Scale). Speech-language assessment. Audiometry.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Behavioral approach as first-line treatment — graded exposure, fading-in technique (gradual introduction of a stranger). Integrated Behavior Therapy (Bergman R.L.) — manualized, with family + school involvement. School-based intervention — gradual increase in communication demands, teacher coordination. SSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline) — in moderate-to-severe cases or in those not responding to behavioral intervention.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Gradual Introduction (Fading-In) Technique — The patient converses with a comfortable person; gradually a stranger is introduced into this context; then the patient transitions to speaking with a stranger. Integrated Behavior Therapy (IBT) — Bergman (Bergman R.L.) — Staged exposure, positive reinforcement, systematic desensitization; 20 sessions. Evidence: Bergman R.L. et al. Behav Res Ther 2013 RCT. Selective Mutism

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AACAP — behavioral intervention first-line, SSRI adjunct. NICE — principles of anxiety disorders apply.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Speech recovers in most children with early intervention. Without treatment, chronicity and transition to social anxiety disorder.

title: Myth 1: “Selective mutism is the child’s ‘stubbornness’”
text: Evidence: selective mutism is an anxiety disorder — the child CANNOT speak, the position ‘does not want to speak’ is incorrect.

title: Myth 2: “If a child does not speak, strong pressure is needed”
text: Evidence: pressure intensifies anxiety and mutism; stepped exposure recommended.

title: Myth 3: “It will resolve with age; no intervention is needed”
text: Evidence: Without early intervention, academic and social impairment persists; risk of transition to social anxiety disorder in adulthood.

title: Myth 4: “Mutism in a bilingual child is normal”
text: Evidence: “Silent period” — normal for a few months when learning a new language; mutism lasting > 6 months or occurring in both languages — consider selective mutism diagnosis.

title: Myth 5: “Only deep psychoanalytic therapy is effective”
text: Evidence: Behavior-based and CBT approaches are first-line; psychoanalytic intervention lacks evidence base.

title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) (Obsessive-compulsive disorder)
text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) (Obsessive-compulsive disorder) Obsessive-compulsive disorder ICD-10 F42 Obsessive-compulsive disorder DSM-5-TR F42.2 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD; ICD-11: 6B20; DSM-5-TR: F42.2) — a disorder characterized by recurrent, ego-dystonic obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts, images, impulses) or compulsions (repetitive behaviors or mental acts). Usually both are present. The patient performs the compulsion to reduce anxiety or prevent a feared outcome. DSM-5 (2013) — OCD removed from anxiety disorders as a distinct category, mo

title: 2. History
text: Esquirol J.E.D. (1838) — “monomanie raisonnante”. Janet P. (1903) — ‘psychasthénie’. Freud (1909) — “Rat Man” case. Mowrer O.H. (1947) — two-factor learning theory (classical conditioning + operant avoidance); basis of ERP. Meyer V. (1966) — first clinical application of Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 (2019) — OCD separated from anxiety disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1.6–2.3% (Ruscio A.M. et al. Mol Psychiatry 2010). Sex: approximately equal; relatively more common in women in adulthood, early onset in childhood in men. Onset: bimodal — prepubertal (10–12 years, males) and early adulthood (20–25 years). Comorbidity: MDD ~60%, anxiety disorders, tic disorders, autism, hoarding, BDD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 40–50% (Mataix-Cols D. et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2013). Neurobiological — hyperactivity of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit (orbitofrontal, cingulate, caudate); serotonergic dysregulation (SSRI effect); glutamatergic dysregulation. Genetic research — SLC1A1 (glutamate transporter), serotonin genes. PANDAS — rare onset of OCD following streptococcal infection (NIMH 2017). Trauma and stress

title: Typical symptom domains
text: Contamination / cleanliness — most frequent; hand washing, disinfection compulsions. Doubting / checking — lock, stove, electrical appliances. Symmetry / precision / ‘just right’ — related to orderliness. Aggressive / sexual / religious obsessions — ego-dystonic, causing distress. Hoarding — Separate category in ICD-11 (6B24).

title: Ego-dystonia
text: The patient accepts that obsessions are their own thoughts, but unwanted, irrational, or unacceptable (insight varies — DSM-5-TR insight qualifiers: good / poor / absent).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Presence of obsession, compulsion, or both. Obsessions: repeated, persistent, unwanted thoughts/images/impulses; creates distress; patient attempts to suppress or neutralize with other thoughts/actions. Compulsions: Repetitive behavior (hand washing, checking, ordering) or mental act (counting, praying) performed as a response to an obsession or according to rigid rules; aimed at reducing anxiety, but either unrea

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — insight specifiers (good or fair; poor; absent — delusional level); tic-related subtype. ICD-11 — parallel; hoarding (6B24), BDD (6B21), olfactory reference (6B22) separate categories. NICE CG31 (2005, 2019 surveillance) — diagnostics via clinical interview + Y-BOCS.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. SCID-5, Y-BOCS (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale) — the gold standard severity scale; CY-BOCS for children. OCI-R (Obsessive Compulsive Inventory-Revised) — self-assessment. Comorbidity (depression, anxiety, tic, autism, BDD, hoarding).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature GAD (6B00) Real-life worries, compulsions absent. Tic (8A05) Motor/vocal; not goal-directed; premonitory urge. BDD (6B21) Appearance-based obsessions. Hoarding (6B24) Difficulty discarding objects. Eating disorders (6B80–6B8Z) Eating behavior is primary. Trichotillomania (6B25.0), excoriation disorder (6B25.1) Body-focused repetitive behavior. Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Y-BOCS / CY-BOCS — gold standard. OCI-R — self-assessment. Comorbidity (depression, anxiety).

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG31 · APA · WFSBP)
text: First-line psychotherapy: ERP (Exposure and Response Prevention) — patient is exposed to feared object/situation and does not perform compulsion. 12–20 sessions. Evidence: Foa E.B. et al. RCTs; effect substantial. First-line pharmacotherapy: SSRIs at high dose — fluoxetine (40–80 mg), sertraline (200 mg), paroxetine (40–60 mg), fluvoxamine (200–300 mg), escitalopram (20 mg; > 20 mg — off-label, ECG monitoring). In OC

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) — Meyer (Meyer V.), Foa (Foa E.B.) — The patient is exposed to feared object (e.g., “dirty” object) and does not perform compulsion (washing hands); anxiety gradually decreases (habituation). Standard course 12–20 sessions, 1–2 times per week; more intensive format (daily) is effective. Evidence: Foa E.B. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2005. CBT — cognitive component — Addition to ERP;

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG31 (2005, 2019 surveillance) — stepped approach by severity; ERP first-line; SSRIs for moderate-to-severe. APA Practice Guideline for OCD (2007) — same; clomipramine strong based on evidence, but second-line due to side effects. WFSBP (Bandelow B. et al. 2008) — SSRI dose ranges and titration. NICE CG31 PANDAS — routine antibiotic prophylaxis not recommended.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course, but significant improvement with adequate treatment. Comorbid depression, tics and autism are markers of poor prognosis. Early onset and poor insight — more difficult treatment.

title: Myth 1: “OCD is just a personality trait related to cleanliness and orderliness”
text: Evidence: Clinical OCD is ego-dystonic, causes distress and functional impairment; obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is an ego-syntonic, distinct disorder. Diagnosis is made by clinical criteria; Y-BOCS measures only severity.

title: Myth 2: “The patient can ‘voluntarily stop’ obsessions”
text: Evidence: OCD is dysregulation of CSTC circuit; not voluntarily controlled; ERP and SSRIs affect it at a neurobiological level.

title: Myth 3: “SSRIs work in OCD at depression doses”
text: Evidence: In OCD, SSRIs require high doses (fluoxetine 60–80 mg, sertraline 200 mg); depression dose (e.g., fluoxetine 20 mg) often does not respond.

title: Myth 4: “ERP causes trauma because it keeps the patient in a feared situation”
text: Evidence: ERP is structured, stepwise, and conducted with patient consent; demonstrates proven long-term efficacy.

title: Myth 5: “PANDAS is the main cause of OCD, everyone should take antibiotics”
text: Evidence: NIMH 2017 — PANDAS is a rare event; routine antistreptolysin O tests and antibiotic prophylaxis are not recommended; only if a classic clinical picture is present.

title: Myth 6: “Allowing compulsions to be performed calms symptoms”
text: Evidence: Permission (accommodation) for compulsions strengthens OCD; reducing family accommodation is a crucial treatment component.

title: Myth 7: “Herbal preparations (St John’s Wort, kava, omega-3) cure OCD”
text: Evidence: none have proven efficacy for OCD; St John’s Wort carries risk of interaction with SSRIs (serotonin syndrome).

Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. 2007. Bandelow B. et al. WFSBP guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and post-traumatic stress disorders. World J Biol

title: Dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (Body dysmorphic disorder)
text: Dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (Body dysmorphic disorder) Body dysmorphic disorder ICD-10 F45.2 Hypochondriacal disorder DSM-5-TR F45.22 Body Dysmorphic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD; ICD-11: 6B21; DSM-5-TR: F45.22) — obsessive preoccupation with an imagined or very slight defect in appearance; this preoccupation leads to repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, skin picking, seeking cosmetic procedures) or mental acts (comparing).

title: 2. History
text: Morselli E. (1891) — ‘dysmorphophobia’. DSM-III-R (1987) — ‘Body Dysmorphic Disorder’ within somatoform disorders. DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 — moved to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in general population: 1.7–2.4% (Buhlmann U. et al. Psychiatry Res 2010). 9–15% in cosmetic dermatology and plastic surgery clinics. Sex: approximately equal. Onset: mean 15–16 years. Comorbidity: MDD ~75%, OCD ~30%, social anxiety ~37%, substance use. Suicide risk high: attempt ~24–28%, completion rate 45 times higher than population (based on reviews by Phillips K.A.).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic overlap with OCD. Neurobiological — orbitofrontal-striatal circuit hyperactivity (similar to OCD); impaired visual processing (Feusner J.D. et al. reviews — patient overfocuses on details, fails to integrate the global image). Social-cultural — idealized appearance in mass media. Childhood peer victimization (humiliation, “bullying”).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Obsessive focus on a specific part of appearance (face, skin, hair, nose, body shape). No actual defect, or a defect that is invisible or unimportant to others. Repeated behaviors: mirror checking, skin picking, comparison, seeking cosmetic procedures, clothing/makeup/camouflage. Cognitive actions: comparing oneself to others. Insight often poor; sometimes at delusional level. “Muscle dysmorphia” subtype — obsession

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Preoccupation with a perceived defect or flaw in appearance; not observable or appears slight to others. B. The patient has at any point performed a repetitive behavior (mirror checking, skin picking, excessive dressing) or mental act (comparison). C. The preoccupation causes clinically significant distress or functional impairment. D. There must be no body image preoccupation meeting eating disorder criteria (ano

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: In the OCD spectrum; muscle dysmorphia qualifier only in DSM-5-TR. NICE CG31 — BDD and OCD joint recommendations.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (patient often does not speak openly due to shame). BDDQ (Body Dysmorphic Disorder Questionnaire) — screening. BDD-YBOCS — severity scale. Comorbidity (depression, OCD, social anxiety, suicide risk). History of anabolic steroid use or cosmetic procedure.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature OCD (6B20) Obsessions are not limited to appearance. Eating disorder (6B80–6B85) Weight and figure are primary; eating behavior is disrupted. Delusional disorder (6A24) Insight absent; often variable in BDD. Social anxiety (6B04) Social evaluation broad; in BDD, focus on specific appearance part. Trichotillomania (6B25.0) Hair pulling primary; appearance distress secondary. Olfactory

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: BDDQ — screening (Phillips K.A.). BDD-YBOCS — modified OCD scale, 12 items. C-SSRS — high suicide risk.

title: 8. Treatment
text: First-line psychotherapy: CBT (adapted for BDD, Wilhelm S., Phillips K.A.) — cognitive restructuring + exposure + mirror retraining + behavioral experiments. 12–22 sessions. First-line pharmacotherapy: SSRIs at high dose — similar to OCD; fluoxetine (40–80 mg), escitalopram (20–30 mg), sertraline (150–200 mg). Clomipramine — alternative. Augmentation — atypical antipsychotic (especially insight at delusional level).

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for BDD — Wilhelm S., Phillips K.A — Manualized 22-session protocol — psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, mirror retraining, behavioral experiments, ritual prevention (ERP), relapse prophylaxis. Body Dysmorphic Disorder Questionnaire (BDDQ) — Phillips (Phillips K.A.) — Screening. BDD-YBOCS — Adaptation of Y-BOCS for BDD. SSRI High Dose — Similar to OCD; response within 8–12 weeks.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG31 — CBT + high-dose SSRI first-line. Phillips K.A. studies — SSRIs effective in BDD; high dose, long-term.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course. Significant improvement with adequate treatment; remission is possible but requires long-term maintenance. Suicide risk monitored.

title: Myth 1: “BDD patients have a ‘real defect’, cosmetic surgery helps”
text: Evidence: Crerand C.E. Ann Plast Surg 2010 — cosmetic procedures do not improve BDD; most patients are dissatisfied with the result or develop a new focus. Surgeons are recommended to screen for BDD.

title: Myth 2: “A BDD patient should be ‘reassured’ by complimenting their appearance”
text: Evidence: praise or reassurance gives short-term relief but strengthens the obsession; reducing family accommodation is a treatment component.

title: Myth 3: “BDD is common ‘self-doubt’”
text: Evidence: BDD is accompanied by functional impairment and high suicide risk (attempts 24–28%, 45 times higher than the general population); it is assessed as a clinical condition.

title: Myth 4: “SSRIs are effective for BDD at depression doses”
text: Evidence: Similar to OCD — high dose required; response in 8–12 weeks.

title: Myth 5: “Muscle dysmorphia is not a disorder, it’s just fitness motivation”
text: Evidence: Muscle dysmorphia occurs mainly in men; it is accompanied by the use of anabolic steroids, compulsive exercise, social isolation, and depression; it is a qualifier in DSM-5-TR.

title: Myth 6: “Seeking sequential procedures from a plastic surgeon is normal”
text: Evidence: Sequential procedures are a sign of BDD; surgeon should screen for BDD and refer to psychiatry.

Oxford Univ Press; 2005. Wilhelm S., Phillips K.A., Steketee G. Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: A Treatment Manual. Guilford Press; 2013. Buhlmann U. et al. Updates on the prevalence of body dysmorphi

title: Olfactory reference disorder (ORS) (Olfactory reference disorder)
text: Olfactory reference disorder (ORS) (Olfactory reference disorder) Olfactory reference disorder ICD-10 F45.8 Other somatoform disorders DSM-5-TR F42.8 Other Specified Obsessive-Compulsive and Related D

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Olfactory Reference Disorder (ORS) (ICD-11: 6B22; DSM-5-TR: F42.8 Other Specified Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorder) — disorder characterized by obsessive belief about a non-existent or grossly over-appraised unpleasant odor emanating from the patient’s body. Patient believes others condemn or embarrass him/her, exhibits compulsive washing, deodorant use, social avoidance behavior.

title: 2. History
text: Pryse-Phillips W. (1971) — term ‘olfactory reference syndrome’. DSM-IV — No separate category (Delusional Disorder as a somatic subtype). DSM-5 (2013) — OCD spectrum noted as a related disorder; but no separate code assigned. ICD-11 (2019) — first formal diagnostic category (6B22).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: precise epidemiological data limited; based on clinical and review reports, considered rare but underdiagnosed (Phillips K.A., Menard W. Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2011). Onset: adolescence–early adulthood (mean ≈ 16 years). Sex: approximately equal. Comorbidity: MDD, social anxiety, OCD, BDD, high suicide risk (suicidal ideation ~68%, attempts ~32% — Phillips K.A., Menard W. Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2011, n=20).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic and neurobiological overlap with OCD and BDD. Insight is variable — sometimes at delusional level. Social-cultural factors — social stigma regarding body odor.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Obsessive preoccupation with body odor (mouth, feet, armpits, genitals, general body) or breath odor. ‘Misreading’ others’ reactions (referential ideas) — coughing, scratching nose, opening a window interpreted as a reaction to the smell. Compulsive behaviors — frequent washing, changing clothes, deodorant, perfume, oral hygiene, gum chewing, vigorous tooth brushing. Social avoidance — avoidance of work and school, s

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (ICD-11)
text: A. Persistent preoccupation that one’s body emits an unpleasant odor or that there is a foul odor in the breath — which is either unnoticeable or minor to others. B. The patient performs repetitive behaviors (washing, odor masking, skin checking) or mental acts (self-comparison with others) in response to obsession. C. The preoccupation causes clinically significant distress or functional impairment. D. Exclusion of

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11 — official status as a separate category. DSM-5-TR — within ‘Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder’.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Medical and otolaryngological examination — excluding genuine halitosis, sinusitis, hyperhidrosis, gastrointestinal diseases. Trimethylaminuria (TMAU) — urine trimethylamine test (rare genetic metabolic disorder, ‘fish odor syndrome’). Insight level assessment. Comorbidity and suicide risk (high!).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Genuine halitosis / hyperhidrosis / TMAU Objectively confirmed. BDD (6B21) Appearance-based. OCD (6B20) Multiple obsessions. Delusional disorder (6A24) — somatic Insight absent; clinical manifestations overlap. Schizophrenia Other psychotic symptoms. Social anxiety (6B04) Fear of social evaluation broad.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Medical examination — dental, ENT, gastrointestinal. TMAU test (urinary trimethylamine). Scale — not specific; adapted use of Y-BOCS. C-SSRS (high suicide risk).

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT — approach tailored to OCD/BDD; exposure (cessation of checking behavior, return to social situations), cognitive restructuring. SSRI high dose — similar to OCD. Augmentation — atypical antipsychotic (insight at delusional level). Social rehabilitation. Suicide risk monitoring.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT (adapted for OCD/BDD) — Exposure + Response Prevention + Cognitive Restructuring. SSRI High Dose — Similar to OCD; 8–12 weeks.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Evidence base is limited. Improvement with SSRIs + CBT; suicide risk monitored.

title: Myth 1: “The patient may genuinely smell bad — a psychiatric diagnosis cannot be made without prior medical examination”
text: Evidence: correct — medical causes (halitosis, hyperhidrosis, TMAU) must be definitively excluded; but if no medical cause and obsessive preoccupation persists, the clinical condition is olfactory reference disorder.

title: Myth 2: “Frequent washing and deodorant use will solve the problem”
text: Evidence: Compulsive behaviors provide short-term relief but intensify the disorder; skin irritation, social impairment increase.

title: Myth 3: “The patient has a simple self-esteem problem”
text: Evidence: Clinical impairment; suicide risk is high (suicidal ideation ~68%, attempts ~32%); medical intervention required.

title: Myth 4: “Only an antipsychotic is effective because it is a delusion”
text: Evidence: insight variable; SSRI high dose + CBT first-line; antipsychotic augmentation only at delusional level.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B22 Olfactory reference disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Phillips K.A., Menard W. Olfactory reference syndrome: demographic and clinical features of imagined body odor. Gen Hosp Psychiatry 2011;33(4):398–406. Pryse-Phillips W. An olfactory reference syndrome. Acta Psychiatr Scand 1971;47(4):484–509.

title: Hypochondriasis
text: Hypochondriasis ICD-10 F45.2 Hypochondriacal disorder DSM-5-TR F45.21 Illness Anxiety Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Hypochondriasis (ICD-11: 6B23; DSM-5-TR: F45.21 Illness Anxiety Disorder — new name, separated from somatic symptom disorder) — persistent preoccupation and anxiety about having or developing a serious medical illness. The patient either checks repeatedly — clinic visits, internet searches, advice from friends — or, conversely, avoids medical care altogether. DSM-5 (2013) — hypochondriasis diagnosis split into two ne

title: 2. History
text: Greek medicine — “hypochondrium” (below the ribs) — ancient humoral theory. DSM-III (1980) — In the category of somatoform disorders. DSM-5 (2013) — separation of illness anxiety disorder and somatic symptom disorder. ICD-11 (2019) — transition to the spectrum category of OCD.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1–6% (Bleichhardt G., Hiller W. Br J Health Psychol 2007). In primary care patients: ~3–10%. Sex: approximately equal. Onset: early to middle adulthood. Comorbidity: MDD, GAD, OCD, panic disorder.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic overlap with OCD and anxiety disorders. Experience with childhood trauma or medical illnesses. Cognitive — catastrophizing of bodily sensations; selective attention; “medical information seeking” (cyberchondria). Modeling — high familial vulnerability to illness.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Fear of developing a serious illness (cancer, heart attack, various chronic diseases). Interpretation of normal bodily sensations (palpitations, headache, sluggish bowel) as markers of serious illness. Behavioral models (two polar opposites): Care-seeking — repeated medical check-ups, multiple doctor consultations (‘doctor shopping’), internet searches (cyberchondria), body checks. Care-avoiding — avoidance of medica

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Preoccupation with having or developing a serious illness. B. Somatic symptoms minimal or absent; if present, preoccupation disproportionate to severity. C. High anxiety about health. D. The patient exhibits excessive health behavior (checking) or maladaptive avoidance. E. Duration ≥ 6 months (DSM-5-TR); typical content of the illness may change over time. F. Not better explained by another mental disorder (MDD, p

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — Illness Anxiety Disorder (F45.21); care-seeking and care-avoiding subtypes. ICD-11 — within the OCD spectrum category (6B23); new placement distinct from classic somatoform location.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Medical evaluation — exclusion of genuine illness (however excessive testing should be avoided). Scale — Whiteley Index, SHAI (Short Health Anxiety Inventory). Comorbidity screening.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Bodily distress disorder (6C20) Somatic complaints dominant. Real medical illness Clinical and laboratory confirmation. OCD (6B20) Multiple obsessions; illness not restricted. GAD (6B00) Multiple areas of worry. Panic (6B01) Fear of ‘heart attack’ during an attack. Delusional disorder (6A24) — somatic Insight absent. Major depressive disorder — somatic focus Affective component predom

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Whiteley Index (14 items), SHAI. Medical examination — once complete, not repeated. PHQ-9, GAD-7 comorbidity.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT first-line — cognitive restructuring (catastrophizing), prevention of body checking and reassurance seeking (exposure + ritual prevention), attention training. Effect: Cooper K. et al. Behav Cogn Psychother 2017 meta-analysis. SSRIs — for moderate-to-severe cases or comorbid depression/GAD. Single physician model (single physician) — patient works only with one primary care physician; avoids multiple checks and “

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for hypochondriasis — Salkovskis P., Warwick H — Cognitive model — “catastrophization” of bodily sensations central. Intervention: psychoeducation, exploration of alternative explanations, behavioral experiments of body checking and reassurance seeking, exposure. 12–16 sessions. Whiteley Index (Whiteley Index) — 14-item Illness Concern Scale — gold standard screening. Short Health Anxiety Inventory (SHAI) — Salko

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Cooper K. et al. Behav Cogn Psychother 2017 meta-analysis — CBT significant effect; medium effect size. Greeven A. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2007 RCT — CBT and paroxetine both superior to placebo.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: CBT or SSRIs result in significant improvement in most patients. Chronic without treatment; persistent use of medical resources.

title: Myth 1: “The patient is ‘faking’ illness, playing games”
text: Evidence: hypochondriasis is a clinical psychiatric disorder; patient’s concern is genuine; not ‘play’ or simulation. Differs from factitious disorder (6D50).

title: Myth 2: “The more medical tests performed, the more the patient will be reassured”
text: Evidence: repeated checking gives short-term relief, then anxiety returns; ‘checking dependency’ develops. Single clinician model and check restriction recommended.

title: Myth 3: “Reassurance (‘you are healthy’) is a treatment tool”
text: Evidence: repeated reassurance reinforces disorder — patient continues seeking proof. Structured clinician response: one-time assessment, then brief standard message.

title: Myth 4: “Internet search helps the patient’s self-education”
text: Evidence: “Cyberchondria” — internet searches increase anxiety, enhance catastrophizing; limitation or structuring recommended.

title: Myth 5: “Hypochondriasis only occurs in elderly patients”
text: Evidence: onset early-middle adulthood; age range wide.

title: Myth 6: “Only antidepressants are effective; therapy is useless”
text: Evidence: Greeven 2007 — CBT and paroxetine both superior to placebo; CBT first-line (long-term effect comparable to SSRIs).

title: Hoarding disorder
text: Hoarding disorder ICD-10 F63.8 Other habit and impulse disorders DSM-5-TR F42.3 Hoarding Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Hoarding disorder (ICD-11: 6B24; DSM-5-TR: F42.3) — a persistent need to acquire or save possessions and persistent difficulty discarding them, leading to clutter of living spaces (to the extent that rooms cannot be used for their intended purpose). Categorized under the OCD spectrum.

title: 2. History
text: Frost R.O., Hartl T.L. (1996) — cognitive-behavioral model of hoarding. In DSM-IV it was a criterion of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 — formally established as a distinct diagnostic category (evidence base — distinct clinical manifestations, course, treatment response).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 2–6% (Samuels J.F. et al. Behav Res Ther 2008). In older adults, prevalence is higher (~6%). Sex: approximately equal; women predominate in clinical samples. Onset: adolescence (mean 11–15 years); severity increases with age. Comorbidity: MDD ~50%, OCD ~20%, GAD, social anxiety, ADHD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 50%. Neurobiological — frontostriatal circuit disruption; activation patterns distinct from OCD (Tolin D.F. et al. reviews). Cognitive deficits — categorization, decision-making, attention (Frost & Hartl model). Emotional attachment to objects; loss trauma. In older adults — trigger for cognitive decline.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Persistent difficulty discarding objects; often excessive acquiring (purchasing, collecting free items) is observed. The thought of discarding or releasing objects causes significant distress. Hoarding items and occupying the living space — rooms cannot be used for their intended functional purposes (the bedroom for sleeping, the kitchen for eating, etc.). Sometimes “animal hoarding” — the mass keeping of animals. In

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent difficulty discarding or parting with acquired items, regardless of value. B. This difficulty arises from a persistent need to keep items and distress associated with discarding. C. Hoarding clogs the living area and significantly disrupts purposeful use of rooms. D. Significant distress or functional impairment (including a dangerous environment for self, family or others). E. Not attributable to a med

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — separate category; insight qualifier. “Animal hoarding” — although not a separate specifier, it is a clinically recognized variant; collaboration with veterinary and public health authorities is required.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Home visit or photographic evidence — condition of living space (Clutter Image Rating). Scale — Saving Inventory-Revised (SI-R). Comorbidity and cognitive assessment (dementia exclusion in elderly — MMSE/MoCA). Safety and health risk assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis (Table 1)
text: Condition Distinguishing feature OCD (6B20) Classic obsessions; hoarding is a response to obsession (fear of harm), not emotional attachment. MDD (6A70/6A71) Not cleaning due to “lack of energy”; no active acquisition of items. Dementia Cognitive decline dominant; accumulation develops later. Autism spectrum (6A02) Limited interests and attachment to objects; social-communicative deficit also present. Schizophrenia /

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SI-R (Saving Inventory-Revised), CIR (Clutter Image Rating). Medical and cognitive examination (MMSE/MoCA in older adults). Safety assessment.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT for hoarding (Frost R.O., Tolin D.F., Steketee G.) — first-line; manualized 26-session protocol — motivation enhancement, cognitive restructuring, decision-making training, sorting and discarding exercises, home visits. Evidence: Tolin D.F. et al. Depress Anxiety 2015 meta-analysis (12 samples, n=232) — symptoms decrease significantly, yet over half of patients still have difficulties after treatment. SSRIs — evi

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for hoarding disorder (Hoarding) — Steketee (Steketee G.), Frost (Frost R.O.) — Manualized 26 sessions — motivational interview, decision-making training, sorting exercise, home visits, cognitive restructuring. IOCDF. Saving Inventory-Revised (SI-R) — Frost (Frost R.O.) — 23 items; three subscales (acquisition, difficulty discarding, clutter). Clutter Image Rating (CIR) — 9-point scale; photo-based assessment of

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Tolin D.F. et al. RCTs — CBT is effective; SSRIs limited. Saxena S. reviews — response to SSRIs is weaker than that observed in OCD.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course, severity increases with age. Significant improvement with CBT, but full remission is rare. Comorbid dementia indicates a poor prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Hoarding is just a ‘collector’ personality trait or laziness”
text: Evidence: Hoarding is a clinical disorder — Frost & Hartl cognitive-behavioral model; distinct neurobiological profile; functional impairment and health risk. Unlike collectionism, items are not systematized and clutter the living area.

title: Myth 2: “Forcibly cleaning the patient’s home ends the problem”
text: Evidence: A forced clear-out without the patient’s consent leads to severe distress, trauma, and re-cluttering within 12 months. Gradual sorting involving patient participation is recommended.

title: Myth 3: “Hoarding is a subtype of typical OCD; SSRIs are sufficient”
text: Evidence: DSM-5 and ICD-11 — separate category; response to SSRIs is poor compared to OCD; CBT manualized protocol is first-line.

title: Myth 4: “Keeping many animals ‘with good intentions’ is good for the animals”
text: Evidence: “Animal hoarding” — results in animals receiving poor hygiene, food, and medical care; high animal mortality, survivors in severe condition; requires intervention from veterinary and public health authorities.

title: Myth 5: “Hoarding in the elderly is ‘normal aging’”
text: Evidence: In older adults, this may be a marker for frontotemporal dementia in particular; cognitive assessment is required.

title: Myth 6: “Once cleaned, the problem is solved”
text: Evidence: Hoarding is a chronic disorder; long-term treatment and community support are required.
