title: Body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders
text: Body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders ICD-10 F63.3 Trichotillomania DSM-5-TR F63.3 / L98.1 Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder) / Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders (ICD-11: 6B25) — a group of disorders characterized by the patient’s repetitive interference with their own body (hair, skin, nails). Main subtypes: 6B25.0 Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder); 6B25.1 — Excoriation / Dermatillomania (skin-picking disorder); 6B25.Y Other specified (nail biting — onychophagia, lip biting, cheek biting). DSM-5-TR — Trichotillomania (F63.3)

title: 2. History
text: Hallopeau F.H. (1889) — term “trichotillomania”. DSM-III-R (1987) — Trichotillomania as an impulse control disorder. DSM-5 (2013) — moved to the OCD spectrum category; excoriation added as a separate diagnosis. ICD-11 (2019) — as a joint category (6B25 umbrella).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence of trichotillomania: 0.5–2%; in clinical samples, females ≈ 10:1. Excoriation: 1.4–5.4%; higher in females. Onset: adolescence (10–13 years). Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, OCD, BDD, ADHD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 30–40%; family history is common. Genetic — SLITRK1 (in humans); SAPAP3 — hypergrooming phenotype in mice. Neurobiological — OCD-like cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical dysregulation, but with a different profile. Behavioral mechanisms: stress response, ‘automatic’ (unconscious) and ‘focused’ (purposeful, with intense attention) subtypes.

title: Trichotillomania (6B25.0)
text: Hair pulling — usually from head, eyebrows, eyelashes; sometimes from other body parts. Visible hair loss. “Pre-pulling tension” or “post-pulling relief” — may not be present in all patients. Trichophagia (eating of pulled hair) — in 10–20% of patients; ‘trichobezoar’ — gastrointestinal obstruction may require surgery.

title: Excoriation / Dermatillomania (6B25.1)
text: Skin picking — face, arm, damaged skin areas (“acne”, insect bite site). Injury, crust, scars. Infection, scarring, cosmetic outcomes.

title: General characteristics
text: The patient makes repeated unsuccessful attempts to stop the behavior. Social isolation due to shame (wearing a wig, covering mouth/hands).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Hair pulling (in trichotillomania) or skin picking (in excoriation) — visible hair loss or skin damage. B. The patient makes repeated attempts to stop or reduce the behavior. C. Behavior causes clinically significant distress or functional impairment. D. Exclusion of a medical condition (alopecia areata, dermatological illness) or another mental disorder (e.g., appearance-motivated behavior in BDD; delusional cont

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — Trichotillomania (F63.3) and Excoriation (L98.1) separate. ICD-11 — under the common 6B25 umbrella; subspecifiers.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (patient often does not speak openly due to shame). Dermatological examination — exclusion of other causes of hair loss and skin lesions (alopecia areata, tinea capitis, eczema). Scale — Massachusetts General Hospital Hairpulling Scale (MGH-HPS), Skin Picking Scale. Comorbidity screening. Trichophagia screening — if gastrointestinal symptoms present.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis (Table 1)
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Alopecia areata Autoimmune; clear borders, “exclamation mark hairs”; no hair-pulling behavior. Tinea capitis Fungal infection; KOH examination. BDD (6B21) Appearance-based obsession; skin picking for cosmetic purposes. OCD (6B20) Multiple obsessions; hair and skin behavior not dominant. Stereotyped movement disorder (6A06) Rhythmic repetitive motor; no specific interference with body.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: MGH-HPS (trichotillomania), Skin Picking Scale-Revised. Dermatological examination. Abdominal ultrasound in case of trichophagia.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Habit Reversal Training (HRT) first-line — awareness training, competing response (e.g., fist clenching), motivation, social support, generalization. Evidence: Bloch M.H. et al. Biol Psychiatry 2007 meta-analysis. ACT (Acceptance and Commitment Therapy) — targets emotional component. Comprehensive Behavioral Treatment (ComB, Mansueto) — HRT + multimodal behavioral intervention. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — evidence base

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Habit Reversal Training (HRT — Habit Reversal Training) — Azrin (Azrin N.H.), Nunn (Nunn R.G.) — Five core components — awareness training, competing response, motivation, social support, generalization. Gold standard in body-focused repetitive behaviors. Comprehensive Behavioral Treatment (ComB) — Mansueto (Mansueto C.S.) — SCAMP model — individualized approach based on Sensory, Cognitive, Affective, Motor, Place mo

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Bloch M.H. Biol Psychiatry 2007 meta-analysis — HRT most evidence-based for trichotillomania. Grant J.E. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2009 — NAC 1200–2400 mg/day efficacy.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course, “waxing and waning”. Significant improvement with HRT; treatment of comorbidity is essential.

title: Myth 1: “Hair pulling and skin picking are ‘bad habits’, not serious disorders”
text: Evidence: Clinical impairment; risks of functional impairment, social isolation, infection, and trichobezoar (surgical).

title: Myth 2: “The patient can stop voluntarily”
text: Evidence: The patient repeatedly tries and fails — this is the main symptom of the disorder; HRT or pharmacotherapy is required.

title: Myth 3: “SSRIs are effective for trichotillomania (like OCD)”
text: Evidence: Response to SSRIs is weaker than in OCD; HRT is first-line; NAC adjunct; clomipramine relatively superior over SSRIs.

title: Myth 4: “Hiding hair (wig, makeup) is the solution”
text: Evidence: Cosmetic camouflage is short-term; primary behavioral intervention required.

title: Myth 5: “Only hypnosis or deep psychoanalytic therapy resolves the underlying behavioral cause”
text: Evidence: the evidence base is limited; HRT-based behavioral approaches are superior.

title: Myth 6: “Skin picking is a response to ‘acne’ or a cosmetic problem”
text: Evidence: Clinical impairment — patient cannot prevent behavior, causes scarring and infection of the skin; clinical intervention required.

title: Myth 1: “PTSD only occurs in war veterans”
text: Evidence: PTSD can develop following any traumatic event — sexual violence (~50% prevalence), physical assault, accidents, natural disasters, medical procedures. Prevalence among veterans is high, but it is also widespread in the general population.

title: Myth 2: “CISD (Critical Incident Stress Debriefing) prevents PTSD after trauma”
text: Evidence: Cochrane (Rose S. et al. 2002) — CISD does not reduce PTSD risk, and in some studies increases it. NICE and VA/DoD do not explicitly recommend. Early intervention should be “watchful waiting”, with trauma-focused CBT only for symptomatic patients.

title: Myth 3: “The patient should not talk about trauma, ‘disclosure’ is harmful”

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Prolonged grief disorder (ICD-11: 6B42; DSM-5-TR: F43.81 — added in 2022) — a disorder of grief and preoccupation lasting longer than cultural and religious expectations following the loss of a close person, causing significant functional impairment. Difference from normal grief: duration, intensity, and functional burden; clinical diagnosis based on specific duration (ICD-11: ≥ 6 months; DSM-5-TR: ≥ 12 months adult,

title: 2. History
text: Lindemann E. (1944) — studies on acute grief dynamics. Bowlby J. (1980) — attachment and loss. Prigerson H.G. et al. (1995–2009) — “Complicated Grief” / “Prolonged Grief” concept; development of diagnostic criteria. ICD-11 (2019) — first official category. DSM-5-TR (2022) — ‘Prolonged Grief Disorder’ added as an official diagnosis.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Development after close loss: 7–10% in general population, 49% after a violent death (Djelantik A.A.A.M.J. et al. J Affect Disord 2020). Sex: higher in women. Risk factors: loss at an early age, sudden or violent death, child loss, anxious/ambivalent attachment. COVID-19 pandemic — may increase the prevalence of prolonged grief (Eisma M.C. et al. 2020).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Attachment theory — impairment in cognitive processing of separation from a close attachment figure. Neurobiological — yearning-related activation of the reward circuit in response to the lost attachment (O’Connor M.F. fMRI studies). Cognitive — “stuck” thoughts, lack of healthy interpretation.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Persistent, intense yearning or preoccupation with the lost person. Several of the following symptoms are persistently present (at least three per DSM-5-TR): Disturbance of the sense of self (“a part of me has died”); Difficulty accepting the loss; Emotional pain related to loss (grief, anger, guilt); Loss of meaning in life; Emotional numbing; Avoidance of social activities; Difficulty maintaining relationships.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Complicated Grief Treatment (CGT) — Shear (Shear M.K.) — 16-session manualized protocol; “loss-oriented” + “restoration-oriented” work; imaginal and situational exposure, positive memories, future orientation. Evidence: Shear M.K. et al. JAMA 2005, JAMA Psychiatry 2016 RCT. Prolonged Grief Disorder-13 (PG-13) — Prigerson (Prigerson H.G.) — 13-item scale; clinical and population screening; PG-13-R update. Inventory of

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Shear M.K. reviews and RCTs — CGT gold standard. Wittouck C. et al. Clin Psychol Rev 2011 meta-analysis — grief-specific interventions superior to universal grief support in prolonged grief.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement in most patients with CGT. Without treatment, chronicity and development of comorbid MDD/PTSD.

title: Myth 1: “Grief always goes through ‘5 stages’ — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance”
text: Evidence: The Kübler-Ross model is a semi-scientific concept; lacks systematic evidence base; grief is a nonlinear, individualized process.

title: Myth 2: “Prolonged grief — pathologized normal sadness, does not require treatment”
text: Evidence: Clinical diagnosis established based on duration and functional impairment; proven interventions have a significant benefit.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant is first-line for prolonged grief”
text: Evidence: Shear JAMA Psychiatry 2016 — CGT first-line; citalopram no better than placebo; SSRIs only in comorbid MDD.

title: Myth 4: “Time heals all wounds — just wait”
text: Evidence: Most people gradually adapt, but 7–10% develop prolonged grief; untreated chronicity.

title: Myth 5: “Talking about grief is harmful to the patient”
text: Evidence: Evidence-based interventions (CGT) work specifically with grief content in structured form; avoidance prolongs and strengthens grief.

title: Myth 6: “Social rituals (charity, commemoration) are harmful; they only distract the patient from good memories”
text: Evidence: Cultural and religious rituals provide support during the grieving process; cultural respect is a crucial component in clinical intervention.

title: Adjustment disorder
text: Adjustment disorder ICD-10 F43.2 Adjustment disorders DSM-5-TR F43.2x Adjustment Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Adjustment disorder (ICD-11: 6B43; DSM-5-TR: F43.2x) — clinically significant emotional or behavioral symptoms that have developed in response to an identifiable stressor (acute or persistent, individual or collective). Symptoms do not meet full criteria for another mental disorder (MDD, GAD, etc.).

title: 2. History
text: DSM-III (1980) — “Adjustment Disorder” as an official diagnosis. ICD-11 — within the stress-related disorders group; general symptom profile ‘preoccupation’ (preoccupation with the stress factor) + adjustment difficulty.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Among the most frequent psychiatric diagnoses in primary care; in clinical populations 5–20%. Sex and age — universal; more pronounced in younger people and during new stress periods. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, substance use, suicide risk (especially in short-term acute form).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Stress factor — a single event (divorce, job loss, illness diagnosis, grief) or multiple/persistent stressors. The role of personality and coping resources — the same stress elicits different responses in different people. Social support — protective factor.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Preoccupation with the stress factor — recurrent thoughts, worry. Difficulty adapting to new situations. Emotional symptoms — depressed mood, anxiety, irritability. Behavioral symptoms — social withdrawal, decreased work/school performance, risky behavior.

title: DSM-5-TR subtypes
text: With depressive mood (F43.21); With anxiety (F43.22); With mixed depressive mood and anxiety (F43.23); With disturbance of conduct (F43.24); With mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct (F43.25); Unspecified (F43.20).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Identifiable stressor response — onset within 3 months (DSM-5-TR) / within 1 month (ICD-11). B. Symptoms clinically significant — distress or functional impairment disproportionate to stress. C. Does not meet criteria for another mental disorder (MDD, GAD, PTSD, complex PTSD, prolonged grief). D. Not normal grief (sorrow). E. Symptoms resolve within 6 months after the stress factor (or its consequences) has termin

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — onset within 3 months; subtype specifiers. ICD-11 — onset 1 month; ‘preoccupation with the stressor’ main symptom; no subtypes and no qualifiers.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview — stressor, symptom onset, prior psychiatric history. SCID-5, MINI. Scale — PHQ-9, GAD-7 symptom severity. MDD, GAD, PTSD, complex PTSD exclusion. Suicide risk (C-SSRS) — particularly high in the acute phase.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature MDD (6A70/6A71) five or more symptoms for two weeks, full criteria. GAD (6B00) ≥6 months (DSM); multiple areas. PTSD (6B40) Traumatic event + intrusions, avoidance, hyperarousal. Prolonged grief (6B42) From a close loss ≥ 6 months (ICD-11) / 12 months (DSM-5-TR). Normal grief/stress reaction No functional impairment or context-appropriate. Conduct-dissocial disorder (6C91) Persistent

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PHQ-9, GAD-7, C-SSRS. Documentation of the stress factor.

title: 8. Treatment
text: First-line: short-term psychotherapy — supportive, problem-solving, CBT-based brief intervention (8–12 sessions). Stress management, strengthening social support, development of coping strategies. Pharmacotherapy — only in severe or comorbid cases; SSRIs short-term; benzodiazepines for acute anxiety for 1–2 weeks. Monitor suicide risk. Removal or modification of the stress factor (if possible).

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Short-term problem-solving therapy (Problem-Solving Therapy) — Nezu (Nezu A.M.) — 4–8 sessions; concrete problem identification, evaluation of solution options, behavioral execution. Supportive Psychotherapy — Validation, emotional expression, social support. CBT in brief form — Cognitive restructuring + behavioral activation. Stress management and relaxation — Breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, mind

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE — no separate guideline for adjustment disorder; general anxiety and depression principles. WHO mhGAP — supportive approach in acute stress reactions, ‘watchful waiting’ in mild cases. Evidence base is limited — the residual nature of the diagnosis.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: In most cases, remission occurs within 6 months. Some persist or transition to MDD/PTSD — follow-up recommended.

title: Myth 1: “Adjustment disorder is not a real diagnosis — it is simply ‘life difficulty’”
text: Evidence: A clinical diagnosis of adjustment disorder requires demonstrable functional impairment or marked distress disproportionate to the stressor. Suicide risk must be assessed in every case.

title: Myth 2: “When the stressor passes, the diagnosis automatically resolves, no treatment needed”
text: Evidence: Some cases persist or transition to MDD/PTSD; short-term intervention prevents such a transition.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant is first-line for adjustment disorder”
text: Evidence: Psychotherapy is first-line; pharmacotherapy only in severe or comorbid cases.

title: Myth 4: “Suicide risk is low in adjustment disorder”
text: Evidence: Acute stress reactions are accompanied by a high risk of impulsive suicide; active assessment is needed

title: Myth 5: “The patient is weak or has a ‘weak character’”
text: Evidence: The reaction is the result of an interaction between stress intensity and coping resources; the “weakness of character” explanation is stigmatizing and incorrect.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B43 Adjustment disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Maercker A. et al. ICD-11 stress-related disorders. World Psychiatry 2013;12(3):198–206. Casey P. Adjustment disorder: epidemiology, diagnosis and treatment. CNS Drugs 2009;23(11):927–938. Nezu A.M., Nezu C.M., D’Zurilla T.J. Problem-Solving Therapy: A Treatment Manual. New York: Springer, 2013.

title: Reactive attachment disorder
text: Reactive attachment disorder ICD-10 F94.1 Reactive attachment disorder of childhood DSM-5-TR F94.1 Reactive Attachment Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Reactive attachment disorder (ICD-11: 6B44; DSM-5-TR: F94.1 Reactive Attachment Disorder) — a disturbance of attachment behavior developing in early childhood due to severe psychosocial deprivation or inadequate care; the child does not seek comfort from the caregiver when distressed, or this seeking is markedly reduced.

title: 2. History
text: Bowlby J. (1951) — maternal deprivation report (WHO). Spitz R.A. (1945) — “hospitalism” in institutionalized children. DSM-III (1980) — “Reactive Attachment Disorder of Infancy” formalized. DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 — RAD and Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (DSED) as separate diagnoses. Nelson C.A. et al. Science 2007 — Bucharest Early Intervention Project — effect of institutional deprivation and early fosteri

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Rare in the general population; even among severely neglected children it occurs in less than 10% (DSM-5-TR); in institutionalized children the inhibited (RAD) type is ~5% (Gleason M.M. et al. JAACAP 2011, BEIP). Higher figures (≈ 20%) refer to disinhibited social engagement disorder (6B45), not RAD. Onset before age 5. Comorbidity: cognitive deficits, neurodevelopmental disorders, depressive symptoms.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Severe psychosocial deprivation — institutionalism, multiple placements, neglect. Disruption of caregiver-child interaction in the critical early period up to 5 years. Neurobiology of the attachment system — oxytocin, prefrontal-amygdala circuit.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Not seeking help from caregiver or minimal attempt while distressed. Difficulty accepting comfort. Reduction of social and emotional reactions (withdrawal, irritability, sadness). Reduction of positive affect. Withdrawn, hypervigilant behavior.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent disturbance of attachment behavior — the child does not seek comfort from the caregiver when distressed or shows minimal response to contact. B. Persistent emotional and social impairment — at least 2 of the following: minimal social-emotional response, reduced positive affect, unexplained irritability, sadness, or fear. C. Disorder developed as a result of severe early care disruption (neglect, multipl

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — RAD withdrawn form; DSED disinhibited form — separate diagnosis (6B45). ICD-11 — same two separate categories.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Interview with caregiver or social worker — care history (institutionalization, placement changes, neglect). Structured interview (DAI — Disturbances of Attachment Interview, Smyke A.T., Zeanah C.H.). Clinical observation of child-caregiver interaction. Autism spectrum exclusion (M-CHAT-R/F, ADOS). Cognitive and developmental assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Autism spectrum (6A02) Social-communication deficit, restricted, repetitive behavior; attachment behavior variable. DSED (6B45) Uninhibited social approach, inappropriate interaction with strangers. Intellectual disability (6A00) General cognitive deficit. PTSD (6B40) Concrete traumatic event; intrusions. Depressive disorder Affective component.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: DAI (Disturbances of Attachment Interview). Strange Situation Procedure (Ainsworth M.) — in a research context. Developmental assessment (Bayley, Mullen).

title: 8. Treatment
text: Provision of a stable, continuous care environment — fostering, adoption; institutional environment is contraindicated. Interventions focused on caregiver–child interaction — Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up (ABC, Dozier M.), Child-Parent Psychotherapy (CPP, Lieberman A.). Trauma-focused approach — TF-CBT added in trauma context. Treatment of comorbid disorders (depression, anxiety, ADHD). Pharmacotherapy — no s

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up (ABC) — Dozier M. — Parent training in 10 sessions; home-based; reinforcement of ‘nurturance’ and ‘synchronous’ interaction. Evidence: Dozier M. et al. Dev Psychopathol 2008;20(3):845–859. Child-Parent Psychotherapy (CPP) — Lieberman (Lieberman A.) — For RAD in the context of trauma; 0–5 years; within the context of parent-child interaction. Disturbances of Attachment Interview (

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AACAP Practice Parameter (Zeanah C.H., Chesher T., Boris N.W. JAACAP 2016). APSAC (American Professional Society on the Abuse of Children) — ‘holding therapy’ and similar coercive methods are prohibited. The Bucharest Early Intervention Project (Nelson Science 2007) — early fostering significantly improves outcomes in institutionalized children.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with early stable care and intervention. Long-term institutional deprivation — residual cognitive and emotional deficits.

title: Myth 1: “Holding therapy” and “rebirthing” cure RAD
text: Evidence: APSAC 2006 — these methods are not evidence-based, are harmful; Candace Newmaker’s (2000) death during ‘rebirthing’ was noted. AACAP and APSAC regard them as an absolute contraindication.

title: Myth 2: “An adopted child will be ‘fixed’ with love”
text: Evidence: Stable loving care is important, but severe RAD requires structured intervention (ABC, CPP).

title: Myth 3: “RAD is a form of autism”
text: Evidence: Reactive attachment disorder is caused by psychosocial deprivation; autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder. In stable care, reactive attachment disorder significantly improves, autism does not.

title: Myth 4: “The patient is ‘manipulative’ and requires strict discipline”
text: Evidence: Clinical manifestations of RAD result from impairment of the attachment system and are not manipulative; a punitive approach exacerbates symptoms.

title: Myth 5: “Only antipsychotics or stimulants are effective for RAD”
text: Evidence: There is no specific FDA-approved medication for RAD; environmental changes and psychosocial intervention are first-line.

AACAP Practice Parameter for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents With Reactive Attachment Disorder and Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2016;55(11):990–1003. Nelson C.A., Zeanah C.H., Fox N.A. et al. Cognitive recovery in socially deprived young

title: Disinhibited social engagement disorder
text: Disinhibited social engagement disorder ICD-10 F94.2 Disinhibited attachment disorder of childhood DSM-5-TR F94.2 Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (ICD-11: 6B45; DSM-5-TR: F94.2 Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder, DSED) — excessive and inappropriate friendliness toward strangers in a child, with approach or departure behavior without caution — resulting from early psychosocial deprivation (institutionalization, multiple placements). It shares the same etiological root as RAD but presents with an opposite clinical man

title: 2. History
text: DSM-IV (1994) — ‘Reactive Attachment Disorder, Disinhibited Type’ as a subtype. DSM-5 (2013) — “Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder” added as a separate diagnosis. ICD-11 (2019) — parallel.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Rare in the general population; in institutionalized children 20%, in foster children 10–15%. Onset before age 5. Significant reduction with early fostering (Bucharest Early Intervention Project), but unlike RAD, DSED sometimes persists even in stable care environments.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Severe psychosocial deprivation — same as RAD. Institutional environment with multiple caregiver rotation — formation of ‘indiscriminate attachment’.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Open approach to strangers, going with them without caution. Reckless physical closeness (hugging, sitting). Reduced checking-back with the caregiver during interactions with strangers. Absence of perceived danger from strangers. Academic and social impairment.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Inappropriately open, friendly behavior with strangers — ≥2 of the following: Reduced or no caution in approaching strangers; Physical or verbal intimacy inappropriate for culture or age; Reduced checking-back behavior for caregiver in unfamiliar place; Minimal or no caution about going with strangers. B. Behaviors are not limited to impulsivity (ADHD) — social engagement component is evident C. Early severe care

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same criteria; DSED separate from RAD. Developmental level by age must be considered — normal social interest in young children should not be confused with DSED.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Interview and observation — child’s interaction with strangers. Care history. DAI (Disturbances of Attachment Interview). Comorbidity screening (ADHD, autism).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature RAD (6B44) Withdrawal, no attachment; open approach in DSED. ADHD (6A05) Impulsivity, but no social engagement component. Autism spectrum (6A02) Social-communicative deficit. Williams syndrome Genetic; “hypersociability” + specific physical features.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: DAI. Observation in unfamiliar environment. Williams syndrome genetic test (FISH 7q11.23) — if suspected.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Stable care environment. Parent training — developing a “safe base” concept for the child; ABC programs. Teaching appropriate distance with strangers. Comorbidity treatment (ADHD). Community and school staff coordination — child safety. There is no specific pharmacotherapy; medications are used only for comorbid symptoms.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up (ABC) — Dozier M — Also used for RAD; in DSED strengthening caregiver-child synchronization. Safety training — Teaching child appropriate distance from strangers; reinforcement of caregiver-checking behavior. DAI — In differentiation between RAD and DSED.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AACAP 2016 — same guidance as for RAD. DSED, unlike RAD, can persist even in a stable environment — long-term follow-up.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With stable care and intervention, improvement occurs; however, DSED sometimes persists long-term. Impulsive behaviors and risks of abuse can persist into adulthood.

title: Myth 1: “An open, friendly child is a positive trait, not a disorder”
text: Evidence: appropriate social distance is a sign of a developmental stage; in DSED absence of boundaries increases child’s abuse risk.

title: Myth 2: “DSED resolves quickly in stable care”
text: Evidence: In contrast to RAD, DSED sometimes persists even in a stable environment (Bucharest study); long-term intervention is required.

title: Myth 3: “DSED is a ‘mild form’ of autism”
text: Evidence: distinct disorder; etiology is psychosocial deprivation; clinical manifestations are opposite (social withdrawal in autism, disinhibited approach in DSED).

title: Myth 4: “You can ‘fix’ a child with punishment”
text: Evidence: Punishment exacerbates the disorder and has a traumatic effect; a positive attachment-based approach is recommended.

title: Myth 5: “Williams syndrome and DSED are the same”
text: Evidence: Williams syndrome is a genetic disorder (7q11.23 deletion), specific physical and cognitive profile; “hypersociability” is present but it is a distinct neurobiological and etiological disorder.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B45 Disinhibited social engagement disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Zeanah C.H. et al. AACAP Practice Parameter. JAACAP 2016;55(11):990–1003. Gleason M.M. et al. Validity of evidence-derived criteria for reactive attachment disorder: indiscriminately social/disinhibited and emotionally withdrawn/inhibited types. JAACAP 2011;50(3):216–231. Nelson C.A. et al. Bucharest Early Intervention Project. Scie

title: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) (Dissociative identity disorder)
text: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) (Dissociative identity disorder) Dissociative identity disorder ICD-10 F44.81 Multiple personality disorder DSM-5-TR F44.81 Dissociative Identity Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID; ICD-11: 6B64 Dissociative Identity Disorder; DSM-5-TR: F44.81) — a severe dissociative disorder characterized by transitions between two or more distinct personality states (“identities”, “alters”). Each identity has a relatively enduring sense of self, memory, behavior, affect, perception, and cognition patterns. Persistent dissociative amnesia is also present (for daily events,

title: 2. History
text: 1791 — Eberhard Gmelin first case description. Janet P. (1880s) — concept of ‘dissociation’. DSM-III (1980) — “Multiple Personality Disorder”. DSM-IV (1994) — Term ‘Dissociative Identity Disorder’. 1980s–1990s — ‘False Memory’ controversy; allegations of ‘iatrogenic induction’ in some diagnostic cases. ISSTD Treatment Guidelines (Adult Treatment, 3rd Revision 2011) — standardized the phase-oriented approach.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in clinical populations: 1–3%; in general population ~1.5% (Sar V. Epidemiol Res Int 2011 review). Sex: 5–9 times higher in females in clinical populations. Onset: symptoms develop in childhood, clinical presentation often at 20–40 years. Comorbidity: MDD, PTSD, complex PTSD, BPD, somatic symptom, eating disorders, substance use, very high suicide risk.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Trauma model — repeated severe childhood trauma (sexual or physical violence, neglect, caregiver violence); 90%+ of patients show trauma history (Putnam F.W. reviews). Neurobiological — hippocampal and amygdala volume reduction; default mode and salience network dysregulation (Reinders A.A. et al. reviews). Attachment — disorganized attachment style in childhood. Iatrogenesis / supporters of the social-cognitive mode

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Two or more distinct identity states — some patients display overt transitions, others appear only with “internal voices,” sense of “loss of control.” Persistent amnesias — daily events, personal information, traumatic episodes. Depersonalization and derealization. Identity transitions as a response to stress, triggers. Self-harm, suicide attempts, somatic symptoms. Complex dissociative symptoms (dissociative seizure

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Two or more distinct personality states — significant discontinuity in sense of self and agency, alterations in behavior, affect, perception, cognition, or sensorimotor function. B. Recurrent amnesias regarding daily events, important personal information, and/or traumatic events. C. Significant distress or functional impairment. D. Not part of a widespread cultural or religious practice. E. Exclusion of substance

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — same criteria; imaginary companion in children excluded as part of normal development. ICD-11 — amnesia is not required: it says “there are typically episodes of amnesia”, whereas DSM-5-TR requires it as criterion B. Trance and possession disorders are separate ICD-11 categories (6B62 and 6B63); in DSM-5-TR, however, the possession form is included in dissociative identity disorder, while dissociative tran

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview — trauma history, dissociative symptoms. SCID-D (Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Dissociative Disorders) is the gold standard. Scale — DES (Dissociative Experiences Scale, ≥30 cut-off, ≥45 DID indicator); MID (Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation). Comorbidity (PTSD, BPD, MDD, substance). Suicide and self-harm risk (high). Medical and neurological — seizures, encephalitis excluded (EEG,

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature BPD (6D11.5) Emotional lability and impulsivity dominant; significant clinical overlap, close comorbidity. PTSD / cPTSD (6B40/6B41) Traumatic intrusions and avoidance are primary; dissociation can be a component. Schizophrenia (6A20) “Voices” differ from schizophrenia — as internal dialogue; no psychotic characteristics. Bipolar (6A60) Affective episodes; no dissociation. Factitious d

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SCID-D-R is the gold-standard structured interview. DES, MID scales. C-SSRS suicide; self-harm assessment. EEG to rule out seizures.

title: 8.1 General principles (ISSTD 2011)
text: Phase-oriented (three-phase) approach: Phase 1 — stabilization and symptom reduction: safety, emotion regulation, coping skills, hospitalization reduction, self-harm management. Phase 2 — processing of traumatic memories: adapted trauma-focused intervention. Phase 3 — integration and rehabilitation: inter-identity communication, functional restoration, relationships. Specific psychotherapeutic approaches — elements o

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Phase-Oriented Treatment (ISSTD) — Three-phase approach; sequence and patient stability are fundamental. Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Dissociative Disorders, Revised (SCID-D-R) — 277-item structured interview; gold standard. Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) — 28 items; screening. Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation (MID) — 218 items; detailed dissociative profile. EMDR — modified — Trauma processi

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: ISSTD 2011 — phase-oriented gold standard. Trauma-based approach and iatrogenesis caution — avoid searching or inducing ‘alters’.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Functional recovery with long-term phase-oriented therapy. High suicide and self-harm risk requires monitoring. Comorbidity treatment is important.

title: Myth 1: “DID is ‘split personality’ as in mass media”
text: Evidence: Film or television portrayals (dramatic transitions, “different people” do not coincide with the more subtle clinical picture in many patients — more “loss of control”, internal voices, amnesia predominates).

title: Myth 2: “DID is a false condition induced by the therapist”
text: Evidence: strong association with childhood trauma (Putnam reviews); neurobiological markers (Reinders fMRI); international research is consistent. However, diagnosis should be cautious — avoiding induction techniques for alters is important.

title: Myth 3: “DID is a rare or fabricated disorder”
text: Evidence: Clinical prevalence in populations 1–3% (Sar 2011); an underdiagnosed condition.

title: Myth 4: “Hypnosis or hospitalization is the main treatment”
text: Evidence: Phase-oriented psychotherapy is first-line; hypnosis can be used as an adjunct (with caution); inpatient admission only in acute self-harm or suicide risk.

title: Myth 5: “A patient with DID is prone to committing violence”
text: Evidence: Patients with DID are more likely to be victims of violence; violence towards others is rare. This parallels the myth ‘people with schizophrenia are dangerous.’

title: Myth 6: “The main goal is to ‘merge all identities into one’”
text: Evidence: Integration is the typical goal, but complete assimilation not achievable in all patients; “cooperation” and “functional activity” also accepted as clinical outcomes.

title: Partial dissociative identity disorder
text: Partial dissociative identity disorder ICD-10 F44.8 Other dissociative [conversion] disorders DSM-5-TR F44.89 Other Specified Dissociative Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Partial Dissociative Identity Disorder (ICD-11: 6B65 Partial Dissociative Identity Disorder) — similar to DID (6B64), but differs in that non-dominant identities do not consistently fully occupy the patient’s behavior or conscious function. Instead, non-dominant identities interfere, but do not fully seize “executive control.” In ICD-11, added for the first time as an official diagnostic category; not separate in DSM

title: 2. History
text: ICD-11 (2019) — recognition as part of the DID spectrum, with the partial form as an official category. New diagnostic framework for conditions recognized in clinical practice as ‘DDNOS’ or ‘DID-NOS’.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Precise prevalence data are limited — believed to be more common than DID. Develops on the basis of trauma. Comorbidity resembling DID.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Same as DID — severe childhood trauma, disorganized attachment, neurobiological dissociative processes.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Two or more distinct identity states. Non-dominant identities intrude — internal voices, thoughts, feelings, actions — but do not fully occupy patient’s behavior and consciousness. Dominant identity controls daily functioning. Less amnesia compared to DID. Distress and functional impairment.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (ICD-11)
text: A. Two or more distinct identity states. B. Non-dominant identities do not consistently take full control of the consciousness and behavior of the dominant identity, but are present as an intrusive experience. C. Significant distress or functional impairment. D. Exclusion of substance or medical condition.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11 — differs from DID by ‘not fully capturing.’ DSM-5-TR — may be assessed within Other Specified Dissociative Disorder (F44.89).

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Same as DID (see 6B64 §6.3).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature DID (6B64) Non-dominant identities consistently seize dominant control + amnesia. PTSD / cPTSD (6B40/6B41) Traumatic intrusions; no separate identities. BPD (6D11.5) Emotional lability dominant. Schizophrenia (6A20) Psychotic symptoms. Possession trance (6B63) Cultural and religious context.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Same as DID (SCID-D-R, DES, MID).

title: 8. Treatment
text: The phase-oriented approach is adapted for DID (ISSTD 2011). For treatment principles, phases, and specific methodologies, see section 6B64 “Treatment” (including “Treatment methods”).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Functional recovery with phase-oriented therapy; similar to DID.

title: Myth 1: “Partial DID is a ‘mild form’ of DID”
text: Evidence: distinct diagnostic category; functional impairment and trauma burden may be comparable to DID.

title: Myth 2: “Internal voices are always a psychotic symptom”
text: Evidence: dissociative voices differ from psychotic symptoms — internal dialogue, ‘own’ feeling, weak response to antipsychotics; SCID-D-R for differentiation.

title: Myth 3: “Antipsychotic ‘cures’ voices in partial DID”
text: Evidence: dissociative voices do not respond to antipsychotics; psychotherapy first-line.

title: Myth 4: “The patient is ‘role-playing’”
text: Evidence: It differs from factitious disorder (6D50) and malingering — no deliberate fabrication; clinical experience is distressing for the patient.

title: 11. Sources

title: Depersonalization-derealization disorder
text: Depersonalization-derealization disorder ICD-10 F48.1 Depersonalization-derealization syndrome DSM-5-TR F48.1 Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Depersonalization-Derealization Disorder (ICD-11: 6B66; DSM-5-TR: F48.1) — a dissociative disorder characterized by persistent or recurrent depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself, disconnected from body and thoughts) and/or derealization (surroundings appearing unreal, like a ‘foggy film’). Reality testing is preserved (the patient knows the experience is unreal).

title: 2. History
text: Krishaber M. (1873) — first description. Dugas L. (1898) — term ‘dépersonnalisation’. DSM-III (1980) — Separate diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — depersonalization and derealization as a combined category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1–2% in clinical form; subclinical experiences at least once in 50% of the population. Sex: approximately equal. Onset: adolescence and early adulthood (mean 16 years). Comorbidity: MDD, panic, GAD, PTSD, BPD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Trauma and stress trigger (especially cannabis, hallucinogen use). Neurobiological — impaired prefrontal-limbic regulation; sensory processing anomalies (Simeon D. reviews). Comorbid anxiety is common, and panic attacks are frequent.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Depersonalization: Sense of observing oneself from outside, feeling like a robot, emotional flattening, feeling that “my body is not mine”. Derealization: Environment appears “faded”, “like a faded film” or “artificial”; distance perception change. Reality testing preserved — patient knows the experience is unreal. Significant distress and functional impairment. Typical course — continuous or recurring episodes.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent or recurrent experiences of depersonalization and/or derealization. B. Reality testing preserved. C. Significant distress or functional impairment. D. Exclusion of substance (cannabis, hallucinogen) or medical condition (seizure, brain injury). E. Not better explained by another mental disorder (transient during panic attack; in the context of PTSD; schizophrenia).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same criteria.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. CDS (Cambridge Depersonalisation Scale, Sierra M., Berrios G.E.) — 29 items. Medical and neurological examination (excluding seizures and brain injury). Toxicology screening. Comorbidity.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Panic attack Short-term in the context of an attack. PTSD (6B40) Against a background of trauma; intrusive symptoms. DID (6B64) Distinct identities. Seizure (epileptic) EEG; postictal state. Schizophrenia Reality testing impaired. Substance-induced (cannabis, LSD) Toxicology.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: CDS is the gold standard. EEG if seizure is to be ruled out. Toxicology.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT — adapted for depersonalization; cognitive restructuring + exposure. Hunter E.C. et al. Behav Res Ther 2005. SSRI — effective for comorbid depression and anxiety; evidence base for the disorder itself is limited. Lamotrigine adjunct — effective in some studies. Against a background of trauma — trauma-focused approach. Abstinence from cannabis and hallucinogen use is critical.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for depersonalization — Hunter (Hunter E.C.), Sierra (Sierra M.) — Cognitive restructuring, exposure, grounding techniques. Cambridge Depersonalisation Scale (CDS) — 29 items. Grounding techniques — 5-4-3-2-1 (5 visible objects, 4 sounds, etc.); sensory attention.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Sierra M. reviews — CBT and adjunctive SSRIs. There is no specific FDA-approved medication.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course, but significant improvement with CBT.

title: Myth 1: “Depersonalization is a sign of psychosis”
text: Evidence: Reality testing preserved; distinct from psychotic disorder; antipsychotics are ineffective.

title: Myth 2: “Depersonalization is transient and does not require treatment”
text: Evidence: The clinical form is characterized by a chronic course and functional impairment; intervention recommended.

title: Myth 3: “Cannabis improves depersonalization”
text: Evidence: Cannabis is a trigger and perpetuating factor; abstinence critical.

title: Myth 4: “Benzodiazepines are the main treatment”
text: Evidence: Benzodiazepines provide short-term relief, but carry a risk of dependence and depersonalization enhancement.

title: Myth 5: “Only antidepressants are effective”
text: Evidence: CBT first-line; SSRIs for comorbid symptoms.

title: 11. Sources

title: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder
text: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder ICD-10 F44.4–F44.7 Dissociative motor and sensory disorders DSM-5-TR F44.4–F44.7 Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder)

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Dissociative Neurological Symptom Disorder (ICD-11: 6B60; DSM-5-TR: F44.4–F44.7 Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder / Conversion Disorder) — impairment of motor, sensory, or cognitive functions normally under voluntary control, not fully explained by a neurological or medical illness. Previously termed “conversion disorder” or “hysteria”.

title: 2. History
text: Charcot J.M. (19th century) — Studies on ‘hysteria’ at Salpêtrière. Freud S. — psychoanalytic “conversion” model. DSM-III (1980) — “Conversion Disorder” within somatoform disorders. DSM-5 (2013) — “Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder” — emphasis on joint neurological and psychiatric assessment. ICD-11 (2019) — transferred to the category of dissociative disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: In primary care and neurological clinics — 5–10% (reviews by Carson A.J. et al.). Sex: 2–3 times higher in females. Onset: adulthood, but also in children and the elderly. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, trauma history, somatic illnesses.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: A traumatic or stressful trigger is common, but in a substantial and variable proportion of patients no trigger can be identified (0–77% across studies; Ludwig L. et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2018 meta-analysis) — which is why DSM-5 and ICD-11 no longer require a stressor for diagnosis. Neurobiological — impaired sensorimotor and cognitive prediction processing; predictive coding hypothesis (Edwards M.J.). “Functional” t

title: Typical symptoms
text: Motor: Weakness, paralysis, involuntary movements (functional tremor, dystonia), gait disturbance. Sensory: sensory loss (anesthesia), visual impairment (functional blindness), hearing impairment. Functional (psychogenic) non-epileptic seizures (PNES): during seizure-like episodes there is no epileptiform activity on EEG. Cognitive: “Foggy” concentration, slow processing — “functional cognitive disorder”.

title: Clinical signs (positive features).
text: Signs that differ from typical neurological patterns (e.g., Hoover sign in motor weakness — positive indicator of functional component). Distractibility — symptom changes when attention is directed elsewhere. Entrainability — tremor adapts to another rhythm.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Impairment of one or more motor, sensory, or cognitive functions. B. Clinical findings demonstrate incompatibility of the disorder with known neurological or medical illness (positive clinical features). C. Symptoms are not better explained by another psychiatric or medical condition. D. Significant distress or functional impairment.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — diagnosis based on “positive features” (not an exclusion method); joint assessment by neurologist and psychiatrist. ICD-11 — in the category of dissociative disorders.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Neurological examination — functional positive features (Hoover, entrainability, distractibility). Exclusion of typical neurological conditions — MRI, EEG, EMG, lumbar puncture (according to clinical presentation). In PNES cases — video-EEG monitoring is the gold standard. Psychiatric evaluation — comorbid trauma, MDD, anxiety. The patient’s diagnosis should be explained positively — “not fabricated, but a functional

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Real neurological disease Clinical and laboratory confirmation. Factitious disorder (6D50) Conscious falsification; motivation is the sick role, no external gain. Malingering Overt gain (legal, insurance). Bodily distress disorder (6C20) Numerous somatic complaints; focus on the body. Hypochondriasis (6B23) Illness preoccupation dominant. Epileptic seizure Video-EEG.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Neurological examination (positive features). Video-EEG — in PNES cases. MRI, laboratory exclusion of neurological disease. Trauma and psychiatric assessment.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Positive explanation of the diagnosis to the patient — “Functional neurological disorder is not fabricated”; the structured explanation of diagnosis is critical for functional improvement (Stone J. summaries). Multidisciplinary approach — neurologist + psychiatrist + physiotherapist. Physiotherapy (for motor symptoms) — evidence-based benefit (Nielsen G. et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2017 RCT). CBT — cognitive

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Positive clinical diagnosis presentation — Stone (Stone J.) — The diagnosis is made by ruling in, not by ruling out; positive clinical signs explained to patient (e.g., Hoover sign demonstrated). Physiotherapy for FND — Specific manual training, movement instruction; Nielsen G. et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2017. CBT for PNES — LaFrance (LaFrance W.C.) — Manualized 12 sessions; seizure diary, cognitive restruc

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: FND-specific international consensus (Stone J., Carson A., LaFrance W.C.). NICE — multidisciplinary approach for functional symptoms.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Improvement with early accurate diagnosis and intervention. Late diagnosis and polypharmacy — chronicity.

title: Myth 1: “The patient is malingering / ‘faking’”
text: Evidence: Functional disorder is a real clinical condition — functional impairment of the nervous system; positive clinical signs prove it. It is distinct from factitious disorder and simulation.

title: Myth 2: “Anticonvulsants are needed for PNES”
text: Evidence: Anticonvulsants ineffective in PNES, cause polypharmacy side effects; correct diagnosis and discontinuation of antiepileptic drugs is critical.

title: Myth 3: “Functional impairment is psychological ‘weakness’, not physical”
text: Evidence: Functional disorder is a biological process of the nervous system; requires joint psychiatric and neurological assessment.

title: Myth 4: “Just ‘dumping’ the patient on a psychiatrist is enough”
text: Evidence: Neurologist and psychiatrist must collaborate; ‘dismissing’ the patient disrupts therapeutic alliance and reduces the chance of improvement.

title: Myth 5: “Functional symptoms are not treatable”
text: Evidence: Physiotherapy, CBT, multidisciplinary approach show a significant effect.

title: Dissociative amnesia
text: Dissociative amnesia ICD-10 F44.0 Dissociative amnesia DSM-5-TR F44.0 Dissociative Amnesia

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Dissociative Amnesia (ICD-11: 6B61; DSM-5-TR: F44.0) — inability to recall important autobiographical information (usually traumatic or stressful), not explained by ordinary forgetfulness. No medical or neurological cause. Subtypes: localized (specific period), selective (part of the period), generalized (entire life history), systematized (specific category), continuous. “Dissociative fugue” — In DSM-5-TR it is a qu

title: 2. History
text: Janet P. — originator of the concept of dissociation. DSM-IV — Dissociative fugue as a separate diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — fugue integrated as a specifier. “False Memory” controversy (1990s) — debate over therapeutically induced “recovered memory”.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1–2%; higher after collective disasters (war, disaster). Sex: more common in females. Comorbidity: PTSD, cPTSD, DID, BPD, MDD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Trauma — response to severe psychological or physical trauma; hypothesized as ‘defense mechanism’. Neurobiological — impaired hippocampal and prefrontal cognitive processing.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Inability to recall the traumatic or stressful event. Localized (e.g., wartime), selective, generalized. Dissociative fugue — unexpected travel, new identity, usually lasts days to weeks. Implicit memory (skills) remains; explicit memory is selective.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Failure to recall significant autobiographical information (typically traumatic), not explained by normal forgetfulness. B. Significant distress or functional impairment. C. Exclusion of substance-related or medical/neurological causes (TBI, encephalitis, dementia). D. Not better explained by DID, PTSD, cPTSD, a somatic symptom disorder, or another mental disorder. Qualifier: with dissociative fugue.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same; fugue qualifier.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + trauma history. Medical and neurological examination — TBI, dementia, encephalitis, seizure excluded. MRI, EEG in clinical suspicion. SCID-D-R. Toxicology.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Traumatic brain injury (TBI) History, MRI. Transient global amnesia (TGA) Acute, less than 24 hours; vascular etiology. Dementia Persistent cognitive decline. Seizure (postictal) EEG. Substance-induced amnesia (alcohol blackout) History. Factitious disorder / malingering Reward motivation. DID (6B64) Dissociative identity disorder.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SCID-D-R. MRI, EEG. Neuropsychological test (memory profile).

title: 8. Treatment
text: Safe environment and supportive psychotherapy. Trauma-focused psychotherapy — phased approach. During a fugue episode — reuniting the patient with family and community. Pharmacotherapy for comorbid symptoms; ‘amobarbital interview’ or hypnosis was historically used — caution due to risk of induced false memory. Long-term psychotherapy — trauma processing.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Trauma-focused phased psychotherapy — Stabilization → processing → reintegration. Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Dissociative Disorders, Revised (SCID-D-R) — Gold standard in diagnosis. Hypnosis — cautious use — False memory induction risk; use only by an experienced clinician.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: ISSTD — general guideline for dissociative disorders. There is no specific FDA-approved pharmacotherapy.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Most cases of the acute form remit spontaneously; Chronic form requires long-term intervention.

title: Myth 1: “Hypnosis is a reliable tool for ‘recovered memory’”
text: Evidence: hypnosis-induced memories can be contaminated with false memory — induced or distorted; particular caution is needed in legal contexts (Loftus E.F. research).

title: Myth 2: “Dissociative amnesia is fabricated or ‘drama’ from movies”
text: Evidence: Clinical condition documented; neurobiological foundations investigated.

title: Myth 3: “The patient ‘must be forced to remember’”
text: Evidence: pressure may create trauma or distress; supportive approach recommended.

title: Myth 4: “Amobarbital interview is effective”
text: Evidence: Historically used, but not recommended in modern practice due to the risk of false memory and adverse effects.

title: Myth 5: “All traumatic memories are ‘real’”
text: Evidence: Some ‘recovered memories’ may be a result of therapeutic induction; cautious clinical approach and source verification are important.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B61 Dissociative amnesia. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. ISSTD. Guidelines for Treating DID in Adults, 3rd Revision. J Trauma Dissociation 2011;12(2):115–187. Loftus E.F. The reality of repressed memories. Am Psychol 1993;48(5):518–537. Staniloiu A., Markowitsch H.J. Dissociative amnesia. Lancet Psychiatry 2014;1(3):226–241.

title: Anorexia nervosa
text: Anorexia nervosa Anorexia Nervosa ICD-10 F50.0 Anorexia nervosa DSM-5-TR F50.0x Anorexia Nervosa

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Anorexia Nervosa (ICD-11: 6B80; DSM-5-TR: F50.0x) — a severe eating disorder characterized by significantly low body weight due to restriction of food intake, intense fear of weight gain, and disturbance in body image. It has one of the highest mortality rates among psychiatric disorders.

title: 2. History
text: Morton R. (1689) — first clinical description. Lasègue C. (1873) and Gull W. (1874) — ‘anorexia hysterica’ and ‘nervous anorexia’. DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — amenorrhea criterion eliminated (diagnosis possible in males and premenarchal).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: in females 0.9–4%, in males 0.3% (Smink F.R. reviews). Sex: 10:1 in females; but the diagnosis is often missed in male patients. Onset: adolescence (14–18 years); second peak at approximately age 18. Mortality: lifetime risk 5–6%; most deaths are medical (cachexia, arrhythmia), 1 in 5 deaths from suicide (Arcelus J. et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2011 meta-analysis). Comorbidity: MDD, OCD, anxiety, B

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 50–60% (Bulik C.M. reviews). Neurobiological — reduced cognitive flexibility, reward circuit dysregulation, atypical response to hunger. Social-cultural factors — thinness ideal; social media influence. Personality — perfectionism, anxiety, family history of eating disorder.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Food restriction — calories, types of food. Body weight significantly low (BMI < 18.5 in adults; children BMI percentile). Marked fear of weight gain or persistent behavior aimed at preventing it. Body image disturbance — “I feel fat” even when underweight. Subtypes: Restrictive type — only food restriction. Binge/purging type — vomiting, laxatives, exercise. Medical complications — bradycardia, hypotension, hypother

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Significantly low weight due to restricted food intake (BMI <18.5 in adults; below age-adjusted norm in children). B. Intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behavior to avoid weight gain, even when weight is low. C. Body image disturbance or lack of recognition of the seriousness of current body weight.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — severity based on BMI (mild BMI ≥ 17, moderate 16–16.99, severe 15–15.99, extreme < 15). ICD-11 — a different severity scale: 6B80.0 significantly low body weight (adults BMI 18.5–14.0; children 5th–0.3rd percentile BMI-for-age), 6B80.1 dangerously low body weight (BMI < 14.0), 6B80.2 in recovery with normal body weight — the diagnosis is retained until full and lasting recovery. ICD-11 has no separate ‘at

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. EDE-Q (Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire) or EDE — gold standard. Medical examination — BMI, vital signs, electrolytes, ECG, bone densitometry. Laboratory: complete blood count, electrolytes (especially K, P, Mg), liver, kidney, glucose, thyroid. Comorbidity (MDD, OCD, anxiety). Refeeding syndrome risk assessment (especially BMI <13 or minimal intake prolonged).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Bulimia Nervosa (6B81) Normal weight; binge eating + compensatory behavior. ARFID (6B83) Weight loss, but no disturbance in body image. Medical condition (cancer, hyperthyroidism, IBS, Crohn’s disease) Clinical confirmation. MDD (decreased food intake) No body image disturbance. Schizophrenia (delusion of poisoning) Psychotic thought basis.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: EDE-Q, EDE. Vital signs, BMI, weight history. Laboratory: complete blood count, electrolytes, liver, kidney, thyroid, FSH/LH, prolactin, vitamin D, B12, iron. ECG — bradycardia, QTc. DEXA — osteoporosis. C-SSRS suicide risk.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE NG69 · APA 2023)
text: Medical stabilization is critical: electrolytes, refeeding syndrome prevention (phosphorus, magnesium, thiamine), cardiac monitoring. Indication for hospitalization: BMI < 13, bradycardia < 40, hypokalemia, orthostatic changes, suicide risk, failure of outpatient treatment. Psychotherapy first-line: FBT — Family-Based Treatment (Maudsley Model, Lock J., Le Grange D.) — gold standard in children and adolescents; 20 se

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Family-Based Treatment / Maudsley Model (FBT) — Lock J., Le Grange D. — 3-phase 20 sessions: (1) weight restoration — family controls food intake; (2) gradually returning control over eating to the adolescent; (3) adolescent-specific topics. Evidence: Lock J. et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010 RCT. Enhanced Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT-E) — Fairburn C.G. — Transdiagnostic (AN, BN, BED combined) approach; 20 session

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG69 (2017) — FBT in children and adolescents; CBT-E in adults. APA 2023 Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients with Eating Disorders, 4th ed. AED (Academy for Eating Disorders) — refeeding syndrome medical care standards. NICE — antidepressants not routinely recommended for AN.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: 50% remission, 30% residual symptoms, 20% chronic course. Mortality high (5–6%). Early intervention (especially FBT in adolescence) significantly improves prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Anorexia is an ‘image’ disorder, not a serious medical condition”
text: Evidence: Arcelus 2011 meta-analysis — AN mortality risk ≈6 times higher than population; highest among psychiatric disorders.

title: Myth 2: “The patient can eat voluntarily — just need to demand it”
text: Evidence: AN is a complex neurobiological and psychological disorder; the ‘volitional eating’ explanation is incorrect and harmful.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant is the main treatment for AN”
text: Evidence: NICE NG69 — antidepressants not routinely recommended for AN; may be used for comorbid MDD (more effective after weight restoration).

title: Myth 4: “AN only occurs in adolescent girls”
text: Evidence: AN also occurs in males (~10%); can develop in middle age; under-detection is common.

title: Myth 5: “The problem is resolved after weight restoration”
text: Evidence: Weight restoration is a crucial step, but without cognitive-behavioral intervention, relapse rates are high; psychotherapy is critical.

title: Myth 6: “Refeeding should be rapid”
text: Evidence: Rapid refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia, cardiac failure) possible; stepped approach and electrolyte monitoring critical.

title: Myth 7: “The patient is perfectionistic and high-performing — this trait should be preserved”
text: Evidence: Perfectionism is among the sustaining factors of AN; therapy is directed at this characteristic.

title: Bulimia nervosa
text: Bulimia nervosa Bulimia Nervosa ICD-10 F50.2 Bulimia nervosa DSM-5-TR F50.2 Bulimia Nervosa

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Bulimia Nervosa (ICD-11: 6B81; DSM-5-TR: F50.2) — an eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating (large amount of food in a short period + sense of loss of control) and compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, exercise, fasting). Unlike anorexia, weight is typically normal or above normal.

title: 2. History
text: Russell G.F. (1979) — term ‘bulimia nervosa’ and first clinical description. DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — frequency criterion reduced to once per week (twice weekly in DSM-IV).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: in females 1.5–3%, in males 0.5%. Onset: adolescence and early adulthood. Comorbidity: MDD ~70%, anxiety, substance use, BPD, history of anorexia. Suicide risk is high.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 50–60%. Neurobiological — serotonergic dysregulation, dopamine reward system. Social-cultural — thinness ideal, dietary history. Personality — impulsivity, perfectionism, low self-esteem.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Binge eating episodes — loss of control, secretive. Compensatory behaviors: Purging — self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics; Non-purging — fasting, excessive exercise. Body image and weight preoccupation. Medical complications: hypokalemia (vomiting), Russell’s sign (calluses on fingers), dental erosion, parotid hypertrophy, esophagitis, gastrointestinal issues.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Repeated binge eating episodes — large amount of food in a short period (≤ 2 hours) + feeling of loss of control. B. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain. C. Frequency: at least once weekly — DSM-5-TR requires ≥ 3 months, ICD-11 ≥ 1 month. D. Self-evaluation and self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight. E. Does not occur in the context of an anorexia nervosa ep

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — severity based on episode frequency (mild 1–3, moderate 4–7, severe 8–13, extreme ≥14 per week). ICD-11 — criteria overlap, but the required duration differs: ICD-11 requires at least 1 month, DSM-5-TR 3 months; atypical bulimia is not a separate code in ICD-11 — it is coded as 6B8Y (other specified). NICE NG69 — diagnosis and treatment.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. EDE-Q, EDE. Medical: electrolytes (K, P, Mg, Cl), liver, kidney, ECG (QTc). Dental examination (erosion). Comorbidity and suicide risk.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Anorexia Nervosa, binge-eating/purging type (6B80) Significantly low weight. Binge eating (6B82) No compensatory behavior. Night Eating Syndrome Nocturnal food intake predominates. Kleine–Levin syndrome Hypersomnia + hyperphagia.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: EDE-Q. Medical: electrolytes, ECG, dental examination. C-SSRS.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT-E first-line (Fairburn) — 20 sessions over 20 weeks; evidence: Fairburn C.G. et al. Am J Psychiatry 2009;166(3):311–319. Fluoxetine 60 mg/day — FDA approval for BN; reduces binge eating and purging. FBT (Lock J., Le Grange D.) — in adolescents. IPT alternative. Medical: electrolyte correction, refeeding, dental care. Bupropion is contraindicated (seizure risk).

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT-E (Fairburn) — 20 sessions; transdiagnostic; disruption of binge-purge cycle. FBT for BN — Adapted for adolescents. Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) — Alternative; slow response, but sustained effect.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG69 — CBT-E first-line; FBT in adolescents. APA 2023.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: 50–70% remission with CBT-E; long-term follow-up is essential.

title: Myth 1: “Bulimia is a ‘diet failure’”
text: Evidence: Clinical impairment; restrictive diet is a typical trigger.

title: Myth 2: “Vomiting is an effective weight loss method”
text: Evidence: Vomiting prevents only 30–50% of calorie absorption; serious medical complications.

title: Myth 3: “Bupropion can be used as an antidepressant in BN”
text: Evidence: bupropion in BN is contraindicated — seizure risk is high.

title: Myth 4: “BN is not a problem if weight is normal”
text: Evidence: Medical complications (electrolyte, cardiac) and psychiatric burden are significant.

title: Myth 5: “Only antidepressants are sufficient”
text: Evidence: CBT-E + pharmacotherapy combination is superior.
