title: Binge eating disorder (BED) (Binge eating disorder)
text: Binge eating disorder (BED) (Binge eating disorder) Binge eating disorder ICD-10 F50.8 Other eating disorders DSM-5-TR F50.81 Binge-Eating Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Binge-Eating Disorder (BED) (ICD-11: 6B82; DSM-5-TR: F50.81) — recurrent episodes of binge eating (large amount of food in a short period + sense of loss of control), without compensatory behaviors. Weight is typically increased, often with obesity.

title: 2. History
text: Stunkard A.J. (1959) — description of binge eating in the context of obesity. DSM-IV (1994) — Listed in the research appendix. DSM-5 (2013) — separate official diagnosis.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 1.9–3.5%; most common among eating disorders. Sex: 1.5–2:1 in females; but also significant in males. Strong association with obesity. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, BPD, substance use.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 40–50%. Neurobiological — reward circuit dysregulation; ‘food addiction’ hypothesis. Emotional eating — stress trigger. History of restrictive diet.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Binge eating episodes — large amount of food in short time, loss of control. Typical features: rapid eating, continuing despite fullness, secretive eating, subsequent shame, guilt. No compensatory behavior. Weight gain and obesity complications (Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular, hepatic steatosis).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Repeated binge eating episodes. B. Episodes associated with at least 3 of the following: Rapid eating Eating until physically full; Binge eating without hunger; Secretive eating (due to shame); Feeling disgusted with oneself, depressed, or very guilty afterward. C. Significant distress. D. Frequency: 1 time per week, ≥3 months. E. Does not occur in the context of bulimia or anorexia; no compensatory behavior.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — severity based on episode frequency. ICD-11 — no severity scale: DSM-5-TR grades by episode count (mild 1–3, moderate 4–7, severe 8–13, extreme ≥14 per week), whereas ICD-11 says only “once a week or more over a period of several months”.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. EDE-Q. Medical assessment — metabolic syndrome screening (glucose, HbA1c, lipids, blood pressure). Comorbidity.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Bulimia (6B81) Compensatory behavior. Obesity (without compulsive eating) No binge eating episode features. Kleine–Levin Hyperphagia + hypersomnia. Prader–Willi syndrome Genetic; hyperphagia out of control.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: EDE-Q. BMI, weight, vital signs. Metabolic panel.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT-E first-line — Wilson G.T. et al.’s randomized trial indicated a significant effect in BED. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) 50–70 mg/day — FDA approval for BED; significantly reduces binge-eating frequency (McElroy S.L. JAMA Psychiatry 2015). SSRI — for comorbid MDD; modest effect on binge eating frequency. IPT alternative. Weight management — diet, physical activity; weight loss is not effective without BED intervent

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT-E for BED — Breaking the binge cycle, alternative coping. Lisdexamfetamine — FDA approval for BED; start 30 mg, target 50–70 mg/day. IPT — Focus on interpersonal issues. Guided Self-Help CBT (Guided Self-Help) — Internet-based, book-based.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG69 — CBT or guided self-help first-line. APA 2023. McElroy lisdexamfetamine RCTs.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: 50–60% remission with CBT-E. Weight management and metabolic complications require long-term monitoring.

title: Myth 1: “BED is just obesity or an ‘overeating’ personality trait”
text: Evidence: Clinical eating disorder; distinguished from an isolated binge eating episode by loss of control and shameful eating (loss of control, shameful eating).

title: Myth 2: “Restrictive diet cures BED”
text: Evidence: Restrictive diet triggers BED — weight control without psychological intervention increases binge eating.

title: Myth 3: “Bariatric surgery cures BED”
text: Evidence: Surgery reduces gastric capacity but does not modify the cognitive-behavioral component; in some patients, a new pattern of “grazing” develops.

title: Myth 4: “Eating is an ‘addiction’ (food addiction), must be treated like drugs”
text: Evidence: “Food addiction” is a concept but not accepted as a clinical diagnosis; standard eating disorder interventions are superior.

title: Myth 5: “BED only requires an antidepressant”
text: Evidence: lisdexamfetamine FDA approval for BED; CBT first-line.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B82 Binge eating disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. NICE NG69. 2017/2020. McElroy S.L. et al. Efficacy and safety of lisdexamfetamine for treatment of adults with moderate to severe binge eating disorder. JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(3):235–246. Wilson G.T., Wilfley D.E., Agras W.S., Bryson S.W. Psychological treatments of binge eating disorder. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010;67(1):94–101.

title: Pica
text: Pica ICD-10 F98.3 Pica of infancy and childhood DSM-5-TR F98.3 / F50.83 Pica

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Pica (ICD-11: 6B84; DSM-5-TR: F98.3) — persistent (≥ 1 month) ingestion of non-food, non-nutritive substances (clay, hair, paper, soap, metal, stones) — inappropriate for developmental age.

title: 2. History
text: “Pica” — from the Latin word for “magpie” (magpie eats everything). DSM-III (1980) — As a childhood disorder. DSM-5 (2013) — diagnosis possible at all ages.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: children 4–26%, higher in intellectual disability, pregnant women 8–65%, iron deficiency anemia. Comorbidity: autism, intellectual disability, iron deficiency, adult malabsorption.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Nutritional deficiencies (iron, zinc) — may be worsened by pica substance ingestion in some patients. Neurodevelopmental disorders (autism, ID). Pregnancy — physiological and micronutrient. Cultural — consumption of clay in some traditions (geophagy).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Geophagy (clay, soil), trichophagy (hair), pagophagy (ice), amylophagy (starch), plumbophagy (paint — lead risk). Complications: intestinal obstruction (trichobezoar), lead poisoning, parasitic infection, dental injury, perforation.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent intake of substances with no nutritional value ≥ 1 month. B. The behavior is not developmentally appropriate (≥ 2 years of age). C. Not a culturally or socially accepted practice. D. If occurring in the context of another mental disorder or medical condition — additional diagnosis required (especially in ID and ASD).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR requires a duration of at least 1 month; ICD-11 sets no duration criterion — it says “persistent or severe enough to require clinical attention”. The developmental age of about 2 years is the same in both.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Interview + observation. Laboratory — complete blood count, ferritin, iron, lead level, zinc. Abdominal imaging (obstruction). Neurodevelopmental assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature OCD (6B20) It is based on obsession. Factitious (6D50) Sick-role motivation. Anorexia binge-eating type (6B80) Body image. Cultural food practices Context.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Iron, lead, zinc, parasite tests. Abdominal X-ray / ultrasound.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Correction of nutritional deficiency (iron, zinc). Behavioral intervention — habit reversal, environmental modification, alternative stimuli. Intellectual disability comorbid with ASD — functional behavior analysis and ABA-based approach. Medical management of complications (lead poisoning — chelation only with specific indication). During pregnancy — nutritional support.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Functional Behavior Analysis (FBA) — Identification of behavior trigger and maintainer. Environmental Modification — Restriction of access to non-food substances. Nutritional Correction — Iron, zinc, vitamin supplements. ABA-based intervention — In ID and ASD.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AAP — pica assessment and lead screening in children.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Remission in children through nutritional correction and behavioral intervention. May persist in the context of ID/ASD; long-term follow-up.

title: Myth 1: “Pica is just a child’s ‘exploratory’ behavior”
text: Evidence: Pica is normal developmental behavior up to about 2 years; subsequent continuation is clinical and poses a risk of complications.

title: Myth 2: “Lead poisoning requires chelation for everyone”
text: Evidence: chelation is indicated only at high levels (BLL ≥ 45 µg/dL typical); environmental remediation first-line at lower levels.

title: Myth 3: “Pica in pregnancy is ‘the baby’s wish’, requires no intervention”
text: Evidence: pica as a marker of iron or other deficiency; nutritional correction recommended.

title: Myth 4: “Pica in an ID/ASD patient is ‘inevitable’”
text: Evidence: Behavioral interventions (ABA, FBA) are effective; the “inevitable” explanation leads to severe complications such as trichobezoar, obstruction.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B84 Pica. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Young S.L. Pica in pregnancy: new ideas about an old condition. Annu Rev Nutr 2010;30:403–422. Hyman S.L. et al. AAP 2020 Clinical Report (ASD). Pediatrics 2020;145(1):e20193447.

title: Rumination-regurgitation disorder
text: Rumination-regurgitation disorder ICD-10 F98.2 Feeding disorder of infancy and childhood DSM-5-TR F98.21 / F50.84 Rumination Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Rumination-Regurgitation Disorder (ICD-11: 6B85; DSM-5-TR: F98.21) — characterized by voluntary or semi-voluntary regurgitation of swallowed food followed by re-chewing, re-swallowing, or spitting out. It is not fully explained by a medical condition (gastroesophageal reflux or other GI disease).

title: 2. History
text: The term ‘merycism’ was used in ancient times. DSM-IV — As an infant and childhood disorder. DSM-5 (2013) — diagnosis at all ages.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: rare in infants and children; 6–10% in patients with intellectual disability; increasing recognition in adults (especially comorbid with eating disorders). Comorbidity: ID, ASD, anxiety, BN, BED.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Behavioral conditioning — ‘post-prandial belching’ followed by regurgitation as a learned behavior. Stress and anxiety. In ID/ASD, self-stimulation with food.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Regurgitation minutes to hours after food intake. Eating disorder outcomes: weight loss, malnutrition, electrolyte imbalance, dental erosion, halitosis. Social consequences: shame, social isolation.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Recurrent regurgitation of swallowed food — DSM-5-TR: ≥ 1 month; ICD-11: several times a week over at least several weeks; re-chewing, re-swallowing, or spitting out. B. Regurgitation is not related to a medical condition (e.g., reflux, pyloric stenosis, duodenal obstruction). C. Does not occur in the context of anorexia, bulimia, BED, ARFID. D. If occurring in the context of another mental disorder (especially ID

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — criteria overlap; the duration and the age threshold differ: DSM-5-TR requires ≥ 1 month, ICD-11 requires several times a week over at least several weeks and a developmental age of ≥ 2 years.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Medical assessment — exclusion of GERD, pyloric pathology, gastroparesis (upper endoscopy, motility study). Manometry — confirmation of functional regurgitation. Weight and nutritional status. Comorbid eating disorder screening.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature GERD Typical regurgitation; pH monitoring. Bulimia (6B81) Vomiting voluntarily for compensatory purposes. Anorexia (6B80) Fear of weight. Gastroparesis Motility study. Pyloric obstruction Endoscopy.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Endoscopy, manometry, pH-monitoring. Complete blood count, electrolytes.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Diaphragmatic breathing — first-line behavioral intervention (Chitkara D.K. et al. Am J Gastroenterol 2006; effect 50–70%). Habit reversal — learning alternative behavior. Biofeedback. Stress management and CBT. In ID/ASD, functional behavior analysis and ABA. Medical: GERD: proton pump inhibitor as initial intervention.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Diaphragmatic Breathing — Slow abdominal breathing for 5–10 minutes after eating — prevents regurgitation. Habit Reversal Training (HRT — Habit Reversal Training) — Developing alternative behaviors. Biofeedback — Abdominal muscle control. FBA — functional behavior analysis (in ID/ASD) — Analysis of behavior trigger and maintainer.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Rome Foundation criteria (functional GI). NICE NG69 — general eating disorder principles.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with diaphragmatic breathing and habit reversal.

title: Myth 1: “Rumination is a form of GERD”
text: Evidence: distinct disorder; manometry and clinical model differ.

title: Myth 2: “Only medical surgery (Nissen) solves it”
text: Evidence: Nissen fundoplication ineffective for functional rumination and contraindicated; behavioral intervention first-line.

title: Myth 3: “The patient behaves ‘volitionally’, requires discipline”
text: Evidence: It is a semi-voluntary behavior, based on conditioning; punishment is ineffective.

title: Myth 4: “Antiemetics are effective”
text: Evidence: Antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron) are ineffective in rumination.

title: Myth 5: “Cannot be discontinued in a patient with ID/ASD”
text: Evidence: Behavioral interventions are effective; active intervention is essential to prevent nutritional complications.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6B85 Rumination-regurgitation disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Chitkara D.K., Van Tilburg M., Whitehead W.E., Talley N.J. Teaching diaphragmatic breathing for rumination syndrome. Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101(11):2449–2452. Rome IV Diagnostic Criteria for Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction. Rome Foundation; 2016.

title: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)
text: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder) Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder ICD-10 F98.2 Feeding disorder of infancy and childhood DSM-5-TR
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID; ICD-11: 6B83; DSM-5-TR: F50.82) — significant weight loss, nutritional deficiency, enteral feeding dependence, or psychosocial impairment resulting from avoidance or restriction of food intake. No body image disturbance or fear of weight gain (key difference from anorexia).
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 2. History
text: DSM-IV ‘Feeding Disorder of Infancy or Early Childhood’ — only in children. DSM-5 (2013) — ARFID expanded to all ages.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 0.3–3.2% (~5–14% in eating disorder clinics). Sex: approximately equal (unlike anorexia). Onset: predominantly in childhood and adolescence. Comorbidity: autism spectrum, anxiety, OCD.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Sensory sensitivity (food texture, smell, appearance) — especially in autism. Fear of choking or vomiting trauma. Low interest in food (low appetite, low food interest).
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 5. Clinical features
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: Three clinical presentations
text: Sensory sensitivity — “picky eating” — limited food variety, texture sensitivity. Low interest in food — low hunger, little interest in food. Fear (choking, vomiting) — avoidance following a specific triggering event. Consequences: significant weight loss or insufficient weight gain (in children), nutritional deficiencies (iron, zinc, vitamins), dependence on enteral feeding, social disruption (school meals, eating w
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. As a result of avoidance or restriction of food intake, at least one of: Significant weight loss or failure to achieve adequate weight gain; Significant nutritional deficiency; Enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplement dependence; Significant psychosocial impairment. B. The disturbance is not explained by existing nutritional deficiency or cultural experience. C. Does not occur in the context of anorexia or b
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same. NICE NG69 does not cover ARFID; no specific recommendation.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview and dietary history. NIAS (Nine Item ARFID Screen) — screening. Medical evaluation — weight, height, BMI, laboratory nutritional deficiency. Screening for autism and OCD. Exclusion of allergy and GI pathology.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Anorexia (6B80) Body image and weight fear are central. Autism spectrum (6A02) Sensory sensitivity component; ARFID can be comorbid with ASD. OCD (6B20) Contamination obsessions primary; ritualized behavior. Specific phobia (6B03) Specific object; multiple food types in ARFID. Allergy / Crohn’s / celiac disease Medical confirmation.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: NIAS, EDE-Q. Weight, height, BMI history. Laboratory: complete blood count, ferritin, zinc, vitamin D, B12, folate. Autism screening (M-CHAT, ADOS).
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 8. Treatment
text: Multidisciplinary approach: nutritionist + CBT therapist + feeding-occupational therapist. FBT-ARFID — adapted by Lock J. CBT-AR — Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for ARFID (Thomas J.J.) — manualized. Stepped food exposure — gradual introduction of new food types. Sensory integration elements (on autism background). Medical: nutritional correction; enteral feeding in severe cases. SSRIs for comorbid anxiety; no FDA-appr
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for ARFID (CBT-AR — CBT for ARFID) — Thomas (Thomas J.J.) — Manualized; protocols tailored to sensory, low interest, fear subtypes. FBT-ARFID — The role of the family in the exposure to food. Stepped Food Exposure — New food approach → touch → taste → swallow steps. Nine Item ARFID Screen (NIAS) — 3 subtype screening.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Expert consensus — graded food exposure. Thomas J.J. CBT-AR — a new evidence base.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With a multidisciplinary approach, improvement in most patients. Long-term follow-up in the context of autism and OCD.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: Myth 1: “ARFID is just ‘picky eating’”
text: Evidence: Clinical diagnosis requires significant functional impairment or nutritional deficiency.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: Myth 2: “The patient can be forced to eat by starvation”
text: Evidence: Hunger strategy ineffective in ARFID and harmful to family-child relationship; stepwise exposure recommended.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: Myth 3: “ARFID is a ‘mild form’ of anorexia”
text: Evidence: distinct clinical entity; body image disturbance and weight concern absent; intervention differs.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: Myth 4: “ARFID on the autism spectrum cannot be treated”
text: Evidence: sensory integration and behavioral approaches are also effective in the context of autism.
sub: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) (Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder)

title: Myth 5: “The patient will outgrow it”
text: Evidence: It can progress without treatment; early intervention prevents nutritional complications.

title: Enuresis
text: Enuresis ICD-10 F98.0 Nonorganic enuresis DSM-5-TR F98.0 Enuresis

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Enuresis (ICD-11: 6C00; DSM-5-TR: F98.0) — voluntary or involuntary urination persisting when the child’s developmental age reaches at least 5 years. Frequency: at least twice a week for ≥ 3 months or significant functional impairment. Subtypes (ICCS — International Children’s Continence Society 2014): Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis — only nocturnal, no daytime symptoms; Non-monosymptomatic enuresis — daytime sym

title: 2. History
text: In the 19th century, familial clustering of enuresis began to be noted in the clinical literature. Mowrer O.H. (1938) — invented the pad-and-bell alarm. ICCS (1989) — international standardization. NICE CG111 (2010) — nocturnal enuresis clinical guideline.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: Age 5: 5–10%, Age 10: 3–5%, ≥ 15 years: approximately 1% (DSM-5-TR). Sex: male 2:1. Spontaneous remission occurs in approximately 15% per year. Comorbidity: ADHD ~30%, anxiety, conduct disorders, constipation.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability approximately 70% (twin and family studies). Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis — pathogenesis: Immaturity of nocturnal vasopressin (ADH) secretion (nocturnal polyuria); Elevation of arousal threshold; Bladder capacity below age norm. Non-monosymptomatic form — bladder overactivity, association with constipation. Secondary enuresis — stress, urinary infection (UTI), diabetes, psychiatric trigger.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Nocturnal enuresis. Daytime symptoms (non-monosymptomatic): urgency, holding maneuvers (Vincent’s curtsy, leg crossing), increased frequency, incontinence. Social-emotional: shame, decreased self-esteem, avoidance of social activities (camping, sleepovers).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 / ICCS 2014)
text: A. Repeated urinary incontinence (in bed or clothes), voluntary or involuntary. B. Frequency: ≥2 times per week, ≥3 months; or significant distress/functional impairment. C. Developmental age ≥ 5 years. D. Not explained by a substance (diuretic) or medical condition (diabetes, UTI, structural anomaly). Qualifiers: only nocturnal / only diurnal / nocturnal and diurnal; primary / secondary; monosymptomatic / non-monosy

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICCS 2014 — subtype terminology standard. NICE CG111 — diagnosis and algorithm. AAP — pediatric assessment.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview — onset, frequency, daytime symptoms, family history. Urinalysis and culture — rule out UTI. Voiding diary 3 days — for daytime symptoms. Constipation assessment (Bristol Stool Chart). Medical: weight, glucose, blood pressure. If structural anomaly suspected — urinary ultrasound; uroflowmetry in non-monosymptomatic case.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature UTI Urine culture positive. Diabetes (Type 1) Polyuria, polydipsia; glucose high. Diabetes insipidus Specific gravity low. Structural anomaly (ectopic ureter) Persistent leakage; ultrasound. Neurogenic bladder Spinal cord pathology. Constipation Clinical and Bristol Stool. Seizure (ictal enuresis) EEG.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Urine analysis, culture. Voiding and constipation diary. Urinary ultrasound (atypical presentation). Comorbid ADHD, anxiety screening.

title: 8.1 General principles (ICCS 2020 · NICE CG111)
text: Behavioral intervention: Conservative recommendations — reducing fluid intake before bedtime, adequate water intake during the day, regular urination, resolving constipation. Positive reinforcement (star chart) — for dry nights. First-line specific intervention: Enuresis alarm — pad-and-bell; ≥ 6 years old, if motivated; long-term good outcome; about 50% achieve 14 consecutive dry nights and about 40% remain dry at f

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Enuresis Alarm — Mowrer — Bed alarm or clothing alarm (humidity sensor); ≥ 4 weeks continuous use; typical use 12–16 weeks. Cochrane meta-analysis — most evidence-based long-term method. Desmopressin — Oral 0.2–0.4 mg or sublingual melt 120–240 µg; 1 hour before bedtime; limiting fluids before bedtime is important (risk of hyponatremia). Voiding and Constipation Diary — 3-day; frequency, volume, bladder capacity, day

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: ICCS 2020 — alarm and desmopressin first-line; “wait and see” until age 5, then active intervention. NICE CG111 — same algorithm. AAP — pediatric recommendations.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Spontaneous remission occurs in approximately 15% per year; with intervention, remission occurs in most patients. Constipation management is important. Comorbid ADHD, anxiety — parallel intervention.

title: Myth 1: “In nocturnal enuresis, iontophoresis (drug electrophoresis) to the groin and buttock area stimulates the urinary center”
text: Why it is widespread: Soviet-era physiotherapy practice; presented as “safe” by family doctors. Clinical logic: If daytime urine output is normal and the problem did not spontaneously arise after any illness, the problem is not at the kidney/bladder/spinal cord level. Pathogenesis is ADH dysregulation, arousal threshold and bladder capacity — electrophoresis does not affect these. Evidence: ICCS 2020, NICE CG111 — no

title: Myth 2: “It will just pass on its own, no intervention needed”
text: Evidence: Spontaneous remission ~15% per year, but untreated persistence creates social-emotional burden; ICCS 2020 recommends active intervention from age 5+.

title: Myth 3: “Punishment or insult corrects a child”
text: Evidence: Punishment is contraindicated; self-esteem reduction, depression risk; positive reinforcement is superior.

title: Myth 4: “Pre-bedtime water restriction alone is sufficient”
text: Evidence: Adjunct measure; ineffective alone in most patients; requires specific intervention.

title: Myth 5: “Imipramine or antidepressants are first-line”
text: Evidence: imipramine in refractory cases; cardiac side effects and overdose risk; alarm and desmopressin are superior to it.

title: Myth 6: “Acupuncture and homeopathy cure enuresis”
text: Evidence: Cochrane reviews — the effect of these complementary interventions has not been proven.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C00 Enuresis. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. NICE CG111. Nocturnal enuresis in children and young people under 19. 2010. Nevéus T. et al. Management and treatment of nocturnal enuresis — an updated standardization document from the International Children’s Continence Society. J Pediatr Urol 2020;16(1):10–19. Caldwell P.H., Codarini M., Stewart F. et al. Alarm interventions for nocturnal enuresis in children

title: Encopresis
text: Encopresis ICD-10 F98.1 Nonorganic encopresis DSM-5-TR F98.1 Encopresis

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Encopresis (ICD-11: 6C01; DSM-5-TR: F98.1) — voluntary or involuntary defecation into inappropriate places (clothing, floor) persisting when the child’s developmental age reaches at least 4 years. Frequency: at least once a month for ≥ 3 months. Subtypes: Retentive (overflow incontinence) — based on constipation; ~80% of cases; Non-retentive — no constipation.

title: 2. History
text: DSM-II (1968) — first recognized; DSM-III (1980) — separate diagnosis. Rome IV — consensus within the functional GI framework. NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN functional constipation guideline (Tabbers M.M. et al. 2014).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: 1–4% among ages 4–17; 3–6 times higher in boys. ~80% are primarily constipation-related (retentive). Comorbidity: enuresis, ADHD, anxiety, autism spectrum.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Constipation — key mechanism (in retentive encopresis); painful defecation → retention → rectal dilatation → sensory reduction → overflow. Trauma, fear, and discipline in the toilet-training process. Diet (low fiber, dehydration). Behavioral and emotional factors — oppositional, anxiety. In rare cases — Hirschsprung disease (rectal aganglionosis), spinal pathology.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Fecal soiling of clothing. Retentive — fecal mass on abdominal palpation; dilated rectum; large (massive) defecation episodes. Social-emotional: shame, social isolation, school avoidance.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Defecation into inappropriate places (clothes, floor), voluntary or involuntary. B. Frequency: ≥1 time per month, ≥3 months. C. Developmental age ≥ 4 years. D. Not fully explained by substance (laxative) or medical condition (Hirschsprung, anatomical anomaly, spinal pathology). Qualifier: with/without constipation and overflow.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN 2014 — functional constipation guideline (Rome IV). NICE CG99 (2010) — constipation in children and adolescents.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview — defecation frequency, pain, toilet training history. Abdominal palpation — fecal mass. Rectal examination — fecal impaction (or other findings, if clinically indicated). Defecation diary (Bristol Stool Form Scale) Medical: thyroid (hypothyroid constipation), serum calcium, celiac disease screening. Atypical presentation: ultrasound, anorectal manometry, suction biopsy (Hirschsprung).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Hirschsprung disease Congenital constipation; narrow, empty rectum on rectal exam; biopsy aganglionosis. Hypothyroidism TSH. Spinal pathology Neurological signs; MRI. Celiac disease Anti-tTG. Anal structural anomaly Physical examination, ultrasound.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Abdominal and rectal examination. Bristol Stool, defecation diary. TSH, calcium, anti-TTG selectively. Ultrasound, manometry in atypical cases.

title: 8.1 General principles (NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN · NICE CG99)
text: Removal of impaction (disimpaction) — PEG (polyethylene glycol) high dose for 3–6 days; oral route preferred; enemas are second-line — more invasive. Maintenance — PEG 0.4 g/kg/day for months to years; keeps defecation regular and painless. Behavioral intervention: Regular toilet time (15–20 minutes after meals, gastrocolic reflex); Correct foot support (defecation position); Positive reinforcement (no punishment). D

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: PEG (Polyethylene Glycol) — Osmotic laxative; disimpaction 1–1.5 g/kg/day × 3–6 days; maintenance 0.4 g/kg/day; months to years; side effects minimal. Toilet Time and Position — 5–10 minutes toilet time 15–20 minutes after meals; foot support — hip flexion straightens the anorectal angle and reduces straining; on videomanometry the angle during defecation is ~100° when sitting and ~126° when squatting (Sakakibara R.

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN 2014 — PEG first-line; enema traumatic and second-line. NICE CG99 — same. Cochrane (Gordon M. et al. 2016) — PEG superior to lactulose.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: PEG and behavioral intervention lead to remission in most patients (50–80% within 1 year). Long-term maintenance therapy is recommended; early discontinuation creates relapse risk.

title: Myth 1: “Encopresis results from psychological ‘stubbornness’ or emotional disorder”
text: Evidence: Approximately 80% of cases are primarily due to constipation; medical/behavioral consultation is the first-line approach, not psychological. The patient’s explanation of “intentional” behavior is incorrect.

title: Myth 2: “A child can be corrected through punishment”
text: Evidence: NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN — punishment is contraindicated; increases self-blame and distress.

title: Myth 3: “Enema is a first-line intervention”
text: Evidence: Oral PEG is superior; enema is traumatic, second-line.

title: Myth 4: “Dietary change alone is sufficient”
text: Evidence: Fiber/water mild adjunct effect; impaction correction and maintenance require PEG.

title: Myth 5: “Encopresis resolves with age, requires no treatment”
text: Evidence: Chronic progression without treatment, social-emotional burden; active intervention recommended.

title: Myth 6: “Probiotics cure encopresis”
text: Evidence: Cochrane — the significant effect of probiotics has not been proven.

title: Bodily distress disorder
text: Bodily distress disorder ICD-10 F45.0 Somatization disorder DSM-5-TR F45.1 Somatic Symptom Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: ICD-11: 6C20 Bodily Distress Disorder; DSM-5-TR: F45.1 Somatic Symptom Disorder — a psychiatric disorder characterized by excessive focus, anxiety, and behavioral interference created by somatic complaints (pain, fatigue, gastrointestinal or cardiopulmonary symptoms), accompanied by functional impairment. Clinical diagnosis is made not on the ‘inexplicability’ of symptoms, but on persistent preoccupation and distress

title: 2. History
text: Briquet P. (1859) — “hysteria” with multiple somatic symptoms. DSM-III (1980) — “Somatoform Disorders” group. DSM-5 (2013) — Fundamental change: requirement for “medically unexplained symptoms” removed; whether the somatic symptom is real or not is not a criterion — the patient’s reaction is the diagnostic focus. ICD-11 (2019) — “Bodily Distress Disorder” — based on the European model of bodily distress (Fink P., Sch

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: In primary care: 5–15%. Sex: 2–3 times higher in females. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, panic, factitious, real medical illnesses. High healthcare utilization and costs.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Biopsychosocial model — biological vulnerability + cognitive-affective emotional components + social reinforcement. Trauma and childhood illness history. Cognitive — catastrophizing and hypervigilance to bodily sensations.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Persistent somatic symptoms (pain, fatigue, gastrointestinal, cardiopulmonary). ≥ 1 of the following: Excessive and persistent thoughts about the severity of symptoms; High anxiety about health; Excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms. Duration ≥ 6 months. Functional impairment. “Doctor shopping”, repeated checking, avoidance behavior.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. One or more somatic symptoms — causing distress or functional impairment to the patient. B. ≥ 1 of the following: Excessive thoughts about the severity of symptoms; High anxiety about health; Excessive time/energy on symptoms. C. Persistence ≥ 6 months.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — “with predominant pain” and severity specifiers. ICD-11 — ‘Bodily Distress Disorder’ — close to the European ‘bodily distress syndrome’ concept (Fink P.); severity (mild, moderate, severe). German S3 Guideline (Funktionelle Körperbeschwerden, 2018) — biopsychosocial approach.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. PHQ-15 (somatic symptom scale), SSS-8. Medical assessment — exclusion of somatic illness (but avoid excessive testing). Comorbidity (MDD, anxiety, factitious, real illnesses).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Hypochondriasis (6B23) Illness preoccupation dominant; somatic symptoms minimal. Real medical illness Clinical and laboratory confirmation; however, somatic symptom disorder may be comorbid. Dissociative neurological symptom disorder (6B60) Specific neurological symptoms; “positive signs”. Factitious (6D50) Factitious; patient role, no gain. Malingering Overt material/legal gain. MDD

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PHQ-15, SSS-8, Whiteley Index (health anxiety). One-time comprehensive medical examination; then minimal repetition. Comorbidity scales.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Biopsychosocial approach and stepped care — primary care physician at the center, with a psychiatrist or psychologist as an adjunct. Single physician model (single physician approach) — all complaints are managed through that physician. CBT — cognitive restructuring, reduction of catastrophic interpretation of bodily sensations, behavioral activation. Evidence: van Dessel N. Cochrane 2014 (CD011142). SSRI — for comor

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for Somatic Symptom — Cognitive restructuring + behavioral intervention (avoidance reduction, exposure). van Dessel N. Cochrane 2014 (CD011142). Single Physician Model — Structured visit; limited number of checks; sequential explanation. PHQ-15, SSS-8 — Somatic complaint scales. Stepped Care — CBT-based brief intervention at the primary care level; then specialized service.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: German S3 Guideline — integrated care at the primary care level. NICE — no separate guideline for somatic symptom disorder; general principles.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: CBT and a multidisciplinary approach lead to significant improvement; chronic course.

title: Myth 1: “The patient is ‘faking’ symptoms”
text: Evidence: symptoms are real for the patient; somatic disorder is a clinical condition, not simulation.

title: Myth 2: “Saying ‘nothing is wrong’ after a medical exam will reassure the patient”
text: Evidence: Negative reassurance is short-term; maintains long-term anxiety. Structured explanation and biopsychosocial model are superior.

title: Myth 3: “Only a prolonged medical investigation will reveal the diagnosis”
text: Evidence: repeated checking increases somatic focus and costs; one-time comprehensive assessment, then limited.

title: Myth 4: “Somatic symptom disorder is only a ‘mental illness’”
text: Evidence: biopsychosocial disorder; biological components (sensory sensitivity, gut-brain axis) are real.

title: Myth 5: “Antidepressant is the ‘treatment’ for somatic symptom disorder”
text: Evidence: SSRI for comorbid symptoms; CBT first-line.

title: Disorders due to use of alcohol
text: Disorders due to use of alcohol ICD-10 F10 Mental and behavioral disorders due to use of alcohol DSM-5-TR F10.20 Alcohol Use Disorder, Moderate or Severe
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Disorders due to use of alcohol (ICD-11: 6C40; DSM-5-TR: F10.20 Alcohol Use Disorder, AUD) — a group of disorders characterized by impaired control over alcohol use, continued use despite physical or psychological harm. ICD-11 subtypes: harmful pattern of use (6C40.1), alcohol dependence (6C40.2), intoxication (6C40.3), withdrawal syndrome (6C40.4), alcohol-induced delirium, psychotic, mood, anxiety disorders.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 2. History
text: Jellinek E.M. (1960) — ‘The Disease Concept of Alcoholism’ — alcoholism as a disease. DSM-IV — ‘Abuse’ and ‘Dependence’ as separate categories. DSM-5 (2013) — unified ‘Alcohol Use Disorder’ (mild, moderate, severe). ICD-11 — episodic harmful use, harmful pattern of use and dependence separated.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 14–29% (NIAAA NESARC); annual 5–14%. Sex: 2–3 times higher in males, but increasing in females. Mortality: about 2.6 million deaths per year worldwide (WHO 2024, 2019 data). Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, PTSD, BPD, other substance use, liver disease, cardiovascular.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability ~49% (95% CI 43–53) (Verhulst B. et al. Psychol Med 2015). Neurobiological — dopamine reward circuit, GABA, glutamate, opioid systems. Environment — peers, stress, alcohol availability, cultural norms. Genetic markers — ADH1B, ALDH2 (protective in Asian population).
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 5. Clinical features
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 5.1 Alcohol use disorder (DSM-5-TR criteria, ≥ 2 out of 11)
text: More/prolonged use; Unsuccessful attempts to cut down; A great deal of time is spent obtaining, using, or recovering from substances Craving; Work/school disruption; Continues despite social-interpersonal problem. Refusal of important activities; Use in a dangerous situation; Continuation despite physical/psychological problem; Tolerance; Withdrawal syndrome.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 5.2 Intoxication
text: Disinhibition, dysarthria, ataxia, nystagmus, cognitive impairment. Severe intoxication — coma, respiratory depression, hypoglycemia, death.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 5.3 Withdrawal
text: Mild: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, nausea (6–24 hours after last drink). Moderate: autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations (alcoholic hallucinosis). Severe: delirium tremens (DT) — 48–96 hours; altered consciousness, hallucinations, autonomic crisis; mortality ~1–4% among hospitalized patients (Schuckit M.A. N Engl J Med 2014); substantially higher in historical untreated series; seizures.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 5.4 Complications
text: Wernicke–Korsakoff (B1 deficiency), alcoholic liver disease, cardiomyopathy, polyneuropathy, fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS).
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR — ≥2 of 11 criteria (mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6); ICD-11 — pattern of use (single episode of harmful use, harmful pattern of use, dependence); hazardous use belongs to QE10, not to 6C4x. sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: WHO AUDIT (Saunders 1993) — 10-item screening. NICE CG115 — diagnosis and treatment of alcohol disorders. SAMHSA TIP — international protocols.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: AUDIT, AUDIT-C screening at primary care level. Clinical interview — TLFB (Timeline Followback) use pattern. Laboratory: GGT, AST/ALT, MCV, CDT (carbohydrate-deficient transferrin), complete blood count. Comorbidity (MDD, anxiety, PTSD, somatic illnesses). Withdrawal risk (CIWA-Ar).
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Other substance use Toxicology screening. MDD with self-medication Affective symptoms are primary. Bipolar disorder Affective episodes. Hyperthyroidism TSH. Seizure disorder EEG.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: AUDIT, CIWA-Ar (withdrawal severity). GGT, MCV, CDT, transaminases. Thiamine level. ECG, echocardiography (cardiomyopathy). Comorbidity screening.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 8. Treatment
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG115 · SAMHSA TIP 49 · APA 2018)
text: Detoxification: Mild (CIWA-Ar <10) — outpatient; Moderate-severe — inpatient (hospitalization); Benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam) — gold standard for withdrawal treatment; Thiamine 100–300 mg IV/IM × 3–5 days (Wernicke prophylaxis — BEFORE glucose). Hydration, electrolyte correction. Pharmacotherapy for relapse prevention: Naltrexone (oral 50 mg or IM Vivitrol 380 mg monthly) — first-line; reduces cravings. Acampr
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Motivational Interviewing (MI) — Miller W.R., Rollnick S — Enhancing readiness for behavior change; targets “ambivalence”. CBT for substance use — Trigger recognition, cravings management, coping skills, relapse prevention. Naltrexone, Acamprosate, Disulfiram — Pharmacotherapy against relapse. 12-Step Facilitation (AA, NA) — Project MATCH RCT — comparative effectiveness of CBT and MI. AUDIT, CIWA-Ar — Screening and w
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG115 (2011). APA Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients with Alcohol Use Disorder (2018). SAMHSA TIP 49 (2009).
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With a multimodal approach, 40–50% achieve long-term remission. Comorbid MDD, BPD, other substance use disorder — poor prognosis.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Myth 1: “Alcoholism is a weakness of character”
text: Evidence: Jellinek 1960; WHO — alcohol use disorder is a medical condition; heritability approximately 50%.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Myth 2: “Detoxification alone is treatment”
text: Evidence: Detoxification is the initial step; relapse-prevention treatment is required; detox alone leads to 90%+ relapse.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Myth 3: “Naltrexone makes alcohol ‘unacceptable’”
text: Evidence: Naltrexone reduces craving and diminishes alcohol’s ‘reward’ effect; differs from disulfiram.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Myth 4: “The patient must hit ‘rock bottom’ before treatment begins”
text: Evidence: Early intervention is more effective; the “rock bottom” concept is not evidence-based.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Myth 5: “Alcohol is the safest substance and requires no treatment”
text: Evidence: WHO — alcohol causes 2.6 million deaths annually (WHO 2024, 2019 data); DT mortality is ~1–4% among hospitalized patients (Schuckit M.A. N Engl J Med 2014); substantially higher in historical untreated series.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Myth 6: “‘A little alcohol is safe’ in pregnant women”
text: Evidence: CDC, AAP — any amount of alcohol during pregnancy creates a risk of FAS; there is no ‘safe’ dose.
sub: Disorders due to use of alcohol

title: Disorders due to use of opioids
text: Disorders due to use of opioids ICD-10 F11 Mental and behavioral disorders due to use of opioids DSM-5-TR F11.20 Opioid Use Disorder, Moderate or Severe
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Disorders due to use of opioids (ICD-11: 6C43; DSM-5-TR: F11.20 Opioid Use Disorder, OUD) — impaired control over opioid use (heroin, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, etc.) or harmful pattern of use. Medical and legal consequences are severe; mortality (overdose) is high.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 2. History
text: Dole V.P., Nyswander M. (1965) — initial studies of methadone maintenance therapy. 2010+ US opioid epidemic — starting with prescription opioids, leading to fentanyl overdose crisis. WHO, SAMHSA, NICE — opioid agonist maintenance therapy (OAT) is the gold standard.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Global: approximately 60 million users (UNODC 2023); in the US in 2022, 80,000+ overdose deaths. Sex: twice as common in males. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, PTSD, BPD, HIV/HCV, cardiac. Mortality: in treated OUD patients, 10–20 times higher compared to the population.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 50%. Neurobiological — effect of the μ-opioid receptor system on the dopaminergic reward circuit. Environment — prescription opioid availability, socioeconomic factors. Pain syndromes — transition from prescription initiation to dependence.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Dependence syndrome (same criteria as AUD). Intoxication — miosis, sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, coma. Overdose — respiratory depression is the main cause of death; naloxone is the antidote. Withdrawal — onset 8–24 hours (short-acting), 36–72 hours (long-acting methadone); rhinorrhea, lacrimation, mydriasis, anxiety, tachycardia, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, piloerection. Withdrawal is not life-threat
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR: same 11-criteria structure as AUD (mild/moderate/severe). Unlike DSM-5-TR, which uses a single severity scale, ICD-11 uses three separate categories: episode of harmful use, harmful pattern of use, and dependence. ICD-11 duration requirement: harmful pattern of use — at least 12 months if use is episodic, at least 1 month if continuous; dependence — at least 12 months, or at least 3 months if use is continu
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: SAMHSA TIP 63 — Medications for Opioid Use Disorder. NICE CG52 — opioid dependence. WHO mhGAP.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Toxicology screening (urine). HIV, HCV, syphilis, pregnancy test. Comorbidity and overdose history. COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale) — withdrawal severity.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Chronic pain (without dependence) Medical indication; pattern of use. Other substance use (sedatives, alcohol) Toxicology. Discontinuation signs (GI, piloerection) — differentiation from functional disorders Medical evaluation.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Toxicology screening. COWS scale. HIV, HCV, HBV, syphilis. ECG (before starting methadone — QTc). Pregnancy test.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8. Treatment
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8.1 OAT — opioid agonist therapy (gold standard)
text: Methadone (in a maintenance clinic, under daily supervision) — full μ-agonist; 60–120 mg/day; long half-life; QTc monitoring. Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) — partial μ-agonist + naloxone; office-based prescription; low overdose potential; “induction” — started when mild or moderate withdrawal signs appear (COWS ≥ 8–12). OAT significantly reduces mortality (Sordo L. et al. BMJ 2017;357:j1550 meta-analysis) and HIV
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8.2 Antagonist
text: Naltrexone (oral 50 mg or IM Vivitrol 380 mg monthly) — patient must be abstinent for 7–10 days before initiation; in motivated patients or in the absence of formal maintenance programs.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8.3 Overdose management
text: Naloxone — IM/IN; widespread; “take-home” programs (community-based) reduce mortality.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8.4 In pregnancy
text: Methadone or buprenorphine — OAT is continued during pregnancy; detox is contraindicated (risk of relapse and pregnancy loss). NAS intervention in the newborn — morphine or methadone.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8.5 Treatment methods
text: Methadone Maintenance Therapy (MMT) — Dole-Nyswander model; clinic-based. Buprenorphine/Naloxone — Office-based; “Suboxone induction” protocol; the ceiling effect gives lower overdose potential. Naloxone Take-Home Program — Community-based; antidote training for family. Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) — 11 items; crucial in induction. Naltrexone IM (Vivitrol) — Monthly; in an abstinent patient.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 8.6 Differences between sources
text: SAMHSA TIP 63 (2021). NICE CG52 (opioid detoxification) and CG51 (psychosocial interventions). WHO — OAT is the gold standard, superior to abstinence-oriented approach.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Long-term stabilization and mortality reduction with OAT. Comorbidity intervention is important.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 1: “OAT (methadone, buprenorphine) replaces one addiction with another”
text: Evidence: OAT is medical treatment — significantly reduces mortality, HIV, crime, social disruption; “sensitive” anti-OAT stance is not evidence-based. WHO, SAMHSA, NICE — OAT is the gold standard.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 2: “Detoxification is sufficient, OAT is not needed”
text: Evidence: detox alone 90%+ relapse; overdose mortality highest immediately after detox (loss of tolerance). OAT reduces mortality by 50%+.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 3: “Ultra-rapid opioid detoxification (UROD) is effective”
text: Evidence: UROD is associated with deaths and serious adverse effects; no evidence of efficacy; SAMHSA and NICE do not recommend.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 4: “Detox is needed in a pregnant woman”
text: Evidence: detox in pregnancy is contraindicated; OAT (methadone or buprenorphine) is maintained.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 5: “Ibogaine or ayahuasca cures opioid addiction”
text: Evidence: No evidence supports this; ibogaine is associated with cardiac arrhythmia (QT prolongation) and fatal cases; not in standard practice.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 6: “Naltrexone is first-line for OUD”
text: Evidence: SAMHSA TIP 63 — methadone and buprenorphine are more effective in reducing mortality; naltrexone in motivated abstinent patients.
sub: Disorders due to use of opioids

title: Myth 7: “Naloxone take-home programs encourage use”
text: Evidence: Walley A.Y. et al. BMJ 2013 — community naloxone programs significantly reduce overdose deaths; do not increase use.

title: Myth 2: “Cannabis withdrawal syndrome does not exist”
text: Evidence: DSM-5 (2013) — withdrawal syndrome as an official category; irritability, sleep, appetite disturbance.

title: Myth 3: “Medical cannabis reduces psychosis risk”
text: Evidence: Marconi 2016 — THC raises psychosis risk in a dose-dependent way: about twofold at average use (OR 1.97) and about fourfold in the heaviest users (OR 3.90); preliminary evidence for CBD, not a clinical recommendation.

title: Myth 4: “Cannabis is not a ‘gateway drug’”
text: Evidence: “Gateway” concept is controversial, but sequential use pattern is statistically evident; causality has different explanations.

title: Myth 5: “High-THC cannabis is safer than regular cannabis”
text: Evidence: THC dose correlates with risk of psychosis, addiction, cognitive impairment; ‘potency creep’ over recent decades.

title: Myth 6: “Synthetic cannabinoids (‘Spice’) are safe”
text: Evidence: synthetic cannabinoids are very potent, unpredictable; acute psychosis and death cases have been recorded.

title: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics
text: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics ICD-10 F13 Mental and behavioral disorders due to use of sedatives or hypnotics DSM-5-TR F13.20 Sedative, Hypnotic, or Anxiolytic Use Disord

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics (ICD-11: 6C44; DSM-5-TR: F13.20 Sedative, Hypnotic, or Anxiolytic Use Disorder) — impaired control over use of benzodiazepines, Z-drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone), barbiturates, and other anxiolytics. Often begins with a medical prescription in clinical practice; ‘iatrogenic dependence’ is common.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 2. History
text: 1960s — clinical introduction of benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide 1960, diazepam 1963). 1980s — recognition of the dependence potential of long-term use. NICE and APA — short-term use recommendation (2–4 weeks).
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Long-term benzodiazepine use in the elderly: 10–20%; problem identification is low. Sex: higher prescription rates in women. Comorbidity: alcohol and opioid use (dangerous combination — overdose risk).
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Iatrogenesis — long-term prescriptions. Adaptation to the GABA-A receptor system — tolerance and discontinuation. Self-medication pattern in patients with anxiety, sleep disturbance.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Dependence syndrome — loss of control, tolerance, withdrawal. Intoxication — sedation, ataxia, dysarthria, disinhibition, anterograde amnesia. Overdose — life-threatening respiratory depression with opioids. Withdrawal — life-threatening (like alcohol): tremor, anxiety, tachycardia, hypertension; severe cases: seizures and DT-like syndrome.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR — 11 criteria (AUD structure). Unlike DSM-5-TR, which uses a single severity scale, ICD-11 uses three separate categories: episode of harmful use, harmful pattern of use, and dependence. ICD-11 duration requirement: harmful pattern of use — at least 12 months if use is episodic, at least 1 month if continuous; dependence — at least 12 months, or at least 3 months if use is continuous (daily or almost daily).
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE — benzodiazepine prescription 2–4 weeks; long-term use should be reassessed. Beers Criteria — avoid benzodiazepines in the elderly.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + prescription history. Toxicology screening. Comorbid alcohol and opioid use (especially overdose risk). Clinical examination — withdrawal signs.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Anxiety disorder Comorbid; substance use is symptomatic. Alcohol use Frequently comorbid. Opioid use Comorbid; overdose risk high.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Toxicology screening. Vital signs (discontinuation)
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 8. Treatment
text: Gradual discontinuation (taper) is the gold standard: conversion to equivalent dose of long-acting benzodiazepine (diazepam), then reduction by 5–10% every 2–4 weeks; total duration often lasts months. Rapid discontinuation can be life-threatening. Hospitalization — severe withdrawal or comorbid substance use. Psychosocial intervention — CBT for anxiety or sleep disorder; this reduces the need for pharmacotherapy. Co
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Ashton Manual Taper — Conversion to diazepam equivalent, then gradual reduction; family support. CBT for Anxiety and Sleep — Alternative to benzodiazepine use; CBT-I for sleep. Toxicological Monitoring — During the maintenance period.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE, BNF — taper protocols. Ashton Manual — practical clinical guide by Heather Ashton (C.H. Ashton); 2002 edition, revised 2011.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with gradual taper and CBT. In older adults, discontinuation is both medically and psychologically difficult.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: Myth 1: “Benzodiazepines can be taken safely for life”
text: Evidence: long-term use — tolerance, dependence, cognitive impairment, fall risk (in the elderly). NICE — short-term use.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: Myth 2: “Rapid discontinuation is safe”
text: Evidence: Rapid discontinuation carries a risk of seizures and death; gradual taper is critical.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: Myth 3: “Z-drugs (zolpidem) are not addictive”
text: Evidence: Z-drugs also cause dependence; AAFP and NICE recommend short-term use.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: Myth 4: “Benzodiazepine + opioid is safe”
text: Evidence: FDA boxed warning — this combination significantly increases the risk of respiratory depression and death.
sub: Disorders due to use of sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics

title: Myth 5: “Detoxification is sufficient”
text: Evidence: After discontinuation, alternative treatment (CBT, anxiety management) is required.

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Disorders due to use of cocaine (ICD-11: 6C45; DSM-5-TR: F14.20) — impaired control over cocaine use or harmful use. Includes intoxication, withdrawal, harmful pattern of use, dependence, induced psychotic and mood disorders.

title: 2. History
text: Coca leaves have been used in the Andes for thousands of years. Niemann A. (1860) — cocaine isolation. Freud (1884) — “Über Coca” — later criticized the clinical effect. 1970s–1980s — ‘crack’ epidemic in the US.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Approximately 25 million people use cocaine annually worldwide (UNODC 2025). Sex: twice as common in males. Comorbidity: alcohol, opioids, MDD, BPD, psychosis, cardiovascular mortality.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 40–50%. Neurobiological — blockade of dopamine reuptake → increased mesolimbic reward; tolerance and down-regulation. Social-cultural — peer, accessibility, socioeconomic.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Dependence syndrome (DSM-5-TR criteria). Intoxication — euphoria, hypervigilance, mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia; in severe cases, paranoid delusions, hallucinations, agitation, myocardial infarction, stroke, seizures. Withdrawal — “crash” — depressive mood, anhedonia, fatigue, hypersomnia, increased appetite, intense cravings; high suicide risk.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR 11 criteria (AUD structure). Unlike DSM-5-TR, which uses a single severity scale, ICD-11 uses three separate categories: episode of harmful use, harmful pattern of use, and dependence. ICD-11 duration requirement: harmful pattern of use — at least 12 months if use is episodic, at least 1 month if continuous; dependence — at least 12 months, or at least 3 months if use is continuous (daily or almost daily).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: SAMHSA TIP 33 — stimulant use.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + toxicology. ECG, troponin (especially if chest pain). HIV, HCV, syphilis. Comorbidity and suicide risk (high during withdrawal).
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Amphetamine/stimulant (6C46) Toxicology differential. Manic episode Substance history and temporal relationship. Psychosis (cocaine-induced and primary) Remission after substance elimination. Hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma Endocrine tests.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Toxicology. ECG, troponin, cardiac assessment. HIV, HCV. C-SSRS.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 8. Treatment
text: Psychosocial — first-line: Contingency management — strongest evidence base (Petry N.M. reviews). CBT; MI; Community Reinforcement Approach (CRA). Pharmacotherapy — No medication is approved by the FDA for this indication. Off-label studies — disulfiram, modafinil, topiramate — mixed results. Comorbidity treatment. Acute intoxication — benzodiazepine (lorazepam); cardiac monitoring; antipsychotic in psychosis.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Contingency Management — Petry (Petry N.M.), Higgins (Higgins S.) — Voucher/reward for negative toxicology tests; evidence base strongest for cocaine. CBT and Community Reinforcement Approach (CRA) — Trigger management, alternative rewarding activities. MI — Motivation for behavior change.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: SAMHSA TIP 33 — contingency management gold standard. NIDA — no specific pharmacotherapy for cocaine.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with contingency management. Comorbid substance use and psychiatric disorder — poor prognosis.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: Myth 1: “Cocaine is a ‘recreational’ substance, not addictive”
text: Evidence: Cocaine has high addiction potential; cardiovascular mortality, psychosis, social impairment.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: Myth 2: “FDA-approved treatment for cocaine exists”
text: Evidence: none yet; psychosocial intervention is first-line.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: Myth 3: “Cocaine ‘crash’ is safe and requires no treatment”
text: Evidence: Suicide risk is high during the withdrawal period; active monitoring is required.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: Myth 4: “Crack and cocaine powder are different disorders”
text: Evidence: Same substance (cocaine); route of administration (smoked vs intranasal) alters pharmacokinetics and addiction speed.
sub: Disorders due to use of cocaine

title: Myth 5: “The ‘crack baby’ concept in pregnancy — lasting harm in children”
text: Evidence: latest reviews — long-term effects of prenatal cocaine exposure are less than initially thought; socioeconomic factors have a stronger impact (Frank D.A. JAMA 2001 review).

sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: USPSTF — screening all adult patients for tobacco use; 5A approach (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) for smokers. NICE NG209 (Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence, 2021).
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (5A). Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND). Expired CO monitoring (motivation). Comorbid cardiac and respiratory assessment.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Differentiation among numerous tobacco products; electronic cigarette nicotine addiction can be presented in multiple ways.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: FTND. Expired-air CO monitor. Spirometry (COPD screening).
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 8. Treatment
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 8.1 General principles (USPSTF · NICE NG209 · APA 2010)
text: 5A model (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange). First-line pharmacotherapy: NRT — Nicotine Replacement Therapy (patches, gum, lozenge, inhaler, spray) — combination (long-acting + short-acting) is superior to monotherapy. Varenicline (Chantix) — α4β2 partial agonist; most effective single agent (Cahill K. Cochrane 2013 meta-analysis). Bupropion SR (Zyban) — dopaminergic and noradrenergic effect. Behavioral intervent
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: 5A model (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange). Nicotine Replacement Therapy Combination (NRT) — Long-acting patch + short-acting (gum, lozenge) ‘rescue.’ Varenicline — days 1–3: 0.5 mg, days 4–7: 0.5 mg × 2, then 1 mg × 2; 12 weeks. Bupropion SR — 150 mg × 2/day; seizure risk. CBT and Motivational Interviewing (MI) — Trigger management, motivation enhancement. Telephone Support Line (Quitline) — Community-based sup
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: USPSTF 2021 — recommends intervention for all cigarette smokers. NICE NG209 — active intervention also in comorbid psychiatric disorders. Cahill K. et al. Cochrane 2013 — varenicline is most effective.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With multimodal intervention, 6-month abstinence is 25–35%. Smoking cessation significantly reduces mortality and illness risk.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: Myth 1: “Tobacco is not addictive and can be quit voluntarily”
text: Evidence: Nicotine has high addiction potential; voluntary cessation success rate is low (~3–5% after 6–12 months); pharmacotherapy increases effect 2–3 times.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: Myth 2: “Weight gain after quitting smoking is harmful to health”
text: Evidence: The average weight gain is 4–5 kg, but the risk of continued tobacco use significantly higher; weight can be managed.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: Myth 3: “Varenicline increases suicide risk”
text: Evidence: the initial FDA warning was later reassessed in the EAGLES trial (Anthenelli R.M. Lancet 2016) — psychiatric adverse event rate not significantly higher than placebo; FDA boxed warning removed in 2016.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: Myth 4: “A psychiatric patient cannot quit tobacco and should not”
text: Evidence: Taylor BMJ 2014 — smoking cessation improves psychiatric symptoms; cessation is effective in patients with schizophrenia or MDD.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: Myth 5: “E-cigarettes are safer than tobacco”
text: Evidence: Current evidence indicates that electronic cigarettes are less harmful than combusted tobacco, but are not “safe”; EVALI, cardiac, respiratory risks; gateway to nicotine addiction in adolescents.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

title: Myth 6: “Quitting is a one-time, all-or-nothing decision”
text: Evidence: Most cigarette smokers make 6–11 attempts to quit; each relapse is temporary, and an ongoing quit-attempt plan is recommended.
sub: Disorders due to use of nicotine

Anthenelli R.M. et al. Neuropsychiatric
