title: Gambling disorder
text: Gambling disorder ICD-10 F63.0 Pathological gambling DSM-5-TR F63.0 Gambling Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Gambling disorder (ICD-11: 6C50; ICD-10: F63.0; DSM-5-TR: F63.0) is a persistent or recurrent pattern of gambling behavior characterized by impaired control, increasing priority given to gambling over other interests, and continuation despite negative consequences. It causes significant functional impairment. Gaming is a separate ICD-11 category — 6C51 Gaming disorder.

title: 2. History
text: DSM-III (1980) — “Pathological Gambling” within the impulse control disorders. DSM-5 (2013) — “Gambling Disorder” was moved to the substance-related and addictive disorders category (similar neurobiology). ICD-11 (2019) — the behavioral addictions block was expanded: alongside gambling (6C50), gaming disorder (6C51) was added as a separate category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Gambling Disorder lifetime prevalence: 0.2–5.3% (wide range). Sex: gambling is more prevalent in men; the sex difference narrows in online gambling. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, other substance use, ADHD, BPD, suicide risk.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 50–60%. Neurobiological — dysregulation of the reward circuit (dopamine), similar to substance use disorders. Personality — impulsivity, sensation-seeking.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Persistent/recurrent gambling behavior. Loss of control. Occupational, family, social, and academic impairment. “Chasing losses” (in gambling) — attempts to win back losses. Lying, financial disruption, concealment. Comorbid MDD and high suicide risk.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: Gambling (DSM-5-TR): ≥ 4 of 9 symptoms within a 12-month period: Gambling with increasing amounts — tolerance; Irritability or restlessness when cutting down gambling — withdrawal; Unsuccessful attempts to cut down; Preoccupation with gambling; Gambling when distressed; “Chasing” after losses; Lying; Loss of relationships/job; Reliance on financial bailouts.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11 (6C50) — subtypes: 6C50.0 predominantly offline, 6C50.1 predominantly online, 6C50.Z unspecified. Diagnosis normally requires ≥ 12 months; the duration may be shortened if all diagnostic requirements are met and symptoms are severe. DSM-5-TR — “Gambling Disorder” (F63.0) is the only behavioral addiction in the main text; DSM-5 (2013) moved it from impulse-control disorders to substance-related and addictive di

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. SOGS (South Oaks Gambling Screen) or PGSI (Problem Gambling Severity Index). Comorbid substance use, MDD, suicide. Assessment of the financial situation.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Manic episode (gambling disinhibition) Affective symptoms. OCD (compulsive checking) Obsessions are primary. BPD (impulsivity) A persistent pattern across all domains. Social gambling (non-problematic) No functional impairment.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Comorbidity scales. C-SSRS for suicide.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CBT — first-line; trigger management, behavioral activation, cognitive restructuring (“near miss” and “gambler’s fallacy”). Cowlishaw S. Cochrane 2012 meta-analysis. Naltrexone, nalmefene — the evidence base is evolving (reviews by Grant J.E.). SSRIs — for comorbid MDD/anxiety. Self-help (Gamblers Anonymous, Gam-Anon) — adjunct. Financial counseling — critical in gambling.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for gambling — Correction of cognitive distortions, exposure (reducing responses to triggers), problem-solving. Naltrexone off-label — Reduction of cravings; 50–150 mg/day. Self-help groups (GA) — 12-step model.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Remission with CBT 30–50%. Comorbid MDD predicts a poor prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Gambling addiction is a ‘character’ disorder”
text: Evidence: DSM-5, ICD-11 — it is a medical/behavioral disorder; neurobiological and genetic predisposition.

title: Myth 2: “The patient will get out of debt with a ‘big win’”
text: Evidence: “chasing losses” is a diagnostic feature of gambling disorder; the pattern of losses is statistically inevitable.

title: Myth 3: “Financial support alone is sufficient”
text: Evidence: reliance on bailouts is a diagnostic feature; psychosocial intervention is required.

title: Myth 4: “The patient will ‘grow out of it’”
text: Evidence: active intervention is required; risk of chronicity.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C50 Gambling disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Cowlishaw S. et al. Psychological therapies for pathological and problem gambling. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(11):CD008937. Grant J.E. et al. Pharmacotherapy for gambling disorder. Curr Top Behav Neurosci 2016;26:135–149.

title: Pyromania
text: Pyromania ICD-10 F63.1 Pathological fire-setting [pyromania] DSM-5-TR F63.1 Pyromania

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Pyromania (ICD-11: 6C70; DSM-5-TR: F63.1) — deliberate, purposeful fire-setting behavior; tension or emotional arousal before the act, relief or pleasure after the act. It is not motivated by financial gain, revenge, or ideology; a rare impulse-control disorder. a rare impulse control disorder.

title: 2. History
text: In the 1830s, Marc described ‘monomanie incendiaire’. DSM-III (1980) — Within impulse control disorders. ICD-11 (2019) — within the impulse control disorders category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Rare — only ~3–10% of arson incidents meet criteria for pyromania (most arson has financial, revenge, or other motivation). Sex: higher in males. Onset: adolescence. Comorbidity: conduct disorder, ASPD, ID, ADHD, other substance use.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Multiple factors — neurobiological impulse control, cognitive deficit, family dysfunction. Comorbid disorders are typical.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Repeated deliberate fire-setting. Pre-act tension/emotional arousal. Admiration for the fire, its attributes (flame, tools). Post-act pleasure, relief. No financial gain, revenge, ideological goal, or psychotic compulsion (delusion).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Deliberately setting fires on more than one occasion. B. Pre-act tension or emotional arousal. C. Fascination with, curiosity about, or attraction to fire and its context. D. The act, its observation, or its outcome provides pleasure. E. The fire is not motivated by financial, revenge, ideological, socio-political, or psychotic motives. F. Not better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode, or ASPD.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — similar. Rare in clinical practice; most fire-setting is motivation-based.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + family/witness information. Motivational history — compatibility with pyromania criteria. Comorbidity (ASPD, conduct disorder, manic, psychosis, ID, ADHD). Legal context — forensic psychiatry consultation.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Conduct-dissocial disorder (6C91) Multiple instances of antisocial behavior. ASPD (Antisocial personality) Persistent antisocial pattern. Manic episode Related to the affective episode. Psychotic motivation Delusion (e.g., “voices”); schizophrenia, delusional disorder. Revenge / financial / ideological Not a clinical diagnosis — forensic topic.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Psychiatric interview. Intellectual assessment. Impulsivity scales (Barratt Impulsiveness Scale). Structured risk assessment in forensic context (HCR-20, VRAG).

title: 8. Treatment
text: Evidence base is limited (rare disorder). CBT — impulse control, trigger management, exposure to alternative behavior. Treatment of comorbid disorders (therapeutic limit in ASPD, behavioral intervention in ID, stimulant in ADHD). SSRI — off-label for impulse control. Legal-psychiatric coordination (hospitalization, court order).

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT for impulse control — Trigger identification, behavior replacement. Comorbidity treatment — Behavioral intervention, specific for ID, ADHD. Forensic risk assessment — HCR-20, VRAG.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Evidence base is limited; comorbid disorder and psychosocial support determine prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “All fire-setters are pyromaniacs”
text: Evidence: Most arson is motivated by financial gain or revenge, not by pyromania; ~3–10% meet clinical diagnosis.

title: Myth 2: “Pyromania is only a childhood phenomenon”
text: Evidence: onset typically in adolescence, but can persist into adulthood.

title: Myth 3: “There is specific effective pharmacotherapy”
text: Evidence: No FDA approval; SSRIs off-label, evidence base limited.

title: Myth 4: “Legal punishment alone is sufficient”
text: Evidence: Clinical intervention and comorbidity treatment reduce relapse risk.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C70 Pyromania. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Burton P.R., McNiel D.E., Binder R.L. Firesetting, arson, pyromania, and the forensic mental health expert. J Am Acad Psychiatry Law 2012;40(3):355–365.

title: Kleptomania
text: Kleptomania ICD-10 F63.2 Pathological stealing [kleptomania] DSM-5-TR F63.2 Kleptomania

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Kleptomania (ICD-11: 6C71; DSM-5-TR: F63.2) — a recurrent impulse to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or monetary value; tension before the act, relief or pleasure after the act.

title: 2. History
text: Esquirol (1838) — “kleptomanie”. DSM-III — Impulse control disorders. ICD-11 — impulse control disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Only ~5% of shoplifting incidents meet criteria for kleptomania (most theft is motivation-based). Sex: higher in females (in clinical populations). Comorbidity: mood disorders 45–100% across series, MDD up to ~65%; anxiety, OCD, eating disorders, substance use.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Hypothesis of serotonin and opioid system dysregulation (Grant J.E.). Comorbid affective and impulsivity disorders.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Failure to resist the impulse to steal items that are not needed for personal use or monetary value. Pre-act increase in tension. Post-act relief, pleasure. Stealing is not motivated by anger, revenge, or psychotic motivation. Objects are typically discarded, given away, or hoarded; sometimes surreptitiously returned.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Repeated failure to resist the impulse to steal items that are not needed for personal use or monetary value. B. Pre-act tension. C. Post-act relief, pleasure. D. Stealing is not motivated by anger, revenge, delusion, or hallucination. E. Not better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode, or ASPD.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same criteria.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. K-SAS (Kleptomania Symptom Assessment Scale) — Grant J.E. Comorbid MDD, anxiety, OCD, eating disorders.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Simple theft Motivation — gain, need. ASPD Persistent antisocial pattern. Manic episode Affective context. Conduct-dissocial disorder (6C91) Multiple instances of antisocial behavior. Dementia Cognitive decline.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: K-SAS. Comorbidity scales.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Naltrexone — Grant J.E. et al. Biol Psychiatry 2009 RCT — efficacy in kleptomania (50–150 mg/day). CBT — cognitive restructuring, covert sensitization, imaginal desensitization. SSRI — for comorbid MDD. Multidisciplinary approach — legal context.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Naltrexone — Opioid antagonist; reduces kleptomania cravings. CBT for impulse control — Trigger management. Kleptomania Symptom Assessment Scale (K-SAS) — Severity scale.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Grant J.E. — naltrexone evidence base.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with naltrexone and CBT. Comorbid MDD predicts a poor prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “All repeated stealing is kleptomania”
text: Evidence: Most theft is motivation-based; kleptomania rare.

title: Myth 2: “The patient can stop ‘voluntarily’”
text: Evidence: impulse control disorder — failure to resist is clinical diagnostic feature.

title: Myth 3: “Legal punishment alone is sufficient”
text: Evidence: Clinical intervention and comorbidity treatment reduce relapse risk.

title: Myth 4: “There is no specific treatment”
text: Evidence: Naltrexone evidence base (Grant 2009 RCT); CBT is effective.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C71 Kleptomania. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Grant J.E. et al. A double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the opiate antagonist naltrexone in the treatment of kleptomania. Biol Psychiatry 2009;65(7):600–606.

title: Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder
text: Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder ICD-10 F52.7 Excessive sexual drive DSM-5-TR — No DSM-5-TR equivalent

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder (ICD-11: 6C72) — a persistent pattern of failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses and behaviors, causing significant distress or functional impairment. Included in the impulse control disorders category in ICD-11. DSM-5-TR has no separate diagnosis (“Hypersexual Disorder” was not included in DSM-5). The term “Sex addiction” is controversial in the scientific communit

title: 2. History
text: Krafft-Ebing (1886) — “hyperaesthesia sexualis”. 1980s–1990s — concept of ‘sexual addiction’ (Carnes P.) became popular, but remained controversial within the scientific community. DSM-5 (2013) — “Hypersexual Disorder” not included. ICD-11 (2019) — Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (impulse control, not addiction) added as an official category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 1–6% (broad range, depending on assessment tools). Sex: higher in males (5:1 in clinical populations). Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, BPD, substance use, OCD, ADHD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Multiple factors — impulsivity, compulsivity, cognitive-emotional dysregulation, trauma. Neurobiological similarities with substance use disorders and OCD. Social-cultural — accessibility of internet pornography.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Excessive time spent on sexual fantasies, urges, or behaviors. Failure of attempts to reduce behavior despite negative consequences. Use of sexual behavior to reduce distress or achieve emotional acceptance. Significant functional impairment due to impaired control of sexual behavior (relationships, work, health, legal). Typical forms — compulsive masturbation, multiple sexual partners, patronizing commercial sex ser

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (ICD-11)
text: A. Pattern of persistent failure to control intense sexual impulses and behaviors. B. ≥ 1 of the following: Repeated sexual activity leads to impairment in other areas of the individual’s life (health, relationships, responsibility); The patient has made repeated and significant efforts to regain control — unsuccessfully. The behavior continues despite negative consequences; The behavior persists even when it does no

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11: impulse control disorders; “sex addiction” term not used. DSM-5-TR: no distinct diagnosis; in clinical practice falls under ‘Other Specified Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorder.’ Diagnosis should not be based solely on spiritual-religious distress.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Scale — CSBI (Compulsive Sexual Behavior Inventory). Comorbidity (MDD, anxiety, BPD, substance, OCD). Screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Legal and relationship consequences.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Manic episode (hypersexuality) Affective context. BPD (impulsivity) A persistent pattern across all domains. OCD (sexual obsessions) Ego-dystonic obsession; ritual. Paraphilic disorder (6D30–6D3Z) Specific atypical sexual object. High sexual interest (normal variant) No functional impairment. Moral-religious disapproval alone Not a basis for clinical diagnosis.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: CSBI. Comorbidity scales. STI screening.

title: 8. Treatment
text: First-line psychotherapy — CBT, ACT, mindfulness-based approach. Evidence base is developing. Naltrexone off-label — opioid antagonist; modest effect in some studies. SSRIs — for comorbid MDD/anxiety. Group support (S-Anon, SAA) — adjunct. Relationship/couple therapy — in comorbid context. There is no specific FDA-approved pharmacotherapy.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) — Trigger management, value-based behavior. Naltrexone off-label — Craving reduction. Compulsive Sexual Behavior Inventory (CSBI) — Severity scale. Self-help (SAA, SLAA; S-Anon for family) — 12-step-based; evidence base limited.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: WHO — ICD-11 official category. APA — DSM-5-TR does not have a separate diagnosis; controversial area.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with CBT and ACT. Comorbidity treatment important.

title: Myth 1: “Sex addiction is a diagnosis like substance addiction”
text: Evidence: ICD-11 — impulse control disorder; ‘addiction’ concept controversial, not adopted in DSM-5.

title: Myth 2: “High sexual interest is a sign of sex addiction”
text: Evidence: Clinical diagnosis requires functional impairment and failure of control; mere high sexual activity is not a disease.

title: Myth 3: “Deviation from moral-religious norms is a basis for diagnosis”
text: Evidence: ICD-11 — religious/spiritual cause not sufficient; functional impairment or marked distress is required.

title: Myth 4: “Pornography use is always a disorder”
text: Evidence: Normal use and compulsive use are different; loss of control and functional burden are diagnostic.

title: Myth 5: “Chemical castration (testosterone suppression) is standard treatment”
text: Evidence: This approach is only applied in severe paraphilic disorders at high risk related to pedophilia according to the WFSBP guideline; not recommended for general compulsive sexual behavior.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C72 Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Kraus S.W. et al. Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder in the ICD-11. World Psychiatry 2018;17(1):109–110. Grubbs J.B., Hoagland K.C., Lee B.N. et al. Sexual addiction 25 years on. Clin Psychol Rev 2020;82:101925.

title: Intermittent explosive disorder (IED) (Intermittent explosive disorder)
text: Intermittent explosive disorder (IED) (Intermittent explosive disorder) Intermittent explosive disorder ICD-10 F63.8 Other habit and impulse disorders DSM-5-TR F63.81 Intermittent Explosive Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Intermittent Explosive Disorder (IED; ICD-11: 6C73 Intermittent Explosive Disorder; DSM-5-TR: F63.81) — recurrent, uncontrolled verbal or physical aggressive outbursts; disproportionately intense relative to triggering provocation. Remorse or shame follows the act.

title: 2. History
text: DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis of IED. DSM-5 (2013) — criteria refined. ICD-11 (2019) — under impulse control disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: 4–7% (Kessler R.C. et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006). Sex: higher in males. Onset: mid-adolescence. Comorbidity: MDD ~70%, anxiety, substance use, BPD, ASPD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 40%. Serotonin dysregulation — SSRI effect. Trauma and abuse history. Disruption of cortex-amygdala regulation.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Recurrent aggressive outbursts — verbal (screaming, threats) or physical (object damage, harm to others). Explosion out of control — the patient is unable to restrain it. The trigger is minimal or minor. Post-act remorse, shame, guilt. Relationship, work, legal consequences.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. One of the following: Verbal or physical aggressive outbursts, without destructive harm, ≥2 times per week, ≥3 months Three or more disruptive/damaging outbursts within a 12-month period. B. Aggression disproportionate to the trigger. C. Outbursts are impulsive (not planned), not for a specific purpose. D. Significant distress or functional impairment. E. Chronological age ≥ 6 years. F. Not better explained by ano

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — criterion A1 (mild) and A2 (destructive) separately. ICD-11 sets no frequency or age threshold; DSM-5-TR requires the A1/A2 split, twice weekly for three months or three destructive outbursts in 12 months, and age ≥6; ICD-11 sets none of these.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + family information. Scale — OAS (Overt Aggression Scale), BPAQ (Buss-Perry Aggression Questionnaire). Comorbidity and exclusion of medical causes (frontal lobe injury, epilepsy, hypoglycemia). Toxicology.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature ASPD (Antisocial) Planned aggression, no regret. BPD Emotional lability and relationships central. Manic episode In the context of an affective episode. Conduct-dissocial disorder (6C91) Multiple instances of antisocial behavior. ODD (6C90) Persistent oppositional component with aggression, but outbursts are not primary. Frontal lobe pathology Neurological. Substance-induced aggressio

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: OAS, BPAQ. Medical and neurological. Toxicology. Comorbidity scales.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Fluoxetine (SSRI) — Coccaro E.F. et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2009 RCT — most evidence-based pharmacotherapy in IED; 20–60 mg/day. CBT — anger management, cognitive restructuring, behavioral activation, relaxation. McCloskey M.S. et al. J Consult Clin Psychol 2008. Mood stabilizers — valproate, lithium (off-label in refractory cases). Comorbid disorder treatment. Legal coordination when needed.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Fluoxetine — SSRI; evidence base from Coccaro RCT in IED. CBT for anger management — trigger identification, cognitive restructuring, time-out, relaxation, problem-solving. Overt Aggression Scale (OAS) — Aggression Scale.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Coccaro J Clin Psychiatry 2009 — fluoxetine evidence-based. McCloskey 2008 — CBT efficacy.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with fluoxetine and CBT. Comorbid ASPD, substance use poor prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “IED is just ordinary ‘temper tantrum’”
text: Evidence: Clinical diagnosis based on frequency and functional impairment.

title: Myth 2: “The patient can stop ‘voluntarily’”
text: Evidence: impulse control disorder — failure of control is clinical feature; evidence-based treatment (fluoxetine, CBT) required.

title: Myth 3: “Benzodiazepine calms aggression”
text: Evidence: benzodiazepine paradoxical disinhibition can occur; contraindicated or used cautiously in IED.

title: Myth 4: “Only legal punishment is effective”
text: Evidence: legal punishment alone ineffective; clinical treatment required.

title: Myth 5: “Antipsychotic is first-line”
text: Evidence: SSRI first-line; antipsychotics in refractory cases.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C73 Intermittent explosive disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Coccaro E.F. et al. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine in patients with intermittent explosive disorder. J Clin Psychiatry 2009;70(5):653–662. McCloskey M.S. et al. title: Conduct-dissocial disorder
text: Conduct-dissocial disorder ICD-10 F91 Conduct disorders DSM-5-TR F91.1 Conduct Disorder, Childhood-Onset Type

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Conduct-dissocial disorder (ICD-11: 6C91; DSM-5-TR: F91.1 Conduct Disorder) — a persistent and repetitive pattern of violating the rights of others or age-appropriate social norms. Typically begins in childhood/adolescence; may transition to ASPD in adulthood.

title: 2. History
text: DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — “limited prosocial emotions” specifier (childhood marker of psychopathic traits). NICE CG158 (2017) — child and adolescent antisocial behavior.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 12-month prevalence 2–10%, median 4%; higher in boys than in girls (DSM-5-TR). Sex: 3 times higher in males. Onset — childhood (before age 10, poor prognosis) or adolescence (age 10+, good prognosis). Comorbidity: ADHD 50%, ODD, MDD, anxiety, substance use, learning disorders.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 40–60%. Neurobiological — amygdala, prefrontal dysregulation, low sympathetic arousal. Environment — childhood trauma, harsh parenting, family dysfunction, peers. Prenatal — tobacco, alcohol.

title: DSM-5-TR 15 symptoms in 4 categories (≥ 3 symptoms in 12 months)
text: Aggression — towards people/animals: threat, assault, use of weapons, physical violence, sexual violence. Object injury: Intentional arson, damage to other objects. Deception/theft: Breaking and entering, lying, theft. Serious rule violation: Staying out at night despite prohibition, running away from home, truancy.

title: “Limited prosocial emotions” qualifier (psychopathic traits)
text: Lack of empathy or remorse; Lack of concern about performance (education, work); Callous lack of emotion; Shallow affect.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR criteria (≥ 3 symptoms from 15 in 12 months; at least 1 symptom in the last 6 months). Severity: mild, moderate, severe. Onset: childhood type (≥1 symptom by age 10), adolescent type.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 — both have the ‘limited prosocial emotions’ qualifier. ICD-11 — ‘Conduct-Dissocial Disorder’; with childhood-onset and adolescent-onset types. NICE CG158 — diagnosis and intervention in children and adolescents.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + parent, teacher. Structured interview (K-SADS). CBCL (Child Behavior Checklist), TRF (Teacher Report Form). The Inventory of Callous-Unemotional Traits — for psychopathic traits. Comorbidity (ADHD, MDD, substance, learning).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature ODD (6C90) No serious legal violation. ADHD (6A05) Impulsivity and attention; common comorbidity. IED (6C73) Explosive type; absence of persistent antisocial pattern. Manic episode Affective context. RAD/DSED (6B44/6B45) Attachment disturbance since childhood. Substance-induced Toxicology.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: CBCL, TRF, ICU. Comorbidity screening. Intellectual and academic assessment.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG158 · AACAP)
text: Parent training programs first-line — for ages 3–11: Incredible Years (Webster-Stratton); PCIT (Parent-Child Interaction Therapy); Triple P. For adolescents: MST — Multisystemic Therapy (Henggeler S.W.) — encompassing family, peer, school, community; FFT — Functional Family Therapy; MTFC — Multidimensional Treatment Foster Care. Comorbid ADHD — stimulant (also reduces aggression). Antipsychotic (risperidone) — off-la

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: “Incredible Years” program — Webster-Stratton — group program for parents of children aged 3–8 years; 14–22 sessions. Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) — 2–7 years; CDI + PDI. Multisystemic Therapy (MST) — Home-based multisystem intervention for adolescents; evidence base strong for severe behavioral disturbances. Functional Family Therapy (FFT) — Family-based, 8–30 sessions. Multidimensional Treatment Foster C

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Clinical guideline CG158. 2017. AACAP Practice Parameter (Steiner H. 2007). Cochrane (Petrosino 2013) — Scared Straight is counterproductive.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With childhood-type and psychopathic traits — risk of ASPD in adulthood ~40–50%. Adolescent-type good prognosis. Early parent training and multisystem intervention significantly improve outcomes.

title: Myth 1: “Harsh punishment/discipline is the most effective intervention”
text: Evidence: Harsh punishment strengthens antisocial behavior; positive parenting training is evidence-based.

title: Myth 2: “‘Scared Straight’ programs ‘correct’ youth”
text: Evidence: Petrosino A. Cochrane 2013 — Scared Straight increases antisocial behavior (OR 1.68; 95% CI 1.20–2.36); contraindicated; sometimes presented as “effective” in media, but meta-analysis negative.

title: Myth 3: “Conduct disorder inevitably turns into ASPD”
text: Evidence: Approximately 50% of cases with adolescent-onset type remit; childhood-onset type and psychopathic traits indicate a poor prognosis.

title: Myth 4: “Stimulants increase aggression”
text: Evidence: In comorbid ADHD, stimulants reduce aggression; use with monitoring of behavior and adverse effects.

title: Myth 5: “Boot camp or military environment cures severe CD”
text: Evidence: No evidence; some studies show counterproductive effects.

title: Myth 6: “Antipsychotics are standard first-line treatment”
text: Evidence: parent training and psychosocial approaches first-line; risperidone off-label in severe refractory cases.

title: 11. Sources

Steiner H., Remsing L. AACAP Practice Parameter for the Assessment and Treatment of Oppositional Defiant Disorder. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2007;46(1):126–141. Petrosino A. et al. “Scared Straight” and other juvenile aw

title: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) (Oppositional defiant disorder)
text: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) (Oppositional defiant disorder) Oppositional defiant disorder ICD-10 F91.3 Oppositional defiant disorder DSM-5-TR F91.3 Oppositional Defiant Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD; ICD-11: 6C90 Oppositional Defiant Disorder; DSM-5-TR: F91.3) — pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictive behavior. Unlike Conduct Disorder (CD), there is no interference with the fundamental rights of others.

title: 2. History
text: DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — emotional component (angry/irritable) separately emphasized.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 1–11% (mean 3.3%) in preschool and school-aged children (DSM-5-TR). Sex: higher in prepubertal boys; postpubertal difference decreases. Comorbidity: ADHD ~40–60%, MDD, anxiety, transition to CD in 30% (severe childhood type).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 50%. Environment — harsh parenting, family dysfunction. Neurobiological — affective regulation, frontal-amygdala circuitry. Temperamental traits (irritability).

title: 8 symptoms in 3 categories (≥ 4 symptoms for 6 months)
text: Angry/Irritable mood. Easily irritated, discontented. Quarrelsome/oppositional behavior: Arguing with adults; non-compliance with rules; deliberately annoying others; blaming others. Vengeful behavior: at least twice in the last 6 months.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: DSM-5-TR — ≥4 of 8 symptoms for 6 months; in at least one context (home, school, peers); in at least one other context with different individuals. Age qualifier: symptoms on most days for 6 months until age 5; age ≥5 — ≥1 per week for 6 months.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — severity (mild, moderate, severe) based on number of contexts. NICE CG158 — guidance for child antisocial behavior.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + parent, teacher. CBCL, TRF, ECBI (Eyberg Child Behavior Inventory). Comorbid ADHD screening. Difference between Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) and depressive disorder.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature CD (6C91) Serious legal violation. ADHD Attention/impulsivity; frequent comorbidity. DMDD (DSM-5) Persistent irritability + severe anger outbursts, ≥ 12 months (with no symptom-free period of ≥ 3 consecutive months); if criteria for ODD are also met, only DMDD is diagnosed. Anxiety disorder Anxiety component dominant. Intellectual disability Behavioral disturbance in the context of co

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: ECBI, CBCL. Comorbid ADHD, anxiety, MDD.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Parent training first-line: PCIT — 2–7 years; Incredible Years — ages 3–8; Parent Management Training (Barkley) — age 6+; Triple P. Comorbid ADHD — stimulant. SSRI — comorbid anxiety/depression. School-based intervention. Suspected child maltreatment or domestic violence — child protection and social service coordination.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) — Real-time coaching by therapist. “Incredible Years” program — Group format. Triple P — Positive Parenting Program — 5-tier system. Parent Management Training — Barkley — training based on behavioral principles. Eyberg Child Behavior Inventory (ECBI) — Parent-rated behavior scale.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG158. AACAP — parent training.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Most patients improve with early parent training. Comorbid ADHD, severe variant — risk of CD/ASPD.

title: Myth 1: “ODD is just ordinary ‘stubborn child’ behavior”
text: Evidence: Clinical diagnosis based on functional impairment and frequency; distinct from normal developmental variation.

title: Myth 2: “Strict discipline will fix ODD”
text: Evidence: Severe punishment exacerbates symptoms; positive parenting training is evidence-based.

title: Myth 3: “Antipsychotic is first-line”
text: Evidence: parent training first-line; antipsychotics are rarely used in refractory cases.

title: Myth 4: “ODD always turns into CD”
text: Evidence: 30% transition to CD; risk higher with childhood type and comorbidity; majority do not convert to CD.

title: Myth 5: “Only the child should be treated, not the family”
text: Evidence: parent training is a central component; child psychotherapy alone is less effective.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6C90 Oppositional defiant disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. NICE CG158. 2017. AACAP Practice Parameter (Steiner 2007). Eyberg S.M. et al. title: Personality disorder
text: Personality disorder ICD-10 F60.9 Personality disorder, unspecified DSM-5-TR F60.9 Unspecified Personality Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Personality Disorder (ICD-11: 6D10; DSM-5-TR: F60.9; 10 categories) — persistent and pervasive pattern in personal and social functioning; thoughts, feelings, and behaviors regarding self and others. ICD-11 has fundamentally moved to a model of a single category + severity degrees + trait domains; the ten classical personality disorders (paranoid, schizoid, borderline, antisocial, etc.) have been abolished as categor

title: 2. History
text: DSM-III (1980) — 11 categorical personality disorders (Cluster A, B, C). DSM-IV (1994), DSM-5-TR (2022) — Same categorical model retained; however, DSM-5 Section III has an alternative ‘dimensional’ model in the research category. ICD-11 (2019) — radical change: Categorical 10 disorders abolished, unified Personality Disorder (mild, moderate, severe + Personality Difficulty) + assessment of 5 trait domains.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: ~9% (Lenzenweger M.F. et al. Biol Psychiatry 2007); BPD ~1.4%, ASPD ~0.6%, schizoid 3%. Sex: BPD higher in females in clinical populations; ASPD higher in males. Onset: adolescence and early adulthood. Mortality: in BPD, suicide 8–10% lifetime; in ASPD, violent death. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, substance use, eating disorders.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Heritability 40–60%. Early trauma, childhood abuse (especially BPD). Disorganized attachment. Neurobiological — frontal-limbic regulation, serotonergic dysregulation.

title: 5.1 ICD-11 5 characteristic domains
text: Negative affectivity — anxiety, depression, variability. Detachment — social and emotional distance. Dissociality — lack of empathy, egocentricity. Disinhibition — impulsivity, irresponsibility. Anankastia — perfectionism, control, rigid rules. “Borderline pattern” — a separate qualifier in ICD-11 (corresponding to BPD, instead of ten separate categorical diagnoses).

title: 5.2 DSM-5-TR 10 categorical disorders (brief)
text: Cluster A (odd/eccentric): Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal. Cluster B (dramatic/erratic): Antisocial (ASPD), Borderline (BPD), Histrionic, Narcissistic. Cluster C (anxious/fearful): Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive (OCPD).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (ICD-11)
text: A. Persistent and pervasive personality dysfunction — in self (identity, self-worth, self-direction) and/or interpersonal (relationships, empathy, intimacy, responsibility) functioning. B. Duration — ≥ 2 years (long-term). C. Not consistent with developmental age, cultural norm, or family situation. D. Severity: Personality Difficulty (subclinical), Mild PD, Moderate PD, Severe PD. E. Feature domain qualifiers (above

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11: Radical departure from the categorical system; requires training in clinical practice. DSM-5-TR: 10 categorical diagnoses retained; Section III alternative model. NICE CG78 (BPD), CG77 (ASPD): Separate clinical guidelines for BPD and ASPD.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + long history. SCID-5-PD (DSM categorical) or ICD-11 PD assessment. Personality scales — PID-5 (DSM-5 dimensional), MMPI-2-RF. Comorbidity (MDD, substance, trauma). Suicide and violence risk.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Change in the context of an affective episode Episodic course; personality stable. Substance-induced Substance history. PTSD / complex PTSD In trauma context; clinical overlap with BPD. Bipolar Affective episodes. Medical condition (frontal lobe, dementia) Neurological.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: SCID-5-PD, PID-5. MMPI-2-RF, MCMI-IV. Comorbidity and suicide.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG78 (BPD), CG77 (ASPD); APA 2024 (BPD, 2nd ed.))
text: First-line psychotherapy — gold standard in personality disorders. Evidence-based approaches for BPD (5): DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Linehan M.) — emotional regulation, distress tolerance, social skills, mindfulness; standard 12 months; MBT (Mentalization-Based Treatment, Bateman A., Fonagy P.) Schema Therapy (Young J.) TFP (Transference-Focused Psychotherapy, Kernberg O.) STEPPS (Systems Training for Emotion

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) — Linehan M.M. — 4 modules (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotional regulation, social skills); individual + group + telephone coaching + therapist consultation. 12-month standard. Evidence: Linehan M.M. JAMA Psychiatry 2015. Mentalization-Based Treatment (MBT) — Bateman A., Fonagy P. — Mentalization — recognition of one’s own and others’ mental states; based on psychodynamic roo

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG78 (BPD, 2009) — DBT, MBT, and similar structured approaches; pharmacotherapy not routinely recommended for BPD itself. NICE CG77 (ASPD, 2009). APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Borderline Personality Disorder, 2nd ed. (2024) — supersedes the 2001 edition.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: BPD — ~85–93% remission over 10 years, ~50% full recovery (Zanarini). ASPD — worst prognosis; but aggression decreases with age. Treatment significantly improves the prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Personality disorders are untreatable”
text: Evidence: DBT, MBT, Schema, TFP — evidence-based approaches; most patients improve significantly; pessimistic prognostic stance is outdated.

title: Myth 2: “BPD patients are manipulative and require strict boundaries”
text: Evidence: Term “manipulative” is stigmatizing and incorrect; BPD behaviors stem from emotional dysregulation; DBT recommends a balance of validation and structure.

title: Myth 3: “Pharmacotherapy cures BPD”
text: Evidence: NICE CG78 — pharmacotherapy not routinely recommended for BPD itself; psychotherapy first-line.

title: Myth 4: “ASPD cannot be treated”
text: Evidence: in severe ASPD, intervention is limited, but in motivated patients structured treatment may yield improvement; nihilistic stance contraindicated.

title: Myth 5: “Personality disorder stabilizes with age and does not require treatment”
text: Evidence: long-term follow-up — BPD remission ~85% over 10 years, recovery ~50%; treatment accelerates this process.

title: Myth 6: “Hypnotherapy, esoteric interventions cure personality disorders”
text: Evidence: No evidence; evidence-based structured psychotherapy is recommended.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D10 Personality disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. NICE CG78. Borderline personality disorder: recognition and management. 2009. NICE CG77. Antisocial personality disorder: prevention and management. 2009. Linehan M.M. et al. Dialectical behavior therapy for high suicide risk in individuals with borderline personality disorder: a randomized clinical trial and component analysis. JAMA Psychiatry 2015;7

title: Prominent personality traits or patterns
text: Prominent personality traits or patterns ICD-10 — No ICD-10 equivalent DSM-5-TR F60.3 Borderline Personality Disorder (matches only the 6D11.5 borderline pattern qualifier)

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Prominent personality traits or patterns (ICD-11: 6D11 Prominent personality traits or patterns) is not a stand-alone diagnosis but a set of qualifiers: they record which trait domains a personality disorder (6D10) or personality difficulty is expressed through. Severity is coded in 6D10 and the domains here; 6D11 is never assigned on its own. Personality difficulty is not a mental disorder in ICD-11 — it sits in the

title: 2. History
text: ICD-11 (2019) — the 10 categorical personality disorders were dropped in favor of a severity rating (6D10) plus five trait domains (6D11.0–6D11.4). The borderline pattern (6D11.5) was added separately as the successor to ICD-10 borderline personality disorder (F60.3); in DSM-5-TR the corresponding diagnosis is Section II borderline PD (F60.3).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Precise epidemiological data are limited; subclinical personality traits are widespread in the population.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Same as 6D10 — genetic and environmental interaction.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: 6D11.0 Negative affectivity — a broad range of negative emotions: anxiousness, irritability, low self-esteem, emotional lability. 6D11.1 Detachment — social and emotional distance: avoidance, restricted affect, refusal of intimacy. 6D11.2 Dissociality — disregard for the rights and feelings of others: self-centeredness, lack of empathy, exploitativeness. 6D11.3 Disinhibition — impulsivity, distractibility, irresponsi

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. The diagnosis is made under 6D10 (personality disorder) or QE50.7 (personality difficulty); 6D11 is added only as a qualifier. B. All domains present to a clinically significant degree are recorded — there may be several. C. The borderline pattern (6D11.5) may be recorded in addition to any combination of domains.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11 — category somewhat similar to the Z-code for ‘clinical attention to personality problems.’

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. 5-domain assessment. Exclusion of full PD diagnosis.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Personality Disorder (6D10) Significant functional impairment. Adjustment disorder (6B43) Response to stress factor. Normal personality variant No functional difficulty.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Personality inventories (PID-5).

title: 8. Treatment
text: Psychotherapy — short-to-medium term; problem-focused CBT or supportive. Stress management and coping skills. Specific intervention for comorbid symptoms.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: DSM-5 — Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5) — Dimensional personality scale.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Improvement with treatment; risk of progression to persistent or full PD.

title: Myth 1: “Personality difficulty is not a real diagnosis”
text: Evidence: ICD-11 is the official code; it makes clinical attention to subclinical personality problems possible.

title: Myth 2: “Personality difficulty inevitably turns into PD”
text: Evidence: Some patients experience deterioration, but most stabilize or improve.

title: Myth 3: “Should only be treated with medication”
text: Evidence: Psychotherapy is first-line; pharmacotherapy for comorbid symptoms.

title: Myth 4: “This category is only for labeling ‘anxious’ patients”
text: Evidence: ICD-11 — clinical response to functional difficulty; provides clinical support.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D11 Prominent personality traits or patterns. 2024. WHO. ICD-11. QE50.7 Personality difficulty. 2024. Tyrer P. et al. Lancet 2015;385(9969):717–726.

title: Exhibitionistic disorder
text: Exhibitionistic disorder ICD-10 F65.2 Exhibitionism DSM-5-TR F65.2 Exhibitionistic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Exhibitionistic disorder (ICD-11: 6D30; DSM-5-TR: F65.2) — persistent or intense sexual arousal from exposing genitals to non-consenting persons; the patient experiences significant distress or functional impairment in response to these fantasies, urges, or behaviors, and/or acts on them with actual non-consenting individuals.

title: 2. History
text: Lasègue C. (1877) — term ‘exhibitionnistes’. DSM-III (1980) — Official diagnosis. DSM-5 (2013) — distinction between paraphilia (atypical sexual interest) and paraphilic disorder (clinical distress or harm to others). WFSBP 2020 (Thibaut F. et al.) — international recommendation for paraphilic disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: males 2–4%; rare in females. Onset: adolescence and early adulthood. Comorbidity: other paraphilia (50–80% of paraphilic disorder patients), ASPD, substance use, MDD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Numerous factors — biological, behavioral conditioning, psychosocial. Comorbid impulsivity and hypersexuality.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Repeated and intense sexual arousal from exposing genitals to non-consenting persons. The patient acts on fantasy, impulse, or behavior or experiences distress. Typical context — street, public transportation. Legal and social consequences (sexual crime).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. ≥6 months repeated and intense sexual arousal from genital exposure to non-consenting individuals. B. The patient has acted on fantasies/impulses or experiences significant distress/functional impairment.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR requires a 6-month duration; ICD-11 sets no duration criterion — it speaks of a “sustained, focused and intense pattern of arousal”. WFSBP 2020 — step-by-step therapy for paraphilic disorders.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Comorbidity (ASPD, substance, other paraphilic). Risk assessment (forensic context).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Hypersexuality Partners with consent. Manic episode Affective context. Dementia Disinhibition due to frontal lobe pathology. Substance-induced Toxicology.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Clinical interview. Risk scales (Static-99R for sexual recidivism).

title: 8.1 General principles (WFSBP 2020 Stepwise)
text: CBT (cognitive-behavioral therapy) — first-line; prevention of relapse, management of cognitive distortions. SSRIs — high dose (fluoxetine 40–80 mg); reduces impulsivity and sexual drive. In refractory cases / severe cases — antiandrogen (CPA cyproterone, MPA medroxyprogesterone). In the most severe cases — GnRH agonist (leuprolide, triptorelin) — chemical castration; continuous monitoring. Legal-medical coordination

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: CBT (relapse prevention) — Trigger management, cognitive distortion. SSRI High Dose — First pharmacotherapy. Antiandrogen (CPA, MPA) — In refractory cases. GnRH Agonist — In most severe case.

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: WFSBP 2020 — step-by-step algorithm.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Reduction of relapse with evidence-based treatment; comorbid ASPD and substance use carry a poor prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Exhibitionism is harmless”
text: Evidence: Psychological trauma for the victim; sexual crime; risk of progression to more severe paraphilias.

title: Myth 2: “Chemical castration is first-line”
text: Evidence: WFSBP 2020 step‑by‑step — CBT and SSRI first; GnRH in most severe cases

title: Myth 3: “Treatment is ineffective”
text: Evidence: CBT and pharmacotherapy significantly reduce recidivism.

title: Myth 4: “Only legal punishment is required”
text: Evidence: Clinical intervention reduces relapse risk.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D30 Exhibitionistic disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Thibaut F., Cosyns P., Fedoroff J.P. et al.; WFSBP Task Force on Paraphilias. The World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) 2020 guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of paraphilic disorders. World J Biol Psychiatry 2020;21(6):412–490.

title: Voyeuristic disorder
text: Voyeuristic disorder ICD-10 F65.3 Voyeurism DSM-5-TR F65.3 Voyeuristic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Voyeuristic disorder (ICD-11: 6D31; DSM-5-TR: F65.3) — persistent and intense sexual arousal from secretly observing undressing, nakedness, sexual activity of non‑consenting persons; patient experiences distress from these fantasies or acts upon them with non‑consenting individuals.

title: 2. History
text: Voyeurism has been described in the clinical literature in parallel with exhibitionistic disorder (6D30).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: the population prevalence of the disorder is unknown; based on voyeuristic acts in non-clinical samples, DSM-5-TR gives a lifetime prevalence of up to ~12% in males and ~4% in females (Långström N., Seto M.C. Arch Sex Behav 2006, n=2450). Most people with voyeuristic behavior do not meet criteria for the disorder. Comorbid other paraphilic disorders. Internet voyeurism (hidden camera, “upskirt”) is an eme

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: General etiology for paraphilic disorders.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Observing unsuspecting individuals naked or during sexual activity without their consent. Typical context — windows, dressing rooms, public places. “Upskirting” — the modern form. Legal consequences.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. ≥6 months repeated sexual arousal from observing non-consenting individuals. B. The patient has acted on these fantasies or experiences distress. C. Age ≥18 (DSM-5-TR; normal curiosity in adolescents is an exception).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR requires a 6-month duration; ICD-11 sets no duration criterion — it speaks of a “sustained, focused and intense pattern of arousal”. WFSBP 2020.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Comorbidity. Risk assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Adolescent curiosity Part of normal development. Consensual viewing (pornography) Consensual context. Manic episode Affective context.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Clinical interview. Risk scales.

title: 8. Treatment
text: WFSBP 2020 step‑by‑step algorithm (same as 6D30): CBT for relapse prevention; SSRI high dose; Antiandrogen; GnRH in the most severe case. Legal-medical coordination.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Same as 6D30.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Reduction of relapse with evidence-based treatment.

title: Myth 1: “Voyeurism is harmless; the victim remains unaware”
text: Evidence: Trauma if the victim becomes aware; a consent violation and a sexual crime.

title: Myth 2: “Pornography use is voyeurism”
text: Evidence: Consensual production and consumption — voyeurism absent; clinical diagnosis focuses on those without consent.

title: Myth 3: “Internet voyeurism is only new; it has no clinical significance”
text: Evidence: “Upskirting”, hidden camera — sexual crime; requires clinical and legal intervention.

title: Myth 4: “Treatment is ineffective”
text: Evidence: CBT and pharmacotherapy are effective.
