title: Pedophilic disorder
text: Pedophilic disorder ICD-10 F65.4 Paedophilia DSM-5-TR F65.4 Pedophilic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Pedophilic disorder (ICD-11: 6D32; DSM-5-TR: F65.4) — persistent and intense sexual arousal toward prepubertal children (typically ≤13 years) for ≥6 months; the patient has acted on fantasies involving children or experiences significant distress/functional impairment. Patient is at least 16 years and victim at least 5 years younger. Important: “Pedophilic interest” (paraphilia) and “Pedophilic Disorder” (clinical di

title: 2. History
text: Krafft-Ebing (1886). DSM-III (1980). WFSBP 2020 — international guideline for paraphilic disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence — precise data are hard to obtain (stigmatized category); DSM-5-TR gives 3–5% as the highest possible figure in the male population; true pedophilic preference ~1%. Sex: almost always in males. Comorbidity: other paraphilic, ASPD, MDD, anxiety, substance use.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Biological — neurodevelopmental anomalies (Cantor J.M. reviews — IQ, neuroanatomical differences). History of childhood trauma or sexual abuse (but most individuals with pedophilic disorder were not victims themselves; the “abused-abuser” concept is only partly supported by evidence). Comorbid impulsivity and hypersexuality.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Persistent and intense sexual arousal toward prepubertal children. The patient has acted on fantasy (sexual abuse of a child) or experiences distress/functional impairment. Subtypes (DSM-5-TR): exclusive type (attracted only to children), nonexclusive type (attracted to both children and adults); male/female/both. Legal consequences (crime).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. ≥6 months repeated and intense sexual arousal toward prepubertal children (typically ≤13). B. The patient has acted on these fantasies or experiences significant distress/functional impairment. C. Patient ≥ 16 years old and at least 5 years older than the child.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR requires a 6-month duration and an age rule (patient ≥16 years and at least 5 years older than the child); ICD-11 has neither a duration nor an age criterion — it only excludes behavior between peers close in age. WFSBP 2020. Structured risk assessment in forensic psychiatry context.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (difficult to confess; patient may conceal). Penile plethysmography — investigation and forensic context. Forensic risk assessment (Static-99R, STABLE-2007). Comorbidity.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Substance-induced disinhibition Toxicology. Dementia (frontal) Cognitive decline, neurological. Intellectual disability In the context of cognitive deficit. Hypersexuality in adults No pedophilic focus. “Hebephilia” / “ephebophilia” Focus on puberty and post-puberty; DSM-5-TR no separate category.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Forensic clinical interview. Static-99R, STABLE-2007. Penile plethysmography (investigation). Comorbidity.

title: 8.1 General principles (WFSBP 2020 Stepwise)
text: CBT and prevention of relapse — first-line; trigger management, management of cognitive distortions, empathy development. SSRI high dose — first pharmacotherapy — reduces impulsivity and sexual urge. Antiandrogen (CPA, MPA) — in moderate-to-severe cases; libido and sexual activity decrease. GnRH agonist (leuprolide, triptorelin) — chemical castration; in most severe or high-risk cases; continuous monitoring (osteopor

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: CBT and Relapse Prevention — Trigger and context management; cognitive distortion; empathy training. SSRI High Dose — First pharmacotherapy. Antiandrogen (CPA, MPA) — Libido reduction. GnRH Agonist — Chemical castration; ongoing monitoring. Static-99R, STABLE-2007 — Forensic risk assessment.

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: WFSBP 2020 — Thibaut et al. — step‑by‑step pharmacotherapy. STABLE-2007 — dynamic risk factors.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Behavior management improves with evidence-based treatment. Comorbid ASPD and substance use — poor prognosis. Continuous monitoring is critical.

title: Myth 1: “Pedophilic interest always means child abuse”
text: Evidence: “Having pedophilic fantasies” and “committing child abuse” are different; some patients never abuse and seek clinical support (e.g., “Dunkelfeld” program in Germany).

title: Myth 2: “All child sexual abusers are pedophilic”
text: Evidence: Most child sex offenders are not pedophilic — the offense is situational, with other motivations. Pedophilic diagnosis requires persistent sexual arousal for ≥ 6 months.

title: Myth 3: “Chemical castration should be mandatory for all patients”
text: Evidence: WFSBP 2020 step‑by‑step approach — GnRH in most severe cases; CBT and SSRI first. Ethical and legal caution.

title: Myth 4: “Once a pedophile, always a pedophile”
text: Evidence: Sexual interest may be stable, but behavioral control can significantly improve with CBT and pharmacotherapy.

title: Myth 5: “Treatment is ineffective”
text: Evidence: WFSBP 2020 and meta‑analyses — multimodal intervention reduces recidivism

title: Myth 6: “The patient is a ‘victim’ of childhood trauma”
text: Evidence: “Abused-abuser” concept not fully supported; most patients were not abused in childhood; victimhood is not the basis for perpetration.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D32 Pedophilic disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Thibaut F., Cosyns P., Fedoroff J.P. et al.; WFSBP Task Force on Paraphilias. The World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) 2020 guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of paraphilic disorders. World J Biol Psychiatry 2020;21(6):412–490. Cantor J.M. et al. Cerebral white matter deficiencies in pedophilic men. J Psychiatr Res 2

title: Coercive sexual sadism disorder
text: Coercive sexual sadism disorder ICD-10 F65.5 Sadomasochism DSM-5-TR F65.52 Sexual Sadism Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Coercive sexual sadism disorder (ICD-11: 6D33; DSM-5-TR: F65.52 Sexual Sadism Disorder) — persistent and intense sexual arousal from inflicting physical or psychological suffering on a non-consenting person. The patient has acted on these fantasies or experiences significant distress/functional impairment. Important difference: Consensual BDSM (Bondage/Discipline, Dominance/Submission, Sadism/Masochism) practice — no

title: 2. History
text: Krafft-Ebing (1886) — term “sadism”, derived from the name of the Marquis de Sade. DSM-5 (2013) — difference between paraphilia and paraphilic disorder. ICD-11 (2019) — “Coercive” emphasizes the importance of consent. WFSBP 2020.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Rare in clinical populations; 5–15% in forensic contexts of sexual offense samples. Almost always in males. High comorbidity with ASPD and other paraphilic disorders.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Biological and psychosocial factors; childhood trauma, antisocial traits. Hypersexuality and impulsivity are frequently comorbid.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Sexual arousal from inflicting suffering on a non-consenting victim. Typical context — forensic offense (rape-sadistic). In severe cases — sadistic murders, serious physical injury. Forensic risk high.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. ≥6 months persistent and intense sexual arousal from physical or psychological suffering inflicted on a non-consenting individual. B. The patient has acted on these fantasies or experiences significant distress.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR requires a 6-month duration; ICD-11 sets no duration criterion — it speaks of a “sustained, focused and intense pattern of arousal”. Consensual BDSM is not a clinical disorder.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Forensic clinical interview. Risk assessment (Static-99R, SVR-20). Comorbid disorders (ASPD, psychopathy — PCL-R).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Consensual BDSM Consensual context — not a disorder. ASPD Violence without a sexual component. Psychopathy PCL-R; clinical overlap. Substance-induced Toxicology.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Forensic clinical interview. PCL-R (Psychopathy Checklist), Static-99R, SVR-20.

title: 8. Treatment
text: WFSBP 2020 step‑by‑step algorithm: CBT and prevention of relapse; SSRI high dose; Antiandrogen; GnRH agonist in the most severe case. Forensic psychiatric supervision; in hospital or correctional setting. In cases with comorbid psychopathy, standard psychotherapy is less effective.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT and Relapse Prevention — Limited effectiveness; limited in psychopathy context. SSRI + Antiandrogen + GnRH — WFSBP 2020 stepwise. PCL-R, Static-99R, SVR-20 — Forensic risk assessment.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: WFSBP 2020 — in severe cases, a combination of CBT, antiandrogen, and GnRH agonist.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: In severe cases, high risk of relapse; multimodal intervention and continuous monitoring are essential.

title: Myth 1: “BDSM = sadistic disorder”
text: Evidence: Consensual BDSM is not a clinical disorder; ICD-11 draws this distinction precisely through the term ‘coercive’. APA and other professional associations do not consider consensual BDSM to be pathological.

title: Myth 2: “Sadistic disorder cannot be treated”
text: Evidence: WFSBP 2020 — multimodal intervention reduces relapse risk; effect is less in comorbid psychopathy.

title: Myth 3: “Only legal punishment is required”
text: Evidence: Clinical intervention recommended jointly with legal oversight.

title: Myth 4: “All sexual murderers have sadistic disorder”
text: Evidence: Most sex crimes are committed by people with ASPD or are otherwise motivated; sadistic clinical diagnosis requires a concrete fantasy pattern.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D33 Coercive sexual sadism disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Thibaut F., Cosyns P., Fedoroff J.P. et al.; WFSBP Task Force on Paraphilias. The World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) 2020 guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of paraphilic disorders. World J Biol Psychiatry 2020;21(6):412–490. Hare R.D. Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R). 2nd ed. 2003.

title: Frotteuristic disorder
text: Frotteuristic disorder ICD-10 F65.8 Other disorders of sexual preference DSM-5-TR F65.81 Frotteuristic Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Frotteuristic disorder (ICD-11: 6D34; DSM-5-TR: F65.81) — persistent and intense sexual arousal from touching or rubbing one’s genitals against a non-consenting person. The patient has acted on the fantasies or experiences significant distress/functional impairment. Typical context — crowded public transport and other crowds.

title: 2. History
text: “Frotteur” — from the French word for “to rub”. DSM-III-R (1987), DSM-IV (1994) — separate diagnosis ‘frotteurism’ (302.89); DSM-5 (2013) — separate category.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: frotteuristic acts may occur in as many as 30% of adult males; 10–14% of adult males seen as outpatients for paraphilic disorders and hypersexuality meet the diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR). Comorbid other paraphilic disorders.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: General etiology for paraphilia; comorbid hypersexuality and impulsivity.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Touching an unwilling person in crowded public places (bus, metro, crowd) Patient escapes — victim cannot complain immediately. Legal consequences (sexual harassment, sexual crime).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. ≥6 months persistent and intense sexual arousal from touching or rubbing against a non-consenting individual. B. The patient has acted on these fantasies or experiences significant distress.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — requires 6 months; ICD-11 has no duration criterion; WFSBP 2020.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Risk assessment. Comorbidity.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Accidental touching (in dense crowd) Consent issues and fantasy not present. ASPD Broad antisocial model. Manic episode Affective context.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Forensic clinical interview. Risk scales.

title: 8. Treatment
text: WFSBP 2020 step‑by‑step: CBT and prevention of relapse; SSRI high dose; Antiandrogen / GnRH in severe cases. Legal-medical coordination.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CBT and SSRIs + WFSBP 2020 protocol — same as 6D30/6D31/6D32 tiered.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Reduction of relapse with WFSBP intervention.

title: Myth 1: “Frotteurism is harmless”
text: Evidence: Trauma for victim; sexual crime and legal consequences.

title: Myth 2: “Just an impulse — does not require clinical intervention”
text: Evidence: repeated pattern requires clinical diagnosis.

title: Myth 3: “Only legal punishment”
text: Evidence: Clinical intervention reduces relapse.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D34 Frotteuristic disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Thibaut F., Cosyns P., Fedoroff J.P. et al.; WFSBP Task Force on Paraphilias. The World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) 2020 guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of paraphilic disorders. World J Biol Psychiatry 2020;21(6):412–490.

title: Factitious disorder imposed on self
text: Factitious disorder imposed on self ICD-10 F68.1 Intentional production or feigning of symptoms or disabilities, either physical or psychological [factitious disorder] DSM-5-TR F68.10 Factitious Disor

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Factitious disorder imposed on self (ICD-11: 6D50; DSM-5-TR: F68.10) — intentional production of physical or psychological symptoms or injury in oneself, presentation of these symptoms to others; no obvious external incentive (distinguishing it from malingering). The patient’s primary motivation is to assume the sick role or be perceived as a patient.

title: 2. History
text: Asher R. (1951) — term “Munchausen syndrome” (from Baron Munchausen’s fantastic stories). DSM-III (1980) — Formalization of Factitious Disorder. DSM-5 (2013) — “Imposed on Self” and “Imposed on Another” subtypes. Eisendrath S.J. reviews — diagnosis and clinical approach.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Rare in clinical populations (1–2% of hospital admissions); under-detection in clinical approach. Sex: more common in females (in the context of the medical profession). Comorbidity: BPD, depressive disorders, history of trauma.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Psychological — deep emotional need in medical role; childhood trauma, neglect. Proximity to the medical system (being a healthcare professional). BPD is frequently comorbid.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Multiple medical consultations and examinations; numerous clinic visits (“hospital shopping”). Multiple surgical procedures. Intentional creation of symptom or injury (bleeding, creating infection, poisoning with medication, fabricating somatic complaint). Clinical presentation “impossible” or atypical; laboratory results contradict the patient’s account. The patient may lie during the interview; the medical history

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Deliberate induction or feigning of physical or psychological symptoms or injury. B. The patient presents themselves as ill or injured. C. Deceptive behavior with no apparent material gain. D. The behavior is not better explained by another mental disorder (delusional disorder, other psychotic).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same. Diagnosis is difficult — requires evidence (insurance documents, information from other clinics, video).

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical suspicion — atypical clinical presentations, multiple clinics, “impossible” symptom. Obtain medical history from other clinics (with patient consent). Insurance and pharmacy records. Observation — detection of fabricated laboratory samples. Comorbid BPD, MDD, trauma history. Legal and ethical coordination.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Real medical illness Clinical confirmation; however, factitious disorder may be comorbid (complex cases). Bodily distress disorder (6C20) Conscious lie absent; patient feels symptoms as real. Conversion (6B60) Not conscious; functional disturbance of the nervous system. Malingering Overt material/legal gain (insurance, legal). Delusional disorder — somatic Insight absent.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Medical history (from other clinics). Insurance records. Psychiatric interview for comorbid disorders.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Non-confrontational approach (Eisendrath) — the diagnosis is explained to the patient within a framework of care rather than punishment; “your distress is real, we can help in another way”. Single physician model — all complaints are managed through that physician. Limitation of invasive procedures and unnecessary examinations. Psychotherapy — supportive, CBT; long-term follow-up. Comorbid BPD, MDD, trauma treatment.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Supportive Psychotherapy — Attention to patient’s emotional needs. Multidisciplinary approach — Medical and psychiatric combined.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Eisendrath S.J. — non-confrontational approach and therapeutic alliance. APA Textbook of Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry (Levenson).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic course; “hospital shopping” continues. Long-term therapeutic alliance and treatment of comorbidities improve prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “The patient is a ‘liar’, legal punishment is required”
text: Evidence: Factitious disorder is a psychiatric disorder — response to emotional need; a non-confrontational approach and psychotherapy are recommended.

title: Myth 2: “Directly saying ‘you are lying’ will ‘correct’ the patient”
text: Evidence: a harsh confrontation causes the patient to “flee” and transfer to another clinic; a gentle approach builds a therapeutic alliance.

title: Myth 3: “Factitious disorder = somatic symptom disorder”
text: Evidence: Factitious deliberate lying; somatic symptom — patient’s genuine feeling.

title: Myth 4: “Invasive procedures that have been started must be carried through”
text: Evidence: Unnecessary invasive procedures are harmful and should be limited after a diagnosis is made.

title: Myth 5: “Factitious disorder cannot be treated”
text: Evidence: the evidence base is limited, but improvement is possible with long-term therapeutic alliance and multidisciplinary care.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D50 Factitious disorder imposed on self. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Eisendrath S.J. Factitious physical disorders: treatment without confrontation. Psychosomatics 1989;30(4):383–387. Levenson J.L. (ed.). APA Publishing Textbook of Psychosomatic Medicine and Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry. 3rd ed. 2018. Asher R. Munchausen’s syndrome. Lancet 1951;1(6650):339–341.

title: Factitious disorder imposed on another
text: Factitious disorder imposed on another ICD-10 F68.1 Intentional production or feigning of symptoms or disabilities, either physical or psychological [factitious disorder] DSM-5-TR F68.A Factitious Dis

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Factitious disorder imposed on another (ICD-11: 6D51; DSM-5-TR: F68.A) — the patient creates or feigns physical or psychological symptoms in another person (typically their own child, elderly or disabled dependent); they bring that person to the hospital as a victim. Originally termed ‘Munchausen by proxy’ (Meadow R. 1977). The diagnosis is made in the perpetrator, not in the victim. This disorder is also a form of c

title: 2. History
text: Meadow R. (1977) — ‘Munchausen syndrome by proxy’ Lancet. DSM-IV (1994) — Listed in the research appendix. DSM-5 (2013) — official diagnosis. APSAC, AAP — child protection protocols.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Rare — annual incidence 0.5–2/100,000 children (McClure R.J., 1996); under-detection. Typical perpetrator — biological mother (~75–80%); victim — child (typically <5 years). Victims’ mortality 6–9% (Sheridan); morbidity high.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Psychological needs of the patient — attention in the medical role, relationships, ‘hero’ image. Occupational burnout. History of trauma or neglect in the patient.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Child’s symptoms occur only in the presence of the mother; improve when the child is separated from the mother. Multiple clinics, atypical symptoms, “impossible” medical history. The mother is a medical professional or has extensive medical knowledge. The mother appears overly polite and is an “ideal caregiver.” Typical induction methods: drug poisoning, mechanical obstruction of food or airway, blood collection, inf

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Deliberate induction of physical or psychological symptoms or harm in another person (victim). B. The patient presents the victim to others as ill or injured. C. Deceptive behavior with no apparent material gain. D. The behavior is not better explained by another mental disorder. The diagnosis is made in the perpetrator, not in the victim.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same. APSAC, AAP — child protection protocols; this clinical condition is also a category of child abuse.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical suspicion — atypical symptom pattern, related to mother. Pediatrician, psychiatrist, social worker multidisciplinary team. Obtaining medical documentation from other clinics. Separation test — monitoring symptoms when the patient is separated from the caregiver. Video monitoring (under child protection and legal intervention) Toxicological and biochemical tests (evidence of creation). Referral to child prote

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Real medical illness Medical proof. Overanxious parent The deliberate induction does not exist; it expresses medical suspicions but does not create them. Real child abuse (other form) Physical abuse, sexual abuse, neglect — different motivation. Factitious disorder imposed on self (6D50) Victim is self.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Pediatric clinical assessment. Medical history gathering. Social service and child protection referral. Legal coordination.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Victim’s safety is the first priority — child separation (from mother or caregiver). Child protection referral — legal protocols. The patient’s (perpetrator’s) psychiatric treatment: Psychotherapy (long-term); Comorbid disorders (BPD, MDD, trauma); Medical occupational context — occupational prohibitions may be considered. Family intervention and sibling protection assessment. Victim child’s psychotherapy — trauma in

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Child Protection Referral — Mandatory when suspicion exists; APSAC, AAP protocols. Multidisciplinary Group — Pediatrician + psychiatrist + social worker + forensic specialist. Separation Test — The mother is separated from the victim; symptoms are observed. Video Monitoring — Under legal and ethical supervision.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: APSAC — child protection protocols. AAP — pediatrician role. Coordination of the legal system is mandatory.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: For the victim — high mortality (6–9%) and morbidity without intervention. For the patient — improvement with psychotherapy; long-term follow-up.

title: Myth 1: “The mother is truly caring, the diagnosis is wrong”
text: Evidence: Clinical features (mother-attributed symptoms, atypical medical history) require substantial proof; clinical suspicion is sufficient for referral to child protection.

title: Myth 2: “This condition is not a psychiatric problem; it is just child abuse”
text: Evidence: both approaches are important — child protection + perpetrator psychiatric treatment.

title: Myth 3: “Treatment of the perpetrator delays cessation of care for the victim”
text: Evidence: Victim safety is the first priority; psychiatric treatment continues separately.

title: Myth 4: “It only occurs in the mother”
text: Evidence: In most cases mother, but other caregivers — fathers, caregivers, healthcare professionals — can also be the perpetrator.

title: Myth 5: “Confrontation ‘treats’ the patient”
text: Evidence: Confrontation may necessitate transfer to another clinical unit; the patient is being followed up; child protection and forensic coordination are mandatory.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D51 Factitious disorder imposed on another. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Meadow R. Munchausen syndrome by proxy. The hinterland of child abuse. Lancet 1977;2(8033):343–345. Sheridan M.S. The deceit continues: an updated literature review of Munchausen Syndrome by Proxy. Child Abuse Negl 2003;27(4):431–451. APSAC Task Force. Munchausen by Proxy: Identification, Intervention, and Case Management. 2018.

title: Delirium
text: Delirium ICD-10 F05 Delirium, not induced by alcohol and other psychoactive substances DSM-5-TR F05 Delirium

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Delirium (ICD-11: 6D70; DSM-5-TR: F05) — a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and consciousness, cognitive deficit (memory, orientation, language, visuospatial) and perceptual disturbances (illusions, hallucinations). Develops in response to a common medical cause (infection, medication, metabolic, neurological). This is a medical emergency — the mortality rate f

title: 2. History
text: Hippocrates “phrenitis” — classic description of delirium. Lipowski Z.J. (1980s–1990s) — modern conceptualization. CAM (Confusion Assessment Method, Inouye S.K. 1990) — gold standard screening.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in hospitalized elderly 15–30%; in ICU 50–80%; post-surgery 15–50%. Comorbidity: dementia (delirium superimposed on dementia), infection, polypharmacy. Mortality and morbidity high; risk of long-term cognitive decline.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Multiple factors: Infections — sepsis, pneumonia, UTI; Medication — anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids; Substance withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepine); Metabolic — electrolyte, glucose, ammonia, uremia; Hypoxia, hypoperfusion; Neurological — seizure, stroke, brain tumor, encephalitis; Pain, constipation, urinary retention; Environment — sensory deprivation, sleep disruption (especially in ICU).

title: Three motor subtypes
text: Hyperactive — agitation, hallucinations — diagnosis is easy; Hypoactive — sedation, withdrawal — frequently underdiagnosed, resembles depression. Mixed — fluctuation.

title: Clinical signs
text: Acute onset (hours–days) and fluctuation. Attention impairment. Cognitive deficits — memory, orientation (time, place, person). Perceptual disturbances — visual hallucinations typical. Sleep-wake cycle disruption. Sundowning — worsening in evening hours.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Attention impairment (focusing, maintenance, shifting) and consciousness impairment. B. Disorder develops over a short period (hours–days); differs from baseline indicators; fluctuates within day. C. Additional cognitive impairment (memory, orientation, language, visuospatial, perception). D. Not fully explained by dementia or another neurocognitive disorder E. Evidence from history, examination, and laboratory fi

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same. NICE CG103 — Delirium: prevention, diagnosis, management (2010, 2019 update).

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) — gold standard screening. CAM-ICU — for the intensive care unit. Medical cause investigation: complete blood count, electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Mg, P), glucose, liver, kidney, TSH, B12, troponin, ECG, urine analysis and culture, blood culture, chest X-ray, brain MRI/CT, EEG (seizure suspicion), lumbar puncture (encephalitis/meningitis). Medication list review — anticholinergics, opioid

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Dementia (6D8x) Gradual onset; attention relatively preserved. Depression (psychomotor retardation as hypoactivity) Affective symptoms are dominant; attention is relatively preserved. Psychotic episode Attention is preserved; onset is different. Non-convulsive status epilepticus EEG. Wernicke’s encephalopathy Response to thiamine; classic triad (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion).

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: CAM, CAM-ICU. MMSE or MoCA (initial indicators of cognitive function). As in the medical workup above. EEG — rule out non-convulsive status.

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE CG103)
text: Etiological treatment is the first priority — correction of infection, metabolic disturbance, medication, and the hospitalization context. Environmental modification — sensory (glasses, hearing aid), daylight, nighttime darkness, quiet environment, presence of loved ones. Bedside care — hydration, nutrition, urination and defecation, movement. Antipsychotic (haloperidol 0.25–2 mg, quetiapine, risperidone) — only for

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Confusion Assessment Method (CAM — Confusion Assessment Method) — Inouye S.K. — 4 core features: acute onset/fluctuation + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness. CAM-ICU — Adapted for intensive care; in patients on a ventilator. Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) — Inouye (Inouye S.K.) — Multicomponent delirium prevention program; evidence base strong.

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE CG103 — etiological and environmental approach first-line; antipsychotics limited. SCCM PADIS Guidelines (for ICU, 2018). Burry L. Cochrane 2018 — antipsychotics do not reduce delirium duration or mortality.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Hospital mortality 25–33%. In survivors — functional decline, long-term cognitive impairment, increased dementia risk. Early etiological intervention improves prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “Delirium is ‘normal for an elderly person’”
text: Evidence: Delirium is a clinical emergency with high mortality; it requires active intervention.

title: Myth 2: “Antipsychotics are a treatment for delirium”
text: Evidence: NICE CG103, Burry Cochrane 2018 — antipsychotics do not reduce delirium duration or mortality; only for severe agitation.

title: Myth 3: “Benzodiazepine is safe for an elderly agitated patient”
text: Evidence: benzodiazepines exacerbate delirium; only in the case of alcohol/BZ withdrawal.

title: Myth 4: “Hypoactive delirium is ‘good’ and requires no intervention”
text: Evidence: hypoactive delirium linked to worse mortality; problem of under-detection.

title: Myth 5: “Sleeping is best for the patient with delirium”
text: Evidence: Daytime activity, presence of close ones, sensory stimulation are recommended; HELP program is evidence-based.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D70 Delirium. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. NICE CG103. Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management. 2010, 2019 update. Inouye S.K. et al. Clarifying confusion: the confusion assessment method. Ann Intern Med 1990;113(12):941–948. Burry L. et al. Antipsychotics for treatment of delirium in hospitalized non-ICU patients. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;(6):CD005594. Devlin J.W. et al. SCCM PADIS Guidelin

title: Neurocognitive disorder (MCI) (Mild neurocognitive disorder)
text: Neurocognitive disorder (MCI) (Mild neurocognitive disorder) Mild neurocognitive disorder ICD-10 F06.7 Mild cognitive disorder DSM-5-TR G31.84 Mild Neurocognitive Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Mild neurocognitive disorder (ICD-11: 6D71; DSM-5-TR: G31.84) — mild decline in one or more cognitive domains (memory, complex attention, executive function, language, visuospatial, social cognition); daily activity is maintained (though compensation may be needed). Also known as “mild cognitive impairment” (MCI).

title: 2. History
text: Petersen R.C. (1999) — clinical conceptualization of MCI. DSM-5 (2013) — Major (dementia) and Mild Neurocognitive Disorders categories. AAN (2018) — Practice Guideline for MCI (Petersen).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence 10–20% in those aged 65+. Annually, 10–15% of people with MCI progress to dementia due to Alzheimer disease. Risk factors: age, ApoE4, cardiovascular.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Alzheimer’s prodromal (amnestic MCI); Vascular Lewy bodies prodromal; Frontotemporal; Medical (depression, thyroid, B12, medication effects).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: The patient or a close person complains of cognitive decline. Mild deficit on standardized tests (typically -1 to -2 SD). Daily functioning is preserved (minimal compensation in complex activities). Subtypes: amnestic (memory dominant — high Alzheimer’s risk), non-amnestic (executive or other domain).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Mild decline in one or more cognitive domains (noted by the patient, informant, or clinician, and confirmed by standardized neuropsychological testing). B. Daily functioning is preserved. C. Not better explained by delirium D. Not better explained by another mental disorder (MDD).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — separation of Major and Mild. AAN 2018 — etiological investigation (Alzheimer, vascular) and biomarkers under development.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + informant. MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment), MMSE. Neuropsychological testing. Laboratory — B12, folate, TSH, liver, kidney, glucose, HIV/syphilis. Brain MRI — vascular, atrophy, other pathology. Biomarkers (if clinical suspicion) — CSF amyloid-β/tau, PET imaging (Alzheimer’s prodrome). Depression screening (GDS, PHQ-9).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Dementia (Major NCD) Daily functioning is significantly impaired. Normal age-related cognitive change Performance normal during testing. Depression (pseudodementia) Affective symptoms are dominant; improves with antidepressants. Delirium (6D70) Acute onset, fluctuating attention. B12 or thyroid deficiency Laboratory; improvement with correction.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: MoCA (a score ≤ 25 indicates impairment) — the validated screen for MCI; MMSE has no established MCI cut-off and is insensitive to mild impairment. Neuropsychological battery (memory, executive, language, visuospatial). Laboratory panel. MRI (routine), biomarkers (selective).

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological treatment — modifiable factors (cardiovascular risk, B12, thyroid, depression, medication). Lifestyle — physical activity (aerobic), Mediterranean diet, cognitive stimulation, social connections (FINGER trial, Lancet 2015 — multimodal approach effective). Pharmacotherapy — no specific approval for MCI. Donepezil and other AChEIs — limited evidence base; not routinely recommended. Lecanemab, Donanemab — ne

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) — Nasreddine Z.S. — 30 items; MCI screening (cut-off 26). FINGER Multimodal Intervention (FINGER — Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study) — Diet + exercise + cognitive training + vascular risk management. Lecanemab, Donanemab — Anti-amyloid antibodies; FDA approval; ARIA monitoring (MRI).

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AAN 2018 — modifiable factors and lifestyle. FINGER trial (Ngandu Lancet 2015) — multimodal intervention. Lecanemab — CLARITY-AD (van Dyck NEJM 2023); donanemab — TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (Sims JAMA 2023).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Stable 30%, transition to dementia 10–15%/year, reversion to normal cognition 15–20%. Amnestic MCI as Alzheimer’s prodrome — high conversion rate.

title: Myth 1: “MCI inevitably turns into dementia”
text: Evidence: annual rate 10–15%; some remain stable or improve.

title: Myth 2: “Vitamin B and ginkgo cure MCI”
text: Evidence: B vitamins only in deficiency; ginkgo Cochrane (Birks 2009) — no reliable evidence of effect.

title: Myth 3: “AChEI is the standard treatment for MCI”
text: Evidence: AAN 2018 — evidence base insufficient; not routinely recommended.

title: Myth 4: “Lecanemab cures MCI/Alzheimer’s”
text: Evidence: Lecanemab reduces clinical decline rate by 27% over 18 months, CLARITY-AD; ARIA and infusion reactions; not “cure.”

title: Myth 5: “Cognitive decline is inevitable with age”
text: Evidence: Cardiovascular risk, physical activity, social connections are modifiable factors.

title: Amnestic disorder
text: Amnestic disorder ICD-10 F04 Organic amnesic syndrome, not induced by alcohol and other psychoactive substances DSM-5-TR F02.8x Major Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition (amnestic

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Amnestic Disorder (ICD-11: 6D72; DSM-5-TR: major/mild NCD; ICD-10-CM F04) — significant impairment in learning and recalling new information; other cognitive domains relatively preserved. Due to a medical condition (Wernicke–Korsakoff, brain injury, encephalitis, anoxia), substance effect, or other causes.

title: 2. History
text: Korsakoff S. (1887) — description of alcohol-related amnesia. Scoville W.B., Milner B. (1957) — H.M. case (amnesia after bilateral medial temporal resection).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Korsakoff syndrome — in 12–25% of chronic heavy alcohol users. Amnesia after traumatic brain injury — in 30–50% of TBI patients. Transient global amnesia (TGA) — prevalence in age 65+ 5–25/100,000/year.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Wernicke–Korsakoff — thiamine (B1) deficiency (alcohol, malnutrition). Traumatic brain injury (TBI). Hypoxia/anoxia — cardiac arrest, carbon monoxide. Herpes simplex encephalitis. Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1). Transient global amnesia (TGA) — suspected vascular etiology. Substance (alcohol blackout, benzodiazepine). Stroke (especially bilateral thalamic or hippocampal).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Anterograde amnesia — impairment in learning new information (core feature). Retrograde amnesia — memory for the period before the injury (“Ribot’s law” — recent memories are lost earlier than remote ones). Confabulation — in Korsakoff syndrome — patient fills memory gaps with fabrications. Other cognitive domains are relatively preserved (intellect, language, visuospatial).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Impairment in learning new information or impairment in recall of previously learned information. B. Memory impairment causes significant functional impairment. C. Does not occur exclusively in the context of delirium or another NCD. D. Evidence — history, examination, laboratory indicate that memory impairment is due to specific cause (medical condition, substance).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR — integrated into Major and Mild NCD structure; amnestic subtype. ICD-11 — separate category.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + informant. Neuropsychological test — memory (WMS-IV, RAVLT, Wechsler Logical Memory). Brain MRI — bilateral hippocampal, medial temporal, thalamic pathology. Vitamin B1 level or empirical thiamine (suspected Korsakoff syndrome). Toxicology. Autoimmune encephalitis panel (in atypical cases). EEG.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Alzheimer’s dementia Multiple cognitive domains, gradual onset. Delirium (6D70) Fluctuation of attention. Dissociative amnesia (6B61) In trauma context; selective past memory; no medical cause. Factitious disorder / malingering Atypical pattern, secondary gain. TGA Acute, less than 24 hours; complete recovery.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: WMS-IV (Wechsler Memory Scale), RAVLT. Brain MRI. Thiamine, B12. Toxicology.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological — thiamine (Wernicke–Korsakoff — 500 mg IV × 3 times/day for at least 3 days, then 250 mg IV or IM once daily × 3–5 days; long-term oral thiamine in alcohol withdrawal). Autoimmune encephalitis — immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis, rituximab). Herpes encephalitis — acyclovir. Compensatory strategies (external memory aids, daily structuring). Treatment of substance use (alcohol). Rehabilitation

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Wernicke–Korsakoff Prophylaxis and Treatment — High-dose IV/IM thiamine; administration before glucose is critical (glucose exacerbates Wernicke’s in thiamine deficiency). Cognitive Rehabilitation — Wilson B.A. — External memory aids (diary, phone reminders), strategy teaching. Immunotherapy (Autoimmune Encephalitis) — Graus 2016 protocol.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Wernicke–Korsakoff — Royal College of Physicians thiamine protocol. Graus F. et al. Lancet Neurol 2016 — autoimmune encephalitis.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: TGA — full recovery. Korsakoff — residual deficit typical; acute thiamine intervention is critical in Wernicke’s encephalopathy. TBI — partial recovery with rehabilitation.

title: Myth 1: “Amnesia can be ‘recovered’ with hypnosis”
text: Evidence: hypnosis can generate false memories; ineffective in organic amnesia.

title: Myth 2: “Oral thiamine is sufficient in Wernicke’s”
text: Evidence: Oral absorption insufficient; IV/IM high dose required.

title: Myth 3: “Glucose ‘cures’ Wernicke’s”
text: Evidence: Glucose given in thiamine deficiency precipitates or worsens Wernicke’s encephalopathy; administer thiamine first.

title: Myth 4: “All amnesia is temporary”
text: Evidence: Korsakoff, TBI-based amnesia typically chronic; rehabilitation yields improvement, but full recovery is rare.

title: Myth 5: “Confabulation is lying”
text: Evidence: Confabulation in Korsakoff syndrome is a neurobiological phenomenon, not a conscious lie.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6D72 Amnestic disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Royal College of Physicians. Wernicke’s encephalopathy and Korsakoff’s syndrome. 2014. Graus F. et al. A clinical approach to diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis. Lancet Neurol 2016;15(4):391–404. Wilson B.A. Neuropsychological Rehabilitation. Wiley; 2009.

title: Dementia due to Alzheimer disease
text: Dementia due to Alzheimer disease Dementia due to Alzheimer disease ICD-10 F00 Dementia in Alzheimer disease DSM-5-TR G30.9 + F02.8x Major Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Alzheimer’s Disease

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease (ICD-11: 6D80; DSM-5-TR: G30.9 + F02.8x Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer’s Disease) — gradual and persistent cognitive decline, initially episodic memory, then multiple cognitive domains and significant impairment of daily functioning. Most common cause of dementia (60–70%).

title: 2. History
text: Alzheimer A. (1906) — first clinical and histopathological description. Amyloid hypothesis (Hardy J., Higgins G.A. Science 1992). NICE NG97 (2018) — dementia clinical guideline. FDA — aducanumab (2021, controversial), lecanemab (2023), donanemab (2024) — anti-amyloid antibodies.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Global 55 million+ dementia patients (WHO 2023); 60–70% Alzheimer’s. Prevalence by age: 65 years 5%, 80+ years 25%+. Sex: higher in females (related to life expectancy). Comorbidity: cardiovascular, depression, anxiety, BPSD (behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Familial Alzheimer’s (1%): APP, PSEN1, PSEN2 mutations (early onset, dominant). Sporadic (99%) — multiple genes (ApoE4 strongest risk; LOAD GWAS loci). Modifiable factors (Lancet Commission 2024; in addition to non-modifiable age and ApoE4): low education, hearing loss, hypertension, obesity, smoking, depression, physical inactivity, social isolation, diabetes, air pollution, alcohol, TBI, vision loss, high LDL. Path

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Typical onset — episodic memory decline (difficulty retaining new information). Stages: Early — memory, anomia, orientation difficulty; Moderate — visuospatial, executive function, daily activities require support; Late — speech severely limited, loss of recognition of relatives, restricted mobility, feeding and swallowing difficulties. BPSD — agitation, aggression, delusions (particularly of theft), hallucinations,

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Major NCD criteria (≥ 1 cognitive domain significant decline + impairment in daily activities). B. Clinical characteristics consistent with Alzheimer’s (gradual, continuous decline, memory predominant). C. Probable AD — genetic mutation and/or 3 elements (memory + 1+ cognitive domain, sustained decline, no other cause). D. Possible AD — criteria not fully met, but atypical clinical presentation or comorbidity.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: NIA-AA Research Framework (Jack C.R. 2018) — biomarker-based diagnosis (ATN — amyloid, tau, neurodegeneration). NICE NG97 — based on clinical diagnosis; biomarkers selective. AAN — diagnostic tools.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + informant. MoCA, MMSE, ACE-III. Neuropsychological battery. Laboratory — B12, folate, TSH, liver, kidney, glucose, HIV/syphilis (medical cause exclusion). Brain MRI (atrophy, vascular changes, other pathology). Biomarkers (selective, if clinical suspicion): CSF amyloid-β42 (low), tau (high); Amyloid PET, tau PET; Blood biomarkers (p-tau217, GFAP) — are under development. Comorbid depression scree

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Vascular dementia (6D81) Stepwise decline, focal neurological signs, vascular MRI. Lewy bodies (6D82) Visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder Frontotemporal (6D83) Personality/conduct or language dominant; earlier onset. Delirium (6D70) Acute, fluctuating attention. Depressive pseudodementia Affective, improvement with antidepressants. Normal pressure hydrocep

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: MoCA, MMSE, ACE-III, neuropsychological. Laboratory panel. MRI, biomarkers. BPSD scales (NPI — Neuropsychiatric Inventory).

title: 8.1 General principles (NICE NG97 · AAN · APA)
text: AChEI (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) — for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease; modestly slows cognitive decline. Donepezil 5–10 mg (later 23 mg), rivastigmine patch. Memantine (NMDA antagonist) — for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s; combination with AChEI. Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) — FDA approval for early symptomatic AD (lecanemab 2023, donanemab 2024); in 18-month trials reduce the rat

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors (AChEI) — Donepezil, Galantamine, Rivastigmine — Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; synaptic acetylcholine increase. NICE NG97. Memantine — NMDA antagonist; reduces excitotoxicity. Lecanemab, Donanemab — Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies; for early AD; ARIA monitoring. Non-pharmacological interventions for BPSD — Validation therapy, music therapy, reminiscence therapy, ABC analysis. FING

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG97 (2018) — AChEI for mild-to-moderate; memantine for moderate-to-severe; combination selective. Livingston G. et al. Lancet Commission 2024 — 14 modifiable risk factors. FDA Lecanemab 2023, Donanemab 2024 — for early AD; ARIA monitoring. APA — guidelines for antipsychotic use in the elderly.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: After diagnosis, median life expectancy is 4–8 years. Rapid course, family history, altered by ApoE4. Comorbid cardiovascular mortality.

title: Myth 1: “Alzheimer’s is normal aging”
text: Evidence: Alzheimer’s is a disease; normal aging can occur without cognitive decline; up to 45% of dementia cases are attributable to modifiable factors (Lancet Commission 2024).

title: Myth 2: “Dementia is inevitable, prevention is impossible”
text: Evidence: Lancet Commission 2024 — management of modifiable factors can delay up to 45% of potential dementia cases.

title: Myth 3: “Lecanemab cures Alzheimer’s”
text: Evidence: lecanemab over 18 months reduces cognitive decline rate by 27%, Clarity AD (moderate effect); ARIA and infusion risks significant; not “cure.”

title: Myth 4: “Antipsychotics are safe for elderly dementia patients”
text: Evidence: FDA black box — antipsychotics increase mortality in elderly dementia patients (stroke, cardiovascular); only for severe agitation/psychosis, short-term.

title: Myth 5: “Ginkgo biloba is a prophylaxis for dementia”
text: Evidence: Cochrane (Birks J. 2009) — ginkgo shows no evidence of efficacy for dementia.

title: Myth 6: “Coconut oil cures Alzheimer’s”
text: Evidence: No clinical evidence; promotion in popular media, not a clinical recommendation.

title: Myth 7: “The patient should not be told the diagnosis of dementia”
text: Evidence: NICE — patient has the right to diagnosis; early decision-making, advance documents important.

title: Dementia due to cerebrovascular disease
text: Dementia due to cerebrovascular disease ICD-10 F01 Vascular dementia DSM-5-TR F01.5x Major Vascular Neurocognitive Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Dementia due to cerebrovascular disease (Vascular Dementia; ICD-11: 6D81; DSM-5-TR: F01.5x and similar) — cognitive decline and impairment of daily functioning developing as a result of cerebrovascular disease (stroke, small vessel disease, hypoperfusion). Second most common cause of dementia (~15–20%).

title: 2. History
text: Binswanger O. (1894) — classic description of subcortical vascular dementia. NINDS-AIREN (1993) — international diagnostic criteria. VASCOG (2014) — Updated consensus (Vascular Cognitive Disorders).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: 15–20% of dementia cases; often mixed with Alzheimer’s. Prevalence increases with age. Risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, smoking, history of stroke.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Multi-infarct dementia. Small vessel disease (subcortical leukoaraiosis, lacunar infarcts — Binswanger). Strategic infarct (thalamic, hippocampal). Hypoperfusion (systemic hypotension, cardiac arrest). CADASIL (autosomal dominant cerebral arteriopathy, NOTCH3).

title: 5. Clinical features
text: “Stepwise” decline (as opposed to the gradual decline of Alzheimer’s). Executive function, processing speed and attention are predominantly affected — memory is relatively less impaired (difference from Alzheimer). Focal neurological signs — hemiparesis, dysarthria, extrapyramidal, visual field defect. Mood disorders (vascular depression), apathy, abulia frequent. Postural disturbances (gait, balance).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (NINDS-AIREN, VASCOG)
text: A. Meeting major NCD criteria. B. Clinical features consistent with vascular etiology: either (1) stepwise decline + history of stroke or (2) executive function and processing speed predominant. C. Brain imaging evidence of vascular pathology — infarcts, leukoaraiosis, microhemorrhages. D. Temporal relationship between cognitive decline and vascular event (Probable VaD).

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: VASCOG 2014 (Sachdev P. et al. Alzheimer Dis Assoc Disord) — introduced the Vascular Cognitive Impairment umbrella term. NICE NG97 — management of vascular risk factors.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + informant. MoCA (attention to executive function subscales). Neurological examination — focal signs. Brain MRI (FLAIR — leukoaraiosis, DWI — acute infarcts, T2/SWI — microhemorrhages). Cardiovascular evaluation — blood pressure, ECG (atrial fibrillation), Holter, carotid ultrasound, echo. Laboratory — HbA1c, lipid, coagulation, hyperhomocysteinemia.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Alzheimer (6D80) Gradual, memory dominant. Mixed Dementia (Alzheimer’s + VaD) In many cases; clinically coexisting. Lewy bodies (6D82) Visual hallucinations, parkinsonism. Frontotemporal (6D83) Personality/behavior dominant. Normal pressure hydrocephalus Triad (gait, urinary incontinence, cognitive impairment). Depressive pseudodementia Affective, improvement with antidepressants.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: MoCA, neuropsychological testing. MRI, cardiovascular. Laboratory panel.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Vascular risk factor management — first-line Hypertension (target SBP <140, sometimes <130); Diabetes HbA1c management; Statin (lipid); Antiplatelet (aspirin) or anticoagulant (atrial fibrillation — DOAC); Smoking cessation; Physical activity, diet. AChEI and memantine — evidence base limited for VaD, but may be effective in mixed dementia; NICE NG97 — considered in mixed cases. BPSD management — non-pharmacological

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Vascular Risk Management — Hypertension, diabetes, lipids, atrial fibrillation, smoking. AChEI/Memantine in Mixed Dementia — Donepezil, rivastigmine off-label in pure VaD; may be considered in mixed cases. Stroke Rehabilitation — Multidisciplinary.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG97 — vascular risk management. AHA/ASA stroke prophylaxis.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Risk factor management reduces the rate of decline. Stroke history and comorbidity determine the prognosis.

title: Myth 1: “VaD is completely different from Alzheimer’s”
text: Evidence: In most dementia cases mixed pathology (Alzheimer + VaD); clinical differentiation sometimes difficult.

title: Myth 2: “There is no specific treatment for VaD”
text: Evidence: vascular risk factor management — first-line and effective intervention; prevention particularly strong.

title: Myth 3: “Aspirin for dementia prophylaxis”
text: Evidence: ASPREE trial (McNeil J.J. NEJM 2018) — aspirin in primary prevention showed no evidence of preventing dementia; only in specific stroke prophylaxis indications.

title: Myth 4: “Homocysteine-lowering vitamins prevent vascular dementia”
text: Evidence: the evidence for homocysteine-lowering vitamins as cognitive prophylaxis is weak.

title: Myth 5: “Stepwise decline is mandatory for diagnosing VaD”
text: Evidence: stepwise decline is typical only in multi-infarct form; in small vessel form decline is gradual.

title: 11. Sources

Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement. Alzheimer Dis Assoc Disord 2014;28(3):206–218. McNeil J.J. et al. title: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (Frontotemporal dementia)
text: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (Frontotemporal dementia) Frontotemporal dementia ICD-10 F02.0 Dementia in Pick disease DSM-5-TR G31.09 + F02.8x (severe) / G31.84 (mild) Major or Mild Neurocognitive Dis

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD; ICD-11: 6D83; DSM-5-TR: G31.09 + F02.8x (severe) / G31.84 (mild)) — dementia developing from atrophy of the frontal and/or temporal lobes; typical onset between ages 45–65 (most common among early-onset dementias). Three clinical variants: bvFTD (behavioral variant) and two forms of PPA (Primary Progressive Aphasia — semantic and non-fluent).

title: 2. History
text: Pick A. (1892) — “Pick’s disease” — description of frontotemporal atrophy. Neary D. et al. (1998) — FTD clinical consensus criteria. Rascovsky K. et al. (2011) — updated criteria for bvFTD.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: 5–10% of dementia cases before age 65; Alzheimer’s dominates after age 65. Sex: equal. Family history in approximately 40% of cases. Comorbidity: ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis) — FTD-ALS spectrum (C9orf72 mutation).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Genetic (40%) — C9orf72 (most common), MAPT, GRN mutations. Pathology — tau (Pick body, MAPT), TDP-43 (types A–D; GRN and C9orf72 mutations), FUS proteins.

title: bvFTD (behavioral variant, ~60% of FTD)
text: Early personality change — apathy, disinhibition, socially inappropriate behavior, loss of empathy. Stereotypical behavior (ritualistic). Hyperoral behavior (food changes, “sweet tooth”). Executive function significantly impaired; memory and visuospatial relatively preserved at onset.

title: PPA — primary progressive aphasia
text: Non-fluent variant (nfvPPA) — grammatical difficulty, slow speech, apraxia of speech. Semantic variant (svPPA) — loss of word meaning, agnosia; fluent, but empty speech. The logopenic variant is associated with Alzheimer’s disease but is distinct.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD; Gorno-Tempini 2011 PPA)
text: bvFTD (Probable): ≥ 3 of 6 behavioral symptoms (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, stereotypy, hyperorality, executive dysfunction) + functional impairment + neuroimaging support. PPA: language is primary deficit; subvariant based on clinical and neuroimaging.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: Rascovsky K. et al. Brain 2011 — Behavioral Variant Frontotemporal Dementia. Gorno-Tempini M.L. et al. Neurology 2011 — PPA.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + informant (behavioral change). Neuropsychological battery (executive function, language). Brain MRI — frontal and/or temporal atrophy. FDG-PET — hypometabolism. Genetic testing (family history). ALS screening (clinical or electromyography).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Alzheimer (6D80) Memory dominant, late onset. Late-onset schizophrenia No atrophy. Mania, depression Affective episodes. Bipolar disorder Affective, cyclic. Personality disorder Persistent, long-standing; change in FTD is new. Brain tumor MRI.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: FAB (Frontal Assessment Battery), neuropsychological. MRI, FDG-PET. Genetic test. ALS screening.

title: 8. Treatment
text: There is no disease-modifying medication — treatment targeting the pathological process is not yet approved (clinical trials ongoing). AChEI — ineffective or harmful in FTD (may worsen behavior); unlike in Alzheimer’s disease. SSRI — for behavioral symptoms (disinhibition, compulsivity, depression) in bvFTD; some evidence. Trazodone — for agitation; studies by Lebert F. et al. Atypical antipsychotic — only in severe

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: SSRI for bvFTD — Citalopram, sertraline — behavioral symptoms. Trazodone — Agitation, sleep. Non-Pharmacological — Environmental modification, structure, caregiver training. Speech-Language Therapy (SLT) — For PPA; compensatory strategies. Genetic Consultation — For family members.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: NICE NG97 — does not recommend AChEI for FTD. Lebert F. et al. Dement Geriatr Cogn Disord 2004 — trazodone.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: From symptom onset, median life expectancy is 6–11 years; FTD-ALS is shorter (3 years). Rapid decline with some mutations.

title: Myth 1: “FTD is a subtype of Alzheimer’s”
text: Evidence: distinct pathological and clinical unit; tau, TDP-43, FUS pathologies; AChEI ineffective.

title: Myth 2: “AChEIs can be used in all dementias”
text: Evidence: AChEIs ineffective or harmful in FTD; NICE NG97 does not recommend.

title: Myth 3: “Behavioral change is only a psychiatric problem”
text: Evidence: Early-onset behavioral change (45–65 years) should raise suspicion for FTD; neuroimaging is important.

title: Myth 4: “FTD is not genetic without a family history”
text: Evidence: 40% of cases have a family history; sporadic cases are also possible; C9orf72 expansion may be occult.

title: Myth 5: “The behavior of a patient with FTD is voluntary”
text: Evidence: behavioral changes are neurobiological in origin — frontal lobe dysfunction; volitional control impaired.

title: 1. Definition and nosology

title: 2. History
text: Marcé L.V. (1858) — first clinical description of postpartum psychosis and depression. EPDS — Cox J.L. et al. (1987) — Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. NICE CG192 (2014, 2020 update) — antenatal and postnatal mental health. FDA — brexanolone (2019), zuranolone (2023) — first specifically approved drugs for postpartum depression.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 10–15% (high-income countries), 20–30% (low- and middle-income countries). “Baby blues” — milder, short-term (1–2 weeks) — occurs in 50–80% of women; does not require clinical intervention. Comorbidity: anxiety, OCD, panic. Risk factors: previous depression, family history, depression during pregnancy, lack of partner support, socioeconomic stress.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Hormonal — sharp drop in estrogen and progesterone after childbirth; allopregnanolone dysregulation. Sleep disturbance with newborn care. Psychosocial stress, relationships, social support. Genetic and prior history of affective disorder.
sub: Mental or behavioural disorders associated with pregnancy, childbirth or the puerperium, without psychotic symptoms

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Major depressive episode symptoms (sleep disturbance, appetite loss, anhedonia, worthlessness, suicidal thoughts). Specific characteristics: affective distancing towards the infant, difficulties in infant bonding, belief in inability to fulfill the maternal role, intrusive thoughts regarding harming the infant (ego-dystonic — similar to OCD; distinct from postpartum psychosis). title: Secondary psychotic syndrome
text: Secondary psychotic syndrome ICD-10 F06.2 Organic delusional [schizophrenia-like] disorder DSM-5-TR F06.2 Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition, With Delusions

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Secondary Psychotic Syndrome (ICD-11: 6E61; DSM-5-TR: F06.2/F06.0 Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition) — psychotic episode developing in the context of another medical condition (autoimmune, infectious, endocrine, metabolic, neurological) or a substance. First-line intervention — treatment directed at the primary etiology.

title: 2. History
text: The term “Symptomatic psychosis” was formulated in the 20th century. Dalmau J. (2007) — discovery of anti-NMDA-R encephalitis; autoimmune psychosis revolution. Graus F. et al. (2016) — autoimmune encephalitis clinical guideline.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: 3–8% of all first-episode psychosis cases have secondary etiologies. Anti-NMDA-R encephalitis — rare but reversible psychosis in young women; paraneoplastic with teratoma. Hashimoto encephalopathy, lupus encephalopathy.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Autoimmune: Anti-NMDA-R, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2 encephalitis; Hashimoto (TPO antibodies); lupus (NPSLE). Infectious: HIV, syphilis, herpes encephalitis, COVID-19. Endocrine: hyper/hypothyroidism, cortisol disorders (Cushing, Addison), parathyroid disorders (hypercalcemia). Metabolic: uremia, hepatic encephalopathy, hyponatremia, hypo/hyperglycemia, B12 deficiency, Wilson’s disease. Neurological: brain tumor, stroke,

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Psychotic symptoms (delusion, hallucination, disorganized behavior). Atypical features (characteristic of autoimmune encephalitis): Rapid onset Motor symptoms (catatonic, dystonias, orofacial dyskinesia); Autonomic disturbance (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia); Seizures; Impairment of consciousness. Compared to classic psychosis (schizophrenia) — atypical presentation raises suspicion.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Psychotic symptoms. B. Evidence of medical condition (autoimmune, infectious, endocrine, metabolic, neurological) or substance effect. C. Psychosis is not diagnosed when it occurs exclusively in the context of delirium (but may overlap with delirium). D. Not better explained by another primary psychotic disorder.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: Graus F. et al. Lancet Neurol 2016 — autoimmune encephalitis clinical approach. ICD-11 — substance-induced psychosis does NOT belong here: it lives in the substance chapter (6C40.6 alcohol, 6C41.6 cannabis and so on). 6E61 covers only health conditions outside the mental-disorders chapter and is assigned alongside the diagnosis of the underlying disease.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical suspicion — new-onset psychosis, especially with atypical features or in young women. Medical assessment: Complete blood count, liver/renal, electrolytes (Na, Ca), glucose, ammonia; TSH, TPO antibodies (Hashimoto); Cortisol level (Cushing/Addison); HIV, syphilis; ANA, lupus panel; B12, folate, ceruloplasmin (Wilson); Toxicology screening. Brain MRI. EEG — non-convulsive status, encephalitis. Lumbar puncture

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Schizophrenia (6A20) Medical cause absent; typical clinical course. Acute and transient psychotic (6A23) Secondary causes excluded. Delirium (6D70) Fluctuation of attention; psychosis in the context of delirium. Substance-induced psychosis Substance confirmation and temporal relationship. Dementia with psychotic features Cognitive decline.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: The above laboratory panel. MRI, EEG. CSF antibody panel. Tumor screening.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological treatment is first-line: Autoimmune encephalitis — IV methylprednisolone 1 g × 5 days → IVIG and/or plasmapheresis; second-line rituximab, cyclophosphamide; Paraneoplastic — tumor treatment (ovarian teratoma surgery); Endocrine — thyroid, cortisol, calcium correction; Infectious — antibiotic, antiviral; Metabolic — correction of the disorder; Medication-induced — discontinuation of the suspected agent. Sy

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Immunotherapy (Autoimmune Encephalitis) — IV steroids → IVIG → plasmapheresis → rituximab/cyclophosphamide. Treatment of Tumor (Paraneoplastic) — Surgical or oncological treatment. Atypical Antipsychotic, Symptomatic — Until etiological treatment produces results; quetiapine and olanzapine are preferred. ECT — in refractory cases — Effective in catatonic or immunotherapy-resistant autoimmune encephalitis.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Graus F. et al. Lancet Neurol 2016 — autoimmune encephalitis protocols. APA Textbook of Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry (Levenson).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Most cases respond to etiological treatment; reversible condition. Anti-NMDA-R encephalitis — 75% good recovery with early immunotherapy.

title: Myth 1: “First-episode psychosis is always schizophrenia”
text: Evidence: 3–8% secondary etiologies; atypical features require attention; medical evaluation is mandatory in first-episode psychosis.

title: Myth 2: “Typical antipsychotic (haloperidol) is safe for every psychotic episode”
text: Evidence: If autoimmune encephalitis is suspected, haloperidol and similar first-generation antipsychotics are contraindicated — risk of NMS, disease exacerbation.

title: Myth 3: “Anti-NMDA-R encephalitis is rare, not worth looking for”
text: Evidence: In a young woman atypical psychosis + movement symptoms + seizures is the classic presentation of Anti-NMDA-R; antibody test saves lives; reversible condition.

title: Myth 4: “If no medical cause is found, a psychiatric diagnosis is made — no further search is needed”
text: Evidence: Atypical clinical presentation requires expanded investigation (CSF, MRI, paraneoplastic panel).

title: Myth 5: “Immunotherapy is not suitable for psychiatric conditions”
text: Evidence: If there is evidence of autoimmune encephalitis, immunotherapy is first-line; standard antipsychotics are ineffective.

title: 11. Sources
