A clinical approach to diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis. Lancet Neurol 2016;15(4):391–404. Dalmau J. et al. Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis: case series and analysis of the effects of antibodies. Lancet Neurol 2008;7(12):1091–1098. Levenson J.L. (ed.). APA Publishin

title: Secondary mood syndrome
text: Secondary mood syndrome ICD-10 F06.3 Organic mood [affective] disorders DSM-5-TR F06.3x Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Secondary mood syndrome (ICD-11: 6E62; DSM-5-TR: F06.3x Mood Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition) — depressive, manic, or mixed mood episodes as a direct physiological consequence of another medical condition.

title: 2. History
text: The term “Organic Affective Disorder” belongs to the 20th century; current clinical practice has moved toward the biopsychosocial model.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Depressive symptoms are prevalent in chronic medical conditions; some meet criteria for clinical depressive episode. Steroid-induced mood disorders — high-dose prednisone 5–18% mania/hypomania, depression. Interferon-induced depression — 20–40% in HCV treatment. Post-stroke depression — 30%.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Endocrine — hypothyroid (depression), hyperthyroid (mania-like), Cushing, Addison. Neurological — stroke (left frontal — depression, right — mania), Parkinson’s, MS, brain tumor, dementia, TBI. Substance/medication — steroids, interferon, dopamine agonists, isotretinoin, β-blocker, anticonvulsant. Metabolic — uremia, B12, folate. Infectious — HIV, syphilis, COVID. Autoimmune — lupus, Hashimoto. Oncology — pancreatic

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Symptoms of depressive, manic, mixed, and hypomanic episodes. Medical condition or substance-related temporal association. Features not characteristic of classic affective disorder (late onset, atypical presentation).

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Persistent mood disturbance (depressive, manic, or mixed). B. Evidence of a medical condition (non-psychiatric). C. Not better explained by a primary affective disorder. D. Does not occur in the context of delirium

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICD-11 — a substance-induced mood disorder does NOT belong here: it lives in the substance chapter. 6E62 covers only health conditions outside the mental-disorders chapter and is assigned alongside the diagnosis of the underlying disease. Consultation-liaison protocols.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + medical history. Medical and laboratory assessment (TSH, B12, cortisol, renal, hepatic). Medication list review. Brain imaging (stroke, MS, tumor). Toxicology. Comorbid disorders.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature MDD first (6A70/6A71) There is no medical cause. Bipolar first History of affective episodes without a medical cause. Adjustment disorder (6B43) Response to stress factor. Delirium (6D70) Fluctuation of attention.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PHQ-9, MADRS, YMRS. Laboratory: TSH, B12, cortisol, ANA, kidney, liver. MRI in atypical cases. C-SSRS.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological treatment — correction of medical condition or medication. Symptomatic psychiatric treatment: Depressive — SSRIs (disease-specific selection; cardiac — sertraline, escitalopram; oncology — mirtazapine); Manic — antipsychotic (quetiapine, olanzapine); in steroid-induced mania, taper steroids or use antipsychotic; Mixed or refractory — ECT. Multidisciplinary approach — psychiatrist, the specialist treating

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: SSRI Illness-Specific — Choice appropriate to cardiac, oncological, neurological context. ECT — In refractory and severe cases.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Most remissions with etiological intervention.

title: Myth 1: “Depression is ‘normal’ for a patient with a medical illness”
text: Evidence: Clinical depression worsens the course of the medical condition; requires active intervention.

title: Myth 2: “Steroid-induced mania resolves on its own”
text: Evidence: dose reduction or antipsychotic addition required.

title: Myth 3: “Antidepressant is first-line in hypothyroidism”
text: Evidence: thyroid correction first; antidepressants for residual symptoms.

title: Myth 4: “Interferon depression is rare”
text: Evidence: HCV interferon therapy 20–40% — active monitoring required.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6E62 Secondary mood syndrome. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Levenson J.L. (ed.). APA Publishing Textbook of Psychosomatic Medicine and Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry. 3rd ed. 2018. Robinson R.G., Jorge R.E. Post-stroke depression: a review. Am J Psychiatry 2016;173(3):221–231.

title: Secondary anxiety syndrome
text: Secondary anxiety syndrome ICD-10 F06.4 Organic anxiety disorder DSM-5-TR F06.4 Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Secondary Anxiety Syndrome (ICD-11: 6E63; DSM-5-TR: F06.4 Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition) — anxiety or panic symptoms as a direct physiological consequence of another medical condition.

title: 2. History
text: Development of consultation-liaison psychiatry; formalization from DSM-III-R (1987).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Frequency of anxiety is high in chronic medical conditions (cardiac, COPD, endocrine). In hyperthyroidism, 60–70% have anxiety symptoms. Caffeine, stimulant-induced anxiety.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Endocrine — hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, hypoglycemia. Cardiac — arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, mitral valve prolapse. Respiratory — COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism. Neurological — TBI, Parkinson’s, MS. Substance/medication — caffeine, stimulant, corticosteroid, β-blocker (paradoxical), benzodiazepine/alcohol withdrawal. Vestibular disorders.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: GAD, panic attack, OCD-like symptoms in the context of a medical condition. Atypical features (late onset, focal symptoms).

title: 6. Diagnosis
text: Medical evidence + distress symptoms + temporal congruence.

title: 6.1 Differences between sources
text: DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 — same.

title: 6.2 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. Medical evaluation — TSH, glucose, cardiac, vestibular. Medication and caffeine history. Toxicology.

title: 6.3 Differential diagnosis
text: Primary anxiety disorders (6B00–6B0Z); Delirium; Adjustment disorder.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: GAD-7, HAM-A. TSH, glucose, ECG. Toxicology.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological treatment. Symptomatic — SSRIs for residual anxiety; benzodiazepines short-term for acute condition. Caffeine restriction.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Etiological Intervention — Correction of medical condition. SSRI For Residual Anxiety — For residual symptoms after correction of medical condition.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Significant improvement with etiological intervention.

title: Myth 1: “Anxiety in a patient with a medical illness is ‘normal’”
text: Evidence: Clinical distress worsens the course of the medical condition; intervention required.

title: Myth 2: “Anxiolytics are first-line in hyperthyroidism”
text: Evidence: Primary is thyroid correction; β-blocker (propranolol) is a symptomatic adjunct.

title: Myth 3: “Caffeine is safe”
text: Evidence: High doses can cause panic, anxiety, and tachycardia; limiting intake is recommended.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 6E63 Secondary anxiety syndrome. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Levenson J.L. (ed.). APA Publishing Textbook of Psychosomatic Medicine and Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry. 3rd ed. 2018.

title: Chronic insomnia
text: Chronic insomnia ICD-10 F51.0 Nonorganic insomnia DSM-5-TR F51.01 Insomnia Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Chronic insomnia (ICD-11: 7A00; DSM-5-TR: F51.01 Insomnia Disorder) — difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, and/or early morning awakening; daytime functional impairment. Duration ≥ 3 months, frequency ≥ 3 times per week.

title: 2. History
text: DSM-IV — ‘Primary Insomnia’; DSM-5 (2013) — ‘Insomnia Disorder’ — primary/secondary distinction abolished. AASM (American Academy of Sleep Medicine) — Clinical Practice Guidelines (2021 CBT-I, 2017 pharmacological). European Insomnia Guideline (Riemann D. 2023). NICE TA922 (2023).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Lifetime prevalence: chronic insomnia 10–15%; insomnia symptoms 30–35%. Sex: 1.5 times higher in females. Increases with age. Comorbidity: MDD ~50%, anxiety, pain, COPD, circadian disorders.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Spielman 3P Model — Predisposing, Precipitating, Perpetuating. Hyperarousal hypothesis — physiological and cognitive stimulation. Behavioral factors — irregular schedule, caffeine, alcohol, screen use, non-sleep activities in the bedroom.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Sleep difficulty (falling asleep), maintenance, early awakening. Daytime symptoms: fatigue, irritability, concentration difficulties, occupational/academic impairment, somatic (headache, GI). Impact on performance, risk of accident.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Sleep difficulty (onset, maintenance, or early awakening). B. Despite adequate sleep opportunities. C. Daytime functional impairment. D. Duration ≥ 3 months, ≥ 3 times per week. E. Not fully explained by another sleep disorder, substance, or medical condition.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM — CBT-I first-line. NICE TA922 (2023) — daridorexant only if CBT-I has been tried and did not work, or is unavailable; that is, CBT-I comes first.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + sleep diary for 1–2 weeks. ISI (Insomnia Severity Index), PSQI. Differential — obstructive sleep apnea (STOP-BANG), restless legs, circadian. Comorbidity (MDD, anxiety). Polysomnography only in atypical cases or suspicion of another sleep disorder.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Obstructive sleep apnoea (7A41) Snoring, daytime sleepiness; polysomnography. Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (7A60–7A65) Shift in the sleep schedule. Restless legs syndrome (7A80) Evening, at rest; relieved by movement. MDD with insomnia Affective symptoms predominate. Hyperthyroidism TSH.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: ISI, PSQI. Sleep diary. STOP-BANG (OSA), Epworth Sleepiness Scale. TSH, ferritin.

title: 8.1 General principles (AASM 2021 · European Insomnia Guideline 2023 · NICE TA922 2023)
text: CBT-I (cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia) — first-line; the gold standard in chronic insomnia; superior long-term efficacy to pharmacotherapy (Mitchell M.D. BMC Fam Pract 2012 meta-analysis). 5 main components: Stimulus control (Bootzin) — bed only for sleep; Sleep restriction (Spielman) — restricting time in bed to equal sleep time; Cognitive therapy — catastrophic thoughts about sleep; Sleep hygiene; Relaxa

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I — Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia), 5 components — Stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, sleep hygiene, relaxation. Digital CBT-I (Digital) — Sleepio, SHUTi — internet-based. Orexin Antagonists — Suvorexant, lemborexant — lower addiction potential. Insomnia Severity Index (ISI — Insomnia Severity Index) — 7-item screening. Sleep Diary — 1–2 weeks baseline indicators

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: AASM Clinical Practice Guideline for Behavioral and Psychological Treatments (Edinger J.D. 2021). European Insomnia Guideline (Riemann D. J Sleep Res 2023). NICE TA922 (2023) — CBT-I must be tried before moving to medication.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Response to CBT-I 70–80%, remission ~40%; the effect is sustained long-term. Without treatment, chronic course and comorbidity (MDD, anxiety).

title: Myth 1: “Sleep medications are the main treatment for insomnia”
text: Evidence: AASM 2021 — CBT-I first-line; pharmacotherapy short-term adjunct; long-term use tolerance, dependence.

title: Myth 2: “Alcohol helps with sleep”
text: Evidence: Alcohol reduces REM, causes midnight awakenings, leads to chronic insomnia.

title: Myth 3: “Antihistamine (diphenhydramine) is safe in the elderly”
text: Evidence: Beers Criteria — antihistamines in the elderly: anticholinergic side effects (falls, cognitive decline); avoid.

title: Myth 4: “Valerian, kava are safe alternatives for insomnia”
text: Evidence: valerian — Leach M.J., Page A.T. Sleep Med Rev 2015;24:1–12 — evidence for effect insufficient; kava hepatotoxicity.

title: Myth 5: “8 hours of sleep is necessary for everyone”
text: Evidence: An individual needs 6–9 hours; daytime function is important.

title: Myth 6: “Waking up during the night is harmful”
text: Evidence: Brief awakenings are normal; stimulus control — rise if you can’t sleep for 20 min.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 7A00 Chronic insomnia. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Edinger J.D. et al. Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an AASM clinical practice guideline. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(2):255–262. Riemann D. et al. The European Insomnia Guideline 2023. J Sleep Res 2023;32(6):e14035. Mitchell M.D. et al. Comparative effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia: a

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) (Obstructive sleep apnoea)
text: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) (Obstructive sleep apnoea) Obstructive sleep apnoea ICD-10 G47.3 Sleep apnoea DSM-5-TR G47.33 Obstructive Sleep Apnea Hypopnea

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA; ICD-11: 7A41; DSM-5-TR: G47.33) — recurrent complete (apnea) or partial (hypopnea) obstruction of the upper airway during sleep; daytime sleepiness, cognitive impairment, increased cardiovascular mortality.

title: 2. History
text: Gastaut H. (1965) — classic description of OSA. Sullivan C.E. (1981) — invented CPAP. AASM Practice Parameters (update).

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: In adults: approximately 13% in men, approximately 6% in women (moderate-to-severe OSA). Increases with age and BMI. Comorbidity: hypertension (50%), cardiovascular disease, stroke, atrial fibrillation, diabetes.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Anatomical — adipose tissue in the upper airway, small mandible, enlarged tonsils/adenoids. Genetic and family history. Posture — worsens in supine position. Alcohol, sedatives — worsen.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Waking up with loud snoring, observed apnea, or choking sensation. Daytime sleepiness (dangerous while driving), fatigue. Morning headache, dry mouth. Concentration, memory problems. Sexual dysfunction, depressive symptoms.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: Polysomnography (PSG) — AHI (Apnea-Hypopnea Index) ≥ 5/hour + symptoms; AHI ≥ 15 irrespective of symptoms.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnostic Testing (2017). Home Sleep Apnea Test (HSAT) — appropriate for moderate-to-severe OSA.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: STOP-BANG screening (Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnea, BP, BMI, Age, Neck, Gender). Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Polysomnography or HSAT. Cardiovascular evaluation.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Insomnia (7A00) Sleeping and retention problems; no snoring. Central sleep apnea Respiratory effort absent. Narcolepsy (7A20) Cataplexy, MSLT. RLS Restless legs.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: STOP-BANG, Epworth. Polysomnography or Home Sleep Apnea Testing. BMI, neck circumference.

title: 8. Treatment
text: CPAP — Continuous Positive Airway Pressure is first-line. For moderate-to-severe OSA; AHI significantly reduced; effect on cardiovascular mortality has not been confirmed in randomized trials (SAVE, NEJM 2016). BiPAP — in refractory cases or CPAP non-response. Weight loss — mild OSA; bariatric surgery in severe obesity. Mandibular advancement device (MAD) — mild-to-moderate OSA, CPAP non-responsive. Postural therapy

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: CPAP — First-line; adherence main problem. Mandibular Advancement Device (MAD) — Mild-moderate OSA; when CPAP fails. Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation (Inspire) — New surgical option; in selected cases. STOP-BANG, Epworth, PSG — Screening and diagnosis.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM CPAP standard, MAD selective. NICE NG202 (OSA-COPD-overlap).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: CPAP reliably reduces symptoms and AHI and improves quality of life; its effect on cardiovascular mortality is unproven (observational studies — Marin 2005 — linked it to reduced mortality, but randomized trials — SAVE, NEJM 2016 — did not confirm this, likely due to poor adherence in trials). Without treatment — stroke, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, increased mortality.

title: Myth 1: “OSA only occurs in obese people”
text: Evidence: Possible in normal-weight patients as well (anatomical factors).

title: Myth 2: “Snoring is the main sign of OSA, nothing more is needed”
text: Evidence: snoring alone not proof; AHI measurement required; untreated OSA high mortality and morbidity.

title: Myth 3: “CPAP only reduces symptoms, does not affect mortality”
text: Evidence: The truth is more nuanced. Observational data (Marin, Lancet 2005) linked CPAP to reduced mortality, but subsequent randomized trials (SAVE, NEJM 2016) did not confirm reduced cardiovascular mortality — likely due to poor adherence in trials (mean ~3.3 h/night vs. the recommended ~4 h). CPAP reliably reduces symptoms and AHI and improves quality of life; its mortality effect remains unproven.

title: Myth 4: “Central sleep apnea and OSA are treated the same”
text: Evidence: Different intervention (ASV — Adaptive Servo-Ventilation for central apnea); differentiation is critical.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 7A41 Obstructive sleep apnoea. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Kapur V.K. et al. AASM Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnostic Testing for Adult OSA. J Clin Sleep Med 2017;13(3):479–504. Marin J.M. et al. Long-term cardiovascular outcomes in men with OSA-hypopnoea with or without treatment with CPAP. Lancet 2005;365(9464):1046–1053.

title: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders
text: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders ICD-10 F51.2 Nonorganic disorder of the sleep-wake schedule DSM-5-TR G47.20–G47.26 Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders (delayed, advanced, irregular, non-24-hou

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders (ICD-11: 7A60–7A65; DSM-5-TR: G47.20–G47.26) — mismatch between the internal circadian rhythm and the external social and light schedule, resulting in insomnia and/or sleepiness. Subtypes: Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (DSWPD), Advanced Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder, Irregular Sleep-Wake Rhythm, Non-24-hour Sleep-Wake (in blind individuals), Shift Work Disorder, Jet Lag Disorder.

title: 2. History
text: In the 1960s, Aschoff J. — foundations of circadian biology. AASM (2015) — clinical practice guideline for circadian rhythm disorders.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: DSWPD — 7–16% in adolescents and young adults. Shift Work Disorder — 10–30% of shift workers. Comorbidity: MDD, anxiety, bipolar, cardiovascular.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Endogenous circadian rhythm disorder (clock gene mutations rare — Familial Advanced Sleep Phase). Environment — light exposure, social schedule. In adolescents, DSWPD — pubertal hormonal changes.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: DSWPD — late sleep and wake times; mismatch with school/work; “night owl” pattern. Advanced — early sleep and wake times; in elderly. Irregular — sleep episodes scattered throughout the day; dementia, ID. Non-24-hour — in blind people; the circadian rhythm does not entrain to the external light signal. Shift Work — shift work; insomnia + daytime sleepiness. Jet Lag — transient, rapid time zone change.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Mismatch between sleep-wake schedule and internal circadian rhythm. B. Insomnia, drowsiness, or both. C. Duration ≥ 3 months (excluding jet lag and shift work). D. Functional impairment.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM 2015 Clinical Practice Guideline.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview + sleep diary for 1–2 weeks. Actigraphy 2 weeks. Dim Light Melatonin Onset (DLMO) — in research context. Exclusion of comorbid sleep disorders.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Insomnia, OSA, depressive disorder, narcolepsy.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Sleep diary, actigraphy. Munich Chronotype Questionnaire.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Bright light therapy — In DSWPD morning; in Advanced evening. Exogenous melatonin — physiological low dose (0.3–5 mg); in DSWPD evening (time critical); in jet lag. Chronotherapy — gradual shift of sleep timing. Sleep hygiene and behavioral intervention. Shift work — strategic resting, dark room, caffeine timing. Non-24-hour in blind patients — tasimelteon (Hetlioz, FDA approved).

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Bright Light Therapy — 10,000 lux × 30–60 minutes; timing adjusted to the circadian shift. Melatonin (Circadian) — Low dose; timing is critical. Actigraphy — 2 weeks. Tasimelteon — FDA approval for Non-24-hour.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With intervention, most patients improve; chronic form requires ongoing strategy.

title: Myth 1: “The adolescent is ‘lazy’ and can get up early”
text: Evidence: the neurobiological basis of DSWPD is circadian delay during puberty.

title: Myth 2: “Melatonin is a sleep medication”
text: Evidence: melatonin regulates circadian phase, its hypnotic effect is minimal; timing is what matters.

title: Myth 3: “There is no treatment for shift work insomnia”
text: Evidence: Strategic rest, light therapy, melatonin, caffeine timing improve.

title: Myth 4: “Jet lag resolves on its own”
text: Evidence: about one day per hour of time-zone change; acceleration with light + melatonin.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 7A60–7A65 Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Auger R.R. et al. AASM Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Intrinsic Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders. J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11(10):1199–1236.

title: Hypersomnolence disorders
text: Hypersomnolence disorders Hypersomnolence disorders ICD-10 F51.1 Nonorganic hypersomnia DSM-5-TR F51.11 Hypersomnolence Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Hypersomnia (ICD-11: 7A21–7A26; DSM-5-TR: F51.11 Hypersomnolence Disorder) — excessive daytime sleepiness or sleep episodes (after ≥ 7 hours of nighttime sleep); functional impairment. In the context of idiopathic hypersomnia, narcolepsy, or other sleep disorders.

title: 2. History
text: In the 1970s–1980s, differentiation from narcolepsy developed; AASM clinical guidelines.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Idiopathic hypersomnia: ~8–40/100,000 among diagnosed cases (Japan — 7.7; US — 37; varies widely with study method). Kleine–Levin syndrome — rare (~1/1 million); recurrent episodes of hypersomnia + appetite/sexual disturbance. Comorbidity: depressive symptoms, OSA, narcolepsy.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Unknown (idiopathic) — neurobiological dysregulation hypothesis. Dysregulation of the GABA-ergic system (idiopathic). Secondary — Kleine–Levin (autoimmune suspicion), post-TBI, MS, depressive disorder.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS). Long night sleep (≥ 9 hours) is insufficient. “Sleep drunkenness” — confusion, disorientation upon awakening. Daytime sleep episodes are prolonged and non-restorative (in contrast to narcolepsy, where they are brief and restorative). Kleine–Levin — 1–2 week episodes of hypersomnia + hyperphagia + disinhibited behavior.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. Even after sufficient sleep (≥7 hours), excessive sleepiness or prolonged sleep. B. Frequency and duration — ≥3 times per week, ≥3 months. C. Significant distress or functional impairment. D. Not fully explained by another sleep disorder, substance, or medical condition.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM Practice Parameters — diagnostic PSG and MSLT (Multiple Sleep Latency Test). Idiopathic hypersomnia — mean sleep latency on MSLT ≤ 8 min; SOREMP ≤ 1 (different from narcolepsy).

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview and sleep diary. Epworth Sleepiness Scale. PSG + MSLT (excluding narcolepsy). Medical assessment — thyroid, anemia, depressive, OSA.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Narcolepsy (7A20) Cataplexy, SOREMP ≥ 2. OSA (7A41) Snoring, AHI ↑. Depressive disorder Affective symptoms. Insomnia (7A00) Insomnia. Kleine–Levin syndrome Episodic 1–2 week hypersomnia + appetite.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Epworth, PSG + MSLT. Medical laboratory tests.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Modafinil, armodafinil — first-line. Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine) — refractory. Low-sodium oxybate (Xywav, FDA 2021) — the only agent approved for idiopathic hypersomnia. Pitolisant (FDA 2019) — approved for narcolepsy; solriamfetol (FDA 2019) — approved for narcolepsy and obstructive sleep apnea; both off-label in idiopathic hypersomnia. Sleep hygiene and behavioral intervention (planned daytime naps).

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Modafinil/Armodafinil — Wakefulness-promoting; first-line; headache, anxiety side effects. Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) — 5 sleep attempts with 2-hour intervals; sleep latency measurement. Pitolisant and Solriamfetol — New medications; in refractory cases.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM Treatment Guidelines (Maski K. et al. 2021).

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic; functional improvement with pharmacotherapy.

title: Myth 1: “Daytime sleepiness is ‘laziness’”
text: Evidence: Clinical condition; increased risk of mortality and accidents.

title: Myth 2: “Caffeine is sufficient for hypersomnia”
text: Evidence: Caffeine adjunct; modafinil or stimulant required.

title: Myth 3: “Hypersomnia is only a symptom of depression”
text: Evidence: idiopathic hypersomnia is a distinct disorder; MSLT differentiates.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 7A21–7A26 Hypersomnolence disorders. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Maski K. et al. Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: AASM Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(9):1881–1893.

title: Narcolepsy
text: Narcolepsy ICD-10 G47.4 Narcolepsy and cataplexy DSM-5-TR G47.4xx Narcolepsy

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Narcolepsy (ICD-11: 7A20; DSM-5-TR: G47.4xx) — irresistible daytime sleep episodes; two types: Type 1 (with cataplexy, orexin-A/hypocretin deficiency) and Type 2 (without cataplexy).

title: 2. History
text: Gélineau J.B. (1880) — the term narcolepsy. Nishino S., Mignot E. (2000) — detection of hypocretin deficiency in CSF in narcolepsy.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence: 25–50 per 100,000. Onset: 10–25 years (bimodal). Comorbidity: OSA, depressive symptoms, OCD.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Type 1 — autoimmune damage to orexin-A neurons (CSF orexin <110 pg/ml); HLA-DQB1*06:02 strong association. H1N1 vaccine (Pandemrix, 2009) — increased incidence of narcolepsy type 1 in Northern Europe and the United Kingdom (Miller E. BMJ 2013). Type 2 — etiology not fully clear.

title: Classic tetrad
text: Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) — irresistible sleep attacks. Cataplexy (Type 1) — sudden partial or complete loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (laughter, anger); consciousness preserved. Sleep paralysis — inability to move at sleep onset or upon awakening. Hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations — visual/auditory hallucinations at sleep transition. Complete tetrad rare; EDS main feature.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria
text: A. EDS ≥ 3 months. B. MSLT — mean sleep latency ≤8 min + ≥2 SOREMPs (Sleep Onset REM Period); or CSF orexin-A <110 pg/ml. C. Type 1 — cataplexy + orexin deficiency; Type 2 — no cataplexy, normal orexin.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ICSD-3 (International Classification of Sleep Disorders) — AASM. HLA typing and CSF orexin — in atypical cases.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview. PSG (night) + MSLT (day) — gold standard. CSF orexin — selective. HLA-DQB1*06:02 — supportive.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Idiopathic hypersomnia (7A21) SOREMP < 2. OSA (7A41) Elevated AHI. Seizure Loss of consciousness; EEG. Syncope Cardiovascular cause. Functional/psychogenic Typical clinical pattern and mismatch with PSG/MSLT results.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Epworth. PSG + MSLT. CSF orexin, HLA-DQB1*06:02.

title: 8. Treatment
text: EDS: modafinil, armodafinil, solriamfetol, pitolisant; stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine) in refractory cases. Cataplexy: sodium oxybate (Xyrem) — gold standard; new — calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium oxybate (Xywav, FDA 2020, low sodium); SSRI/SNRI (venlafaxine, fluoxetine); pitolisant. Behavior — planned daytime naps (15–20 min) Driving restriction if EDS present.

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Sodium Oxybate (Xyrem/Xywav) — GHB; two doses at night; effect on cataplexy and EDS. Modafinil/Armodafinil — First-line for EDS. Pitolisant — H3 receptor antagonist; for EDS and cataplexy. SSRI/SNRI for cataplexy — Venlafaxine, fluoxetine off-label. MSLT — mean latency ≤ 8 min and ≥2 SOREMP diagnostic.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: AASM Treatment Guidelines (Maski 2021). FDA approvals — pitolisant 2019, solriamfetol 2019, Xywav 2020.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Chronic; functional improvement with pharmacotherapy. Comorbidity (MDD, OSA) intervention essential.

title: Myth 1: “Narcolepsy is just EDS alone”
text: Evidence: Tetrad (EDS + cataplexy + paralysis + hallucinations); SOREMPs differentiating in MSLT.

title: Myth 2: “Cataplexy is a seizure”
text: Evidence: consciousness preserved; EEG no epileptic activity; emotional trigger.

title: Myth 3: “H1N1 vaccine causes narcolepsy — vaccines should be avoided”
text: Evidence: Risk indicated specifically with Pandemrix (AS03) (2009–2010 Northern Europe, Britain); other vaccines are safe; avoiding vaccination overall is not recommended.

title: Myth 4: “The patient can drive”
text: Evidence: Driving must be restricted in a narcoleptic patient with EDS.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. 7A20 Narcolepsy. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Maski K. et al. AASM CPG. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(9):1881–1893. Miller E. et al. Risk of narcolepsy in children and young people receiving AS03 adjuvanted pandemic A/H1N1 2009 influenza vaccine. BMJ 2013;346:f794. Mignot E. et al. The role of cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin measurement in the diagnosis of narcolepsy. Arch Neurol 2002;59(10):1553–1562.

title: Erectile dysfunction (ED) (Male erectile dysfunction)
text: Erectile dysfunction (ED) (Male erectile dysfunction) Male erectile dysfunction ICD-10 F52.2 Failure of genital response DSM-5-TR F52.21 Erectile Disorder

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Erectile Dysfunction (ED; ICD-11: HA01.1 Male erectile dysfunction; DSM-5-TR: F52.21) — persistent difficulty in obtaining or maintaining an erection sufficient for sexual intercourse. Duration ≥ 6 months, in most attempts.

title: 2. History
text: 1998 — FDA approval of sildenafil (Viagra) — revolution in ED treatment. AUA (American Urological Association) Guideline (Burnett 2018, 2024 update). EAU (European Association of Urology) Guidelines.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: 5–10% at age 40, 50%+ at age 70. Risk factors: diabetes, cardiovascular disease (ED as cardiovascular early marker), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, obesity, depression, antidepressants.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Organic (~70%) — vascular, neurogenic, endocrine (hypogonadism), medication-related. Psychogenic (~10%) — performance anxiety, relationship problems, depression. Mixed (~20%). Princeton III Consensus (Nehra 2012) — ED an early cardiovascular marker, cardiac risk assessment important.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Difficulty obtaining or maintaining erection. Presence or absence of morning or nighttime erections (for psychogenic vs organic differentiation) Relationship and emotional burden.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (AUA 2018 · EAU)
text: A. Persistent difficulty obtaining and/or maintaining erection. B. Duration ≥ 6 months, in most attempts. C. Distress or relationship impairment.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: AUA 2018/2024 and EAU — stepwise approach.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (sexual and medical history, relationships). IIEF (International Index of Erectile Function) / SHIM. Laboratory — morning testosterone, glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile, prolactin, thyroid. Cardiovascular evaluation. Penile ultrasound (vascular suspicion) — selective.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Hypogonadism Low testosterone + symptoms. Premature ejaculation (HA03.0) Ejaculation time. Hypoactive sexual desire (HA00) Decreased desire dominant. Peyronie’s disease Penile curvature and pain.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: IIEF. Medical and laboratory (above). Cardiac evaluation (ECG, stress test if needed).

title: 8.1 General principles (AUA 2018/2024 · EAU stepwise)
text: 1st line: Lifestyle — smoking cessation, weight, physical activity, cardiovascular management; PDE5 inhibitors — sildenafil (25–100 mg), tadalafil (5–20 mg as needed or 2.5–5 mg daily), vardenafil, avanafil; absolutely contraindicated with nitrates; caution with α-blockers. 1st line (in hypogonadism): Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) — only for confirmed hypogonadism (≥ 2 morning measurements low + symptoms); m

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: PDE5 Inhibitors — Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitor; absolutely contraindicated with nitrates. Intracavernosal Alprostadil — PGE1; if PDE5 fails. Vacuum Device — Non-invasive; use with caution in anticoagulant use and bleeding disorders. Penile Prosthesis — Refractory ED; high satisfaction. International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF) — Severity scale.

title: 8.3 Differences between sources
text: Burnett A.L. et al. AUA Guideline. J Urol 2018, 2024 update. Salonia A. et al. EAU Guidelines 2023.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: PDE5 with 70% efficacy; refractory cases 2nd–3rd line; cardiovascular risk management reduces mortality.

title: Myth 1: “ED is a normal part of aging, requires no treatment”
text: Evidence: ED is an early cardiovascular marker; active intervention is essential.

title: Myth 2: “Over-the-counter ‘natural’ potency enhancers are safe”
text: Evidence: FDA warnings — many “natural” products contain undeclared sildenafil/tadalafil — interaction with nitrates, risk of death.

title: Myth 3: “Testosterone replacement therapy is needed for every ED patient”
text: Evidence: AUA — only in confirmed hypogonadism; routine TRT not recommended.

title: Myth 4: “Shock wave therapy (Li-ESWT) is standard treatment”
text: Evidence: AUA 2024 — under investigation; not standard first-line.

title: Myth 5: “Yohimbine is an effective natural alternative”
text: Evidence: Ernst E., Pittler M.H. J Urol 1998;159(2):433–436 — small effect, side effects of anxiety and hypertension; PDE5 superior.

title: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)
text: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation) Male early ejaculation ICD-10 F52.4 Premature ejaculation DSM-5-TR F52.4 Premature (Early) Ejaculation
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Male early ejaculation (PE; ICD-11: HA03.0; DSM-5-TR: F52.4 Premature Ejaculation) — ejaculation occurring involuntarily within a short time, often before or within ~1 minute of penetration; loss of control and distress. Subtypes: Lifelong (primary) — present from onset; Acquired (secondary) — developed later; Variable and Subjective — Waldinger classification (ISSM recognizes only the first two forms).
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 2. History
text: Semans J.H. (1956) — ‘stop-start’ technique. Masters & Johnson (1970) — “squeeze” behavioral technique. ISSM (2014) — Althof S.E. international diagnostic and treatment guideline. 2009 — dapoxetine first approved drug for PE in the EU.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in males 20–30% (self-reported); with strict ISSM criteria 4–5%. Age-related variability low; occurs in all age groups. Comorbidity: ED, anxiety, depression, relationship strain.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Neurobiological — serotonergic (5-HT2C, 5-HT1A balance); genetic component (lifelong). Psychological — performance anxiety, early sexual experience, relationship problems. Acquired — ED, prostatitis, hyperthyroidism, substance use.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Intravaginal ejaculation latency time (IELT) short (lifelong ~1 min; acquired ≤ 3 min). Loss of control. Distress, avoidance, relationship tension.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (ISSM 2014 · DSM-5-TR)
text: A. Ejaculation always or almost always before or within ~1 minute of penetration (lifelong) or a clinically meaningful decrease in latency time to ≤ 3 minutes (acquired). B. Inability to delay in all or almost all penetrations. C. Negative personal consequences — distress, avoidance.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ISSM (Althof S.E. et al. J Sex Med 2014). AUA and EAU guidelines.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (sexual history, IELT, control, distress). PEDT (Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool) — 5-item. Comorbid ED assessment (IIEF). Endocrine and urologic (acquired form).
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature ED (HA01.1) Difficulty maintaining erection. Variable PE Not a clinical entity — normal variation. Subjective PE IELT normal, but perception disturbance. Prostatitis Pelvic pain; acquired PE.
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: PEDT, IIEF. IELT (chronometry — when recommended). Endocrine and urologic (suspected acquired).
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 8. Treatment
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 8.1 General principles (ISSM 2014 · AUA · EAU)
text: Behavioral methods (first-line or combination): Stop-start (Semans); Squeeze technique (Masters & Johnson); Pelvic floor exercises (Pastore A. RCT 2014). Dapoxetine — short-acting SSRI; 30–60 mg 1–3 hours before intercourse; approved for PE in EU and many countries. It is not approved for PE by the US FDA. SSRI off-label daily — paroxetine (10–40 mg) highest efficacy (Waldinger meta-analysis); sertraline, fluoxetine,
sub: Early ejaculation (premature ejaculation, PE) (Male early ejaculation)

title: 8.2 Treatment methods
text: Dapoxetine — Short-acting SSRI; when needed; EU approval. Topical Anesthetic — Lidocaine/prilocaine (EMLA cream 20–30 min; Fortacin spray ~5 min prior). SSRI Daily (off-label) — Paroxetine highest efficacy. Stop-start and squeeze techniques — Behavioral methods; singly or in combination. Pelvic Floor Exercises — Pastore RCT — IELT increase.

text: Dapoxetine and SSRIs increase IELT by 2–4 times; behavioral combination supports long-term effect.

title: Myth 1: “PE is only a psychological problem”
text: Evidence: Lifelong PE is associated with serotonergic neurobiology; the effects of dapoxetine and SSRIs confirm this.

title: Myth 2: “Dapoxetine is FDA-approved in the US”
text: Evidence: Dapoxetine is not approved by the US FDA for PE; it is approved in the EU and many countries; in the US, PE is treated off-label with daily SSRIs.

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction (HSDD; ICD-11: HA00; DSM-5-TR in females Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder F52.22, in males Male Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder F52.0) — persistent decrease or absence of sexual fantasies and desire for sexual activity; with distress. Duration ≥ 6 months; situational or generalized; lifelong or acquired.

text: Kaplan H.S. (1977) — inclusion of the desire phase in the sexual response model. Basson R. title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Biological — hormonal (testosterone, estrogen), medication-related (SSRIs, OCs, antihypertensives), chronic diseases. Psychological — depression, anxiety, body image, trauma history. Relationship — conflict, partner sexual dysfunction. Social-cultural — taboo, lack of knowledge.

title: Anorgasmia
text: Anorgasmia ICD-10 F52.3 Orgasmic dysfunction DSM-5-TR F52.31 / F52.32 Female Orgasmic Disorder / Delayed Ejaculation

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Anorgasmia (ICD-11: HA02.0; DSM-5-TR Female Orgasmic Disorder F52.31 in women; Delayed Ejaculation F52.32 in men) — persistent difficulty, delay, or absence of reaching orgasm after sufficient sexual arousal; or reduced intensity of orgasm. Duration ≥ 6 months; situational or generalized; lifelong or acquired.

title: 2. History
text: Masters & Johnson (1970) — classic description of orgasmic phase disorder. ISSWSH and ISSM guidelines.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Women experience clinically significant anorgasmia in 5–10% of cases; men experience delayed ejaculation in 1–4%. Sexual side effects occur in 30–70% of patients taking antidepressants (SSRIs).

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Medication-related (SSRI, antipsychotic, opioid). Neurological (pelvic surgery, MS, diabetic neuropathy). Endocrine (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia). Psychological — anxiety, trauma, knowledge deficiency. Age and hormonal changes.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Difficulty or absence of achieving orgasm. Decreased intensity of orgasm. Distress, avoidance.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR)
text: A. Delay, absence, or reduced intensity of orgasm following sufficient sexual arousal — in all or almost all instances (75–100%). B. Duration ≥ 6 months. C. Distress.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ISSM Delayed Ejaculation Guideline. ISSWSH — orgasm dysfunction in women.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (sexual history, orgasm with masturbation, orgasm with partner). FSFI (in women) / IIEF (in men). Medication and comorbidity analysis. Endocrine (testosterone, prolactin, thyroid).

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature HSDD (HA00) Decreased desire dominant. Retrograde ejaculation Orgasm present, ejaculate into bladder. SSRI-induced Medication-related timing. ED (HA01.1) Erectile disorder.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: FSFI, IIEF. Hormonal panel. Neurological and urologic (acquired suspicion).

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological approach — management of medication, endocrine, neurological causes. SSRI-induced anorgasmia: Medication switch — bupropion, mirtazapine, vortioxetine alternative; Dose reduction; drug holiday (with caution in SSRIs); Bupropion adjunct; Sildenafil adjunct in women for SSRI-induced dysfunction — Nurnberg JAMA 2008 RCT. Psychotherapy and behavior — orgasm-oriented therapy (Heiman & LoPiccolo); CBT, mindfuln

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Bupropion — As adjunct or switch in SSRI-induced anorgasmia. Directed Masturbation — Heiman & LoPiccolo program; effective for primary anorgasmia in women. Mindfulness-CBT — Brotto research; in female sexual dysfunction.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Nurnberg H.G. et al. JAMA 2008 — sildenafil in SSRI-induced female sexual dysfunction. Brotto L.A. mindfulness studies.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: For women, directed masturbation yields 60–90% efficacy for primary anorgasmia; in SSRI-induced cases, pharmacological strategies provide improvement.

title: Myth 1: “Women must achieve orgasm through penetration”
text: Evidence: Most women (~70%) require clitoral stimulation; orgasm with only penetration is normal variation, not anatomical norm.

title: Myth 2: “Anorgasmia is a sign of ‘frigidity’ in women”
text: Evidence: Anorgasmia often related to knowledge, technique, anxiety, or medication; not a character trait.

title: Myth 3: “SSRI-induced anorgasmia is transient, requires no treatment”
text: Evidence: Chronic; pharmacological interventions or adjunctive strategies are effective; ongoing distress is clinically significant.

title: Myth 4: “Over-the-counter ‘orgasm enhancers’ are effective”
text: Evidence: Evidence is weak; FDA has warned about hidden components.

title: Myth 5: “Vibrator use deprives the patient of orgasm with a partner”
text: Evidence: On the contrary, it is effective in training for primary anorgasmia; can be integrated into an intimate relationship with a partner.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. HA02.0 Anorgasmia. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Nurnberg H.G. et al. Sildenafil treatment of women with antidepressant-associated sexual dysfunction. JAMA 2008;300(4):395–404. Brotto L.A. et al. Psychological and Interpersonal Dimensions of Sexual Function and Dysfunction. J Sex Med 2016;13(4):538–571. Heiman J.R., LoPiccolo J. Becoming Orgasmic. Prentice Hall, 1988.

title: Sexual pain-penetration disorder (vaginismus) (Sexual pain-penetration disorder)
text: Sexual pain-penetration disorder (vaginismus) (Sexual pain-penetration disorder) Sexual pain-penetration disorder ICD-10 F52.5 Nonorganic vaginismus DSM-5-TR F52.6 Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disor

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Sexual pain-penetration disorder (vaginismus; ICD-11: HA20; DSM-5-TR: Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder F52.6) — during penetration attempts: (a) difficulty, (b) genital or pelvic pain, (c) fear of pain, (d) tension of pelvic floor muscles. Classic vaginismus and dyspareunia are combined in this entity. Duration ≥ 6 months; lifelong or acquired.

title: 2. History
text: Sims J.M. (1861) — description of vaginismus. Masters & Johnson (1970) — pelvic floor tension. DSM-5 (2013) — vaginismus and dyspareunia combined into GPPPD. ISSWSH and ACOG guidelines.

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Prevalence in women is 5–17% (in clinical and non-clinical samples). Lifelong vaginismus — in young women, at first penetration attempt. Acquired — trauma, infection, atrophic vaginitis, post-surgery.

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Biological — atrophic vaginitis (postmenopausal), vulvodynia, endometriosis, infection, surgical wound. Psychological — sexual trauma, anxiety, abstinence education, fear of pain. Relationship and partner factors.

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Reflexive tension of pelvic floor muscles during penetration. Pain (burning, stabbing). Penetration avoidance. Gynecological examination also difficult or impossible.

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR)
text: A. At least one of the following: Difficulty in penetration; Pain in vulvovaginal or pelvic region during penetration attempts. Fear of pain associated with anticipation of penetration. In attempted penetration, tension of the pelvic floor muscles. B. Duration ≥ 6 months. C. Distress.

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: ISSWSH and ACOG.

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Clinical interview (sexual history, pain characteristics, trauma). Careful gynecological examination — with caution, with patient consent. Vulvodynia screening (Q-tip test). Infection, atrophic vaginitis, exclusion of endometriosis. Pelvic floor assessment.

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Vulvodynia Localized vulvar pain, Q-tip positive. Atrophic vaginitis Postmenopausal, estrogen deficiency. Endometriosis Deep dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea. Infection (candida, vaginosis) Exudation, microbiological.

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Gynecological examination. Pelvic floor assessment. FSFI; pain scales.

title: 8. Treatment
text: Multidisciplinary approach — pelvic floor physiotherapy + CBT + education. Pelvic Floor Physiotherapy — biofeedback, manual therapy, dilator therapy (gradual size increase). CBT and exposure therapy — fear of pain and avoidance; ter Kuile M.M. RCT. Sensate focus and couple therapy. Topical anesthetic (lidocaine) — in provoked vulvodynia (Goldstein A.T.). Local estrogen for atrophic vaginitis. Botulinum toxin A — in r

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Dilator Therapy — Gradual increase in size; combined with relaxation. Pelvic Floor Physiotherapy — Biofeedback, manual therapy. CBT/Exposure — Fear of pain and avoidance. Topical Estrogen — Atrophic vaginitis. Botox (off-label) — For refractory vaginismus; selective.

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: ter Kuile M.M. et al. CBT vaginismus. Goldstein A.T. et al. ISSWSH vulvodynia consensus.

title: 9. Prognosis
text: With a multidisciplinary approach, prognosis is good (70–90%); in refractory cases, botox or intensive psychological intervention.

title: Myth 1: “Vaginismus is an emotional rejection of the partner”
text: Evidence: Reflex muscle tension — outside conscious control; accusing the patient is harmful.

title: Myth 2: “Vaginismus cannot be treated”
text: Evidence: CBT + dilator + physiotherapy combination 70–90% efficacy; ter Kuile RCTs.

title: Myth 3: “Treatment should be done to increase penetration frequency”
text: Evidence: target is reducing patient distress, restoring sense of control and choice; not a performance indicator.

title: Myth 4: “Local anesthetic is effective for all sexual pain”
text: Evidence: Effective in provoked vulvodynia; use limited in generalized vaginismus — main problem is muscle tension.

title: Myth 5: “Forcing ‘compulsory exercise’ helps with penetration attempts”
text: Evidence: urgent, painful repetition increases avoidance and fear; gradual, controlled exposure effective.

title: 11. Sources
text: WHO. ICD-11. HA20 Sexual pain-penetration disorder. 2024. APA. DSM-5-TR. 2022. Ter Kuile M.M. et al. Therapist-aided exposure for women with lifelong vaginismus: a RCT. J Consult Clin Psychol 2013;81(6):1127–1136. Goldstein A.T. et al. Vulvodynia: Assessment and Treatment. J Sex Med 2016;13(4):572–590. Bergeron S. et al. Genital pain in women and men: It can hurt more than your sex life. Sex Med Rev 2020.

title: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders
text: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders ICD-10 F52.8 Other sexual dysfunction, not caused by organic disorder or disease DSM-5-TR — —
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 1. Definition and nosology
text: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders (ICD-11: HA40) — a set of qualifiers identifying the etiology of sexual dysfunctions (which may involve desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain) arising in the context of another physical illness, medication, substance, or mental disorder. Cases that do not fit specific HA01–HA20 categories or are comorbid. Subtypes (ICD-11): a medical condition, i
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 2. History
text: DSM-IV (1994) — substance-induced, DSM-5 (2013) — “Substance/Medication-Induced Sexual Dysfunction”. 2000s — SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction was widely described (Montejo A.L. studies). PSSD (Post-SSRI Sexual Dysfunction) — Bahrick A. (2008), EMA 2019 confirmation.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 3. Epidemiology
text: Sexual dysfunction with SSRI use 30–70%. ED in diabetic men 35–75%. High prevalence in cardiovascular diseases. Antipsychotics (especially risperidone, paliperidone) cause sexual dysfunction through hyperprolactinemia.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 4. Etiology and pathogenesis
text: Medications: SSRI, SNRI, antipsychotics (D2 blockade, hyperprolactinemia), antihypertensive (beta-blocker, thiazide), opioids, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride — suspected Post-Finasteride Syndrome), anticonvulsants. Substances: alcohol, opioids, chronic cannabis use, stimulants. Medical diseases: diabetes, cardiovascular, neurological (MS, Parkinson’s disease, spinal trauma), endocrine (hypogonadism, hyperp
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 5. Clinical features
text: Decreased desire, excitement/erection dysfunction, anorgasmia, pain — etiology-dependent. Temporal relationship — onset with medication/substance. PSSD — persistent sexual dysfunction after SSRI discontinuation, genital numbness.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 6. Diagnosis
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 6.1 Unified diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR)
text: A. Clinically significant sexual dysfunction symptomatology. B. Evidence from history, physical examination, or laboratory results: symptoms are a direct consequence of medication, substance, or medical illness. C. Distress.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 6.2 Differences between sources
text: Montejo A.L. et al. — SSRI-induced dysfunction. EMA (2019) — included PSSD in SSRI label.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 6.3 Diagnostic algorithm
text: Full medication and substance history. Medical and endocrine assessment (testosterone, prolactin, glucose, HbA1c, lipids, thyroid). Sexual function scales (FSFI, IIEF, ASEX). Mental comorbidity screening. Pelvic examination (in women).
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 6.4 Differential diagnosis
text: Condition Distinguishing feature Primary HSDD/ED/Anorgasmia There is no evidence of a medical or pharmacological cause. Depressive disorder Anhedonia, mood symptoms dominant. PSSD Sexual dysfunction persisting after SSRI discontinuation.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 7. Examination and assessment
text: Hormonal panel, glucose, lipids. FSFI, IIEF, ASEX (Arizona Sexual Experience Scale). Pelvic or urological examination when indicated.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 8. Treatment
text: Etiological approach — first-line: Medication-related — dose reduction, medication switch (bupropion, mirtazapine, vortioxetine, aripiprazole — in antidepressant or antipsychotic strategies); Medical condition management (diabetes, hypertension, hypogonadism). Adjunct pharmacotherapy — sildenafil (PDE5) in ED and SSRI-induced female dysfunction (Nurnberg JAMA 2008); bupropion adjunct. In hyperprolactinemia — antipsyc
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 8.1 Treatment methods
text: Medication Switch — SSRI → bupropion/mirtazapine/vortioxetine; risperidone → aripiprazole. Sildenafil Adjunct — SSRI-induced dysfunction (male and female); Nurnberg JAMA RCT. Bupropion Adjunct — In desire and orgasm disorders. Antipsychotic Switch (aripiprazole) — In case of hyperprolactinemia. Patient Education — Informed consent; discussing long-term risk.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 8.2 Differences between sources
text: Montejo A.L. et al. — antidepressant sexual side effect algorithms. EMA 2019 — PSSD risk information. NICE and APA guidelines — management of antidepressant sexual side effects.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 9. Prognosis
text: Most cases improve with etiological management and medication switch; PSSD may persist for a long time in some cases.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: 10. Myths and misconceptions
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: Myth 1: “Antidepressant sexual side effects are ‘temporary’ and require no intervention”
text: Evidence: Montejo studies — side effects are persistent (30–70%); require active management.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: Myth 2: “PSSD is not a clinical entity”
text: Evidence: EMA 2019 — PSSD risk included in SSRI label; clinically recognized entity.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: Myth 3: “Antipsychotic sexual dysfunction is the same for everyone”
text: Evidence: risperidone and paliperidone high hyperprolactinemia risk; aripiprazole and quetiapine less; switching is effective.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: Myth 4: “Sexual dysfunction due to a medical illness is only a consequence of the illness, no intervention exists”
text: Evidence: In diabetic ED, PDE5 inhibitors are effective; sexual function improves with cardiovascular rehabilitation; active intervention is important.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: Myth 5: “It is not necessary to discuss sexual side effects before starting an antidepressant”
text: Evidence: informed consent is ethical and clinical requirement; later emerging side effects lead to patient distrust and reduced treatment adherence.
sub: Aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders

title: MONITORING AND EXAMINATION STANDARDS
text: This appendix presents standard protocols for safety monitoring in the use of psychotropic medications and for monitoring the medical condition of psychiatric patients.

title: A.1. Metabolic monitoring during antipsychotic therapy
text: Atypical antipsychotics — especially olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine — Metabolic syndrome increases the risk (weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, diabetes).

title: Monitoring chart (APA/ADA 2004, ADA/APA/AACE/NAASO consensus):
text: Parameter Onset 4 weeks 8 weeks 12 weeks Quarterly Annual Personal/Family history ✓ ✓ Weight, waist circumference ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Blood pressure ✓ ✓ ✓ Fasting glucose ✓ ✓ ✓ Fasting lipid profile ✓ ✓ ✓ (every 5 years) If abnormality is detected: Weight gain ≥7%: consider medication switch (aripiprazole, ziprasidone — metabolically neutral); HbA1c ≥6.5% or fasting glucose ≥7: referral to a diabetes specialist LDL ≥3.4 mmol

title: Specific monitoring for clozapine (due to agranulocytosis):
text: Duration Frequency First 18 weeks Weekly WBC and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) From week 18 to month 12 Every 2 weeks 12+ months Monthly ANC indicators: ≥2.0 × 10⁹/L Normal — continue treatment; 1.5–2.0 × 10⁹/L (warning zone): monitoring twice a week until the value stabilizes or rises; <1.5 (red zone): clozapine is stopped immediately, hematology consultation; In benign ethnic neutropenia the thresholds are 0.5 ×

title: ECG monitoring with antipsychotics:
text: QT interval prolongation risk: specifically ziprasidone, haloperidol IV, ondansetron combination; Baseline ECG in patients with risk factors (heart disease, electrolyte disturbance, >65 years); QTc >500 ms or >60 ms increase from baseline — Medication change; Medications increasing risk: thioridazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol (IV, high dose).

title: Hyperprolactinemia:
text: Risperidone, amisulpride, paliperidone — high risk; Symptoms: amenorrhea, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis. Baseline prolactin; repeat if symptoms recur.

title: A.2. Lithium monitoring
text: Narrow therapeutic window — level 0.6–1.2 mEq/L, >1.5 toxic. Parameter Onset Every 6 months Annual Lithium level ✓; weekly until stabilization Every 3 months in the 1st year, then ✓ Creatinine, eGFR ✓ ✓ TSH ✓ ✓ Electrolytes ✓ ✓ Calcium ✓ ✓ ECG ✓ (50+ years old) Pregnancy test Female of reproductive age Signs of lithium intoxication: Tremor (more severe); Bradycardia, arrhythmia; confusion; Diarrhea, vomiting; Slow, c

title: Valproate:
text: Parameter Onset Every 6 months CBC (thrombocytopenia) ✓ ✓ Liver function (AST, ALT) ✓ ✓ Valproate level With symptom or suspicion Monitoring signs of pancreatitis Every visit Pregnancy test MANDATORY in women of reproductive age Every quarter Critical: valproate should be avoided in women of childbearing potential because of the risk of neural tube defects and cause of cognitive impairment only with effective contrac

title: Carbamazepine:
text: CBC, liver — baseline, 1 month, quarterly; HLA-B*1502 test in patients of Asian origin (Stevens–Johnson risk); Level drop due to auto-induction in the first 4 weeks — check level.

title: Lamotrigine:
text: Slow titration — Stevens–Johnson syndrome risk; Starting 25 mg/day (weeks 1–2), 50 mg/day (weeks 3–4), then to target dose; Along with valproate: doses halved (25 mg every other day) — valproate slows lamotrigine metabolism; If a skin reaction occurs — immediately discontinue.

title: A.4. Monitoring of SSRIs and SNRIs
text: Hyponatremia risk — especially in elderly, in those using diuretics; Baseline Na, after 1 month, then with symptom; Increased suicidality, especially with onset in patients under 25 — close monitoring during first 1–2 months; QTc prolongation — escitalopram, citalopram (at high doses); Serotonin syndrome (MAOI or triptan, etc., in combination) — symptom education.

title: A.5. Benzodiazepine use
text: Maximum duration: 2–4 weeks; Long-term use inevitably leads to addiction; Reduction schedule (tapering): 25% every 2 weeks, sometimes slower; Withdrawal symptoms (rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor) are normal and temporary.

title: A.6. Psychotherapy monitoring
text: Quality indicators: Session duration, frequency; Patient symptom scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7, etc.) every 4–6 weeks; Functional indicators; Assessment of therapeutic alliance (Working Alliance Inventory). Achieving external goals; Signs of relapse. Supervision and peer consultation — in complex cases, and whenever the clinician asks for it.

title: PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY SITUATIONS
text: In a psychiatric emergency, time is the scarcest resource. Decisions are measured in minutes and must almost always be made on incomplete information. This appendix is written for precisely those moments: it offers concise, sequenced action lists rather than extended discussion. These lists do not replace clinical judgment; they serve as a safeguard against the step most easily overlooked under pressure.

title: C.1. Active suicide risk
text: Assessing suicide risk is a conversation, not a questionnaire. Ask directly: the question does not plant the idea — more often it gives the patient the first chance to say it out loud. What you are listening for above all is how far the intention has taken concrete shape.

title: Primary assessment:
text: Are there suicidal thoughts? Plans? Means? How concrete the plan is: when the patient names a time, a place and a means, the risk rises sharply; a general “sometimes I want to die” is of a different order; Previous attempts — the strongest predictor; Substance intoxication — inhibition decreased; Protective factors — family, religious beliefs, future plans.

title: High risk signs:
text: A concrete plan and easy access to the means; Recent situational change (loss, severe illness); Loneliness and chronic pain; Psychosis or severe depression; The early phase of recovery from depression — energy returns while mood is still low; Adult male, disability, alcohol.

title: Management:
text: Low-moderate risk: Safety plan — written; Reducing access to means (gun removal, medication in small quantities); Close outpatient follow-up (a repeat visit within 24–48 hours); The crisis line number; Family involvement (with consent). High risk: Hospitalization (voluntary or involuntary); Close observation — one-to-one if the risk is very high; Removal of dangerous means (sharp objects, rope, access to windows); Co

title: Involuntary hospitalization within the Azerbaijani framework:
text: “On psychiatric assistance” Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan; A decision on involuntary hospitalization is made by two psychiatrists, followed by the legal procedure; After the commission’s decision, a court order within the period established by law (see: “Legal and ethical aspects”).

title: C.2. Delirium tremens and alcohol withdrawal
Symptoms:
text: Tremor — hands, then general; Anxiety, agitation; Hallucinations — visual and tactile (“insects under the skin”); Disorientation; Autonomic hyperactivity — tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, hyperthermia; Seizures (~5–10%).

title: Treatment (in ICU or IMU setting):
text: Benzodiazepine — diazepam 10–20 mg IV (not IM) every 15–20 min until sedation is achieved; then maintenance regimen; Alternative: lorazepam (in those with hepatic dysfunction); Thiamine 100–300 mg IV — Prevention of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Give before glucose administration. Fluid and electrolyte replacement; Magnesium sulfate, potassium — often low; Mortality: ~1–4% in treated inpatients; substantially higher (15

title: C.3. Serotonin syndrome
text: Cause: SSRI + MAOI, SSRI + triptan, SSRI + tramadol, SSRI + linezolid, SSRI + methylene blue, etc.

title: Symptoms:
text: Mental change — agitation, confusion; Autonomic — tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, sweating; Neuromuscular — tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus (lower extremity — specific sign).

title: Treatment:
text: Immediate discontinuation of causative medication Support — fluids, electrolytes, cooling; In severe cases cyproheptadine 12 mg initial, 2 mg every hour maximum 32 mg/day; Invasive intervention (intubation) in severe hyperthermia.

title: C.4. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
text: Cause: antipsychotics (especially high potency, e.g., haloperidol), acute initiation or dose increase.

title: Symptoms (4 main):
text: Muscle stiffness (“lead pipe”); Hyperthermia (38–42°C); Autonomic lability (high blood pressure, tachycardia, sweating); Mental state change (confusion → stupor → coma). Laboratory: creatine kinase (CK) markedly elevated (>1000 U/L), myoglobinuria, leukocytosis, ALT/AST elevated.

title: Treatment (ICU):
text: Immediate discontinuation of antipsychotics Cooling. Fluids (risk of rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury); Dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV — reduces muscle rigidity; Bromocriptine 2.5–5 mg every 8 hours — dopamine agonist; ECT in non-responsive cases. Mortality: 5–20%; considerably lower with early recognition and timely treatment.

title: C.5. Acute dystonia
text: Cause: antipsychotic initiation, especially potent D2 antagonists.

title: Symptoms:
text: Acute muscle spasms — neck (torticollis), tongue, eyes (oculogyric crisis), spasm of the esophagus; Life-threatening — laryngeal spasm.

title: Treatment:
text: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IM/IV — relief within 15 minutes; Benztropine 1–2 mg IM/IV; Reducing or changing the dose of antipsychotics Prophylactic anticholinergic in high-risk patients.

title: C.6. Acute mania and psychomotor agitation
Management:
text: Safe environment — quiet, free from stimuli; Verbal de-escalation first step; Medication: - Oral preferred: haloperidol 2–5 mg + lorazepam 1–2 mg; - IM when indicated: haloperidol 5 mg + lorazepam 2 mg (50/50 syringe) or olanzapine IM 10 mg (not together with a parenteral benzodiazepine); Involuntary hospitalization if indicated; Physical restraint — only as a last resort, when life is at risk, and only briefly.

title: C.7. Acute psychosis
text: Similar to the protocol above. Differential: organic causes, substance intoxication, postpartum psychosis, NMS.

title: Symptoms:
text: Stupor, mutism; Catalepsy (‘waxy flexibility’); Negativism; Mannerisms, stereotypies; Echolalia, echopraxia.

title: First-line treatment:
text: Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV/IM test — Significant response within 1–2 hours → diagnosis and treatment of catatonia; If there is a response, increase the dose to 4–24 mg/day; No response — ECT as second-line treatment, highly effective; Avoiding antipsychotics during acute phase is necessary — they may provoke NMS. Search for organic causes (encephalitis, epilepsy), mood disorders, schizophrenia, autism, certain substances.

title: MILITARY MEDICAL EXAMINATION (IN AZERBAIJAN)
text: This appendix provides practical guidance on psychiatric aspects for assessing fitness for military service in the Republic of Azerbaijan.

title: D.1. Legal basis
text: “On military duty and military service” Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan; Regulation on military medical examination; Ministry of Defense Normative acts; Table of diseases — divided into two parts: mild and severe degrees, groups A–D.

title: Main components of the examination:
text: Complaints and history (patient and close relatives); Previous medical records; Clinical interview and mental status examination; Experimental-Psychological Examination (EPE) — by a psychologist; Laboratory and instrumental examinations when necessary; Differential diagnosis, and assessment of disease severity; Conclusion.

title: Typical psychological tests (used in the EPE):
text: MMPI-2 (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory-2) — personality profile; Raven’s Progressive Matrices — intellect; Luria tests — memory, attention; Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS); Rorschach test — a projective method (its contemporary reliability is contested); Beck, Hamilton scales — mood.

title: D.3. Psychiatric disorders and military fitness assessment
text: Classification by group (adaptation — based on local normative acts):

title: Group A — fully fit for service
text: No psychiatric history or minor transient issues.

title: Group B — fit with minor limitations
text: Mild personality traits (below impairment threshold); Transient adjustment disorders; Mild sleep disturbances; Neurotic disorders in remission state.

title: Group C — fit for service with limitations
text: Moderate psychiatric disturbances in partial remission state; Specific personality disorders; Past PTSD, compensated; Moderate neurocognitive dysfunction.

title: Group D — unfit for service
text: Schizophrenia spectrum; Bipolar disorder; Severe depression; Active PTSD/complex PTSD (Karabakh War veterans — separate treatment program); Substance use disorders; Severe personality disorders; Intellectual disability (severe); Severe forms of autism spectrum disorder; Disorders with active suicide risk; Paraphilic disorders (severe, active).

title: D.4. Post-traumatic stress and veteran assessment
text: In veterans of the Karabakh War: Complex PTSD high prevalence — trauma-focused intervention; Alcohol and substance use are comorbid; Depression, suicide risk; Family dysfunction; Moral injury — ethical conflict during war (killing, witnessing); Burnout and re-traumatization risk factors. Specific rehabilitation programs: Evidence-based trauma therapies (PE, CPT, EMDR); Group therapy for veterans; Family therapy; Medi

title: RELATED NEUROLOGICAL CONDITIONS
text: Brief description of neurological diseases important for clinical practice in areas intersecting psychiatry and neurology.

title: Epileptic syndromes and psychiatry:
text: - Interictal personality changes (Geschwind syndrome — hyperreligiosity, hypergraphia, “viscosity”); - Interictal psychosis — long-standing TLE; - Postictal psychosis — psychotic episodes within 24–72 hours after a seizure; - Ictal anxiety and dissociative experiences; Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) — psychiatric comorbidity most common: Absence epilepsy — attention problems, differential with ADHD; Juvenile myoclonic

title: Psychogenic (non-epileptic) seizures (PNES) — dissociative neurological symptom disorder (6B60.4):
text: Video-EEG — gold standard differential; PNES frequently comorbid with epilepsy, 10–30%; Treatment: CBT-PNES, slow tapering of anticonvulsants.

title: Psychiatric side effects of antiepileptics:
text: Levetiracetam: Aggression, irritability, depression; Phenobarbital, primidone: depression, cognitive slowing; Topiramate: cognitive dysfunction, depression; Lamotrigine: mood stabilizer.

title: E.2. Headache and psychiatric comorbidity
text: Migraine — depression risk 2–4× higher; anxiety disorders; Cluster headache — depression, suicide risk; Chronic daily headache — analgesic overuse (medication overuse headache — MOH) — frequently comorbid mood disorder; Recurrent tension-type headache — associated with intense stress, anxiety.

title: Management:
text: SSRI/SNRI improves many types of headache; TCA (amitriptyline) historical standard for migraine prophylaxis Topiramate, valproate (not in women of childbearing age) for prophylaxis; CBT is effective for chronic headache; Avoidance of opioids and excessive analgesic use.

title: E.3. Cerebrovascular diseases (stroke)
text: Post-stroke depression: 30–40% in the first year; Post-stroke mania: Rare, in right frontal or thalamic lesions; Pseudobulbar affect (pathological laughing/crying): dextromethorphan-quinidine combination is the established treatment; Vascular cognitive disorder/dementia: classified under 6D81; Rehabilitation: Multidisciplinary, psychiatric support plays a central role.

title: E.4. Parkinson’s disease
text: Depression: 30–50%; Anxiety: 30–40%; Dopamine agonist-induced impulse control disorder: 13–36%; Psychosis in Parkinson’s disease: mainly visual hallucinations, often induced by levodopa; Dementia in Parkinson’s disease: 6D85.0; REM sleep behavior disorder: an early marker for Parkinson’s disease. Treatment characteristics: Use of antipsychotics in Parkinson’s disease: quetiapine, clozapine (D2 minimal blockade); Halo

title: E.5. Multiple sclerosis (MS)
text: Depression: 30–50%; Anxiety: 30%; Bipolar-like symptoms: 5–10%; Pseudobulbar affect; Cognitive dysfunction — in most patients; Lethargy and fatigue — closely associated with depression, differential diagnosis difficult. Interferon-beta may worsen depression (evidence conflicting) — monitoring required.

title: E.6. Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
text: Post-concussion syndrome: headache, dizziness, memory issues, mood changes; Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE): repeated injuries, sports (boxing, American football); PTSD + TBI — very frequently comorbid; Personality change (6E68) — in frontal lesions.

title: E.7. Dementia (detailed in Section 17)

title: The essence and place of the protocol
text: Nocturnal enuresis in children (World Health Organization (WHO) ICD-11: 6C00.0; DSM-5-TR: F98.0) is a condition of involuntary nocturnal urination (enuresis) that persists beyond the age norm (over 5 years). It is observed in approximately 5–10% of 7-year-old children, in 3–5% of 10-year-olds, and in 1–2% of adolescents. title: Practical recommendations
text: Essential conditions for the effective implementation of the protocol: 1. Parental motivation is an essential condition. During the first two weeks, parents must wake several times a night and actively awaken the child within 5–10 seconds. This is a heavy burden for the family and requires prior consent. A weekly meeting with the parent is an integral part of the protocol. 2. Reduction of fluid intake is prohibited.
